Well I suppose since everyone else is reviewing it poorly, I should jump on and say some things too. Now, before I begin I must say that I actually enjoyed GTA V back in the day. Back when it was first out on consoles, my friends and I would hop online and play some online multiplayer. Then, when nobody else was online, I'd play the story and oh boy did I enjoy the story. The story, in my eyes, is such an interesting tale that it deserves your upmost attention. For those who don't know, it features three main characters who pull off heists and other criminal jobs. In most of the missions, you get to control two or even all three characters. This allows a very fun gameplay experience as you can switch between these characters fast and with ease. Now the story alone sounds like a blast but this game has one more component that ultimately ruins this game and that's online. Online sounded so promising! You and your friends could take to the streets of Los Santos and do various missions, races, and fun gamemodes. They even promised heists just like in the story. For starters, heists weren't placed into the game for a very long time but at least we got races and various missions. But those were limited. There was only a handful of missions before you had to grind them just to get guns and planes and cars, even an apartment. Online started to get more and more bad with each passing day. Soon enough, joining an online game meant either getting killed constantly by randoms or getting killed by hackers all while racial and sexist slurs are thrown at you. Online devolved into this toxic community where you couldn't get anything done or just have some fun. Pretty soon Rockstar started pushing out FREE updates. This is a godsend! Free updates hear we come! Except...they were♥♥♥♥♥♥ Sure we got new cars, new houses/apartments, new boats and new planes but there was one glaring problem. They all costed way too much in game money. The only way to afford these new big boy toys was to either grind missions until sunrise or buy sharkcards. Sharkcards allow you to use real world money to buy in game money which seems fine at first but it gets worse. The updates started to roll out more and more fun vehicles that were locked behind ridiculous amounts of money. Every update, the prices for the newly introduced vehicles rose. So it was either grind for about a week and get one new vehicle or buy a sharkcard. This became a problem as you had to keep buying sharkcards over and over just to keep up and get the new content. They also released these online only supply running missions where you and your crew drive some supplies to a warehouse and eventually sell it while people try to attack your shipment. The problem with that is how almost everyone in online is a total♥♥♥♥♥♥and will just destroy your shipment for no reason. You get the supplies, you die. You get them again and you die again. They released more and more updates around this concept but it just doesn't work at all considering online is filled with ruiners of fun. They just released another update very similar to this concept which doesn't help Rockstar at all. But TakeTwo, Rockstar's parent company, decided to really dig their grave. They sent a cease and desist to OpenIV, a tool which lets you mod GTA V, and thus they had to take it down. This, for me, is what ticked me off. They just openly shut down modding with almost no warning whatsoever. They completely ruined the game with their "free updates" and now they really ruined it. With all that said, I do not recommend this game for $60 or really any price at all. Rockstar only cares about the money they earn from online that they don't cater to others. They still have yet to released a singleplayer DLC which was promised a couple of years back. Innocent people are getting banned left and right for no reason while cheaters still lurk in the online mode. This game does not deserve your time, especially not the online mode. The story is really good but only enjoyable till you 100% it. Then you can't really do anything else considering you can't mod it anymore. This game is not worth $60 or even $20. Oh how the mighty have fallen.

Final Review/Wall of Text:
(I am not here to complain about DLC and micro-transactions (until the end a little); we all know that it sucks, but that doesn't automatically disqualify the game.)
Mechanics:
Overall, they took every single thing that was great about Human Revolution and improved it.
- Overhauled Hacking (New UI, new software, hotkeys to perform actions)
- Highly improved takedowns (Pull someone around a corner or over a counter, multiple camera angles, better positional tracking)
- Stealth/Non-Lethal (more augmentations, non-lethal Typhoon, multi-target ranged aug, rewarded for stealth)
- Dialogue (You see word for word what Jensen will say, tons of options (even more based off of your actions/discoveries), C.A.S.I.E. aug allows interruptions and doesn't use the cheesy pheromones)
Level Design/Gameplay:
Take Detroit and Hengsha from Human Revolution. Combine them. Prague.
- THE HUB IS HUGE... THE... the... t h e... yeah, "the" as in one. As incredible as it is, Prague is the only hub level and it bums the crap out of me because of how stupendous it was and how I just want more, but can't have it.
- Okay, so that is kind of a lie... there is one other hub, but it is part of a quest and is likely the product of a hub that was supposed to be much, much bigger but got cut short.
- Prague (You will get lost, every nook and cranny has something interesting, friendly to all playstyles, TONS of enterable buildings, apartments, shops, sewers, etc., attention to detail is through the roof which is probably why there was only one)
-General mission levels (Start with Dubai which is beautiful and a great introduction, every level is fair to all playstyles and you CAN find a way through even if you think that initially you can't, exploration is HIGHLY rewarded and I love it)
- General Gameplay (It's just fun, man. No matter how you want to play: straight-forward and balls to the walls or exploring everything and like a ghost, it is an absolute blast.
Missions/Characters:
The story missions are cool. The side missions are cooler.
- Story Missions (You're going to be conflicted as crap, multiple factions to side with, memorable and fear-inducing choices for each side, CONSPIRACYYYYYYY)
- Side Missions (SO MANY. They don't stop comin' and they don't stop comin' and they don't stop comin' and they are really good. Not like Skyrim's radiant AI stuff. These are legitimate stories of their own with interesting characters, important choices, relationships to be made, the list goes on. Huge props in this section.)
- Voice Acting (Tons and tons of work done, mostly impressive work, Elias Toufexis, so many small random conversations to listen in on)
- Characters (I've heard people complaining that Jensen doesn't belong in this game. I agreed at first, but then I started to understand why he seemed so withdrawn at the beginning and came to really care about the people and the causes at hand. Additionally, the people MAKE you care for them. There are some people I just want to blow away for doing things to people I cared for dearly.)
Negatives:
It's like a big beautiful house: solid foundation, great framework, beautiful finish work... but no one living inside.
- Main Story (The story is cut short. Fiercely. Word is that Square Enix forced them to cut tons of content in order to make DLCs and another game. It isn't that the story is bad, just that it ends right when you think you are making some serious progress.)
- Paragon (It doesn't seem that your choices have much of an impact. I will have to do a second playthrough with some changes to my behavior, but I don't think that most of what you do impacts the way things play out.)
- Breach (I couldn't even get past the first set of server blocks because my guy doesn't seem to have Remote Hack... dunno, man. I wasn't that stoked for it anyway.)
- Slight Animation Desync (Not a huge deal, but the lips sometimes get out of sync with the voice. I mostly just look at people's eyes and it doesn't bother me.)
Overall:
It really sucks that Square Enix has done what they have regarding cutting the game, DLC, microtransactions, and the like; however, I don't believe it discredits this game. This game was an absolute blast and the only reason I am so bummed about the swift end is BECAUSE it was so incredible... I just want more, man. I guess Square realized what they had and knew that'd be the case, so why not make me pay if I want more?
Just play it for the enjoyment of playing it, but don't get too deeply invested in it if you're not okay with the Squeenix chop-shop treatment.

NOTICE:     I have played this game both on Play Station 3 (when it first arrived), and now on PC.
Rockstar and it's parent, Take Two, have a very serious issue pertaining to their game security.
Unless you play this game in singleplayer (which has an excellent story and is worth the time), the online is a sham.
There's a great chance that you'll hop online to find yourself suddenly collected with every other player in the lobby to a strange point on the map, where the supposed hacker drops huge bags of money. Hopefully you've left GTAV online at that point, but if you stayed, there's a good chance you'll have that money taken away, your character reset, and all the many hours of your life...gone...
Grand Theft Auto Five: Online functions as a peer to peer user statistic game. Instead of the central server receiving chatter from each individual, the game allows each peer to connect and send information to each other. This is a HUGE backdoor for 'scripters' and 'hackers', as it allows them to create false information to the server, which in turn is the reason why it is no longer safe to play in an online session full of unknown players.
Every time I've played this game, EVERY TIME I connect to GTAV online, I have to leave the session because my character suddenly burst into flame, exploded, or gained several million dollars in money bags. Certainly like every other sensible gamer out there, I don't want to risk getting banned, so more recently, I've been forced to go into Invite Only sessions due to the risk of getting banned.
By cutting the gamer's ability to use mods on this game, Take Two and Rockstar have cut the gamer community in monumental ways - the very core of playing and modding a game, making it better looking or better functioning, has been removed and for those who have used these mods, their accounts could be, or have been banned, often inexplicably!
The companies behind GTAV and GTAV online, especially the latter, won't admit to the naturally flawed nature of their game. You can't have a peer to peer stat game like this and expect the best of every player; it's impossible to expect humans to behave appropriately when there's very little repercussion against fighting someone across the globe, yet Rockstar and Take Two have begun smashing the ban hammer on any 'offenders' and those who are 'possible offenders' without giving a viable explanation via the tickets.
Be aware then, that if you receive a ban, Rockstar isn't going to help you. They've got your money, and that's all that matters.

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is a marked departure from the earlier games in the series, in terms of gameplay. While the basis of the game (suppress and flank) remains, the ability to "dig in", ala Gears of War, fundamentally changes how you play. It is now much easier to kill the enemy yourself, as the cover mechanic significantly changes how the gunplay works. Cover, along with a health regenerating system, renders this a very different experience to either of the preceeding games. That being said, this is still a very good game, and the best in the series in my opinion. From story telling to the raw experience of the levels, everything is more polished than either of the previous games managed to achieve.
From a technical perspective, the decision to use Unreal Engine 3 was a wise move, as the gameplay feels fluid and graphically still holds up today. Everything visual and technical has been stepped up a few notches from the previous entries in the series.
Highly recommended to FPS fans.

This game was marketed as a Zelda clone.  However, it is not even close.  The only similarities are, bows, bombs, and swinging a sword.  It ends there.  There are no original gadgets, no compelling storyline, no challenging boss fights, and no challenging puzzles.  The entire game feels extremely limited.  There is no real mystery to character development and the storyline is petty.  All of the mobs require the same logic to defeat and there are very few variations of them.
If this were to be a clone, then where are all of the extra gadgets and related puzzles?  The only extra "gadget" you get is the ability to jump over 1 block.  There are a total of ~10 types of creature to defeat, but really only 4 different types: flyers, biters, sword swingers, and archers.  All of them are weak against everything.  So there is no real need to mixup your playstyle.  Bosses show a little bit of variety, but are too simplistic.
The competition offers variance between mobs.  Some mobs can only be killed with bombs, others with the bow.  You could use a boomerang to stun them or grab what they dropped.  The puzzles in the competition actually required thinking.  This game blatently points out what exactly needs to be done to solve just about all of the puzzles.
So, if you want an incredibly easy and boring ripoff, this is your game.  Otherwise, I'd only consider purchasing this during summer sale at the price it is worth - ~$3.

Landstalker meets The Legend of Zelda. There are obvious nods to The Wind Waker in the world setting and locales right down to an ocean landscape dotted with islands, but that did not stop Cornfox & Bros from developing their game the way they wanted. The isometric view harkens back to an era that has long since disappeared in the realm of Z-targeting and free roam cameras - a programming art that was funnily enough perfected in The Wind Waker.
The story starts off simple enough with a young man's father having disappeared in the search for Oceanhorn. The main character sets off with an interaction level akin to the Zelda titles; jars are picked up and smashed on the ground, grass blades are slashed, boulders are blown apart by bombs. However there is an enjoyable yet simple physical meat to the main character in Oceanhorn. Even something as basic as wading in water brings about a speed penalty. A sign that the developers pay attention to the minutia of videogames.
The graphics are gloriously bright and colourful. The story won't set your imagination alight with wonder but it does the job. And the music is outstanding - sooner or later you'll be humming and whistling to the overworld theme.
It's a pity that this game may fly under the radar despite the reception it could and should achieve. Games like this don't come around too often anymore considering the monopoly of Zelda, so don't be deceived by the "smartphone game" approach by some commentators. Oceanhorn is a delight and I look forward to whatever else comes out from the Finnish caverns of Cornfox & Bros.

I don't remember how I came to own this game. Probably a Humble Bundle, but not sure. What I do know is that I didn't pay the asking price of $15, and it's not worth it at that price.
So, what is it? It's a game about two brothers trying to find a miracle cure for their father, who appears to be terminally ill. I say appears to be because nothing in the game is actually explained. You're expected to come up with the how's and why's of everything you encounter, similar to a "create your own adventure" type game, only your adventure is down a straight and narrow path.
The controls are simple. I used a 360 controller and everything comes down to four buttons. Left stick controls older brother, right stick controls younger brother, left trigger makes older brother grab things, right trigger makes younger brother grab things. Simple as you like.
Let's get into the actual game, shall we. For roughly two hours, you'll guide the two brothers to their destination, doing very basic platforming, repeatedly. There really is no challenge to it, no thought required. As you do the very basic platforming, you come across some rather interesting landscapes. Herein lies one of the two main issues I have with the game. You'll come accross some interesting stuff in your journey. However, nothing, and I do mean absolutely nothing, is explained. As I mentioned earlier, you're left to come up with your own reasons for what you're seeing. Some people may enjoy that. I really didn't. Thought and care obviously went into the game world, so why not give an explanation as to what is going on? SPOILERS AHEAD:
For instance, one part of your journey takes you through an area littered with the bodies of freshly dead giants. The actual gameplay through this area is quite brilliant, but I kept thinking to myself, "what happened here?" The answer never appeared. Soon, I was traversing through a new part of the land, the giants completely forgotten.
The other problem I have with it is how MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD:
The older brother dies. Let's recap his death shall we? They rescue a girl from some religious fanatics. The older brother shows her the map of where they need to go, and she leads the way. Eventually, she guides the brothers into a cave, where she inexplicably turns into a spider and attempts to kill them. What transpires is a very easy boss fight in which the the brothers work together and rip off her legs. Of course, while ripping off her last leg, the older brother gets stabbed in the chest. When this happened I just said to myself. "alright, you ripped of the other five legs with no problem , now you get shanked? Lol." Also, why would a spider posing as a girl get caught by religious fanatics? This happened a good distance away from her cave, BTW. As in, she had no reason to be there.
Also a small gripe I had is the ending. The ending is very somber, yet the music has this fantasy action hero type vibe. It's really strange and didn't fit at all, at least to me.
All in all, this game was decent. Had the potential to be great, but forcing the player to come up with reasons for everything happening in the game really took away from it. The platforming was also so basic that it didn't feel like much of a game. It felt like reading a pop-up story more than playing a video game. There is no replayability here. The $15 asking price is way too steep. Thankfully, the game seems to be on sale a lot. If you don't own it and want to play it, $5 or less is what you should pay.

Ah, Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons. I watch TotalBiscuit often and agree with him in many things, but I can't call this game mind-blowingly great. That said, I thoroughly enjoyed my playthrough of this game, so please don't think that I don't like this game.
The premise of the game is that you play as 2 sons of a father who's seriously sick in a medieval/fantasy world. The Brothers set out to bring him the one thing that can cure him, the Water of Life, found in a mystical tree in a faraway land. The twist is that rather than playing one brother and having the other be controlled through AI, you have to control both of them at the same time. This is why the game highly recommends using a twin-stick gamepad.
The control scheme certainly is less than common, but don't think that it is unique: I remember playing The Grinch on my good ol' PS1 15 years ago, where you could switch between the Grinch and his dog, Max in terms of camera perspective, but the character not bound to the camera could be controlled by the right stick on the controller (assuming you had a DualShock controller, which the original PlayStation did not come bundled with - "shocking", am I right?).
But that game did not have the control scheme as its main gimmick. Brothers takes this idea and creates some unique interactions which require good timing and coordination. It sounds easier than it actually is in practice to not lose track of which stick controls which brother. The thing is, once you get used to it (I'd say it took me between 1 and 2 hours to do so) the game becomes somewhat easy, or simple. You can only come up with so many puzzles that only require two analog sticks and two "use" buttons (one for each brother). To be honest, I felt myself starting to feel a hint of boredom in the latter half of the game.
I think that this is not only due to me getting past the novelty of the controls. While the story is certainly heartwarming and/or heartbreaking at times, I found it difficult to connect with either of the brothers. Maybe I'm just a bad brother, but maybe it's because of the design decision to not have them speak (or rather, to have them speak in an incomprehensible manner).Without getting to know their more subtle personality quirks, there's no way I could identify with, and subsequently care for, them. It does not help that much of the already linear journey is pretty generic for a fantasy world: a village, fields, a dungeon, a battlefield etc., but I must admit that I appreciated the areas designed for humongous people. It really puts the size of the brothers in perspective to that of the world.
Graphics-wise however, the game excels at making the environments fantasy-esque. The game makes good use of the Unreal Engine 3, and the outdoor areas always have a way of inferring an overwhelming sense of scale. The music complements this well, although again, near the end I did start feeling the most common themes outstaying their welcome.
In conclusion, Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a good game, and I heartily recommend it anyone. Keep in mind that it is pretty short, but it is also in many ways one-of-a-kind. I think that no matter the genre of your choice, Brothers is a title worth picking up.

Cute, fun game in need of some minor touch-ups.
Pros:
-Lovely and diverse environments, cute characters.
-Frequent timed and seasonal events to spice things up.
-Simple and enjoyable fighting mechanics
-Cute pets! (Even more variety would be nice.)
-Ability to build whatever, wherever. Want to claim a broken-down castle in a snowy biome and rebuild it? Go ahead. Want to steal an NPC's lunar palace and build a workshop/dungeon out of her cellar? Do it.
-Pretty customizable protagonists, solid variety of gear and weapon options.
Cons:
-Can be a bit grindy.
-At times, rather difficult to explore and find certain portals, even despite having a compass. Flying and superior underwater breathing mechanics should be made available, at least for end-game players.
-Furniture variety, building materials, and building options need to be expanded. It would be nice to have more than two types of bed, for example; to have glass; and to be able to change the colors of furniture (baroque furni is lovely, but the same red & gold gets boring after a while).
-After a while, much of the game starts to feel the same. It would be nice to see more unique enemies and different types of buildings/underground routes to explore. Better enemy drops would also be nice, and not just recipes--after you hit level cap and reach endgame, fighting anything other than bosses feels very pointless.
-Inventory and storage space. While your inventory isn't particularly small, lack of storage can nevertheless make it a problem. Even the best storage (titanium chest) is far from large enough to contain all the drops, gems, potions, and materials you'll need to hoard--resulting in the need to crank out a bunch of them and stow them wherever you can, then pop back and forth between them to try and organize everything. To make matters worse, storage isn't synced across worlds, so trying to move or manage multiple bases is a true headache. It would be nice to have a single upgradable chest that could sync across multiple bases, even if it's DLC or an end-game item.
-Last but not least, glitches that need to be addressed. The notorious audio glitch is a problem, and not the only one. Personally I haven't encountered any bugs that make the game unplayable, but the glitches are currently an annoyance.
Overall this is a great game, and it's still very young. The developers seem to be very on top of things, listen to feedback, and release new content and updates often. Despite some minor drawbacks, I have high hopes for this game's future.

So I literally played 9 hours of this game and realized after those 9 hours of no problems whatsoever that people were giving this mixed reviews due to performance issues and developer greed from DLC. And having bought the deluxe edition that comes with the season pass I too got those DLC. And being perfectly honest, playing the 9 hours that I played, I easily got about the same amount of credits and praxis kits from side quests and exploring. Even if I didnt i honestly havent used much augs aside from the reflex enhancer or whatever that lets you take down multiple people and never really needed credits for anything. And I feel like by the time I would NEED credits or a ton of other augs that I wasnt able to get in the first place, I would be able to get them by the time I needed them. So far I've also not shot a single bullet/tranq/stun dart so I've had no use for ammo, and have yet to kill anyone either.
Those are just kind of the ways I've been dealing with the issues, by basically not realizing they were happening in other places and well.... playing it like Deus Ex. The best I can say about the graphical crashes and fps issues is turn off MSAA and just turn your graphics down if that doesnt do enough for you. You might not be able to play the game on ultra, deal with it. Otherwise the game itself is literally Human Revolution 2.0 and I honestly really like it. You get all the augments from HR as well as some additional ones that are super fun to use. A couple other newer features I noticed was the different ways to run between cover, making stealth a lot simpler and makes it harder to accidently screw up while up against cover. You're able to actually climb up and over certain cliffs and obstacles that open more than just one floor up to you. You can climb up buildings to access a lot of different entry points. I guess a better way to describe it would be that they increased your overall mobility. Running is a bit faster and you dont run out of stamina in 2 seconds without an augment, and jumping and climbing is easy as well.
The world itself has so much more detail compared to HR. From what I've heard theres only one real hub world but its so big and I don't even think Ive hit every part of it. Im only on the second real main mission too due to just exploring and side questing. Everything about the world just seems a lot more colorfull too, not in like a super rainbow way, but its better in comparison to just black, dark grey, and yellow Detroit and Hengsha. It honestly looks beautiful in comparison if you ask me and I don't even think Im running it on Ultra.
Overall I'd say this game is a huge improvement from Deus Ex: HR. And I will absolutely be playing through this multiple times to check out the different choices, as well as finishing every single side quest i can. Its great! 9/10

Shortly described this is a Survival running horror game that has randomized elements as the map is different on every play trough. The hallways even change during the same session if one walks away far enough so it really is random.
Difficulty is quite tough and constant restarts actually reminds me of Receiver, a game that is not a horror game but has the same random map every time you play it and similar kind of (illusion) of choices - and both have quite tough difficulty that goes up slowly but surely.
I have no idea what people mean when they say in some reviews that this game is a walk in the park - they must mean earlier versions as after some 3 hours i have managed to beat the game only once using save points. So many things CAN and WILL go wrong even after you think you have the mechanics figured out.
For me the concept just works. I have a lot of horror games in my library but not a nifty little horror game title like this.  This game will not blow your mind and redefine the horror genre but in my books it doesn't need to. It is enough to preferably bring a new element and solid gameplay and you have a game worth it's price and this the game is able to do.
This is not a large game like Penumbra series/Amnesia nor is it a design marvel of a game squeezed into a tight space such as Anna.
Cons? Few but there are some. Rough edges here and there are annoying. Clicking on items is best done by clicking franticaly it seems. Beginning of the game is also weakest. For example if the game is so well into randomized hallways then i'd prefer to skip the early pleasantries after awhile. Also ghosts coming trough the floor at you can be a problem when changing floors so stairs require your full attention. I was also killed for the first time before i even got the flashlight. Tiny details like these which dont matter at all after some hours but add to the rough feeling in the first 30minutes. i'd also not see the face of the Hat Man at all during death. Like games better that leave it to players own imagination what happens when you get caught.  (sound can also  be sometimes more effective than visuals)
3 hours clocked at this time and will be expecting at least some hours more as i have not yet grown tired of the game. i'd say this is a good addition to the horror library.

Hat Man: Shadow ward takes place in an Asylum, you will play either as the Father or the Mother of a young girl that tried to commit suicide, which caused her to be assigned in a mental asylum for the insane in hopes that she does not do anything to further harm herself. When you first start the game, you are greeted with a note saying that she has somehow "Gone Missing". When you exit the elevator, everything will look just fine except for the fact that it's completely devoid of life. But as soon you will find a cursed book which will cause everything to change. The once normal looking asylum will reveal it's true state, a rotting and decrepit mess. Grab your flashlight and start collecting 22 pages in a way similar to slenderman! This is based on true stories and sightings of the one that we call "The Hat Man". He, along with his shadow people will try and get you so they can take your soul. The game relies heavily on the sound and atmosphere, keeping you on your heels from the start, the only thing i can reccomend is if you see "The Hat Man" just run, run and don't look back. When your lights flicker, then your problem is just starting, friend. Get out as soon as possible. Whispers will tell you that there is a page nearby. The Hat Man and his lackeys aren't the only thing you have to worry about though, there are other ways to die too! There's an eastern egg featuring everyone who helped this game be realised, as well as the devs near the start (if you're interested). The voice-acting isn't the best, but it's just a fresh company, we can't really expect much. The graphics are also not bad. The game is still good though. Hopefully this will be one of many to come!

I've been playing it non-stop since a mate got it for me for xmas. Just like watching the show - some of the gags are reused obviously, but that's the point.. it's like current time nostalgia. I was impressed with how many gags are in the game from recent series (I've only been watching South Park for about three years and haven't had much of a chance to go back and watch the original series yet - so it was nice to 'get' all the references, unlike a lot of the Stick of Truth, which I will go back and play again after watching the original seasons).
The gameplay is more streamlined than the first game, which I would normally be annoyed about but I have actually enjoyed. Clothing has been separated out from attribute bonuses which is nice, as it allows you to wear whatever the hell you want, and you're not gimping yourself because you don't want to wear the ugly outfit.
One disappointing thing is that if you get the Gold pack you start off with extra crafting materials and items that really make the items you collect throughout the entire start of the game completely redundant. It's kind of annoying - but I guess if you just want to enjoy the jokes and 'watch' the game it's fine.
The actual battles have been changed from final fantasy style turn based timers to a grid based version that plays primarily to lining enemies up and bouncing them off each other with knock-back bonuses.. it's quite fun.
Also - <spoiler> you can totally triple class. </spoiler> :D

GunZ: The Duel was an amazing game, classless, and if you removed macroing, and the obscene ammount of hackers, it was extremely skillbased. You built your class and your style on your loadout and what you could physically do with your keyboard and mouse.
GunZ 2: The Second Duel is more of a homage in name and look of the original. They have modernized it by adding in classes, and restricting the once open source attack combonations you could do to a streamlined and broader appeal. It saddens me to see what I saw in GunZ gameplay as a step into the future of gaming take a side-step. The game is still in the works but the devs have set their sights and outlined what GZ2 is going to be like and have decied to try something different. If you liked the original you will definatly find GunZ 2 unfulfilling.
Besides that if I had to choose between GunZ where its hard enough to connect to at this point and is being neglected (no fault for the creators as it is an old game). I would choose to play GunZ 2 with a warm embrace, but I would continue to look back longingly for GunZ. Hopefully there will be another newer game that will take the original and revitalize what is was with graphics, better moderating, and a more seamless feel.

This game makes me conflicted, sure it's a little fun for a little while but there are issues with it aside from the host lag which I will cover first.
Any game you get into, whoever is host will be on a killing spree, they are neigh impossible to hit, and hit you easily. I've gotten host, and had the same thing happen to me. It's ridiculous how easy it is to rack the whole team up as the host.

Going into Torchlight II, I knew I was going to enjoy it even though I have never played a Diablo game before (which is apparently this game is heavily based off of). I love the RPG genre, I love addictive looting, and I love games that can hook me in through addictive and long gameplay. After playing it, I can safely say that this game is amazing.
Torchlight II is brimming with so many great elements that make the overall experience great. The game runs smoothly, the graphics and lighting are very well designed, and the sound design is top-notch. What makes this game great though is the gameplay, looting, and questing. There is plenty of stuff to do in this game from levelling up through experience pointsm skill trees, and finding new weapons and armor. Randomly generated dungeons, however, are very effective because if you decide to play through the game again (which you probably want to, so you can experience knew classes), it never feels repetitive and instead feels fresh. So far, I do not find this game repetitive in the slightest.
The game is worth it. The game is high quality, and the fact that you can buy it for $20 is a steal. It's even more of a steal for me, since I bought it for $7. The game is worth your money and time, and I highly recommend Torchlight II.

This game totally caught me by surprise. It's an incredibly well done Zelda clone(circa Link to the Past) with a healthy dose of the elevation-based problem solving from the classic Genesis adventure Landstalker. The game takes all it can from Zelda right down to the pieces of heart collectibles and block pushing puzzles to the simplistic but effective hack and slash combat. Heck, even the world map is itself a total Windwaker copycat(however nowhere near as tedious or annoying).
It adds it's own features here and there such as a leveling system, quests and a tad more open exploration than certain Zelda titles, and a more involved story but it's part and parcel a huge homage to the trend setting franchise. In no way is that a knock to the game's character because it's all done nearly as well as an indie dev could do so.
The music is another feature that struck me as well. It's another high quality aspect of an already high quality product, even if it sounds slightly Zelda-ish at times (when you first leave your house, you'll instantly get the feeling you've been here before).
If you're someone who loves Zelda or hack and slash adventures in general, you can't go wrong with picking this game up. It would seem so far that it's going to be at least a solid 20-30 hours to fully complete also, possibly more so it's totally worth the price for a game that even begins to touch the greatness that is Zelda.

Hello review readers! The fact that you're reading this review means you're either potentially interested in this game or have played it & want to get another guy's opinion on the game you have been playing. I am currently still playing the game and have not finished it, about 5-6 hours in.
The game has full controller support (using xbox 360 controller for pc) and I would recommend playing it in this way. It is possible to play with mouse and keyboard, after testing both I decided to stick with he controller.
It's possible to change some graphical settings (shadows, screensize, etc.) up to a given point, I would have liked to have seen a little more options for this to make the game prettier/uglier depending on your hardware, but the basics are there.
What annoys me a little bit is that it seems to be poorly optimised for PC at this point. Meaning: even though you might have a high end gaming system, sometimes you will get the occasional FPS drop or screen tear here & there. Nothing major & gamebreaking though, but it did cause me to tone down the graphics a bit for more consistent FPS.
Nevertheless: the game has vibrant colours & is fun to look at, despite it not being "graphically advanced". The cartoony atmosphere grows on you, and I would not want to see this game with realisticly drawn characters & backgrounds, it feels fine the way it is.
I have not had any crashes yet & the game runs flawlessly, people on the community forums have reported otherwise and I did see dev responding to these topics regularly. If you are unsure if you can run this game, better ask people on the forums with similar specs what their experiences are.
The gameplay in my eyes, at first, was a bit "easy". Meaning: if you're looking for a "hard" game you will find little joy playing Oceanhorn. I'm not sure what age group i'd recommend this game for but i'd say something in the lines of 6+. If you (or your kid) can play games like Spyro the dragon or Skylanders/Disney Infinity, they can play this. It's not very hard, but to fully play the game they will need to understand the English language, be it to follow the story or just to read clues / where they should go next. The game starts off easy & keeps on making the puzzles more difficult, having you look around & go "hmm, what now" at regular intervals, keeping it interesting.
You get some freedom as in where to travel at any given point, yet, until you get some basic things handed to you by following the storyline (*minor spoilers, mouse over to show*
), there is little to do other than follow the main route. It's a fake sense of freedom, but a sense of freedom nevertheless. After gaining a certain item or ability, you will often backtrack on the map or take sidepaths to reach areas you could not reach before.
The music is catchy at some points, making me hum it in the background while inside a dungeon / traveling around the world. They chose to not give the main character a voice in this game, as is common in a lot of these games, which I still kind of miss - I get that this is done to make the hero more relatable to you, giving you the option to give him your voice, but having a totally mute main hero has been done countless times and I find it more enjoyable when this isn't the case. That being said: the voice actors from the other people around the world sound kind of bland and I'm under the impression some bad/good guys were all voiced by the same person. They could have spiced this up a bit.
The story feels a bit cliché to me, as an adult, but what more do you need than save princesses and find your family to go on an adventure right?
Conclusion: Don't regret being curious enough to buy this game, have been having a lot of fun with it, albeit making the game/puzzles a little bit harder would not hurt. Very good step in game for friends/family who are not that experienced with gaming. Consider it a stepping stone into adventure/puzzle games to later hook them on something more complicated like Zelda, Tomb Raider, Prince of Persia, ...
If you must have a score, I rate this game 67/100, it would have gotten 70/100 if the voice actors could loosen up a little :-)

Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas caused a splash when it dropped on iOS back in 2013. It was plain to see that the game was an almost cut and paste rip, at least visually, from The Legend of Zelda: Windwaker, but it's unfair to call Oceanhorn a clone. To me, 'Clone' is a pejorative term reserved for the scores of cheap knock-offs occupying iOS, Android and Greenlight. Oceanhorn is better than that. It's a love letter to the Zelda series that brings similar, high quality design practices and gameplay values to gamers on iOS and PC. It doesn't quite sail into the same realm as Nintendo's flagship series but it's the closest another developer has ever come.
There's not much worth knowing about Oceanhorn's story, it's much the same as any Zelda game - so, as deep as a puddle and just about as interesting .The fabled sea monster called "Oceanhorn" has come back to your island, leaving your father to go fight it while you sleep. You find yourself alone with nothing but your mothers magical pendant to guide you, and off you pop on a Windwaker-style adventure in your dinky little boat- which, thankfully, doesn't talk this time.
You'll sail to new islands, each inhabited by people with interesting stories to tell, explore vast dungeons, and encounter creatures that are most definitely not ripped off from the Zora or Rito people.
Equipped with your sword and shield, you'll take on dangerous foes and some surprisingly well designed boss monsters. Combat isn't as tight as the Zelda games but it's an admirable impersonation, especially for a game that has made its way over from iOS. Controls can be a bit finicky and loose at times but they are otherwise fine, feeling just as good with the mouse and keyboard as they do with a gamepad.
The developers try their hardest to conjure up the same sense of adventure that can be found in A Link to The Past and Windwaker, and for the majority of the game they succeed. It's unlikely you will forget that you are playing a game very heavily based on a well-known franchise, but it's enjoyable nonetheless.
The game doesn't hold your hand, opting to leave you wander off in your own direction with nothing but the words of other people to guide you. You are free to travel around and explore, neglecting the main story, if you so choose.
Diving in to the meat of the game has you kill easy monsters in deep dungeons, solve simple puzzles, and collect elemental powers (where have we seen that before?). It's fairly standard stuff that even the Zelda franchise has dined out on for far too long. There's nothing particularly outstanding about any of Oceanhorn's action but its richly crafted, sun-kissed worlds are immersive and fun to explore. Ironically, for a game based around traversing large bodies of water, sailing isn't that fun. In fact, it's a bit dull - a complaint that was frequently directed at Windwaker, also. Any frustrations inspired by the mediocre sailing will at least be washed away by Oceanhorn's gorgeous soundtrack.
Audiovisual presentation is an area where Oceanhorn zips past its, rather sparse, competition. A beautiful world-class composer crafted soundtrack and pretty landscapes are destined to keep a smile on your face and a tune in your head.
In truth, Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas can be a bit shallow, but it's hard to dislike a game so lovingly crafted - and with such respect for the source material from which it was created. Temper your expectations and you'll find an engrossing adventure that pays homage to one of gaming's greatest, never managing to step out of its shadow.

Early Access game, so obviously theres going to be bits that need ironing out and points that needs tweaking.
The difficulty is just right for this kinda game, lead to an INTENSE gaming session. (The difficulty overall changes depending on how many players are in the game, so yeah thats a nice system.)
The gameplay is damned good, with this drop in/drop out system included.
Its fun and energetic, calling for good team cooperation.
OOOOOOOOOOK now onto the gripes:
Music:  OK while the music is good at points, I find that the best bits tend to be looped poorly, it kills the mood, a minor gripe but something to take note of. in other cases there simply ISN'T any music... not even something to set the mood.
Animations: Ok overall good, but there some minor things that need a tweak, such as the stop animation: when running and ya stop, your still running on the spot...
Subtitles: Overall ok, but when it goes into a large lump of text, it tends to only show a small amount of it before the character talks ahead of the text shown, as it doesnt show the next bit of text. Need to work on that timing there.
Controls: OK, rip and tear time:  The Store page claims it has FULL CONTROLLER SUPPORT. I call bull on that, I got a gamepad that works like an XBOX controller, but the game doesnt recognise it at all, works with other games just fine. Might wanna get on that Guys!
And the dodgeing... in a game that lacks a block abillity ya could give a little bit more leeway with the dodging...
Campaign: pretty good, got me interested, but I wonder, will we be fighting ONLY grimm? I mean theres no way that Grimm could do HALF the things done in the story. so fighitng ONLY Grimm wouldn't make much sense.
Oh, and the chat system, im not sure if this is a recurring problem but I'll say it anyway: The text chat during one game ceased to operate mid game. It just wouldnt show up, completely invisible.
Even laggy games show their text chat, that needs a look at. Just hoping it was a glitch.
The MOBA Leveling System: Love it, it keeps the playing field level, so that no one player is so high a level that others cant compete or keep up. A good way to have levels involved without it beign a DOMINANT FEATURE in gameplay. Very good, I wouldnt change a thing, except maybe add some more skills, but that would depend on HOW the campaign overall will work in the future.
Overall a Healthy Early Access game that demands to be played!

I'm sure we've all at one point in our lives watched or read a movie/show or novel, that we've really felt we had a connection with. Something that spoke to us on a deeper level for whatever reason that may be. Perhaps it reminded us of an experience we had in our lives or conveyed a message where you really understood, or had some characters you could totally empathize with.
Because of it, we ended up growing a deep attachment to the point where no matter what flaws the thing might actually have, we could easily overlook it because… well, it didn't matter.
It didn't affect our experience or why we got so attached to it.
And even if others did find flaws with it, we didn't care. As, they didn't have the same experience that you did.
To us, it was perfect. Even if, objectively speaking, The perfect movie, the perfect game, the perfect novel cannot exist.
I was lucky enough to come across the record-breaking RWBY: Grimm Eclipse and it absolutely blew me away. So much so, I had to play it, not for a few hours, but hundreds of hours before getting close to satisfied. And it was after the hundred hour milestone that I knew I had found my new perfect game.
Except, I know that - critically speaking - if I called this "perfect," or "a masterpiece," or any other overly superlative adjective, there would be those of us who would argue the semantics of describing it such a way 'cause, at the end of the day, it's an opinion that's subjective. Yet I don't know why this word is so looked down upon when we're talking critically about something - Of course I know if a game or film isn't perfect. The mechanics aren't the deepest, and I'm sure if I thought deeply about it, I will find flaws and weaknesses - I don’t know because the game speaks to the heart rather than to the mind. (some dont see that in shows and games, and misses it)
Though, none of that actually matters to me because I felt it achieved everything it need to, and there's so much I love about this game that I wouldn't change a single thing about it.
I exited the game with that same bittersweet joy of meeting a lost friend you won't see again for a long time with a reignited passion for this medium I love so much, and that's not one thing you can just put on a 1-to-10 review scale. To me it was a masterpiece. And no amount of lackluster AI, character writing, or any other flaw could take that away from me. But I know that not everyone will share the same experience I did, or come to the same conclusion. There will be people it didn't appeal to. Some will have gotten too caught up in the hype, or simply couldn't connect to it as much for whatever reason, and that's
.
No one will ever create a piece of work that would appeal to absolutely everybody, so why is it that we pretend a good review is something that can objectively break down what makes a piece of media good or not?
Many self-proclaimed critics of movies/shows I've seen always harp back to the writing and characters as the absolute backbone of what makes something good. As if there's only one specific formula to making a great movie or show. Which is something
.
Sure there is a guidebook and theories to what makes good film making and story telling, which applies to the majority, but we shouldn't forget what they are: A guide. Not an absolute.
And there are exceptions to every rule - both for all mediums including shows and games.
Every game/show sets out to achieve something different and part of the charm of certain...
(including a conclusion)
... At the end of the day, shows/games are a form of art. A way for the creators to communicate to the audience in some way. Whether it be an idea, a feeling, an experience or something else.
Which is why I feel like the best critics are people who can break down why a movie/show or game appeals to them, and what aspect of it would appeal to an individual audience member. Rather than a blanket statement of why it's objectively good.
So instead of condemning subjectivity, why aren't we embracing it?
It is possible to embrace critical thinking while acknowledging the subjectivity of it.
I've seen far too many people try to hide their actual taste because they think it's too eccentric or too trashy or something that isn't critically acclaimed. There's nothing wrong with your favorite game/show, even if it doesn't take all the boxes and characters or writing or cinematography or if you just like it for some really stupid reason. And it's definitely nothing wrong with thinking some critically acclaimed games/shows are just 
(btw think deeply about it before reacting ^)
Your taste reflect who you are as a person, your interests are shaped by your experiences, and upbringing that made you the individual you are today.
So why the hell shouldn't you be proud of that?
It shouldn't be about having superior taste, it shouldn't be about showing off how much  knowledge you have. And it definitely shouldn't be about showing how much smarter you are than other people.
It should be about keeping an open mind, embracing individuality, and most of all having fun!
Whatever shows/games hold a special place in your heart, are special because that's the person you are. So don't forget that.
Finally I guess all I really wanted to say through all this mindless rambling without any real point I was trying to make was that, I bought
the other day, and I liked it a lot. It was pretty great.

The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is an atmospheric indie horror-adventure game.  You play as father/mother in search of your daughter wich was sent to an asylum because she attempted suicide. The asylum is haunted by shadows and The Hat Man.
You walk throught the asylum and search for pages. You might think this is another Slender clone, but no it's not! In this game the pages tell a story. I'd rather compare this game to Daylight.Both games take almost the same time to complete. Daylight had a bigger budget than this game bud it didn't acomplish at least half of what this game does. I sugest getting this game instead of Daylight (I tryed both and I regret getting Daylight).
Here is a list of things that make this game great:
-The Hat Man
The Hat Man is an original creature. I find it very cool.
-fantastic atmsophere
-builds tension
The game builds tension. As you walk through the hallways they become darker and darker(by darker I mean scarier). Sometimes they even give you the sensation of deja vu.
-dynamic map(the map is different every time which adds replay value)
-it has puzzle elements
-it has good sound effects
-it has achievements
-you can play as 2 characters the father or the mother.
-it has achievements
-it's pretty short but who says games should take hours to finish? The game has replay value due to randomly generated map and playing as diffrent characters.
In conclusion  The Hat Man: Shadow Ward it's great if you like horror game. I consider it a little gem.

Prepare to die screaming…or more likely laughing at the horrendously bad voice acting of ‘The Hat Man: The 20+ Pages’……wait….wrong game (and more on the voice acting later).
Alas, just as has happened with so many other indie horror games in recent years and with the advent of the Slender series, ‘The Hat Man:  Shadow Ward’ (the ‘for real’ name) falls victim to the same ‘collect quest’ gameplay  mechanic.  This means that you need to find a set number of pages from your daughter’s diary to complete the game.  Ultimately, that’s the basis of the game:  you either play as the father or mother in search of said daughter, who has gone missing from the seemingly empty asylum she was committed to which is now populated by shadow people/The Hat Man (BTW – the idea of shadow peeps is based loosely on fact and there are many documented cases, and even some decent movies, about people that have seen or had encounters with these so-called ‘Shadow People’).  Thankfully, you don’t just search for pages as you also need to find some other items to progress deeper into the asylum and defeat The Hat Man (who I guess is like the pimp of the shadow peeps) to get your daughter back.
One of the more unique attributes of this game (though it’s been done before) is that sound is utilized to pinpoint the location of pages/other items you need by means of whispery voices.  Also, the sound design of this game isn’t half bad for being a budget title, with some of the sound effects/ambient music being pretty creepy in my opinion.
Now as promised, I must go back to my earlier comment about the voice acting.  Granted, this game is super short and can be beat in less than half an hour, so you may think that voice acting wouldn’t be too important in such a game…..but it kinda, sorta totally is.  Essentially, it’s hilarious.  No, seriously, I’m not joking.  I mean, it’s so stupendously bad that it’s good (I don’t know how that works; it defies the human intellect to comprehend how that can be) but it’s true.  I figure most people will laugh at it, though some may actually want to cry at how bad it is.  And for all those 100% achievement unlock Steamers out there – prepare thine selves!!  There is actually an achievement for listening to your daughter reading the pages of her diary as you collect them.  Sure, this game can fairly easily be ‘100%’d’ and the aforementioned achievement is easy enough to unlock, but don’t go joy-puking your faces off just yet as I seriously believe that listening to all of the pages may very well land you in an asylum. I personally just barely managed to keep my sanity intact while unlocking this achievement, so don’t say I didn’t warn you.
This game can be fun for like 2 hrs tops, but I wouldn’t recommend it at full price, even if it is a budget title. With decent voice acting, who knows, perhaps this game could have been terrifying.  As it is, it will likely be overlooked by most gamers, but it is somewhat interesting and good for a laugh….or cry, so give it a shot.

The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is a indie horror game.
Your daughter is assigned to an asylum because of attempting suicide. Somehow she has gone missing and it is up to you to find her.
At the beginning you can choose if you play as the father or the mother (no difference to game, just difference voices).
Soon after the start you will realize that The Hat Man is nothing more as another Slender clone. You move through the rooms and try to find all pages (notes from your daughter) while the Hat Man is trying to chase you.
The Hat Man is fairly slow and not a real danger at all. You can easily walk through the rooms and collect the pages. To finish the game it takes something around 30 minutes.
The graphics are not great at all. The whole game is very repetitive, all rooms look the same.
The sound is okay but the voice acting is really awful.

With rudimentary resources and technology, this game perfectly utilizes everything on hand and make them great.

This game does not dehumanize you into a human killing machine, everything from the game reminds you contantly you're still a human, fighting in a war, you feel sorrow, happiness, love and all. Imitation really is the best form of flattery. If you're a Zelda fan who's thirsty for adventure, look no further. For a port of a mobile game, Oceanhorn manages to look pretty. The visuals have been polished and everything looks shiny and new, but there are some framerate problems. The art style is pretty much ripped from The Wind Waker, so fans should feel right at home. Speaking of The Wind Waker, you get a boat! This is how you travel from island to island. Unfortunately, your boat doesn't talk and you can't steer it yourself. Traveling between islands is an on-rails affair, but there are enemies to keep you on your toes and driftwood to be smashed for the loot it contains. There's also a leveling system that basically replaces bigger quivers and bomb bags from the Zelda franchise. You gain experience from slaying baddies and attaining in-game achievements, which can force you to backtrack but do add to the longetivity of your adventure. Puzzles are a bit on the easy side and some items are a bit too familiar, but why fix gameplay that isn't broken? If you're a Zelda fan, Oceanhorn is a must-have for your Steam library.
+ Gameplay is immediately familiar
+ Environments are lovely, varied, and don't overstay their welcome
+ Great soundtrack
- Framerate issues
- Controls could be tighter
- Not being able to sail the ocean yourself is a bit of a bummer

I'm sure we've all at one point in our lives watched or read a movie/show or novel, that we've really felt we had a connection with. Something that spoke to us on a deeper level for whatever reason that may be. Perhaps it reminded us of an experience we had in our lives or conveyed a message where you really understood, or had some characters you could totally empathize with.
Because of it, we ended up growing a deep attachment to the point where no matter what flaws the thing might actually have, we could easily overlook it because… well, it didn't matter.
It didn't affect our experience or why we got so attached to it.
And even if others did find flaws with it, we didn't care. As, they didn't have the same experience that you did.
To us, it was perfect. Even if, objectively speaking, The perfect movie, the perfect game, the perfect novel cannot exist.
I was lucky enough to come across the record-breaking RWBY: Grimm Eclipse and it absolutely blew me away. So much so, I had to play it, not for a few hours, but hundreds of hours before getting close to satisfied. And it was after the hundred hour milestone that I knew I had found my new perfect game.
Except, I know that - critically speaking - if I called this "perfect," or "a masterpiece," or any other overly superlative adjective, there would be those of us who would argue the semantics of describing it such a way 'cause, at the end of the day, it's an opinion that's subjective. Yet I don't know why this word is so looked down upon when we're talking critically about something - Of course I know if a game or film isn't perfect. The mechanics aren't the deepest, and I'm sure if I thought deeply about it, I will find flaws and weaknesses - I don’t know because the game speaks to the heart rather than to the mind. (some dont see that in shows and games, and misses it)
Though, none of that actually matters to me because I felt it achieved everything it need to, and there's so much I love about this game that I wouldn't change a single thing about it.
I exited the game with that same bittersweet joy of meeting a lost friend you won't see again for a long time with a reignited passion for this medium I love so much, and that's not one thing you can just put on a 1-to-10 review scale. To me it was a masterpiece. And no amount of lackluster AI, character writing, or any other flaw could take that away from me. But I know that not everyone will share the same experience I did, or come to the same conclusion. There will be people it didn't appeal to. Some will have gotten too caught up in the hype, or simply couldn't connect to it as much for whatever reason, and that's
.
No one will ever create a piece of work that would appeal to absolutely everybody, so why is it that we pretend a good review is something that can objectively break down what makes a piece of media good or not?
Many self-proclaimed critics of movies/shows I've seen always harp back to the writing and characters as the absolute backbone of what makes something good. As if there's only one specific formula to making a great movie or show. Which is something
.
Sure there is a guidebook and theories to what makes good film making and story telling, which applies to the majority, but we shouldn't forget what they are: A guide. Not an absolute.
And there are exceptions to every rule - both for all mediums including shows and games.
Every game/show sets out to achieve something different and part of the charm of certain...
(including a conclusion)
... At the end of the day, shows/games are a form of art. A way for the creators to communicate to the audience in some way. Whether it be an idea, a feeling, an experience or something else.
Which is why I feel like the best critics are people who can break down why a movie/show or game appeals to them, and what aspect of it would appeal to an individual audience member. Rather than a blanket statement of why it's objectively good.
So instead of condemning subjectivity, why aren't we embracing it?
It is possible to embrace critical thinking while acknowledging the subjectivity of it.
I've seen far too many people try to hide their actual taste because they think it's too eccentric or too trashy or something that isn't critically acclaimed. There's nothing wrong with your favorite game/show, even if it doesn't take all the boxes and characters or writing or cinematography or if you just like it for some really stupid reason. And it's definitely nothing wrong with thinking some critically acclaimed games/shows are just 
(btw think deeply about it before reacting ^)
Your taste reflect who you are as a person, your interests are shaped by your experiences, and upbringing that made you the individual you are today.
So why the hell shouldn't you be proud of that?
It shouldn't be about having superior taste, it shouldn't be about showing off how much  knowledge you have. And it definitely shouldn't be about showing how much smarter you are than other people.
It should be about keeping an open mind, embracing individuality, and most of all having fun!
Whatever shows/games hold a special place in your heart, are special because that's the person you are. So don't forget that.
Finally I guess all I really wanted to say through all this mindless rambling without any real point I was trying to make was that, I bought
the other day, and I liked it a lot. It was pretty great.

The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is a indie horror game.
Your daughter is assigned to an asylum because of attempting suicide. Somehow she has gone missing and it is up to you to find her.

The Hat Man is fairly slow and not a real danger at all. You can easily walk through the rooms and collect the pages. To finish the game it takes something around 30 minutes.
The graphics are not great at all. The whole game is very repetitive, all rooms look the same.
The sound is okay but the voice acting is really awful.
The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is not scary at all and especially not worth 4,99€ (former price was 14,99€).

Playing this game from the begginign and even through the updates, it has been a dissapointment. The over all story isn't bad, it still needs a lot of work, but the main problems are this; its pretty much just another slenderman-styled game in terms of objective and enemies, the graphics are not that great, it is way too predictable, the hatman himself is a poor adversary and too slow, even in the updates, and he is not scary. It would have been much wiser to replace the tophat with a fedora and made him look like the infamous shadow man seen throughout man decades by many people. I played a game like this back in April, called Daylight.
While that game seems to have had a higher budget, they both accomplish the same thing fairly effectively. The gameplay is quite similar.
Not a bad game, and it tries to do a few things that are quite difficult to do. Mostly get things to happen in the right order, with the player looking in the right place at the right time... without forcing them to.
As with Daylight, the results are mixed. Mind you I am not aware of any game which has pulled that off without issues.
A fun ride, if a bit short... which is good otherwise you'd become used to it.
Don't look too hard at it and just enjoy the playthrough. Sort of like a made-for-TV horror movie.
Popcorn optional.

Here are my main gripes:
Has potential, but I feel like I was ripped off when I paid 14.99 for a 250mb game. I feel like a 4.99 price tag would be more appropriate.
The voice acting is painful. I'm pretty forgiving of things like this, but wow. It actually made the game less scary because some of the comments were very out of place and sarcastic. When you're doing a horror game, the feeling needs to be raw with genuine fear. How are we supposed to be afraid if you aren't?
I don't feel like I have enough time to sit and listen to the journal entries. Whenever I try to listen to or read one so I can learn about the story, hatman comes and kills me. I don't know if this is a glitch or normal, but I can't learn about the story if I get killed every time I'm reading the journal. I really wanna know what's going on with the lady's daughter but I still haven't much of a clue as to what's going on in the asylum.
Here is what I liked:
Running around collecting pages/piecing together a story.
Some folks feel like it's too bright, but I disagree. You can't have shadows without light.
When the bad voice acting wasn't ruining my immersion, I was actually scared of the hatman and rushing through the asylum trying to find everything without dying. Though I wish he was a little less agressive so that I could have more time to explore and see the rooms/read journals.
So with all of this being said, I'm still trying to complete the game. These are just my opinions for right now and may likely change.

"What is it that makes a great soldier? Is it his brain? Or his heart?"
These are the words spoken by Sergeant Matt Baker. A platoon sergeant in the US Army's 101st Airborne Division, and one of the iconic protaganists of the Brothers in Arms franchise. Brothers in Arms, as i've stated before in my previous reviews, is my favorite WW2 themed franchise; and with good reason. But Hell's Highway is it's own seperate animal. While retaining the core story, characters, and features that the series is known for, Hell's Highway takes the traditional BIA formula, and injects it with steroids. Everything the previous games did right, this game does it better. But, it's not my personal favorite in the series. That title belongs to Earned in Blood. The reason for that is because Hell's Highway has a few strange design choices, and nitpicks that hold it back from being my go-to. That being said, overall, I think Hell's Highway IS the best when compared to the rest of the franchise. Just not my favorite. But, enough beating around the bush. Let's get into it, shall we?
Story: Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is set in the midst of Operation: Market Garden. The massive air and land invasion of Nazi-occupied Holland of which the end goal was to liberate the Netherlands, break through to Germany, and end the war before Christmas. However, due to the overconfidence of some Allied commanders that the Germans were on the verge of collapse lead to them overextending the Allied elements, and eventually to the failure of the operation. In Hell's Highway, you take on the role of Sgt. Matt Baker. A platoon sergeant in the US Army's 101st Airborne Division that takes part in the airborne side of the invasion (obviously). Baker finds himself in a tough spot at the outset of the game. Due to all of the casualties taken and friends lost during D-Day, the company has taken on many new uppity replacements. Those that survived the initial invasion are obviously a bit urked by how excited the newbies are for combat, and thus, Baker, as a platoon leader, must try to convey some sense of order. After the company settles with it's compatriots, it's time for the real deal. You'll be travelling to many locations throughout Hell's Highway. From the colorful and vibrant Holland countryside, to the bombed out ruins of war-torn cities. All the while coping with the sorrow and guilt of those that we've lost thus far. Hell's Highway's story is second-to-none in the realm of WW2 shooters, even today. Rivaling that of the HBO series Band of Brothers if followed across all three installments. That should tell you all you need to know if you're asking if the story's any good.
Graphics: Hell's Highway is an absolutely beautiful game, even by today's standards. The vibrant colors, overall fidelity, and lighting are stunning when looking at the time the game was released. Visual feedback and most animations are good as well, though there are some that could do with some improvement. Overall, there's not much to complain about on the graphical side of things.
Sound: Hell's Highway's sound design is well above average, i'd say. It's a definite improvement from the previous installments, but some weapon sounds could certainly stand for some improvements. The MG-42, for example still retains that downright annoying Hollywood stock machine gun sound. It sounds more like a broken chainsaw belt than the menacing "Hitler's Buzzsaw" that we all know. But, that's more of a nitpick than anything. Voice acting is great, as always in BIA. And they actually added more explosion sounds this time around! Overall, sound design is good. If you're not a stickler for it, there's not much to hate.
Gameplay: Now we're getting into the meat and potatoes of it. Gameplay is, by far the catagory that Hell's Highway stands out in. It's been completely revamped and streamlined for 7th gen, and it's a monumental improvement from previous installments. The "feature" where your character waves his weapon around like a cracked out zombie has been completely removed, the movement system is much more fluid with the addition of a sprint function, and the ability to jump and vault over walls, and with the addition of a sticky cover system, you'll no longer have to worry about having to run all the way across an open field just to hide behind a conveniently placed rise in the dirt. Additionaly, new weapons have been added, and many have been improved. The franchise's staple feature, the squad command mode has also been reworked and streamlined to be much more useful. This combined with some greatly improved level design results in the game being fun, and makes the player feel as though they're making progress, and not just going from firefight to firefight. Overall, the gameplay in Hell's Highway's the best it's been in the franchise, hands down.
Conclusion: Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is a great game. And a great BIA game at that. As I said before, it's my personal belief that Hell's Highway is the best in the series from an "everything included" point of view. Just not my personal true favorite. It more than earns the title of "cult classic" in my opinion. And is one of the best WW2 shooters out there. If you're looking for gritty, emotional, blood-soaked rollercoaster of a WW2 game, you can't go wrong.
Final Score: 9/10
