So I've never written a full blown review before but I'm a long time tekken fan and I have to say of the main tekken games, since I never played the tags or street fighter x tekken games, this might be the weakest one. Yes the art and graphic quality is high, yes the fighting is straight forward and crisp... until you get into the fact that the rage system is rediculous and there isn't even a option to turn it off. People can use weapons in rank and there once again is no option to turn it off. The music is the worest of any tekken game I've played... Let me just break it down in pros and cons I guess.
Pros
Fighting feels rewarding as usual and the style of the combat hasn't really changed.. well yes it has (getting to that). You wont be able to just buttom mash here, well for 95% of the characters at least,you have to take the time to learn moves and in my book thats a good thing.
Graphics are good even on the lower settings (though the frame rate drops heavy on levels like the snow one) I can play on medium at above 50 easily but it will drop to like 25, the dynamic setting thing that is suppose to reduce quality to save preformance just doesn't work.
Customization is neat, I would be lying if the crazy freaks you encounter wasn't amusing (waiter/chef Dragnov is terrifying when he uses his rage move) That said it can also be seen as a negative if you expect any real veriety, you can't make a character look like any of their past variations, there are only a few options for that.
Cons
Rage, this is just stupid, you can't turn it off at all, in any mode on or offline, and its a dumb feature that tekken didn't need. Tekken's strength was that despite its rediculous story and silly moments the actual fighting mechanics made it feel grounded and plus having a move that gives you armor that deals over 50 hp is just rediculous, its takes away a lot from the more complex strategy part of the fighting because it devolves into a stand still of waiting out the rage art. Yes they look cool most of the time but it doesn't belong in tekken.
Also there aren't any variations for them except for King.
Weapon add ons, once again you can't turn off this feature as of right now and you can use them in rank, in god damn online rank.
New characters, the new characters added to the roaster are increadibly underwhelming. They aren't interesting at all with the exception of the cancerous Lucky Chloe (which as a character doens't even make sense, a blonde hair blue eyed idol japanese girl for an american organization, G corp, which means Kazuya brought her in? dafaq?)
Old characters, this is 2017, Ps4, xbone, PC, there is no excuse for not having the older characters in the game. The roster is a good size yes but its dumb not to have the characters from previous games, esspecially when you have gutted so much from it to begin with. I don't care if they "dead" in the story, it would not take much to add them when its already taken so long to come out. And if they do come out later but as paid DLC then F*ck this game, and you know what f*ck it already for having a character that is only avalible to you if you preordered. Its a competative online fighitng game, your wallet shouldn't dictate whether or not you are in the meta for a game you have to buy to begin with.
Akuma (explained further in story but for here lets just say adding a range character with multiple supers is stupid as ♥♥♥♥)
*****No Tekken force, time attack or survival mode!!! ******
No instant replays, the slow down effect is cool and it has made some increadible moments, but those moments are then lessend by the fact that you don't get an instant replay to revel in it.
Sound, while the hit sounds are on point the music is just god aweful, I don't even think this is subjective, its just bad, its doens't match the feel of the fights let alone the pace half the time. I don't recall tekken having this issue in the past. There is maybe 2 good songs everything else is either just completely unmemorable/generic or aweful.
Plus for the PC version you can't change the music at all, only the ps4  version has that option.
And now Story, yes story, this has to be the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idea I have ever seen, adding Akuma. The story already is poorly handled and just not long or satisfiying in the slightest. But on top of that  to have Akuma as a cannon part of the story is just stupid, esspecially with the role he is given too. Imagine for a second that you are watching a long running show you enjoy, and then all of a sudden, a character from a completely different series is introduced as a cannon part of the story out of no where. This is like if in Naruto, Vegeta was brought in to defeat Sasuke and Madara at the request of Itachi in a flash back because Itachi once saved Vegeta's life. That would be the dumbest♥♥♥♥♥♥ever. For those of you who don't watch or know Naruto, them just think of one of your favorite shows and throw Mojo jojo in as a cannon person to defeat the main villain.
OOOH we aint done.
There are no end arcade Scenes!!!! NONE. This is part of what makes tekken special, they have hands down the best scenes for psudo character stories at the end of their arcade mode but its not here! The extra chapter story mode thing doesn't make up for it in the slightest. Arcade mode is just pointless now, after already removing other modes thats just stupid.
This is a gutted Tekken game, completely bare bones, My final verdict is that if you are new to tekken go ahead and pick it up if you enjoy fighting games, you wont see all the big issues with it since you don't what what you should be getting though its not worth full price by a long shot. If you are a tekken fan don't get it yet, go play the older games more and when this one comes down in price then grab it. So I guess overall don't get it, replayability only goes so far when you are doing so little in the replay.

Being an Android user, this came out of the blue for me. As a huge fan of the Legend of Zelda, and Zelda-likes, this is very much welcomed to my library.
The visual aesthetic is pretty much Wind Waker, with a touch of Minecraft inspired cubic layouts.
Gameplay wise, there is a very simple two button combat system. Your input options change dynamically as you approach objects you can interact with, which can work very well. Managing items is simple and forgiving; you're given more inputs for quick access than I've seen in most Zelda titles.
While the puzzles are mostly tried and true block and button puzzles, its a great trip back to nostalgia lane and leaves me wanting more modern releases from this genre.
Unlike other games of it's genre, there's a levelling system to Oceanhorn. Your character gains experiences through defeating monsters and completing specific goals. Then, through the adventurers guild, you are given access to different weapons and features in the game. This is a great way to tie progress to your regular combat and accomplishments throughout the game.

Any review ONLY complaining about framerate or performance should automatically be discounted as useless. A game is much more than its performance. Incidentally, the performance is fine on high end hardware. If you're not running a maxed out build and are expecting to run this game on 4k ultra, your expectations are out of whack. The game runs 60ish fps on a 980ti with high-to-ultra settings, MSAA disabled, and a few other tweaks. In other words, it performs just fine.
But that's irrelevant, this game isn't about perf, it's about gameplay. And the gameplay is solid.
Story is great, movement feels good, world is fairly large and open. There's at least a good 40hrs of gameplay, seems like (haven't even unlocked special augs). If you're a Deus Ex fan, this game feels a lot like the franchise. Nothing's changed-- you still aug, hack, sneak, and occasionally run and gun. Lots of different ways to play missions (stealth vs shoot, lots of paths), tons of secrets. Some might consider this game a little stale based on past games (it feels very much like HR), but if you've been following along, you've already noticed that most of the story arcs have been fairly repetitive. They're following a formula here, and it's completely unsurprising.
What you're buying: a solid and lengthy single player story-based FPS. What you're getting: exactly that. Buy it if you like the franchise. If you don't know anything about Deus Ex, start from the beginning.

Okay, so, a lot of people out there complain about the dlc characters, online and offline modes, etc. But for me as a big fan of the series, I DON'T CARE ABOUT DLC CHARACTERS OR ONLINE MODES.
I think it's cool that they added this stuff, but if anyone, that includes me, wants to use dlc characters and play online, i'd say just be patient until they fix everything. Yes, the fact that they released with all of those unfixed patches and bugs is a ♥♥♥♥♥ and a half to deal with, but for now just focus on the core of the game.
So that being said, my honest review of MKX is... it's a great game. Bugs aside, it offers a fresh reboot to the series, even if the story mode lacked a bit storywise. The gameplay feels slick and fun, all of the characters are given unique movesets to shake things up, and the new X-ray moves and fatalities are... to say the least, brutal. If you are going to play this on PC, make sure that you have as computer with an updated graphics card, enough space for the game so that you won't settle for the minimum requirements, and other things of that nature, because no one wants a laggy and slow MK experience.
One of the new modes they added was the ability to join one of the factions, like Lin Kuei or Black Dragon, and fight in a competitive online modeto win gold and rewards.
So all in all, this was a great game. Slick gameplay, brutal X-rays and fatalities, unique characters, and the new online mode. It would have been a better experience for everyone if they released it fully without its bugs and patches, but until then they are slowly building it back up to what fans expected. Just make sure your computer has the power to handle it.

Not working correctly on launch day, broken puzzles in the krypt, erratic frame rate in the Shaolin Temple stage, memory leaks, high CPU usage, erratic performance on high end AMD cards(6970, 7950, 270x, 280 etc.), fatality glitches, unable to unlock items achieved from mobile version of MKX, 15GB patches that delete saves and a host of other bugs listed on the STEAM discussion forum of MKX. Thankfully the only bugs I suffered from are the first 3. Now the first 2 bugs have been fixed and the framerate in Shaolin Temple have improved slightly. Running on a Phenom ][ 965, 16GB of RAM and 5850  at 1680 by 1050 with all the effects reduced to low or disabled, I was pleasantly surprised to find it playable at 60fps.
On the gameplay side they have really delivered. A massive improvement over the last game. The character roster is more or less as big as the last one with a twist though, each character has 3 different fighting styles. Something brought over from the PS2/XBOX/GameCUBE era of MK. Also they have increased the number of towers available compared to the single 300 challenges tower from the last MK. There's so much one can do with the offline content that online play can be completely ignored. The story mode is shorter than the last one but frankly speaking the real meat is in it the arcade mode and I am quite surprised to see people getting riled up over the short campaign in a fighting game. The only mode I wish to see return is the tag mode. It was quite fun in the last game.
Online multiplayer seems to be a mixed bag and rightfully so because everyone runs on different ISPs. However compared to the last one this one is definitely better. I did manage to get a few games going with Australians and Indonesians. Lag was noticeable  but it was playable.
In closing, this is a competent fighter which stands right next to Street Fighter, King of Fighters and Killer Instinct. Quick review after 40+ hours in the game (I play a lot offline, it doesn't count those usually).
First, for those of you wondering, this game plays without a hitch on an i5-3450 with a mere Intel HD 2500 gpu, on Windows 7-64 bit with 16 GB RAM at 1360x768 with no framerate slowdowns.  It probably will play on Intel laptops with at least an Intel HD 2500 gpu, that's impressive.
The combat is a lot like Darksiders or The Witcher 1.  Basically, you fight in a chain of attacks, usually moving in with each step in the chain.   There are abilities attached to each type of weapon.  You can fight with Daggers, Fae Daggers, Longsword, Chakram, Great Sword, Staff, Sceptre, Bow.   Each of these has a specialty tree where you learn additional passive and active abilities.   The active abilities have certain effects with certain special maneuvers learned.  So a Chakram attack can be held down with left click to create a large defensive spin area attack that applies the magic effect of the Chakram (burning, shock, etc) on everyone in the spin area.   It's quite simple to do and understand.
One of the beauties of this game is that every maneuver or ability you learn has a short movie in-game to examine, even before you learn it.  This gives you a good sense of the timing to achieve it and how it works.   A visual approach is used in almost everything.
And the visuals are impressive.  You have a long view  of the terrain before any level of details lower and if cautious can often see your unaware enemy before you must engage, allowing you to avoid many engagements.  (There are ambushes though, and some enemies are much more alert, so there is still inevitable excitement in any journey.)  The style is exactly as in the pictures and movies on the Store Page.   You can customize your character a fair amount, nose, eyes, gauntness, coloration, hair almost as much as in Skyrim.   The graphics are in the vein of Warcraft but higher resolution and more detailed.   The scenery is colorful.   The animations are very good, both in combat and not.
The Lore is at least as good as Skyrim.  But to be honest, Bethesda lore is always contradictory and confusing, books often are wrong or disagree with the game.  Amalur has lore also, it is less contradictory and confusing, but it is likewise not consistent with the actual game.  I don't think one should really depend on such Lore as meaningful in either set of games.  The difference is that here, the books tend to agree with the reality in the game.  In Skyrim or Oblivion, or even Morrowind, the Lore does not agree with all that is in the game.  About a third of it is totally wrong, and another third of it is inconsistent or just filler.   You'll find less of those inconsistencies in Amalur, but some exists and some is filler.
Combat is fluid, once learned it is easier than in Bethesda games.   Weapons apply much of the magic damage by the abilities and special moves, so there is a lot of value to loot and to armor.   Loot is easy to come by, one does not need to get the special help loot in one of the DLCs to do well, but the package deal is a good price.   I still have not even opened the DLC loot chest.   The most difficult level is level one, not because the in-game tutorial is hard, it is not, but because at each level you seem to grow stronger faster than the opposition.   Also, because it seems that the game's local monsters do not get stronger as you level, although that's a bit debateable.  They are at least capped in certain regions is my guess.
This means that although you are free to go almost anywhere, which is something sandbox RPG players like, you will find it tougher in the expected areas farther from your beginning and closer to the War's front.   You therefore get a sense of improving power as you level, as well as more flexibility in your skills.
I find the game fair at all difficulty levels, play as you wish, difficulty levels can be changed on the fly, so the game is very user friendly.
The dialog is spoken, and although there may not be quite as much dialog as in Skyrim or Oblivion, it's close to as much, well voiced, and more to the point.   I believe this is an area where the game shines.  Quests seem to make sense, even the side quests have value and of course they make you see all parts of the world while being done.  There are a ton of quests and all dialog whether in a quest or not is well done and germane to either the quest or adding flavor to the game world.
The music, the art, the graphics, the animation, the color palette, the characters, the combat, the quests, the open world, the gameplay, the voicework  -- all combine to give you a full, consistent, enjoyable experience.   It combines the feeling of a personal MMO done right with that of an RPG adventure done right, with good action, lots of story, player progression that matters, and so many ways to achieve things and interact with a world you will care about.
There is little to fault here.   Are you afraid of having too little money ... there are crates that spawn everywhere, they aren't chests but remind one of the common loot crates on the Docks of Oblivion's ports.  Break them and you will get some coins over time.  So money is not an issue, although this is not the best way to make money.   Common enemies will respawn in the wild, perhaps even invading a town from time to time.   The guards will respond, but they can take their time, if you kill these interlopers you get a chance for more loot.  Things like this calm you in feeling you can make progress if you fall behind and that there is safety in familiar places you befriend.   Yet, there are ambushes regularly triggered, making good sense in the game, causing either rebel thiefs or beasts to challenge you in various locations as you simply travel about.  This adds to immersion.  There are many special hidden chests, some not so hidden that you can't find them if you look in every tree trunk or every path off the main beat.   But also there are some skills you can acquire to make your mini-map and map help you find more seriously hidden items that you might not find at all otherwise, even secret doors or secreted areas.  Every skill tree has value and you are not limited to any one class or tree or weapon specialization.  Whether you wish to be a better merchant or find hidden areas as a Thief, or cast many spells as a Mage, or fight as a skilled Warrior, you can always mix and match as well. Reset your skills for a price in gold, re-imagining your character.  If you like, craft potions, enhance weapons, salvage anything.
This is a great game, frequently 75% off, so you will not be disappointed.   I can't speak to whether or not the game is too hard or too easy, I would say it after some adjustment is probably easier than the Elder Scrolls series, but that doesn't make the journey any less enjoyable.   So if you want to travel in a beautiful story world with lots to do, in a more colorful and cartoony world that still has all the detail in graphics and story that you ache for, this is a game to recommend highly to you.
Enjoy.  It is often on sale at 75 % off.   Buy it then.  The complete pack is usually $10 and the main game alone is $5.  It's a shame, these developers deserved a chance to make many more games, they would have been equal to the best.   This game has so many extra features done flawlessly, like the map and the movie clips for skill moves, that one has to wonder how this company ever went broke.   A great shame.
NOTE:  This game does seem to require an EA account, but it's easy to register and works flawlessly otherwise.   For me it checks in via internet with the EA servers for authentication every time it starts up.  It may be possible to play the game without this internet access, but I mention this as information.

Hell’s Highway is the third (and most likely final) installment of the Brothers in Arms series.
Just like the older games, Brothers in Arms is a tactics based shooter, but unlike the other games, Hell’s Highway adds many different systems that the others games lack. Accuracy is tighter than the other titles of the series, grenades are easier to throw, the game introduces the “dig-in” mechanic, you get a couple new squad types, and various forms of cover can be destroyed.
The story continues to follow Sgt. Matt Baker as he continues to fight and slowly falls victim to the horrors he has faced, and it’s just as great as, if not greater than, the previous games.
In short, this game is more up-to-date then previous titles and feels much more polished than the other games. But at the same time, it still captures the emotional experience that made Brothers in Arms stand out.

Next, characters. I've played Ruby and Yang so far. They play somewhat differently, though the simplistic combat system doesn't do a very good job of letting them really shine the way they could/should. I've no reason to believe that Wiess and Blake don't also play differently. The variety is there, without a doubt. Whether the game can take great advantage of it remains to be seen.
Combat system: I dearly hope the combat system does evolve , as right now it's way too simple. Just mash the melee button, and occasionally use your specials. At the least, Ruby has one 'ranged' attack that you can add in her melee 'combo'. Swing melee, then ranged, and she'll do the whole "swing scythe and shoot what you're scything" thing. It doesn't really lead into any sort of actual combo though. Yang, in my experience, would break her combo to fire her ranged attack no matter when I pressed the ranged attack button. The combat system dearly needs some level. Also, I'd trade your first born child for a block button.
Levels: You got four of them. That's it. Okay, Early Access. The lack of content is understood. Right now, you can blow through the game with four players in maybe 45 minutes.
Difficulty: Solo, this game is frustratingly difficult on my first playthrough. With a group for my second playthough (RRYY), it was laughably easy.
All in all, I can't really whole heartedly recommend the game due to lack of content, but as an Early Access title, I'm willing to not not-recommend this game. The potential for a great game is there. It desperately needs more of a combat system than "mash melee", and I dearly hope future patches improve upon it. If you're a RWBY fan though, and willing to accept Early Access for what it is, I'd have to recommend the game. So put me down for a tentative Recommend.

Pros:
_Looks alright: The game is colorful and bright, nothing particularly ground-breaking here, but not bad.
_Good music.
_Controls well: I don't know how it played on the iPad, but it plays well here for both Mouse-Keyboard and gamepad.
_The Legend of Oceanhorn, Ocarina of Uncharted Seas: It's clear where the game got its inspiration from. Although the tight-level design and interesting mechanics of Zelda isn't really here (Let's be honest, you shouldn't expect it to be), the game manage to  the Zelda games justice, to a degree, without ripping it off too much. It's like Oceanhorn sat next to Zelda on a test and manage to pull off a B- without the teacher's suspicion.
Cons:
_Where is my windowed mode? Man, TB is gonna freak the ♥♥♥♥ out: Ya, for some reason you can't have windowed mode. You can have borderless though, so that's good. But for people who connects their PC to a TV, you'll have to play this game on  a huge resolution.
_The leveling system: This is where the whole "this game used to be on iPad" thing showed its head. You "level up" by completing challenges, but you don't get anything from it, other than just some ingame coins. That is some IOS stuff right there. But no big deal. UPDATE: There's actually more than the leveling system than that, so scratch this off of the list of cons.
_Voice acting is meh.
Overall, you would like this game if:
_You think IOS ports to PC can be done and are looking for some proof.
_You think IOS ports to PC CAN'T be done and are looking to prove yourself wrong.
_You like The Legend of Zelda games.
Is this game worth $15: Yes. It's pretty good. Not in the GOTY sense, but it's very, very decent, borderline excellent for its price.
Seriously, though, I can't believe this game is an IOS port...

There’s no way of skirting the issue – this game is a Zelda clone, through-and-through. From the bombs and arrows to the comically oversized chests you find them in, Oceanhorn is a mere re-skin mod away from being the Zelda release for PC we all so desperately long for. In fact, this may well be the closest we will ever get.
Is that necessarily a bad thing? I don’t think so. While it shows little in the way of originality, it does a great job of reproducing the magic spark that keeps players coming back. Make no mistake – this is no cheap copy, and will easily keep you entertained for hours. It would have been great to see Cornfox & Bros. take a few more risks to give the game more of a distinct personality, but don’t let that stop you from casting off on this excellent adventure on the open seas.

I was really enjoying this game until one particular boss fight and the difficulty just SPIKED!
There's a video explaining how XCOM developers tried to force players to play under a time limit in a Turn Based Strategy game, players absolutely hated it and modded it out so they could play the game THEIR way, slow and strategic, because the game, XCOM, runs on a Random Number Generator (RNG), if you select a soldier to attack he's given a % chance to hit an alien bad guy, even at 99% players often joke/complain that they miss almost every single time, so the RNG is WAY against you!  This is why players wanted to take it slow and make sure it's a 100% chance to HIT instead of any chance to miss right?  Developers didn't like that so they added turn limits to the campaign, forcing players to take risks to which it made some missions damn near impossible to complete because of risk taking against an RNG system that was against the player.
This was similar to that, this boss battle changed the way I had to play IMMEDIATELY and I was just getting used to the combat system, I was taking my time and figuring out a strategy on how to deal the most damage and keep enemies at bay.  The battle is hard enough as you're chasing an enemy and her "allies" keep pushing you back to begin with, and then IN COMES BOOTAY!  Who chases you from behind, and she's on a timer where no matter who's turn it is, she interrupts it with an attack.  So between dealing with the allies pushing me back trying to catch the main baddy and a giant woman chasing whom btw the game decides to put RIGHT BEHIND YOU to the point where you can't even react in time NO MATTER HOW FAR YOU PUSH IN THE BATTLE!  Makes this boss battle unbeatable, because the developer is punishing you for taking your time and strategizing.
The Youtube video raises a fair and great point on poor game design like this, on how companies need to think about how to reward players for playing a certain style they want you to play instead of punishing you.
I also realize this game wasn't made by Obsidian and it shows considering the controls, Stick of Truth's controls were just fine, but they made the keybinds in this one so awkward to the point where i had to get a controller.
Also the game has DRM by Ubisoft, thanks, that ALWAYS helps paying customers >:P!

Pre-ordered the Digital Deluxe for $100 local currency; only to find that the pre-order items I was so keen on obtaining
are
.
After an insanely large day one patch (requiring almost as much space to "install" as the game is large... I required 40 GB free to
the 48 GB game... I had to uninstall other games to get that much free space) I get a message saying any saved games I might have had are incompatible... never mind the one time use items.
After getting to the first grate you smash & deciding the game is running *very* slow I quit & go online to find that low frame rates are a known issue. Go to turn down my settings just in case... to find the game no longer works. At all. Even the launcher will no longer launch; silent no error messages crash. But hey... it's still synchronizes my game to the Steam cloud just in case something goes wrong & you know... the Steam cloud some how eliminates those one time use DLC items.
Skip it until it matures; roast Square Enix & bash "lightning" (since that IP is their baby) if it doesn't.
P.S. Please open support tickets about the one time use pre-oder DLC. I already did myself.
The 524.7 patch build went of more sanely then the day one patch; Steam indicated the download was only a few megabytes. Unknown if there was any size install issues as I still have 42 GB free from the day one patch.
This patch fixed whatever the problem was with my system; however patch notes are vague at best... there is no way to determine what was causing my problem of unplayability.
Indications are that this build did not solve the problems for many people; however Steam indicated ~45,000 people in game this morning so it did help lots of people I'd say.
Game play wise now that the game is working:
The game takes everything Deus Ex: Human Revolution was & makes it better.
The levels & hubs feel bigger with more options to take to solve various problems. The hubs in general feel like they take place in an actual city now.
The new augments are interesting & having the peps moved to internal is nice but overall they're not an amazing change; the early on "power management" is very annoying.
The crafting system boils down to having a basic store with you at all times; no running out of ammo for all your weapons as long as you can get your hands on a few things to turn into crafting components.
The redesigned weapon system is very nice with the ability to disable or enable items on a gun.
4x scope on your assault rifle too much for the guy just around the corner? No problem; just disable it for that one shot.
Detail wise the game has had a lot done to it. Graphically everything looks... nice. Mirrors don't have reflections which is a bit of a disconnect & cars still seem like they're out of a ~2000 game but the cars are much better then they were in DEHR. Everything else looks lovely. It's not the best looking game on the market by far but everything is nice & crisp & seems mostly natural.
Also many things appear to be remembered by the game engine. For instance one problem in the game allows you to solve it by just telling the cops... which results in a firefight you're not part of. During said firefight one cop lost her helmet... 3 cut scenes later (and 2 area transitions?) when I saw her again she still did not have her helmet.
Over all the game is fun to play & basically takes everything DEHR was & makes it better; however it's growing pains are too much even after the first patch.
Beyond this one use DLC is still not was advertised on the store page upon purchase & because of this there turns out to be
reason to have pre-ordered the game.

Graphics: 7/10: It has a very creepy and proper feel to it, but the graphics can get a bit old after a while. Granted it's in beta, so hopefully during official release it will have been touched up. The monster has a rather nice graphics effect when it gets closer and can be seen, granted the ACTUAL Hat Man, is rather hard to make out within the fog till he's right up on you.
Sound/Music: 6/10 The sounds and audio are great at first, but after a while they stop being scary, especially when you're having trouble finding pages and are feeling frustrated. The heartbeat mechanic of Hat Man getting closer, is a rather awesome way to tell how close he is and act accordingly, but during the last several pages, when he is popping up all the time (in some of my videos like ever 30 seconds or less), it can get extremely annoying as it becomes all you hear. Still it's in beta, hopefully that'll be polished a bit to where he doesn't pop up so often when you're being super cautious or it isn't as deafening. This is a game you have to play with the sound though, otherwise finding pages will be EXTREMELY hard.
Gameplay: 7?/10: I put the ? because I may changed it and move it up, at the present point, I still haven't beaten the game (13 out of ?? pages), though I've finally started to get the hang of it. Hat man is a nice enemy as you can sneak by him and even juke around him (this requires some skill), the stealth works very nicely in the game and leads to some funny survival moments. As you collect more, it seems that real traps start to appear (or there is just a giant pitfall to your death at one point). My only issue with the gameplay is that it's not entirely clear what somethings are for, namely the Matches...I've found Matches, I think they unlock more pages (as I get stuck on 7 pages, find a box and boom I start finding more), maybe a tiny bit of clarity on that...granted could be a journal page I haven't gotten to read yet.
Overall: 7/10 likely to improve up with future edit. It's a good game, if you like this type of game. It could be a little more clear on some issues and have some audio configuration options (there is no way to effect the sound which means if you record, you'll be lower the games sound level during editing). I'd say buy it, especially before it gets closer to finished and increases in price.

Hell's Highway feels a full generation away from it's predecessors - the graphics are vastly improved and the tech can finally tell the story with all the drama and tension that they've been aiming for since the beginning.
It also feels like a new generation in terms of the fact that a lot of the gameplay has been streamlined (grenade throwing has been tightened up, thank god), and, in my opinion, these changes have made the game easier. The new appearance of OP weapons like the bazooka team and the player-controlled tank make it a cakewalk to mop up whole squads of enemies in one shot. Your Thompson is also replaced early on with a barrel-cartridge tommy gun that feels like it never runs out of ammo. You can, with relative ease, stand back and pick off enemies from afar with the new cover system that allows you to peek around corners and focus your fire, and if you do happen to flank the enemy, often they'll stand straight up and into your squadmates' gunfire, dying in seconds. All these additions detract from the immersion, and make the game feel a little more arcadey, even thought the core gamplay mechanics are nearly identical to the previous games. All in all, this game feels much more polished and fancy, but loses some of the pulse-pounding, gritty tension of knowing that even if you're prepared, bum-rushing that dug-in squad could get you killed.
The one thing this does best is make you feel. By the last levels of the game, you'll almost want to stop playing, and the push through burning wreckages and sand dunes, being harried by multiple enemy squads, will feel dreadful, but you know that you have to keep pushing through in order to complete the mission, which is exactly how the characters feel. The narrative continues the story of Matt Baker, who is experiencing some deep PTSD/mental illness. It's incredibly bleak all the way through, and centres around a specific and almost rushed-through moment in the original game, which is retroactively filled out to fantastic effect for the player, explaining the actions of some of the characters all the way through the series. There is a subplot about a cursed weapon that it also tries to retrofit, but this doesn't stick quite as well.
So that's it - I've played all three games in the series, one after the other, in the space of a couple of weeks. This used to be my preferred game, and it's the one I've played most, but after playing them back to back, Earned in Blood is easily my favourite, and balances a quality narrative, with realistic and rewarding gameplay, a battlefield that sounds truly alive, memorable level design, and just the right level of difficulty that rewards good tactics. The original game falls on the side of being a little too clunky, and this falls on the side of being a little too streamlined, for my tastes. In saying that, because the narrative intertwines throughout the three games, you really must play all three in order to get the full effect. Clever move, Gearbox.
I recommend this more than RTH30, but less than EiB.

A refreshingly relatable and grounded take on war in videos games. Relying more on character and personal moments than big overly produced set pieces. That's not to say the actual action isn't great, it's full of the same nitty gritty combat of any other solidly crafted war shooter. But it's not what makes Hell's Highway stand out, it's the smaller details that do. The tension of combat and planing out your battles, the humanity and development given to your comrades, the atmospheric levels full of booming sounds of the battlefield and eerie silence of empty village streets and farms. Many games capture the sheer power and brutality of war. But only a small handful capture the real warriors themselves. The thoughts and feelings of men forced to fight and die in a cause they may not fully understand nor sometimes even fully care about. Hell's Highway is one of those rare games that does.

There are thousands of free games out there but only a select few that are of the quality of Super Crate Box.  This game feels a lot like the arcade classic Mario Bros. with the weapon selection of Serious Sam.  Vlambeer is well respected for their high-quality arcade throwbacks and this is no exception.  The pure simplicity of this addicting game is the only decent excuse not to charge anything for this experience.  Once you get a hang of the game you just want to keep playing round after round.  There is no reason not to give this game a try but if you need more convincing I'll try my best.
In Super Crate Box you play as a tiny character running around one screen maps.  Your goal is to collect as many crates as possible.  Each crate counts as one point towards your score and equips you with a new weapon.  You do not receive any points for taking out the enemies but you must do so anyway because if one touches you then its game over.  If one of the enemies escapes your fire and makes it to the bottom of the map they will come back down the top.  These enemies will turn red and move at double speed.  This is an incredibly fast paced game and most rounds won't last more than a minute.
The weapons obviously play a huge roll in helping you survive.  There are fast weapons like dual pistols, machine guns, and miniguns; each shooting faster than the last but with more recoil.  There are explosives such as mines you lay down, straight shooting bazookas, and bouncy grenade launchers.  The katana, shotgun, and to some extent the laser rifle all good for close quarters combat.  You'll need a variety of weapons to deal with the three different types of enemies.  There are lots of little runners that go down quick, big runners that are slow but take a lot of hits, and flying skulls which are weak but hard to hit.
Strategy is actually quite important for both survival and high-scores.  On one hand you need to know when to go and grab boxes to increase your score.  While on the other hand you don't want to put yourself in a tight spot, especially when you never know which weapon you will pick up next.  There are times when you have a good weapon you'll just have to clear the screen and give yourself some breathing room.  As you play you'll unlock a handful of extra weapons, a couple new characters, and a total of three increasingly difficult stages.
This really is a wonderfully crafted game that begs to be played over and over again.  Most of the weapons are immensely satisfying as you cut down the hordes of enemies.  It always feels like with just a little luck or just a bit of extra caution you get achieve a slightly better score.  After you die a single button press instantly brings you right back into the action for another shot.  You really can't go wrong with Super Crate Box.  Jump on Steam and add this little gem to your library.

After playing for 9 hours Oceanhorn is a fun journey, in a world I am keen to explore more of. This is my very first experience with the game and I am pleased to say a positive one.
Well done to the dev's.
This is a great game, particularly when you need a break and just want to enjoy a relaxing, non-difficult RPG.
Xbox 360 controller works perfectly for me. No control issues. Games runs very well considering my older system.
The gameplay, whilst basic, since the game originated from a mobile platform, does have me coming back for more, trying to find and complete all quests.

Waking up during a stormy night you find your father has left, leaving a notebook and strange necklace behind. What happened? Where did he go? It's your job to find out.
Oceanhorn is a port of a mobile game from 2013, rather then being a direct port much effort has gone into remastering the game for PC. Was it worth the wait?
. Graphically speaking it's just as amazing as the first time you may have played it. Adding 4k+ res, realtime AO, soft shadows, AA, higher draw distance and 60FPS support among other things. While the game played well with keyboard+mouse or controller, everything was completely rebindable.
Staying true to the Zelda formula while keeping a charm of its own, you travel the between islands on your ship gradually piecing together the story. Each island has it's own distinct themes and challenges while some just serve as hub points for restocking and gathering new information about undiscovered locations. Progress will result in level ups which unlocked a range of upgrades including a peashooter for firing off your ship. Later stages traveling becomes quite dangerous so these extra defenses are critical.
Dungeons generally consist of simple puzzles and key finding while backtracking to unlock areas you were unable to access earlier. Select islands contain boss fights and victory often rewarded unique abilities which also helped with opening secret areas. While you do spend much of your time traveling to locations already seen it's not a problem at all, as you will also find many new npcs and sidequests along the way.
Oceanhorn is a little on the easy side but the beauty of the entire package completely out weighs the lack of challenge. The game does ramp up in the later stages and you'll need to learn different attack patterns of enemies to guarantee success. Already mentioned the graphics are very distinct, the closest game to the mark would be Lili: Child of Geos (another decent phone port). With a captivating story, relaxing soundtrack and a whole bunch content to discover. For the asking price it's well worth the investment. Cheers.

Action-Adventure RPGs are a dime-a-dozen these days, Is Oceanhorn a worthy addition to said genre ? The short answer would be "Yes and No"
Let's get into it.
This is not the original launch of the game, first being released on iPad where it got good reviews. So first things first, how well was it ported to PC ?
Please keep in mind that my time with the game was through a pre-release version, that being said :
-Frames locked at 60 max (Vsync on or off).
-Vsync off will result in screen tearing.
-Operates fine with mouse and Keyboard as-well with a controller.
-Most of the keys are rebindable but not all. You can rebind the movement and action keys which are most important, but you can not rebind generic commands such as "Pause" , "Menu", Numeric for items (1,2,3,4) and you can not assign keyboard commands for mouse actions (attack, use item and turn camera). Overall i found this to be acceptable but not ideal.
-No bugs, glitches, crashes or any issues from my time with the game
-Decent graphics options for quality / resolution etc.
The developer claims that this was a huge overhaul and from my time with the game i found this to be true. So overall it's ok technically speaking. My only issue is with the frame lock and tearing, hopefully the dev will have this sorted soon. OR RIOT!!! :D
Now that we are done with that on to the game!
The overall feel of Oceanhorn resembles the Zelda series, featuring a mute hero, a handful of magical artifacts that you will collect across very different environments in order to save the world!...what else ?... oh and find out what happened to your father!
The journey will take you from verdant landscapes to sun-scorched deserts to treacherous dungeons, all of these environments are beautifully crafted and never outstay their welcome.
The "I am on a adventure!" feeling is present throughout the game. A big part of that feeling is caused by the epic soundtrack which blends perfectly with your surroundings, never breaking the feeling and always adapting itself to the situation at hand.
The gameplay is rather stiff for a Action RPG and while it may be fine for ipad it's definitely sub-par for a PC title. This is a issue because from my point of view the actual combat-gameplay is the bread and butter for a game of this type. You start with a STICK for a weapon (yes a actual stick!) but you soon find your fathers sword and shield! You can block with said shield using shift and you can move around while holding block, but when you attack with your sword you are rooted in place, making for a bit of a frustrating experience when a enemy moves 5 pixels out of range you need to stop attacking, move and start attacking again.
While you traverse Oceanhors worlds you will level up and unlock new items and abilities which will allow you to solve previously impassable puzzles. So if you are a completionist there is plenty of backtracking for you in Oceanhorn.
Speaking of puzzles...these are for the most part no-brainers, with the occasional brain teaser, i did not mind this to much as i never enjoyed being stuck on a puzzle but if you want something more complex you will have a hard time finding it here.
What about the difficulty ?
Well there is no hand-holding and the game rarely points you in the right direction.
For example, if you chose not to talk to all of the towns folk or read all the messages scattered across the land you will not get access to all the locations you can explore. A location will only unlock for you if someone tells you about it or you read about it somewhere.
The actual combat is not that challenging and you will have no problems dispatching creatures or learning a bosses patterns so you can counter it.
Let's wrap this up...
If you are looking for a leisurely-paced enchanting adventure and you are not to fussy about combat then look no further.
Sure... it is not perfect and it may not be the embodiment of modern day ARPGs but it more then makes up for it in feel and style.
Overall a good game at a very attractive price which i am happy to recommend!

Just got this as a Christmas present. I put it in my wishlist since I use that as a "Check back later and see if that early access game is any good now" list, but sadly, my friends think it's an actual wishlist. Oh well, definitely not the worst Christmas present I ever got. That being said, the game suffers from nowhere near enough content. In line with this being an Early Access review, I'm going to assume anyone looking to buy this is willing to accept that lack of content, so I'm not docking any points there.
Next, characters. I've played Ruby and Yang so far. They play somewhat differently, though the simplistic combat system doesn't do a very good job of letting them really shine the way they could/should. I've no reason to believe that Wiess and Blake don't also play differently. The variety is there, without a doubt. Whether the game can take great advantage of it remains to be seen.
Combat system: I dearly hope the combat system does evolve , as right now it's way too simple. Just mash the melee button, and occasionally use your specials. At the least, Ruby has one 'ranged' attack that you can add in her melee 'combo'. Swing melee, then ranged, and she'll do the whole "swing scythe and shoot what you're scything" thing. It doesn't really lead into any sort of actual combo though. Yang, in my experience, would break her combo to fire her ranged attack no matter when I pressed the ranged attack button. The combat system dearly needs some level. Also, I'd trade your first born child for a block button.
Levels: You got four of them. That's it. Okay, Early Access. The lack of content is understood. Right now, you can blow through the game with four players in maybe 45 minutes.
Difficulty: Solo, this game is frustratingly difficult on my first playthrough. With a group for my second playthough (RRYY), it was laughably easy.
All in all, I can't really whole heartedly recommend the game due to lack of content, but as an Early Access title, I'm willing to not not-recommend this game. The potential for a great game is there. It desperately needs more of a combat system than "mash melee", and I dearly hope future patches improve upon it. If you're a RWBY fan though, and willing to accept Early Access for what it is, I'd have to recommend the game. So put me down for a tentative Recommend.

If you're looking for a new Horror game that presents a great atmosphere and makes the hairs on the back of your neck stand up, The Hat Man: Shadow Ward just might be for you. Taking inspiration from Amnesia: The Dark Descent's ambiance, puzzle/collection-based objectives from a variety of games, and cues from psudo-folklore-derived games like Slenderman, The Hat Man has a lot of familiar and tried-and-true aesthetics while presenting new gameplay elements that are quickly becoming extremely popular for video games, especially in the Horror genre--namely, that it's very replayable. The map generates randomly, and if you stray too far from any one spot, it will have changed completely when you try to return to it.
If there's one thing that the Horror genre in general relies on, it's atmosphere. As a music composer/writer, I can say with great confidence that what I say next cannot be easily refuted, which is thus: A game that desires to scare, unsettle, unnerve, and frighten, must take great care in creating an experience that tips the audience off-balance, makes them lose their footing, and just when they think they're back on their feet, you pull the rug out from under them. If a Horror game cannot disturb and create suspense, it is operating completely wrong.
Now, of course, your mileage may vary, and various games may not neccessarily scare you. But, for me, anyway, The Hat Man does a great job at creating suspense and keeping me on my toes; like watching the fishing reel scene from Jaws, you'd be utterly amazed at what happens when you just focus on the ambience and the sound effects. In truth, they can sometimes be quite scarier than what's actually trying to scare you. In this regard, I think the developers of this game chose a great collection to work with. This game relies on building suspense and atmosphere rather than relying on conventional jump scares like most other Horror games. In fact, there's only maybe a handful of them in this game, if you can even call some of them so. A refreshing and welcome change of pace, in my opinion.
All-in-all, a fun game. I can't wait to see what is added and done in the final release. If it's great already, I can scarcely imagine what will happen in the future. To the developers, I say great job, and keep at it.

Good game for the price.  Has its ups and downs.
Things I think could be improved...
Building your home doesn't have that incredible accomplishment factor many games have.  There really isn't that desire to improve on your house as the enemies in the location you choose will be more of a nuisance than anything else.  You'll want to bring your stuff to a tougher island but moving everything is a pain.  I think having a ship or boat that can be built upon and flown to each island would make building it up more enjoyable.
Chests with larger storage have to be researched and created and then replace the old ones making moving all your items again and again very frustrating.  A direct upgrade system on each chest would be much better.
There's not any reason to play further once you beat it.  You can reroll another character but it feels very grindy.  Otherwise the RPG element is fantastic!
The graphics and gameplay are fluid and crisp.  The ability to reset and redistribute your upgrade points is nice too.  Co-Op is a blast and connecting with friends is easy and not at all difficult.
I'm still happy with my purchase but I do think it could use some tweeks.

This is my review for Tekken 7 on PC. I will break it down in pros and cons rather than writing an essay though the only thing I would like to highlight is the fact that as a fighting games fan and modder I love any fighting game appearing on PC.
PROS:
1) A Tekken game on PC finally.
2) Very well optimized on PC.
3) Nice graphics if you got the rig to push it to max.
4) Healthy roster of characters to choose from.
5) Excellent character customization options.
6) Treasure battles are fun.
7) Good netcode.
8) Good interface.
9) Great fighting mechanics, easy to play but difficult to master.
10) Great looking stages.
11) Excellent keyboard support for players who use it.
12) Good music.
CONS:
1) No crossplay.
2) Frequent disconnects while connecting to online matches.
3) Overall graphics are good but textures look dated sometimes.
4) Limited modding potential (not really a con but as a modder I do consider it a con).
5) Rare FPS drops but they happen for no reason.
6) Sound effects (like hitting an opponent) are not impactful or say they sound old.

For the first full-fledged Tekken game to be released on  the PC, this is doing fantastic. I haven't stopped playing it since I bought it. It is totally fun and there is a lot of learning to it.  The online is great, the matchmaking was at first shaky but I think it has improved. No unfair matchups where beginners got automatically matched up with seasoned vets (although you can choose to do so when setting your preferences before the warm-up screen.) Customization is plentiful with almost endless possibilities in decking out your characters.
As far as negatives go, story mode/arcade mode can have a bit of an improvment. There is one big story arc, of course involving the 3 main members of the Mishima bloodline, Heihachi's wife, Kazumi, and Akuma from Street Fighter. The other characters have a little episode for each one, involving one match (kind of like Street Fighter V's character episodes but I think SFV had 3 matches for each character) and a little cinematic scene. A little more involvement from the  non-Mishima characters could have been nice. Also, besides the Story mode and the 5-match Arcade mode, Treasure battle is the only offline game mode available (at the moment at least). No team battle, no Tekken bowl/ball mode (although there is a rumor one will be implemented), no Tekken Force mode. This is a more online-centered title imo, as they are taking Capcom's route in making a competitive esports tour involving numerous tournament appearances.
TL;DR:
Pros:
- Online matchmaking
-Character customization
-The main story is interesting compared to previous titles.
-Can watch movies of previous titles and view artwork.
Cons:
-Lack of various offline game modes.
-Very short episodic stories of non-Mishima Characters.
-Shin Akuma is cheap as hell (but if you played SF or CVS games, you knew that)

First off, I would love to mention that this is my first time playing Tekken.... EVER.
In fact, it is really rare for me to even play fighting games since I tend to button mash and get bored quite frequently with no motivation to learn combos and my character. Other than Smash 4, I have never felt inclined to continue to play a fighting game. As of this review I have currently clocked in around 15 hours worth of Tekken 7, most of which has been practicing and getting destroyed on quick match online play. I have slowly started to understand the basics of play, and how characters and fighting in general works in this game.
Like many other 3D fighter games, it is very difficult to just jump right in and play. Most of the enjoyment come from strategically demolishing your enemy with various combos that took hours upon hours to practice. One must really put in some time to understand the mechanics of the game and their character to find more enjoyment out of this game. This is a great game, a great PC port, and to my suprise, very very fun! I never imagined I would enjoy a 3D fighter after giving up on many 2D fighters but I did. In addition I recently purchased a beginner arcade stick off amazon called the Qanba Drone, seems solid for the price of around 75 USD. Install - Took me ages, around 36Gb from start to finish. There are updates at around the 10Gb mark approximately once a month, and more frequent updates of a few hundred Mb. Seems strange considering the launch title is only 3.6Gb or something. So if you've got a slow connection, you may be waiting a while
Game - Framerate can be a bit strange during cut-scenes and the opening sequences of fights, reaching about 15-20fps at times, but that generally clears up, and is not present later even during intensive particle showers etc.
Story - Yeah. Good.
Online - For me, not good. I've played about 30 games online, and about 27 of them have been against Scorpion. This wouldn't normally be a problem, as you can just learn defence against one character, but it's practically unplayable with the crippling lag I get. A good second between button press and actual movement means I can only really hold my own against an opponent who doesn't know he's playing, or one with worst lag issues than mine. That being said, when you find that one match in one hundred without lag problems, it can be quite enjoyable. As long as you aren't on the recieving end of the abuse of scorpions teleport.
Msc - Good roster of characters, missing some of the origional (Don't hate me for this, but I wanted to see some Meat. He was awesome), all of which have a pretty good list of combos. At first though you might think a character has fewer combos than other characters, e.g. Shinook has one page, where Kenshi and others have nearer two, but 'very hard' practise mode against Shinook should give you an idea of the combos that are still possible with that reduced list...
Would recommend in spite of the online problems, it's well made (apart from online), and I haven't had any hard crashes outside online, and when you nail the AI on hard, it's rewarding. The Krypt is also quite amusing, just turn your volume down - those goddamn spiders aren't scary, they just come at you with a thousand decibels behind them...

As my frien put it, "I would happily spend $100 on GTA with all the content is has now." And so would I.
Modding a game for the most part is almost entirely benefitial to the game. You've seen it with Bethesda titles such as Skyrim and Fallout, and was very true for even GTA VI. Modding allows for communities to form and interact with one another to find ways to make a game even better. It's a passion and it takes hard work and dedication to create custom content for the games we already love. We do it not to insult the creators, but to make our own stories and discover our own artistic interests. If the creators of a game refuses to improve their games, then the community will. Plain and simple.
Games such as GTA V that are more susceptible to alterations and modifications only entice players to jump on the creative train and take their shot at making something wonderful. If the game one makes is easily manipulated, then one cannot complain that people take advantage of it. It's better to encourage modding than to spend thousands of dollars to prevent it, something Rockstar clearly has not done. There will always be someone willing to change the code and enter a section of the game's engine that was never inteded to be breached.
Singleplayer is a portion of ther game entirely different from its multiplayer countrpart. Taking away modding from a singleplayer game serves absolutely no purpose and should never be done. That's why people mod singleplayer sections of game, to not ruin the multiplayer experience.
Take Two, this was a huge mistake and it should be considered fraud. Thousands of players have purchased GTA V multiple times, and you should have no right to ban players based on your
of cheating. People who have spent $180 on your game should not be banned because of a flaw in your game design. No one asked you to create a currency in your game, and no one said you had to create free DLC. You could have simply left the game alone and let the communty imprive it. Banning players for singleplayer modding is a great way to kill a game you spent millions on developing. Stop acting like you're underpayed and underappreciated. These reviews should have been the first thing you thought about when making this decision.
Modding is an art form, it's the same reason people become game developers. You can't just hinder someone's want for creativity. Next time think with your brain instead of your wallet.

The town of South Park is much bigger now, there's more characters, deeper/better combat, the RPG system is more robust and deep, the writing and humor is noticeably funnier (and offensive for even a South Park episode). There's also much more combat now than SOT, it just happens more frequently,  it's a good thing.  And the mini-bosses are hilarious.

Brothers - A Cool Game Mechanic Spoiled by a Disturbing Story.
Recommend the game if you like morally ambiguous or cathartic texts (The Punisher, Death of a Salesman, etc.)
Do not recommend if you like to feel good after a game.
Two brothers try to help their ailing father, and they end up on an adventure which traverses a vast and magical world.  The game is set apart by the emotional depth of the brothers' relationship as well as an unusual game mechanic.  Prior to beginning their adventure, the game specifically prompts players to use a controller.   This is because both brothers are simultaneously playable, one with the left joystick, the other with the right.  By forcing the player to guide both brothers together through every event, the game further develops the bond between brothers through gameplay.  In other words, this mechanic enhances the game's storytelling.  The puzzles within the game also match this singular control scheme.  In combination, these aspects drive fun gameplay while drawing the player deeper into the author's story.
Remember how I said the mechanic was spoiled by that story?  A disturbing story that leaves you wondering whether you really should have tried to help these two brothers.  (Possible spoilers?)  Here is a summary of the game:  Two brothers take their dad to a doctor, release an attack hound on a little boy, steal toys from children, trample a senior citizen's flowers, torture animals, break prisoners out of jail, run from wolves, go white-water rafting, go hang-gliding, enslave animals they steal from a veterinarian, work said animals to death, mutilate corpses, bathe in blood, mutilate corpses, bathe in blood again, pretend to be god, release a monster onto a village, run from whales, mutilate more corpses, torture a bug, finish the story.  Oh, did I mention that they mutilate corpses?  Needless to say, I felt ashamed of my actions by the end of the game.  If you believe the ends justify the means, you should enjoy how the gameplay complements the storyline.  However, I, in the end, just felt mean.

I've played this game before it was launched, when there was only the demo back 2 years ago and I don't remember why it didn't convinced me. It was probably the price, or maybe that I didn't hang off Skyrim, but on a sale I say it's absolutely worth it. I've played like 10 hours or so and I've been gratefully surprised. I've read some reviews and comments bashing about the combat system but it isn't bad at all. Yes, only 3 spec trees, but as you skill up those trees you'll be given fates that will make your character really unique. So, in my opinion, the game is a mix between the Batman titles (has the agility of combat), Dragon Age (talents, specs and lore) Skyrim (the feeling of freedom/sandbox) and Diablo (the loot), this mix is, at least for me, a really good combination to renew the genre.

So I bought this game a few months ago, not expecting much.  Honestly, I was expecting it to be one of those games I play for a couple of days and then lose interest in.  I was very wrong on that account.  This is actually one of the best, if not the best, RPGs that I have ever played.  There were a few cons of course, but I will get to that in a little bit.
Because The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion was the last RPG I played before this game, I could not help but to make comparisons during my entire time playing this.  In terms of graphics, I found Amalur to be far superior than Oblivion.  When you are walking in caves and you see all of the flora just come to life as you walk past, it is just captivating.
In terms of story line, I would say that they are about equal, but then again, I have not gotten all that far in Oblivion's storyline (I spend most of my time doing the side quests, build my character up some for the really tough bosses).  If I compared Amalur to Morrowind however, I would pick Amalur's storyline anytime.  Because unlike Morrowind, in which the storyline has you do all of these tasks to the point that it feels crazy, Amalur is fairly straightforward.
Voice-acting, I don't really care for.  But from what I can tell, the voice of the characters in Amalur tends to have this almost...ghostly quality?  Almost like you are hearing someone in another room rather than them talking right next to you.  I guess you will either love it or hate, but for me?  I was indifferent.
There are plenty of side quests to take part in, just like in Oblivion.  Like Oblivion, you can take part in faction quests.  Like if you want to be the head of a Mage's guild in Oblivion, then you can do the same for Amalur.  However, while it it can take a few days or so to finish a faction quest in Oblivion, you can knock them out in Amalur in like, a day because the quests are so much easier and there are fewer actual quests to complete for the faction.
There is a huge variety of character customization.  Do you want to play a male or female character?  Go ahead.  Do you want to play as an Elf or a Human?  Go ahead.  If memory serves me right, then I think there are four races to select in Amalur, but the building of the skill-set does not occur until you actually start game play.  Like you do not decide immediately if you want to make your character a mage.  You can decide where you want to place your character's skill alignment later on and even then, you are fully able to go back and change your character's style whenever you want.  If you decide you want a hammer wielding mage, but decide later that you want to have a magic wielding thief or warrior, then you can do that.
I guess now I can get into the overall pro's and con's.
Pro's
-Absolutely amazing graphics
- Wide skill-set available
-You can change your skill-set whenever you want with no consequences other than what your character can or cannot wear or what they can do in combat.
-Game play tends to be fluid and smooth, particularly with the combat.  You can dodge-roll or teleport out of the way of an attack and the game is not in first-person so you can see more.   I will get to con's later
-Once the main storyline is complete, you can still continue on side-quests
-Items will not weigh more than others.  While some weapons will impact attack speed, they will still only occupy one item slot in your backpack.  For example, your hammer, while slower in combat than your daggers, will still occupy the same space in your backpack as the daggers.
-There is a hide-helmet option so that even if your character wears a hood or helmet, you will not see it in game play yet you will still have the effects.  I personally loved this feature.
-Easier than Oblivion, but the boss fights can still crush you if you are not ready
-Good enough that it deserves a sequel
-My overall verdict?  I enjoy this game way more than Oblivion.
Con's
-Camera angles tend to lag every once in a while, to the point where you might have difficulty seeing an enemy
-Character may freeze while running.  As in your character will just stop moving while running.  This can be overcome by rolling or teleporting, but it can be troublesome to freeze in the middle of a fight.  Also, this freezing will occur A LOT, and as such you will be rolling or teleporting almost all the time.  It took a couple of days for this to occur to me though.
-Voice-acting is so-so.
-From what I have heard, you can only reach level 41.  That is it.  But you can still reset your skill points later on.  Keep in mind though that this means you will not be able to completely max out all skills and abilities.
-I have had difficulty completing a side-quest because every time I try, the game shuts down.  I do need to give it another try though.
-Last I checked, the company that developed this game went bankrupt.  So do not expect a sequel or any patches.
Overall, I say check this out.  I got it for $9.99 and this game was most definitely worth the price.  It is fun, beautiful, and the ability to change your skill-set helps to take away the pressure of having to stick with one field.

How would I sum this game up ? Mediocrity at it's best. I mean the game is fine, it has all the necessary things for an action RPG, but the thing is you never get lost in it, the game doesn't suck you in as other games in this genre do. I just didn't feel that pull to return to the game, to find out what happens next.
I've played a few action RPGs - Mass Effect 1-3, Witcher 1,2, Fallout 3, Fallout New Vegas, TES: Oblivion, Skyrim and all of them made a much better impression on me.
The strange part is I can't actually point to one single thing that is wrong or broken in this game. I said it in the beginning - it's an ok game. But maybe that's it's downfall - it's just ok, it's kind of bland, nothing that stands out. It ticks all of the boxes for an RPG but never excels in any of them.
It's a forgetible experience for me and I jumped to other games very quickly. Compare that to my 100+ hours in each of the Fallout games and you can see the difference.
So would I recommend this game ? Well it depends. If you're a seasoned RPG player, then I'd say skip this game. It just doesn't have anything to offer that you haven't already experienced in other games in this genre. If you the type that absolutely has to play all RPGs out there, consider this game only if it is on sale.
Now, for someona who is only starting his adventure with RPGs, I think this game might be a good starting point. It has all the basic mechanics in it, it will introduce you to the concept of open world games and it will only get better once you move on to other, better titles.
I myself might pick it back up some time down the road, or maybe not. Right now there are more fun games in my catalog waiting to be palyed.

Good old-school Action/RPG
PROs
- Huge world: it is a MMO turned Single Player, so you get huge areas and countless quest hubs
- Class system allows lots and lots of different Character builds
- Fast travel to avoid running too much around
- Longevity: 60-70 hours needed to complete it
- DLCs are worth the money (do not forget it is EA!)
- Awesome actions/skills
- Crafting allows a lot of customization of gear
CONs
- Repetitive dungeon design: after you have visited 5, you've seen them all
- Recycled enemy design: same mobs in all areas
- Too many sidequests: you will end up overlevelled pretty soon
- Main quest is quite boring, expected better from R.A. Salvatore
- Too many item drops vs. small inventory = lots of travelling to sell trash
- Menu design

A masterpiece. Really, there is not a thing I do not like about Hell's Highway. Well, actually, there is one: The story won't continue and that's something I just can't get over. But let's be professional here.
This is one hell of a fantastic shooter. You continue in the story of Sgt. Matt Baker a paratrooper of 101st Airborne Division. He and his men have already gone through hell in Normandy and now there is another one ahead of them: Operation Market Garden.
is fantastic, controls are easy to learn and handle. 3rd person view, utilizing a cover and issuing orders for squads under your command. Game will quickly teach you how to use tactical manouvering and suppresive fire. Forget Call of Duty, you are no supersoldier who can take out whole garrison single-handed. No. You need to rain lead down on your enemy, so they won't dare to stick their heads up. Once they are pinned, you can outflank them and finnish from the side. Especially on higher difficuilties, the game require you to think tactically. That's what I like most.
is one of best I ever encountered. Characters are unique, while still remain ordinary troops. No stereotypes like e.g. psycho gunner, excellent sharpshooter, and demolition guy. No, no. Brothers in Arms is all about grunts, ordinary soldiers. It's about their feels, their stories. Many of your soldiers have their own backstory (sometimes linked to previeous installments in the series), they have a different level of relationship with Sgt. Baker. Some would go to fire for him, others are questioning his ability to lead them. New guys who want to prove themselves, old friends, loyal to the end. Each with great voice-acting. Warning: there will be emotions. Thanks to excellent animation of facial expressions, you can read thoughts of your men to the point, where you will truly be part of the story. You will mourn the fallen comrade, you will mourn dead civilians. Their blood will be on your hands and altough there are no choices in this game, you will feel responsible for some of your actions nonetheless. Story is something, which make this game a real gem of WWII shooters.
And here we are - the thing I don't like. After Market Garden, there was yet another hell awaiting for paratroopers of 101st and 82nd Airborne Division. The snowy, freezing hell of Ardenne forest. Yes, Battle of the Bulge, it was supposed to be a cap stone of the story of Matt Baker and his soldiers. In the end of Hell's Highway, there is a rift, there are emotions and there are questions unanswered. I want to know how will it all end. After all, Matt made it through hell. I wonder how he would handle snow. But game devolopers will never answer my prayers...
Anyway, this is a game I recommend to any and all who like historicaly acurate WWII shooters, who like great story and who like to think tactically and feel the war as a soldier, not some god-like spec op superman.
