Horrible, repetitive, broken piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥
There is no "simulation" here. Just click away and pay attention to arrows on the screen. If you ride a horse, an enemy will bloxk you even if they are in the middle of the battle turned with their backs towards you. They will pull out a shield in the last second and your lance will miraculously bounce off of it. it's also possible to stop the momentum of a full galloping warhorse and a knight with a lance by using only a small knife. Apparently, a passive block with polearm against a b@stard sword will not break it, since weapons are made of titanium alloy, even the wood ones.
The AI cheats. There is no such thing as realism in this "game". Try shooting in the foot of a warrior or his head, and his shield takes the arrow to the centre. Try to ride miles away from the enemy troops and get a spear in the head whilst galloping full speed on a horse. The enemies are either whalers with 120 years of experience, or athletic champions. I did not ask for Medieval Matrix.
But hey, if you happen to shoot a bow from 10 miles away you will hit someone's head, killing them instantly. Which is completely realistic, not. I have done archery and I have credentials to prove it and it's impossible to hit a small target consequtively in the same spot that is more than 150 meters away, especially with medieval longbow, That just doesn't happen.
No matter how good your troops are - most engagements you are either doing nothing or you are fighting alone. And since you don't have the money to actually support large amounts of troops, or that money comes with tons and tons of repetitive grinding (which is so borning, it made my eyes bleed) - you fight mostly by yourself. The enemy generals will destroy any force of elite men you have, and it will take you days to bring it back to the same standard just to see it completely obliterated again.
The game lives on by itself, but not in a good sense. Things happen around you for no rhyme or reason, one lord hates your guts, then suddenly he likes you. Your fife can get raded 10 times in a row whilst all the other villages in its vicinity are untouched or not be touched at all, the village you own could go from prosperous to poor in a day and you'd have no clue why it happened.
Castle sieges are a thing of legend. Since 50% of the game is spent laying sieges, it's what you will be doing quite often. this is how it goes:
1. Lay siege
2. Tell your troops to stand back
3. Spend three hours shooting the men on walls and colleting their arrows
4. Storm the last 4 guys with your 75 men
If you dare assault the castle walls with your elite army against 30 peasants, you will be a witness to rain of men and women, falling dead from its walls because apparently they can't swing a word to save their life.
The game suffers from unecessary complex design in some parts and unforgivably simplisitc decisions by game devs in other areas. For example, when you auot-resolve a battle, the troop quality is not taken into account. This is very easily remedied by changing the mathematical formula and adding values to the troops depending on their strength. But no. The game takes the number of troops, subtracts it from the number of the enemies, then multiplies it by god knows what randomness factor. Let me just tell you: if you auto-resolve - everyone dies. On your side. Yes, that army you've spent 40 real life hours building just cause some lucky forest bandit threw a spear 100 meters away taht hit you dead in the eye through a steel grand-helm.
The combat system is awkward, the gameplay is repetitive and unvaried. The mods do not change the fact that this game is outdated in every sense.
The community is half-jokers half-pseudohistorians that claim they have been fighting in Medieval times and had extensive training for decades, whilst they fail to acknowledge simple historical facts.
The arguments end up with insults, since everyone here is an agressive dilettante, and also because apprently HEMA teaches you medieval history as well and is the only agency that knows anything about anything to do with close combat weapons.
I am very sorry I bought this, even though I knew I wasn't going to like it.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a wonderful game that has little bad to it (in my eyes)
Lets start with the bad
-some animation issues can occur, while most of this didn't happen to me, I still occured a running in place motion (easly fixable with either a patch or graphics mod)
-*OPINION ALERT* I personally am not used to the leveling system, it does provide a stratagy where you can either go for more health or special, or go for better special attacks (not both) so this is more of a personal downside
Now for the overwhelming good
-Teamwork is key, meining that everyone has a role to play so the newbs and pros alike can both do the same amount of work
-The voice acting is spot on, every character speaks like they're in the acctual show
-combat is fluent, by that I mean that my gril (Ruby) isn't underpowered or overpowerd, as everyone's combat is fluent
-Story, right now, the game only has 4 chapters. All of the chapters have something new to offer, lets go in order
1st chapter - Helps you get used to the controlls and teaches you the mechanics of the game without a tutorial
2nd chapter - teaches you new enemy types and a new type of defence mode, defend to get to the next section
3rd chapter - showes more enemy types and shows where the story would take place in relation to the show
4th chapter - begins the insaine Dark Souls difficulty, lots of Grimm while trying to escort a dust powered bomb to a cavern
-Music fits in with the show!

-"you will only understand the story if you've seen the show" no dip sherlock
-"The SFX are too lowed" I never experienced this and everything sounded great for me

To start off, I've been hyped for this game since it was a simple demo done by the developer in his spare time. And it's definitely blossomed with RT's resources to help him. The combat is quick and fast-paced and you definitely lose yourself in it. I can say with complete honesty that I've enjoyed this game so far.
That being said, I do have a few gripes. Foremost of which is that I keep crashing at the start of Mountain Glenn. I thought it was just a fluke the first time, but the moment I reached the top of the small hill at the start of the level, my game crashed again (Three times and counting). I hope that this is a known bug rather than due to my hardware limitations, otherwise I'm screwed. I doubt that it's due my hardware, though, because my game played just fine in the previous two levels before crashing at the exact same spot. UPDATE: The devs provided methods for fixing this which worked marvelously for me. At first I thought it made it worse because the startup froze and I thought I would've had to restart my computer, but I managed to close it out and the second startup worked like a charm. I'm now able to complete Mountain Glenn.
There's no tutorial, but there is a control map...that's only accessible in game. Seems kinda foolish to require people to jump into a game before being able to see what the controls are.
A manual lock on would be appreciated. Unless there already is a manual lock on and I just don't know about it because there's no tutorial or control map. In which case I would appreciate someone pointing it out to me.
Some smaller gripes are that the Aura recharge sound is kinda dumb. Yeah, I get it, Rooster Teeth started with Halo so the recharge sound is kind of an homage, but it's still pretty dumb. The sound effects stay at the same volume. You can lower music and voice, but all the sound effects (of which there are a lot of happening at any given moment) remain level. The walk cycles are pretty rough. And finally, an in-game voice chat function for Quick Games would be cool. UPDATE: There's now an SFX slider which is great.
UPDATE: Ruby is OP as hell. If you want to steal everyone's kills and make it to Level 10 long before everyone else, pick Ruby and shovel points into the Crescendo skill tree. Insta-gib entire hordes and free yourself up to dash in and steal kills.
Which brings me to my next point, EXP sharing would be nice. As it is, there's hardly any incentive to work together (except for the Flawless bonus, but it's only worth a measly 50 EXP per horde wave). Just share a percentage of your kill with teammates so everyone isn't rushing to get the most kills.
Bottom line: For $15, I'd say this game is fairly than worth it. It's still in Early Access, so I'm not miffed about all the issues. Hopefully they're resolved or otherwise explained.

NOTE: This is a review which is basing the game on its own merits, not upon the expectations forged from its predecessor. I've heard many things about the first GunZ, the good and the bad, but have never played it. Along with this, the game's only in beta, so I can only assume that MAIET will improve on where it's lacking during this phase.
From a free to play third person shooter, there are a few things that we may expect. A super-quick run-and-gun with flashiness abound from every corner. A grand selection of characters and weaponry to suit our style of play. Maybe even a few stylish maneuvers to truly show who can walk the walk and who falls flat on their face. Quite a few games have done this for me, but none on Steam. Unfortunately, GunZ 2 doesn't seem to have this pat down yet.
The first screen I'm given once I could finally get a spot in the game was a choice between four characters. They all seemed different in their own ways, making choices between a katana-wielding sniper, a small arms specialist with dual daggers, an assault-based gunner with a bat in tow, and a hulking minigunner with his own shield as his melee weapon of choice. I was originally set on choosing the first character, feeling it would be a good start for beginners. However, this leads to the game telling me I could only have one character, needing to pay for the other three if I wanted them (thankfully with in-game gold). A bit of a hassle, but something I could've expected from a free to play game. Unfortunately, what I didn't expect was the inability to switch to weapons on other characters, locking you with what you have until you could purchase another character, which would lock you with the weapons on THAT character when you decide to play as them. The potential for variety does exist, but not at this particular point.
Upon running through the tutorial, I tried to experience all of the potential speed that this game had to offer. This involved a double-tap in any of the four major directions, as well as a vertical or horizontal wall run. Ground dashes and air dashes seemed like the most it could offer for mobility, and although it was exhilarating the first ten times or so that I dashed, I found out that I would have to keep this constant state of mad tapping for at least ten minutes at a time, assuming the fifteen minute timer on the top of the screen was true. Not only would this be a strain on whatever key I'd be mashing, it would also inevitably be a strain on my tapping hand as well. The worse part of this is that when I compared dashing to simple walking, there really didn't seem to be much of a difference. Perhaps it would be useful to get away from a closing melee strike or maybe fool around with an enemy sniper, but strafing just feels like the better choice with less effort needed. Apart from that, it seemed that movement was slow and clunky, and melee combos feel like they lock you down on the ground if you try to do anything fancy. Bullet guns do bullet things and that's fine by me.
Now I was offered two choices in terms of play: either multiplayer, going man to man against others, or a campaign mode with some semblance of a story. I decided to try the campaign first, thinking that I should probably hone my skills before I jump into the fray. The result of this was essentially a shooting gallery of enemies, the ranged ones staying back and the melee ones running a straight course to cleave you. To my surprise, the sniper rifle of the first character pierced through several enemies at once and it gave me a good chuckle, but I was eventually overwhelmed due to inexperience and the expectation that melee would be useful against them (it wasn't). I ended up playing a few matches of the multiplayer modes afterward and the result was interesting. Movement seemed a bit erratic at times and although melee was powerful, it usually left anyone who used it being shot. Along with that, connection issues made this even worse with some players juking in unusual ways in combination with the dashing and others straight-up teleporting. I decided to leave this for another time and look at the other options I had.
Customization is what you could expect of it. There were several outfits for each character and various guns that had increased strength in comparison to what guns you're initially equipped with, all of which can be bought with gold. Along with these were costume pieces that you could purchase with real money. I didn't pay much attention to the particular things that the cash items might give, but it was understandable to me that you would have to spend quite a while grinding up gold to purchase the items you would want. Along with the customizing, there was also the ability to create certain upgraded weapons with materials. It was unknown to me from the start how to obtain them, possibly from leveling, the campaign mode, or with some real money usage, but after looking at that, I decided to leave the game for the time being.
In summary, GunZ 2: The Second Duel is currently at a disappointing state. Somewhat clunky movement, connection issues popping back up every now and again, the gold pay for matches played feels lower that it should be, and the inevitable wait on the title screen for a slot to be found in the servers makes this an unappealing game, even with its Early Access tag. I can only hope that MAIET makes improvements for this game soon so it can reach a more playable and fun state, but until then, this just isn't a game I would want to spend my time on.

There's usually issues with any sort of crossover to PC game, but this has handled wonderfully on my system (which is by no means a top of the line build) and I didn't have to adjust the graphics down to be able to play comfortably.
Just buy it. At times it can seem a little bit childish or PG but it's never long before something jumps out at me and scares my pants off. You really won't be disapointed by this.

Aside from the striking visuals, it's hard to recommend this game. It's too easy and obvious for adults and way too hopeless and violent for kids. The action/puzzle/platformer set pieces are straightforward and contrived, the narrative is razor thin, and the payoff at then end is limited. The controls are somewhat clumsy (but functional) on a controller, but virtually unplayable on a keyboard.
I'll give it a 6/10. Play it if you're curious but by no means treat this game as a must-own.

Lately, after playing quite a few hours and enjoying the game, I looked through reviews to see what others thought and found a number of things from the negative sections that seemed a bit off to me. While some people gave valid points to issues in it, I think there are several things that people complain about that aren't really all that valid, and have decided to make my own review because of it. Lets get to the bad stuff first.
Cons:
- Subtitles need some work
- No difficulty adjustment for replaying levels
- A few graphical and audio glitches here and there
- Some work needed on blocking off areas you aren't supposed to be in
These were the main things that come to mind for me. Some people have listed other things that I quite frankly don't think need to be on the list. First one is the price tag. Is the game in it's currents state worth $15? No, but it's early access. I feel like people see early access and think of something like Day Z. That game in it's current state is worth what is charged to most people. Problem is that game has been in early access for years. There are other games like it that are at the end of the early access games, and some that just stay there but are pretty much done but use it to say that they periodically add large content patches like Minecraft does. This game, as of the time of this review, has just hit early access, and RT is fully taking advantage of the title. This game is far from a finished product and you slapping down the $15 is kinda like a donation with benefits really. You give them money so they can keep making the game, they give you access to it while it's in developement and can give feedback. If you want a polished, complete game worth $15, don't get it. If you want to support the concept and idea of the game, or RT in general, pick it up. There are also complaints about combat being too repetative, but I feel like unlocking the challange perks and remebering the blast attacks adds more than people give it credit for. More variation is not something I would be opposed to, but at this point I don't think the combat deserves such a bad rap from people. Also, people don't seem to like levels not carrying over. The thing is, with this type of game that just wouldn't work. If I hit level ten then rerun from the beginning, I'm gonna be destroying everything no problem. Add that to the fact that I wouldn't be able to get anymore perks since I'm at the level cap and couldn't expiriment with new skills, and you see that it just doesn't work. As long as they find a good way to keep levels going when they add more levels and content, this system works just fine. Lastly, I've seen complaints that swarms of enemies keep you from combing too easily with attacks that can't be intterupted. Personally, I havn't had a problem with this after my first playthrough. I won't go into details as this is long enough already, but teamates are there for a reason and so are evades. Use them right and you should be fine.
Now to the good things.
Pros:
- Well voice acted
- Great art design and character models
- Interesting abilities and a nice leveling system
- Characters keep their personalities from the show
- Alternate paths and challanges give some level of replayability.
- Interesting enemies with variation
I can't say much to the plot since it isn't very developed so far, but I think it looks good for now. We won't realy know until more comes out. Hopefully this sheds some light on the game for everyone, along with why some of the cons really aren't cons.
Final verdict, get it if you like the idea of the game and want to support it or RT, as it is fun so far and has great groundwork, but don't expect a huge amount of content until later in development. Happy hunting!

So, to start. My pseudo-review will be very very biased. I've been watching the show since day one and I can tell you right now if you like the show then buy this game. It's... euphoric being able to play as the titular characters of such a well made series such as this. Also to point out, I am by no means a reviewer. Just some guy with a keyboard who likes to think he knows what he's talking about.
In regards to the game, I have a few gripes and suggestions.
Overall the game is well made, and as it is in Early Access, good things are yet to come. The combat is tight, the story - what we know so far - seems intriguing and the characters are who we know and love from the show that many of us have been watching for years.
That all being said, the complaints.
- The fast paced nature of the combat leads it to feeling very floaty. There is no so called "meat" to the fighting, and while as a spectacle to watch it's very enjoyable, playing it feels like I'm fighting air for the most part. If there was more weight to the combat than the game would have been a perfect 10, but as it stands it needs some improvement.
- The talent trees are weak. Bearing in mind the game is in Early Access this is easily forgivable so long as they work on them soon. However the progression system is one that I appreciate greatly, as playing Ruby for 3 hours didn't end up just being a total waste of time, and I was able to unlock - subjectively - cool new abilities fairly rapidly.
- The last and largest complaint I have about the game is the in-match levelling system. The problem with this is fairly substantial. The problem, in short is that of the rich getting richer while the poor stay poor. What I mean by this is if you have an ability that does a large amount of aoe damage - Crescendo for example - and you stand in a cluster of enemies and use that ability two or three times in a row, you're going to kill all of the enemies, and if it's a wave based event, you're likely to get the MVP bonus. The problem with this is that the person who did the most work is being fairly rewarded, sure, but the other players on your team are then losing experience that was availble to them. It also perpetuates this cycle of you killed the most things, resulting in the most experience. That Experience allows you more upgrades than your team. Those upgrades generally increase the ease of which you kill things. Thus giving you more ways to gain more xp. Once you reach level 10 all the xp you're gaining is wasted and your teammates are just flat out losing the xp that they should be obtaining. This means that by the time you're done chapter one, if you've hit level 10 on the third mission - which is really rather easy - then your teammates may not get to cap at all, which is distressing because the cap allows for a really cool ability.
-As for suggestions, the first two complaints are likely to be fixed during the early access program. The last also has an easy solution - more levels, and shared xp. Instead of giving the whole amount of xp to the person who got the killing blow, givem them 50%-100% increase and give the others a flat rate. So if I fought an Ursa, and landed the killing blow, if I get 60xp give my team 30. For the Grimm that award only 5 this could be ignored but for the ones giving 15 and up there should be some padding for the team. More levels would also aid this so that the xp that you are gaining isn't just going into the void, and your team can actually benefit from you killing things after capping.
As it stands the game right now is a 7.5/10 and should probably be avoided for the most part by non-RWBY fans - unless you're looking for a MOBA style spectacle fighter. Which in hindsight makes no sense but if you've played the game you'll understand.

A great action adventure role-playing game with a vast open world to explore and many quests to complete. Plenty of skill trees to try out and crafting to do, from potions to blacksmithing to enchantment. Suffers from clunky interface and at times it can feel grindy. All the characters are however, well voice acted and can bring a lot of life to the game. Finally, all cutscenes (and dialogue) are skippable. So yay to that. Worth purchasing during the sale, at $10 for base + all DLC.
Perhaps the greatest cons that are holding this game back in my opinion, is the very clunky interface when it comes to inventory and quest management. Instead of pressing, say, "I" to open up an inventory screen, you have to press ESC to go to the menu and access your inventory from there. You can also only track one quest at a time, and can only view other quests on your local map provided that you're in the correct zone (this took a bit to figure out, but once it was figured out the single-quest tracking no longer posed a problem). Any other quests outside of your zone will not show up on your minimap. The game also has lots of loading screens, though they are rarely more than 10 seconds each, split between instances and interior / exterior transitions.
The game's combat can be very fun, a hack and slash sort of feel, with contextual 'moves' to use (i.e. pausing just before a second attack and you will launch enemies into the air) and the variety of skills to invest into can really mix up the gameplay. There's also a fate meter, which is essentially an execution bar where you go into a rage and deal extra damage whilst everything around you moves in slow motion, then you can execute enemies which kills all 'knocked down' enemies around you, whilst granting you bonus XP. You have your wizard, rogue and warrior skill tree. You have two weapon slots to quickly switch between as well as a 1-9 spell slot (casted by right clicking). The control might feel a bit console-like at first, but it's no where near as bad of a port as some other games have been (i.e. dark souls). Simply put, very playable. The graphics also look aesthetically pleasing, no real complaints.
There's a lack of "open world" things to do beyond questing and hunting mobs, though there is more than enough dialogue to fill in each city / town / hub as well as letters and books to collect.
A revamped interface (as in, an actual in-game UI inventory screen, quest tracker and similar, would be significantly more palatable than its current clunky interface) and the addition of a few mounts could really improve this game.
Probably an 8/10. Definitely should pick this up during the sale (currently at 10$ for base game + all the DLC, which are worth the money).

So heres a general overview: you start with character creation. you choose what you/your familys backround is, and that decides your starting stats, gear, wealth, and renown. important things, so choose wisely. I prefer a balanced start. So maybe my father was a smith, and I was a trader growing up, but i had a lust for money and power to leave. So from there, you choose your first additional skills. these are vital. you have a lot of choices for character customization. skills ranging from strength and agility, so like hp, damage, run speed, looting abilities, etc to intelligence and charisma so like extra inventory, prisoner management and leadership to allow you to hire troops and take prisoners of war to sell for money.
So you've choosen what you like, maybe a warrior, or a bowmen, trader, or scout. You open up to the campaign map. This is where you can see all of calradia, and how you go from place to place. You select a destination, and while you travel or sleep, the world around you evolves. this is one of the coolest parts. the AI kingdoms, bandits, caravans, peasants, etc will all fight, trade, make peace, etc and over time, you may see entire kingdoms wiped out. Lords of factions will change sides, mutiny, etc.
So now its up to you to make a difference! you decide how! There is plenty of tasks/missions/quests to perform. Kings, Lords, GuildMasters in towns, village elders in villages, and random people in the taverns will have work available to you. from delivering letters and wine, to hunting down bandits and persuading high ranking lords. Or ignore everyone. Just hunt down bandits and sea raiders, they are enemies to everyone except themselves so you can pile their bodies as high as you'd like, or keep them alive and sell them for extra cash. One of the nice parts of warband is with a positive relation with a town, its owner, and its guildmaster, you can invest in a business with the guildmaster with your "denars" aka money. this will provide weekly income based on the areas trade. you can even micro manage it, lets say you have a workshop to make tools with iron, but in that city it costs 200 denars for the iron, but by buying it a city over, you can get the iron for 100 denars each. so you take the cheaper iron and give it to your workshop, and now you're making more money off of your product. once you have enough of these going, you can fuel yourself and a small army and still make a profit. Dont worry about the city/settlement being taken over by another faction either, they make money off you so they want your business either way.
Which brings us to the bulk of/end game. So everything you do has long lasting effects in the game. Even if you just kill some bandits, recovering lords use small bandit parties as a way to make-up for big losses. They can train up veteran troops and make some cash. Raid some ones caravan for example. Alot is a stake here. So you obviously have to fight the troops, which can easily go wrong if you arent prepared. Then you get some loot, which is nice. But thats not the end. So both settlements, the one it came from and the one it was going to, just lost out on profit from those items they were trading. The one the caravan belongs to, is actually super♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you, cuz not only did you kill a bunch of men they had hired and paid for, but you essentially set yourself up for war. You have relations you can view with HUD and menus with Factions, Kings, Lords, Ladies, Settlements, and Villages. Almost everyone has a relation bar, but most of them dont matter except those big ones I listed.
So you could gain relations with a faction, and join them. Just by doing quests for the king and gaining the smallest relation, just a few missions, you have a chance for them to randomely offer you vassalage and a fief. Meaning you would be a lord and own a village that you can collect taxes on, upgrade, defend, recruit from, etc. The drawbacks and benefits are mostly obvious. So now you make money off this village, have high relation with it to get lots of recruits/better recruits, and have protection from a large faction. On the down side, your faction may at any point call on you for war, start a multi-front war no one could win, or your enemies may come and raze and loot your village while you are away.
Or you could just take one your self. The average castle has around 150-250 defenders plus whatever lord(s) parties from that faction decide to show up. You unfortunately can't just take a single village for yourself. You can steal cattle or loot and raise them, but in order to collect taxes and control them, you need to take either a castle or town/settlement. This is one of the funnest but also most difficult parts of the game. Seiges.

Brothers- A Tale of two sons is a 3D platformer developed by starbreeze studios.
The story is simple, yet it is conveyed perfectly. You play as two brothers who are tasked to retrieve some medicine for their sick dying father. In order to do so, they will have to cross giant bridges, bloody graveyards, giant oceans and meet a variety of colourful characters. Through out the story you will feel a variety of emotions including joy, happiness, wonder, fear, amazement and sadness. There is no voice acting in the game, and honestly there doesn't need to be as you can understand what the characters are saying through their actions.
The game will last you 3 hours or a bit more if you want to collect all achievements and explore a bit. There isn't much replayability to be had here.
Gameplay revolves around a mix between platforming and puzzle solving. Bearing in mind that you NEED A CONTROLLER to play this game, the controls are quite good. You control the movement of one brother with the left analogue stick and another with the right stick. It might seem tricky at first, trying to control both the brothers at the same time, but after a while you will get the hang of it.
The graphics are cartoony and good to look at. The lighting does a great job at making the colours more attractive to the eye. There are also p[enty of scenes that look so good that you want to take  screenshot of as well.
I highly recommend this game to people you want to a rememberable adventure with a few platforming and puzzles thrown in.

The building system is pretty basic block placing with multiple variants and furniture you can add to your buildings. This makes it more simplistic while still retaining the enjoyment of building an epic building,fort,bunker, town of your very own. There are many several world island types. I would definitely recommend to any fan who enjoys being dropped off in a strange world and building yourself up from nothing.

Really good base for what could eventually be one of my favorite games ever.  While I also would've really liked a turn-based RPG approach, a hack n slash is definitely the best way to transition RWBY into a video game.
Characters -
The characters themselves need to be worked on a lot more. They have a bit of a samey feel from one another, and it's not like you don't have a lot of things you could do for each of them to make them unique from one another. The upgrade tree could definitely go more in-depth and allow you to truly customize the way you play. Ranging from max aura, aura recharge, movement speed, attack speed, max special meter, increased special meter gain, and more. I really like what they're currently doing with upgrading your special abilities, they just need to branch out a bit. I also think they should add more special abilities per character, and allow you to pick 3 of them at any time.
Also, they really need to add more dialogue. The story is pretty much nonexistent in this game, as it is currently, it just seems like its nothing but random training assignments from various mentors from Beacon with very minimal communication between the actual team members.
Once they've gotten team RWBY down, all nice and polished, they should definitely add more teams! We all know people want to see JNPR. Not really sure how they would exactly handle this. Perhaps allow the host of a lobby to select what team will be used for the current map? But that's looking a bit too far right now, let's focus on getting RWBY completely done, in my opinion.
Levels -
The game so far is really, really barebones and doesn't justify the 15$ price tag. There's just not much here. If you're buying your way into this at its current state, you should be doing it solely to provide feedback. There's a handful of levels to play through, most in which consist of defense sections with the exception of the last one, which is a modified payload mode. It definitely needs more variety from that standpoint. Having to defend every 5 minutes in each level is pretty tedious, and there's so many things you could do in exchange. Don't get me wrong, a few defense sections are okay. But they should be among a bunch of other gamemodes in order to mix things up to keep the player interested. Don't be afraid to become inspired by other games such as Warframe and TF2 in order to come up with new possible ways to make levels vary. It would be really cool to just have a level where your goal is to collect hidden artifacts, much like the beginning of Volume 1, and you have to fight the Crow and Scorpion Grimms.
It would be absolutely insane if they allowed us to do 8 player co-op, where two teams of 4 have to complete objectives in different parts of the map. Much like what went on during the first training session in RWBY Volume 1.
At the end, it is a really good base for what could become a great game. It is very, very far from it right now. I recommend it solely to people who want to provide feedback and help the game grow. But if you want your totally epic RWBY game that's finished, you'll have to wait a while for this game to make more progress.

I've been a fan of the Gunz series for quite some time, even with all the ups and downs the original Gunz had gone through. Really the only thing that drove me away from the first was the invasion of hackers, either wise I'd probably would've been playing it until this finally launched.
Let me make something clear that this game definitely has taken another route than the original Gunz template laid out. Mainly the whole "style" attributes are gone but I do believe this helped open the game up to many more players as well as bring a lot more importance onto every aspect the game has to offer, instead of just a small segment. The customization, while not currently as diverse as I'd like, has the potential for a lot of growth. Currently there are 4 classes and most of them boast weapons unique to their class. The only similarity currently is Ivan (Silent Avenger) and Rena (Shadow Dancer) sharing the same automatic weapon type (an SMG). However they all have a firearm that is unique to them as well as a melee weapon that is unique to them as well that have quite the diverse abilities for them. Rena for instance wields two short sword nodachis (the game calls them daggers for some reason) and as a result she has the longest combo both on ground and air. She is also, I believe, the fastest character in the bunch; though all of them are pretty quick. While on the other hand you have Max, who wields a giant melee shield into battle. This shield may be a bit slow and boasting a low combo count, but it certainly hurts to get hit with. Not to mention he has the only block that completely protects against most firearms. His trade off is being one of the slowest classes and also having a pretty short reach with his firearms, though you can get some lucky shots with the minigun.
But I do like that each character is now unique. In the original Gunz, there were several classes to choose from but I never really noticed any difference between them besides what weapons they started off with (which could all be changed to whatever you wanted later on). Now I mentioned customization is a bit lax atm as all the classes are pretty much restricted to their own weaponry currently. I don't know if they plan to allow mixing up weapons later on or keeping them restricted to help make the classes stand out, we'll just have to see where it goes.
Now the only major drawback to this game so far has been on the server side of things. Unfortunately it is quite a bit difficult getting into the game (with the low server capacity cap, currently only 4500). However another server side issue is the downside to peer to peer network. Unfortunately lag plays a huge factor when it comes to fast paced games and even with a strong connection, you can end up with a nasty lag situation all depending on who the host is. There aren't really any official servers people play on but more so user hosted matches. This ultimately can lead to many instances where some players can connect just fine but others have horrible connections or spike all over the place, simply because of the distance to the current host. Now the host can be changed via an option to help mitigate this issue, but unfortunately you're still at the mercy of whoever is in the room. While someone's own internet may be pretty good, that doesn't necessarily make them ideal hosts. Not to mention that the more people trying to connect to one game, the worse a lag situation can get. I discovered this issue playing Tenchu Z on the Xbox 360. The multiplayer lag in that game increases expotentially depending on how many participants are in the group (max 4 players). At 4 players, the game is essentially unplayable for anyone but the host. However when you remove that 4th person, at 3 players the game is a lot more stable. Likewise dropping it down to 2 people, depending on who is hosting, there may be little to no lag at all. But it never mattered who was hosting or how good their connection was, the second a 4th player was involved, the match would always lag horribly.
Now the devs for Gunz 2 are working on increasing the server capacity and trying to improve their network to help make the experience much more stable for everyone but that stuff takes time. However, that is why the game is in an early-access stage (something many players tend to forget). There are many improvements to be made and stuff to add to the game to make it an amazing experience. However, Gunz 2 certainly can be an amazing title as long as it could pull its act together and remain strong, especially for a free-to-play title. Which by the way, they took a bit note from the original Gunz in how to handle the free-to-play market. There was a big divide between players who bought their gear in game and players who purchased better gear using actual currency, essentially creating a pay-to-win model. Though Gunz 2 handles this well by only having cosmetic things attached to the real currency, while every gear piece can be purchased with in game currency. Definitely an improvement and something that lets many new players come enjoy the game without feeling at a disadvantage because they don't want to make a real money investment to a game they may or may not spend a lot of time with. Now people who want to put a little cash into their characters can help make themselves stand out and feel unique, without gaining an unfair advantage over other players.

Brütal Legend is awesome and metal. Brütal Legend is also a mediocre and forgettable open world/hack & slash/strategy game. A prime example why Steam needs a “meh” button for the reviews.
Brütal Legend is a tribute to metal. Not cash-in whiny pop metal, but real, classic, early seventies, head-banging, engine-worshipping, leather-winged heavy metal. It is a temple for bands like Black Sabbath, Judas Priest, or Motörhead– just to name a few from the in-game soundtrack.
This game is so metal that its cast has such names as Jack Black as the protagonist, Rob Halford as the first main boss, and Ozzy Osbourne as the shopkeeper. This game is so metal that the entire landscape is never-ending scenery of heavy metal album covers. This game is probably as metal as metal you can get without dipping your computer in molten steel.
Brütal Legend is also incredibly mediocre. It wants to combine three genres: GTA style open world exploration/driving, hack & slash brawling, and real-time strategy. The problem is that it isn’t remotely good in any of those.
The brawling is dumb, although fun: you mindlessly mash two buttons and hope that the enemy runs out of health faster than you do.
The RTS part consists of spawning an endless stream of units until one army reaches the end of the battlefield to wreck the opponent’s production stage. To be frank, it is downright boring.
Still, the driving takes the cake. The controls are worse than you can imagine (worse than Borderlands could ever be), and when you have to race on narrow platforms over bottomless pits… get yourself a pack of Xanax.
I wouldn’t call Brütal Legend bad… the soundtrack and most of the plot about leading a metal-fuelled revolution against the demon-like oppressors can easily entertain you from start to finish, but you will always have the feeling that the game mechanics could have been a lot better.

The great thing about this game is it doesn't take itself seriously and just tries to be a fun experience. And it does a good job of it. You play a roadie called Eddie Riggs (voiced by Jack Black) who dies and gets transported to another world which is a land that is the embodiment of heavy metal. Eddie gets involved with a resistance movement trying to fight back against Doviculus and his Tainted Coil army. The game features a lot of gameplay elements from melee combat, to driving sections and even RTS sections, all contained in a large sandbox map.
Good Points:
- the games humour and story is enjoyable if a little cliched at times. The voice cast is excellent and features appearences from metal celebrities. (Ozzy Osbourne as the Guardian of Metal is my favorite).
- the heavy metal themed world in this game looks really cool and even the enemies and allies are imaginatively designed to match the heavy metal theme
- the soundtrack in this game is brilliant with loads of metal songs. (some have to be discovered on the map to unlock though.
Bad points

The game lacked a lot of impact for me and the story wasn't anything to write home about. However it was still a nice experience and the art style and graphics are quite nice.
(I played this game entirely on the xbox 360 gamepad by the way.)
This game felt like a dark childrens book, it was quite whimsical at times, very funny and silly, but it got hauntingly dark too. And thankfully, without remorse. That, is a very strong mark for this game. I think this may be a spoiler, but I was really expecting it to undo what it had done. I am very glad that it didn't.
Before I get to where I want to go, I want to talk about the controls. The controls tangled your fingers up into a knot, I don't really mind that. But with the very simple control layout, this game controlled very basically. The controls were not interesting in the slightest and really it just boiled down to building a control scheme onto that same controller in essence. Wasn't really anything ground breaking. You could change your camera view, move two characters with the analouge sticks. And then you have two action triggers/keys, for each of the respective characters. So really you'd just move around and press the action trigger/key and see what happens.
By the way, this game's store page lied, you DON'T need a xbox 360 controller to play this game. You can play it on the keyboard too as I could tell in the options menu.
Anyway, I don't really know how to explain why it felt like and experience to me over a story. Perhaps it has to do with how shallow everything felt regarding characters. I felt like absolutely no one had a real backstory or depth besides the young boy. Using them to interact with the world had very expressive reactions. The older brother was boring, he was completely neutral the entire story and just struck me as a faceless robot kind of chugging along on this quest. Even his 1 flashback was really shallow and boring and felt irrelevant. It just reminded me of the father i'm trying to save. It didn't give the brother any face-value and only seemed to show aggression to his brother at time when his brother was unokay with something. That or he'd just show leadership or be protective of his brother. Other than that, he had absolutely no depth whatsoever and he was easily forgettable. Really, I felt only interested in him cause he looked cool. I didn't like the little brother because he looks like a doof to me. But after watching the little bothers events and personality and backstory unfold a little bit (not enough I'd say) he was much more interesting and likeable.
Next up is the graphics. Graphics were good, I mean. I am unsure about the detailing, at times they felt not shaded enough, detailed enough, or they didn't flow together well enough. Though the graphics and displays and scenery was good enough to definitely warrant a second playthrough with your finger on the steam screencapture key, that's for sure. Definitely good desktop wallpaper material in here. Also can be aspring for some artists I can imagine.
There were some moments of tenseness in this game, surprisingly. As the game got progressively dark and took a really unexpected dip into limbo-like depressive stuff all of a sudden. I think there was only one or two parts that really made me have to actually pay attention to my controls, very sure it was once only. And that was a damn good part, glad it wasn't necessary to the story, felt very important to me though. And I like that, i'm glad I got a opportunity to side-track in the game and find things that were important to me instead of the characters. It was nice.
That being said, this games trip into darkness and doing scenarios that aren't often done in video games was truly surprising and i'm really glad they didn't regret any of the decisions they decided to do in it. Because I feel like that's what saved the game for me a little bit. It was a nice journey and it was fun and relaxing.
Most deaths in this game really only occur when the controls are a little too unclear, but you figure out what went wrong almost immediately, so it's not big deal.
That being said, I'd really like to give the developers a BIG thumbs up to one part they made me do. It was something I never want to do in a video game ever again, it just felt all kinds of wrong and messed up to me. I'd like to compliment another part about it, but. I won't, cause spoilers. But, it was good. And i'm glad you didn't reverse it.
Also, lastly. The music. ...It was really easy to ignore it. It really was. It wasn't bad by any means, but it wasn't anything to remember. When my mind actually did pick up some of the tracks, I was instantly dissuaded to bother youtube searching it because that same track felt like a reoccuring theme in any "deep" moments. Whenever something interested happened or a cutscene happened, tracks that sound like that song I heard. Sounded just like remixed versions of it with added or removed instruments and spacing between instrument play times and so on so forth to fit the timing they wanted to match or feelings they wanted to convey in the cut scenes. So the only interesting track was pretty much just rehashed to me in a uninteresting way and most of the scenes were impactful. Even the ones that were supposed to bother you.
Also with that, I don't get why they put this skyrim-sounding song at the end of the game. It really made no sense, it was all epic and then nothing happened. After everything that happened in the game, it made absolutely no sense when it played. It didn't match the mood of what was going on at all. I don't know who's choice that was, but it wasn't a good one.
Anyway, while the game was lackluster in personality I feel, as far as experience goes it was quite something and it was definitely a pleasurable way to spend my morning and part of my afternoon. I would recommend this to someone who wouldn't mind going on a enjoyable light puzzle/adventure. If you want to get your hands on this game, sure, I suppose 14.99 is a fair asking price. However I think paying ten bucks for this product is a good buy, any less than that is too low for what you're getting.
Anyways, thanks for reading my review. I hope it helped you in your decision to get this game or not. Have a good one.

Beautiful game. I have to say, I originally was put off by what seemed like clunky mechanics, and wondered why there was no support for a second player. I wondered about the simplicity of the game, the lack of instructions, and the seemingly cliched task of going to find a cure for a sick father. I wondered about the slightly odd meshing of textures that the game presented; the contrast of a stylized background with semi-rough looking foreground. But all of that became something that was so much more than it initially seemed to be. It became what is an incredibly emotional, poignant, and immersive experience. The clunky graphics prove to be a product of two brothers working together on a difficult journey. The lack of instructions speak to the experience that the two brothers face, a sort of unknown journey that they must puzzle their way through. The seemingly boring outset of the game ends up being a wonderful checkpoint for the story to come full circle to.
The game is mechanically simple, you use just a single controller with a joystick and trigger controlling each brother. There are never in game instructions, and all that you finally get through is done by experimentation. Some of the tasks seem pointless, and I will admit that initially I was struck with the lack of any driving reason to continue in first 1/10 or so of the game. However, as the story develops, you become more and more excited to continue on in the journey and learn more about the world that the game takes place in. The narrative travels through several different areas which tell a story in their own right. Several times, the brothers come across opportunities to help others, and to discover a little bit about the place that they inhabit. The game does a great job of giving you a little sliver of story that you then can infer about, and use your imagination to embellish.
The game is graphically quite beautiful, and it does a remarkable job conveying the atmosphere through the use of lighting and really well done models. The water is gorgeous.
The game has several themes that run through the course of its story, which I will not spoil because really what you should be doing is picking this up right now and playing it through.

For South Park fans - yes.
Otherwise - play South Park: The Stick of Truth first.
It took me about 33 hours to get 100% completion on the highest difficulty.
At the time of playing, the highest available difficulty was called Mastermind Difficulty.
That's the one I played on and the one that allowed me to unlock "The Token Experience" achievement.
Apparently, in one of the recent patches, a new difficulty level has been added. I haven't played that one.
The Stick of Truth.
It also reminded me of some good old Heroes of Might & Magic.
This time the guys are playing superheroes. They want to build a franchise similar to the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but they disagree on who should get their own movie and tv series, so they split into two groups.
Around that same time, cats start disappearing around town. You, as the New Kid, join Coon & Friends (Cartman's group) and you have to help solve that case.
It looks just like the TV series. The cartoon-y graphics are exactly what you would expect from a South Park game.
Most of the time there's no room for visual fireworks, but I gotta say - some of the special attack animations are great (I love the one with Jimmy running through the cities and around the world).
This is the biggest improvement since the previous game, especially around battles. You now have to move your heroes around the battlefield since their attacks affect specific areas. This requires better tactics and hero/skills selection.
All of the menus (inventory, character progression, skills, crafting, maps, etc.) are now handled through an in-game smart phone. Each area is a separate app where you can view available items and make changes.
Most of the time it's just ok. It's there and it nicely combines the South Park themes with superhero motives.
But there are some moments, where it's just awesome! I really liked the songs playing at Raisins, but my absolute favourite was the one during the Spontaneous Bootay fight.
In some of the locations you can hear the radio playing various songs from the TV series, which is a nice treat for old-time fans.
I honestly regret that the soundtrack is not available for purchase.
It's an open-world RPG. You run around town performing side missions, collecting items, following the main plot and fighting.
What's done really great here is character progression. At specific points during the story-line you get access to new skills, abilities and side-kicks who can help you access areas that were previously blocked.
As I mentioned before, the fights are much more interesting this time around. Your character can mix skills from different superhero classes (after you unlock them). But you can only have four skills at any given time (three regulars + one special). That means you have to pick and choose what you think will work best with skills used by your currently selected battle companions. And then try to position your fighters correctly on the battlefield to use those skills effectively.
There's one more thing you can do within the game - use toilets located around town. Each toilet has a mini-game with different difficulty level. It's a QTE button-mashing game which is surprisingly fun. I played with a controller which required me to hit highlighted buttons while turning the analog sticks in circles. Not sure how that works with a mouse and keyboard, but it was a good finger-bending exercise.
At the time I played the game only two DLCs were available.
First one was the Relics of Zaron, providing you with some character costumes and perks. The latter were very powerful if used at the beginning of the game, resulting in some unbalanced gameplay.
The second one was Towelie: Your Gaming Bud. At various points in the game, Towelie would appear to give you some "valuable" advice. This was in fact useless and not even funny. I can't recommend getting this, unless you got it for free as part of the Season Pass.
Even though the Fractured But Whole has better gameplay mechanics, I think I enjoyed The Stick of Truth more. Nonetheless, this is still a very good game - the South Park spirit is strong and I did have a lot of fun playing it.

Firstly I would like to point out that this game is not at all bad, there are people who like this game and/or will like this game. However, it just is not for me... Here is why:
Although the AI in this game brings a challange and the stealth aspects of the game (which is how I like to play) are decent. The movement of the player feels weightless as if you are floating through the air at high speed, I could almost compare it to being in a spectator mode. Controls are decent aside from the EXTREME mouse sensitivity (which even on 6% is quite intense). There is a bit to be wondered about the tutorial in regards to weapon customization and how some aspects of the game work (such as enemies spotting you etc) however I believe the intent is for you to try it out in these "test" zones so you can see for yourself. There REALLY ARE options in terms of your approach to things so if you want essentially linear maps with lots of options (some of which are only available if you have the right character build" than you will not be disapointed.
All in all the gameplay can be fun but I simply can not get into it with all the off putting asthetics of the game. I am sure there will be people that like the way it feels and the way the animations etc. look, but for me, it just doesn't hit the spot.
One last thing.  If you are second guessing your purchase based off performance issues, I am running this on ultra (with the already mentioned FPS dropping settings turned to "medium") at 60 fps on a GTX 980 with no troubles at all. DO NOT miss out on trying this game simply for that purpose.

This game is a pain in the butt.  While I enjoy a game that is challenging, this game is beyond ridiculous.  First, it is a rogue game.  So, you have to start over from the beginning every time you die.  Second, the levels are randomized.  So, you can't really get to know the levels really well in order to beat them.  You can get lucky and have a string of levels that are super easy.  Or, you can get ♥♥♥♥ed and have a string of levels that are super hard.  There are strategies for how to beat most of the enemies, but, again, I feel as though it all depends on the set up of the level.  The set up can make an enemy more dangerous than usual...
I've die more than 600 times and I still haven't beaten the game.  Little achievements like obtaining the short cuts make me ecstatic.

This game is really hard. Rogue Legacy is the closest thing I've played to this difficulty and that game is like dropping a rock in a puddle compared to this game.
With precise controls but an unforgiving world it is not impossible by any means but it is certainly a sharp learning curve. Every enemy and obstacle requires it's own precise approach. At first you will die within seconds, constantly. Then you learn how not to be quite so reckless and can live for more than a minute. Then you slowly master handling different enemies and train your brain to know how to jump and manuver in certain ways. This will get you far but will not win the game for you. Only perfection can do that. Sloppy jumps and not moving just right at the right time will kill you in this game.
If you enjoy punishing yourself with gameplay though this is the game for you. Just don't think you can casually play it and make any headway unless you're an idiot savant or something. Learning to be good at this game is like NASA space flight training. Its rough, will take copious amounts of time, and there will be a lot of dropouts.

I wish that Jack Black was in more games. Brütal Legend is an open world, action RPG from Double Fine Productions. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
I think the obvious answer to this is Jack Black.
If you’re a fan of Tenacious D, this game is pretty much Tenacious D: The Game.
The soundtrack is fantastic. Whether you’re cruising around in the Deuce or just wandering around seeing the sights, the blend of well known metal music and original composition is glorious.
There is a satisfyingly ample amount of items for you to unlock in the “Motor Forge”. Their are weapon upgrades for the Deuce, weapon upgrades for your character, and additional attacks to use. There are also purely cosmetic items to acquire, however, like paint jobs, new clothes, and giant stone heads.
There is a large array of enemies for you to hack to pieces as well as indigenous fauna for you to harass. All the designs are brilliant and very much metal influenced.
The story is great, the dialogue is funny, and the game never takes itself to seriously. This is a trait which we don’t see enough these days.
The map is surprisingly big and makes for a good amount of exploration.
The Bad
I’ve got nothing here, sorry.

There’s no DLC, so, once the game is over, it’s over. This makes me a sad panda.
Verdict: Yea
If you’re a fan of jack Black, Tenacious D, or metal music, then BL is very much the game for you. You can pick it up in the Steam Store at your earliest convenience. It is money that you won’t regret spending. As always, thanks for reading.

There appears to be some sort of crafting system, though I have yet to figure out how it works. You get 3 lives to use in campaign mode per period of time (I think probably per day, but I'm not sure). After that it is three dollars to bring yourself back to life. However, it is still quite fun.
All in all, the actual core game has some promise, but I'm pretty disappointed with the lag, class system, unintuitive item crafting, and the $3 pricetag on campaign mode continues.

So heres a general overview: you start with character creation. you choose what you/your familys backround is, and that decides your starting stats, gear, wealth, and renown. important things, so choose wisely. I prefer a balanced start. So maybe my father was a smith, and I was a trader growing up, but i had a lust for money and power to leave. So from there, you choose your first additional skills. these are vital. you have a lot of choices for character customization. skills ranging from strength and agility, so like hp, damage, run speed, looting abilities, etc to intelligence and charisma so like extra inventory, prisoner management and leadership to allow you to hire troops and take prisoners of war to sell for money.
So you've choosen what you like, maybe a warrior, or a bowmen, trader, or scout. You open up to the campaign map. This is where you can see all of calradia, and how you go from place to place. You select a destination, and while you travel or sleep, the world around you evolves. this is one of the coolest parts. the AI kingdoms, bandits, caravans, peasants, etc will all fight, trade, make peace, etc and over time, you may see entire kingdoms wiped out. Lords of factions will change sides, mutiny, etc.
So now its up to you to make a difference! you decide how! There is plenty of tasks/missions/quests to perform. Kings, Lords, GuildMasters in towns, village elders in villages, and random people in the taverns will have work available to you. from delivering letters and wine, to hunting down bandits and persuading high ranking lords. Or ignore everyone. Just hunt down bandits and sea raiders, they are enemies to everyone except themselves so you can pile their bodies as high as you'd like, or keep them alive and sell them for extra cash. One of the nice parts of warband is with a positive relation with a town, its owner, and its guildmaster, you can invest in a business with the guildmaster with your "denars" aka money. this will provide weekly income based on the areas trade. you can even micro manage it, lets say you have a workshop to make tools with iron, but in that city it costs 200 denars for the iron, but by buying it a city over, you can get the iron for 100 denars each. so you take the cheaper iron and give it to your workshop, and now you're making more money off of your product. once you have enough of these going, you can fuel yourself and a small army and still make a profit. Dont worry about the city/settlement being taken over by another faction either, they make money off you so they want your business either way.
Which brings us to the bulk of/end game. So everything you do has long lasting effects in the game. Even if you just kill some bandits, recovering lords use small bandit parties as a way to make-up for big losses. They can train up veteran troops and make some cash. Raid some ones caravan for example. Alot is a stake here. So you obviously have to fight the troops, which can easily go wrong if you arent prepared. Then you get some loot, which is nice. But thats not the end. So both settlements, the one it came from and the one it was going to, just lost out on profit from those items they were trading. The one the caravan belongs to, is actually super♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you, cuz not only did you kill a bunch of men they had hired and paid for, but you essentially set yourself up for war. You have relations you can view with HUD and menus with Factions, Kings, Lords, Ladies, Settlements, and Villages. Almost everyone has a relation bar, but most of them dont matter except those big ones I listed.
So you could gain relations with a faction, and join them. Just by doing quests for the king and gaining the smallest relation, just a few missions, you have a chance for them to randomely offer you vassalage and a fief. Meaning you would be a lord and own a village that you can collect taxes on, upgrade, defend, recruit from, etc. The drawbacks and benefits are mostly obvious. So now you make money off this village, have high relation with it to get lots of recruits/better recruits, and have protection from a large faction. On the down side, your faction may at any point call on you for war, start a multi-front war no one could win, or your enemies may come and raze and loot your village while you are away.
Or you could just take one your self. The average castle has around 150-250 defenders plus whatever lord(s) parties from that faction decide to show up. You unfortunately can't just take a single village for yourself. You can steal cattle or loot and raise them, but in order to collect taxes and control them, you need to take either a castle or town/settlement. This is one of the funnest but also most difficult parts of the game. Seiges.
So I just recently started playing again, and heres an overview.
240 days have passed since I started travelling Calradia. My beginnings were miserable. After helping rid this Swadian town of bandits, feeling confident, I lead 7 men to their death and was a prisoner for 2 days. After escaping, I learned from my mistakes. I spent lots of time traveling and avoiding large parties and fighting the smaller ones, performing tasks for guildmasters and lords. Overtime, I gained lots of wealth through fighting bandits and missions. I collected large sums sellings loot and prisoners and small trades. When I would get around 3-10k denars, i would invest. Now I have 5 breweries, 3 dyeworks, and a mill. Same with my troops, I slowly recruited more, now i have 28 Swadian Sergeants, 2 Swadian Nights, and 2 Swadian Infantry. Using the training fields on the map are a good a way to train your troops up to 2nd or 3rd tier before leading them to a slaughter. Just remember it costs denars to upgrade your troops. So my plans are to continue to set up more businesses to boost my income as much as possible. While i've invested likely over $50k denars, after troop wages I profit around 1400 denars a week, its makes my armies future proof. So if i have to stay and defend a fief, or a seige takes a long time, I wont have to worry about troops abandoning me with lack of wages. I also need to level up my character and gain renown it order to increase my party size. Even though my troops are mostly elite, as mentioned, castles generally have more than 100 defenders, so thats about the size party you'll want to amass. What I plan to do, is when I am high enough level and have a disposable weekly income of at least 2k or more I will go to Swadian (or what used to be) Villages for 2-3 days and recruit volunteers. Then I will take them to a training field and promote them all to militia and footmen. Then the attack begins, the target, the remains of swadia. While I prefer swadian troops, they fought a 3 front war and are almost gone. Only the kings castle, 1 town, and 1 other castle remain. So I plan to take one amid the chaos. Which may be bad, as the Nords are the aggressors, and they offered me vassalage, and im starting my own kingdom.
Nonetheless the goal is bring Calradia under one crown, and how you do is up to you!

This will be a LONG review, so I'll put a TL;DR at the bottom.
Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is an open(ish) world RPG. At least, that's how most people see it. The biggest downfall of the game is that the public image of the game is so far offset from what the game actually is. Many people dismissed it at first as a Skyrim-clone, which could not be any further from the truth.
Skyrim focused on having deep RPG stats, and sacrificed the prospect of having enjoyable combat to make sure the stats were deep and balanced. Most of Skyrim's combat boils down to "run up to something and click repeatedly until it dies", which made the combat wear over very quickly on me. Instead, Amalur focused on having fun combat first and foremost, and as a result some of the stat building is not as deep or complicated as Skyrim's. Instead of having deep stats and simple combat, Amalur has deep combat and somewhat simple stat building.
Amalur's combat systems are inspired by character action games, such as Devil May Cry or God of War. You have a primary and secondary attack (which are determined by what weapons you have equipped. Different weapon types give you different movesets), a dodge, magical abilities, and a Devil Trigger, which is called Reckoning mode. You can juggle some of the game's smaller enemies, and there are some advanced systems in the game such as dodge cancelling, which will come naturally to any character action fan. It feels fun and genuinley rewarding to try out the dozens of different weapon combinations, though one of the most effective weapon combo is introduced in the game's tutorial -- Longswords have a built in juggle, and you can juggle enemies with a bow and arrow. It's a fun combination, but far better ones exist if you experiment with the combat system.
The fun combat is further aided by the fact that you can build your character in almost ANY way and it's valid. Wanna build a Rogue-Mage hybrid? It's a thing. Wanna do a boring, straight Warrior? Unimaginitve, but it works. Wanna be a mix of all three classes? YES, you can do that! This is one of the few RPG's I've ever played where you can build however YOU like and it'll work. Most RPG's have a feeling that there are only one or two classes which are the best, and you shouldn't bother with anything else. But in Amalur you're free to build however you want.
I also enjoy the character building more than Skyrim's because you get two different types of skill points every time you level up. You get skill points for leveling up combat abilities, and skill points for leveling up other abilities such as lockpicking or crafting. Remember in Skyrim how you'd level up and then you wouldn't actually get any more powerful because you put your skill point into alchemy or something instead of one-handed? That isn't a problem here. You will have constant character growth both in terms of power, and crafting abilities. I feel like you start out weaker than an average skyrim character in this game, but you gain power FAR more quickly. It's a rather fast and enjoyable pace for character development.
The enviornments are a little more of a mixed bag. They're far more varried and beautiful than Skyrim's enviornments, but you aren't allowed to freely explore them like how you could in Skyrim. Try to explore too far into the world and you'll be insta-killed by enemies who vastly overpower you. But, once you do get to those better enviornments, you'll marvel in their extreme beauty. Some of the vistas I saw were jaw-dropping.
The music is also an upside. Ever head of Grant Kirkhope, the musical composer behind Banjo Kazooie? He did the music for this game, and it's just as good, if a little more serious than Banjo Kazooie's wacky toons.
Now, for the downsides. You level up very quickly, and there's an abundance of side-quests in the game so you can reach max level without even trying. This is especially true if you buy the DLC's. The DLC's are very well made, but don't increase the max level at all, so it becomes even easier to overlevel if you buy them.
Remember those skills I mentioned which aren't combat oriented? Some are far, FAR better than others. Firstly, there's little point in leveling up lockpicking, because there are TWO lockpicking skills (lockpicking and dispelling). Even if you're a master lockpick, you won't be able to get all the chests in the world, because you're not a master at dispelling. Meanwhile, if you max out blacksmithing, you can make armor BETTER THAN A FULL LEGENDARY ARMOR SET GIVEN TO YOU RIGHT BEFORE THE FINAL BOSS. With blacksmithing AND sagecrafting maxed out, it's possible to have so much health regen that you can never see yourself take damage. Which brings me to the main bad point of this game...
The game is too easy. Play on Hard mode first. Even then, the game won't be especially hard. I've heard of mods that make the game harder, but I can't personally speak to their effectiveness. If you're here for an immense challenge, you won't find it.
Additionally, to those of you who enjoyed how open Skyrim was, Amalur is a little more confined. Instead of being a huge open world, there are about 20 or so large zones which're broken up by linear paths. Imagine it as a group of small, diverse worlds to explore, as opposed to one huge one which looks mostly the same. And exploration of some zones is locked off by main quest progress.
Speaking of the main quest, the story is rather run-of-the-mill. It has some very good concepts, but execution is rather lackluster. You probably won't care about the story much, for the main quest or sidequests. Though, it's worth mentioning that some characters are VERY well written. Your main motivation for reaching end game won't be beating the game, but instead to kill your nemesis who is built up very well throughout the game.
TL;DR
Did you think Skyrim could've used better, deeper, Devil May Cry like combat?
Do you hate when an RPG forces you to choose between leveling up combat abilties, or crafting abilities?
Do you like the idea of being able to build your character in any way and still having it be a viable build?
Are you okay with a game having amazing music and breathtaking vistas, at the cost of a little less of an open world?
Are you okay with the fact that this game won't be very hard, even at the highest difficulty?
Then Kingdoms of Amalur is for you.

Portal Knights is a fun sandbox-like game. I say "like" because it is pretty linear and gives you a very obvious direction to go, in which you are unable to do much else unless you follow said direction. That being said, you are able to modify the terrain around you in a way very similar to games like Minecraft.
There is a sense of RPG as you are able to choose between one of three different classes, each with their own obvious abilities and disadvantages. You are able to gain exp and level up, gaining access to perks and different tiers of weapons and armor so long as you have advanced along that path spoken of earlier, for example, tier 2 or 3 weapons will need special ores only found in later worlds.
Aesthetically, the game is very fluid and pleasing. The effects are colorful, bright, and generally very well done.
Unfortunately, I don't recall any storyline, the game kind of throws you into it, though figuring it out is pretty quick and easy.
This review is coming from a single player perspective, I don't remember if multiplayer was/is and option at this time. If you're looking for something that will constantly challenge you with new obsticles and content, this may not be the game, as it does get extremely repetitive. The grind is.. grindy.
Overall, its fun for a few hours, maybe a day or two, but I likely won't get back into it unless I'm really bored. Definitely don't advice getting it at full price, wait for a sale. 6.5/10.

I wasn't initally interested in Tekken 7.
I've had fond memories of the game since Tekken 3 on the PS1 and Tekken 5 DR on the PSP but was never more than a casual scrub who played local with friends. Even after finding out about the pc port all I thought at the moment was, "oh cool" and nothing more.
Fast forward a week after launch and I'm casually browsing youtube before bed and happened to stumble on Tekken 7 previews and gameplays. I can't really remember what sold me but I nonetheless purchased the game. If anything, it'll be cool to just play a few matches and finish the story and it'll be worth its price.
It's now been a week and a half later, It would be safe to say that Tekken 7 has been more than I expected. After my first few plays online, realized how bad I played and while I did win a few matches, it just wasn't satisfying mashing buttons or repeating the same combo. This became more evident after watching a few tournaments online, and what a blast they were to watch. Enough so that I may have put off playing the actual game but I definitely did benefit from them to just get used to common Tekken strats, the community itself, and a heck ton more technicalities to the game.
So what's even the point of this bed time story?
Well in short: If you're on the fence about getting Tekken 7, I would implore you to watch a tournament (like the recent CEO 2017) and get a proper look at the world of Tekken. Not only for the fights but also the passion from the Tekken community, one that has veterans playing since the first installment of the game. Hopefully you too are inspired enough to pick up Tekken 7 and pick up fighting games in general, definitely one of the more rewarding genres in gaming.
