Kingdoms of Amalur, also could be called the poor people's Skyrim. The game itself is decent at most. Not a game to buy at full price however, wait for a sale is my suggestion in the highest form. HOWEVER, the game has it's pros and cons, as does even the best of games. Here's my review in my, now normal, manner of doing this.
Character customization: The character customization is limited to really race, gender and face. Very little body change outside of gender. You have two versions of human and two versions of elf. You have your face changing and your tattoo, piercing and hair and hair color. The usual facial change. Now, the difference is you can change it any time outside of console commands after you get your first "home", which is nice.
Gameplay: Gameplay for combat is general hack and slash, not much to say about it, only distinct feature is pressing X or whatever the console equivalent is to trigger fate mode at full bar where you deal extra damage and can kill a person for extra xp after a QTE which is also used in boss fights. Otherwise, hack and slash with bow use. The leveling system you gain three trees: Might, Finesse and Intellect. Honestly, this is basically Fighter Mage Thief tree. Finesse for thief, intellect for mage, might for fighter. You can multiclass as well up to all three trees being used. The more points in a tree the better stats you get for it. You also have your general skill points in other professions of sorts. The armor is restricted by level and tree so you can only use an armor if you have so many points in a tree.
Story: Haven't finished the game but the story from what I played is decent at best, some plot holes like HOW you got the abilities you have and it starts with the entire bit about you dying, it can be assumed you being brought back is how, but doesn't really explain it much.
Graphics: It's cartoony looking. It's much less graphically intense, so might be easier to run for the comps without a good graphics card. The sights are decent as well as character design.
Difficulty: The difficulty never changes. You have to do it manually.  You get higher level and it never gets any more difficult. After awhile, you get so high level, it doesn't even matter anymore.
Over all. There's not really a way to recommend or not recommend KoA. It's a decent game if it goes on sale, but not a game to invest too much time into.

"Manos": The Hands of Fate is a nice novelty of a sidescroller, being an adaptation of a 49-year-old no-budget B-movie. It's also rife with references to other infamously bad movies, most featured on Mystery Science Theater 3000, with the exception of Plan 9 From Outer Space, Troll 2, and The Giant Claw. The game is an action-platformer remniscent of Castlevania, but you get a gun instead of a whip. You can also get a shotgun that fires 3 shots (like the Spreader from Contra), but you lose it if you are hit once. You can also find other items by shooting the hand statues through the levels. There are flashing Hands Of Fate items that increase your max health too, and you can an achievement if you find them all. Another novelty worth mentioning is the film grain, which can be turned on and off in the Options menu.
The game is rather short however. I was able to beat it within a half-hour. Beating the game also unlocks Torgo, who moves faster, but slides to a stop (lke Luigi). It's nice for $5.

Did you watch the movie? Of course you did, you're reading this review!
There are shot for shot pixel art drawings of certain pieces, midi-style soundtracks of various movie themes, nods to other MST3K references and you can play as Michael (the dad) and TORGO (upon completing the game)! I beat this thing in under an hour and it was pretty fun.
Sure maybe there wasn't a part with a plane fight or an underground sanctuary, but if it was accurate to the movie then I would have cut off my Manos long before the 30 minute mark. (It's honestly a pretty forgiving and solid action platformer.)
If you're an MST3K fan then just shut up and buy it. If you're just into collecting games or action platformers then wait for the 2 dollar mark in price, it's a decent play.

I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #30: Brutal Legend
Brutal Legend is an unapologetic love letter to hard rock and heavy metal music.  If you are a fan of this kind of music, that alone is enough for me to recommend this game.  But as it happens, Brutal Legend also happens to be pretty fun.
The story in Brutal Legend is pretty damn silly.  It's not meant to be taken seriously.  But if tongue-in-cheek humor is not what you are looking for, then you should look elsewhere because Brutal Legend brings it in spades.
The gameplay is a mix of combat and exploration.  The beginning is fairly combat heavy, but as I wrapped up my first hour of play I started to get a sense for more of an open world feel to the game.  Combat itself is fast paced.  You start with a huge axe for melee attacks, but you also get a guitar which shoots lightning (don't ask, just go with it).  But the game will also build on these basic attacks and unlock combination attacks and "guitar solos".
Along with the combat and exploration, the game also features vehicles.  It was a lot of fun the first time I hopped in a vehicle and started mowing over enemies.  I also did a boss fight entirely in vehicle, which offhand I can't remember ever doing that in a game before.
I didn't find the gameplay terribly difficult, at least at the beginning.  I played on normal difficulty and did not find it to be much of a challenge.  But it's always hard to judge from the first hour of the game, as it's not unusual for the difficulty to ramp up as the game goes along.
The art is pretty solid.  The environments were pretty varied, but it's the character design that really stands out.  And as you would expect for a game playing homage to rock and metal, the soundtrack is magnificent.  I love that Brutal Legend has a real soundtrack and not just some generic guitar riffs.  It's a great mix of rock and metal.
I had way too much fun with Brutal Legend not to recommend this.  Unless you just hate music, I don't think you'll be disappointed.

I would not recommend this game at the time. Maybe later down the road they will improve it, but I'm not entirely hopeful.
They stripped down a lot of what made Gunz 1 good, and tried to "reimagine" it into Gunz 2. What we're ultimately left with is with a rather generic third person shooter where the winner of a fight is often decided by who has to reload first. There's very little incentive or swordplay, which, ironic enough, is what Gunz 1 was best known for. The Swords, not the guns. They fixed that error in Gunz 2 by focusing almost completely on the guns. The melee feels extremely clunky, the wall running and climbing is extremely unintuitive, and it becomes literally just a bullet hell.
I played my fair share of matches, and they all went exactly the same. Nobody bothered to melee, and when someone tried, they were immediately punished with nearly instant death. Switching between gun and sword is far less intuitive than in its predecessor, so the fluid blend of gun and sword is moot, with the person eventually deciding that it's easier to just use a gun. The result is that the entire core gameplay, (without fluid wall running, useful melee, or intuitive switching) becomes a bunch of people shooting at each other from long distances, neither of them able to effectively close the gap. And when you take into consideration that the netcode is rather lackluster at the moment, players will often jerk around heavily, stripping what could be an intense firefight into little more than just a bullet hell. Spraying and praying that you can get a hit.
I somehow managed to do relatively well at this, despite everything, but as someone who was very excited about the revival of one of my favorite games, I can't help but feel that this strong focus on lackluster gunplay is going to be a feature. Even winning a match felt like an empty victory. I also feel that death comes far too quickly in the game. The bullets seem to do a rather high amount of damage, and there's very little response to inform you that you are in danger of dying. One "redeeming" quality about melee, however, is that once an enemy initiates melee combat with you, you have virtually no defense. They finish their combo, and you fall down, and then you get killed.
Granted, it's in early access, so I might come back to it someday. But as it stands, this is not the game I remember fondly, and outside of a couple familiar levels, there's nothing linking it to the original. Fans of Gunz 1 will likely be disappointed by the sequel they waited for.

I played this entire game without getting a game over in combat. There are ways to get game overs outside of combat and each one is hilarious. The plot is like an episode of South Park and even references characters who were in the very early seasons as well recent seasons.
Gameplay:
Outside of combat, gameplay is very similar. However, the equipment you will be changing for bonuses is no longer weapons and clothing but instead a bunch of accessories that give boosts to certain new stats. Each one will change what is basically your power level and you will constantly needing to change it to survive further in the game.
Inside combat is the real fun part. It is still turn-based combat with the ability to use your farts but it works in different ways. Farting is very useful on your opponents turn as you can skip their turn entirely, freeze time to deal minimal damage to certain enemies (still skipping their turn), create a clone of yourself that steals their turn entirely, or change it from day to night and vice-versa. You now have a moveset instead of attacking with a melee and ranged weapon or using spells. You get different superpowers throughout the game that are with certain classes, which you can change during the story or wait to about the end to just gain access to all of them. You only have 4 slots so you need to think about which you want equipped for battle.
Placement of your character, buddies, and the enemies is also VERY important as attacks will have different ranges and possibly allow you to deal damage by knocking enemies into either a buddy, object, or another enemy. It feels like chess, but way more fun.
Characters:
All of them are hilarious in their own way. The character I used the most was Wendy Testaburger/Call Girl as she just seemed to have the best moveset for every scenario. Craig/Super Craig was also very useful as he could♥♥♥♥♥♥off opponents and have them attack him and his shield. Kyle/Human Kite was a good support character as he can give you a shield, pull you back if you're almost surrounded and heal you, or shoot lasers out of his eyes. I didn't get to experience some of the characters but there are some that could be useful for your playthrough such as Mysterion's Multi Attack, Toolsheds ability to hit multiple enemies if they are in an X, or Fastpass's ability to switch places with an ally.
Conclusion:
If you liked South Park: The Stick of Truth, you have a higher chance to enjoy this. If you like RPG's and tactical gameplay, than you should defiinitely pick this up.
PS Towelie's commentary was also pretty funny. However, the Escape From Shady Oaks level crashed A LOT for me.

Short review:
If you have any interest at all in Japanese historical drama, play the free chapter, even if you don't care about anime babes. Beware of semi-serious translation issues in the paid DLC.
Long review:
I'm incredibly conflicted about this game.
Let's get this out of the way first: If you're here for titillation, you'll be disappointed. Despite appearances, this version of ChuSingura is pure story with zero hardcore content. But the experience is all the more worthwhile for it.
The story and characterizations are fantastic. If you have a pre-existing interest in Japanese period drama, this game will scratch your itch like few others before it. If you don't have that itch, ChuSingura may very well create it for you. The art varies in quality, with backgrounds being decent at best, but where it really counts — character design — the art is nothing short of excellent. The Japanese voice acting is good enough that each of the 40+ (!) voiced characters in the story take on their own unique personalities.
However, there's a serious problem: translation quality and editing. This problem is not apparent right away, nor present all the time, but it worsens as the story proceeds. By the fourth and fifth DLC chapters, entire portions of the story are barely more than nonsense gibberish. That these sections are interspersed between blocks of sensible, well-formatted and edited text makes it all the more frustrating. The project was clearly split between multiple translators and editors of vastly different levels of skill and care. Some portions are terrific; some feel like they were put through Google Translate and copy-edited by a grade schooler, if at all.
The story and characters are so captivating that the translation issues never prevented me from wanting to continue. The sheer quantity of content is also massive for the price. Each chapter in ChuSingura is equivalent in size to most other visual novels, though that's partly because the writing is padded and falls into some of the bad VN tendecies of over-describing things that are readily apparent. Still, this is the first time I have spent 60 hours on a VN with a single coherent narrative as opposed to various "routes" that don't relate to one another. In terms of scope,  ChuSingura is equivalent to an epic saga of novels such as the Song of Ice and Fire, back to back to back.
This review, much like my own perspective on ChuSingura, seems stuck between positives and negatives. That's unfortunate, because I enjoyed ChuSingura immensely and truly wish I could recommend it without reserve. To that end, I strongly urge the developers to dedicate a translation checker and editor to fixing up the latter portions of the paid DLC. If they could raise the quality level of the worst sections to match the best sections, ChuSingura would be at the very top of my list of visual novels.
Until that time, I give ChuSingura a double thumbs-up for the free portion and a single thumb up for the paid DLCs. Despite its drawbacks, ChuSingura's story and characters will remain with me for a long time to come.

Portal Knights. I bought that game while it was still in early access. I tried it out and liked it, and now that it is in early access no more, i even liked it more. Currency came in, and now with version 1.1 there is even new stuff, trials and some merchants! Here some +es and -s.
General:
+ It's looks are promising.
+ It's a blocky game.
+ The characters look nice.
+ The tutorial part is easy to understand.
+ Nice level-up system. You just kill mobs and complete quests on islands you unlock by crafting portal stones and fixing a portal with them to reach other islands with higher level difficulties. At night time, mobs called "Hollow Knights" spawn. They are much stronger than the normal daytime mobs, but that is only fitting. It only lets you know you just have to stay at home during night. (Those mobs are still killable though, but requires skill and gear to defeat them.) With a maximum level of 30.
+ Crafting utilities and cool gears!
+ Relatable to Minecraft's Skyblock maps (One lone island in a void world), but with portals, and bigger islands and different biomes and reagents!
- Sadly, some dungeons are badly generated, allowing you to jump straight toward the treasure chest for example.
- I hope more islands, recipes and merchants will be coming soon too. When you reach level 30, and already have everything, it urges me and the others to lay the game down for like until the next patch.
Combat:
+ Whenever you attack, you'll automatically lock-on target, allowing you to face the mob, so you just can run around and avoid some special attacks, while still facing the target, allowing you to beat them easily, though they can be quite challenging.
+ Some mobs are a real challenge. Just gear up and make sure you avoid those attacks, and be careful not to draw attention of another mob! Personally I love combat-related challenges, as long as there is a balance in it.
+ 3 epic bosses to fight. Beating them grants you access to even higher level content!
- You have to be really careful at first, as you start with a rickety wooden sword and no armour at all.
- The combat system requires getting used to at first.
I would gladly recommend this game to anyone else. :)

Basic description:
Just play it, it is pretty amazing.
It's short and easy, but it's also cute and sweet.  And the ending is a real tear jerker.  So sad, which I like because you don't see that very often in a video game.  Most endings are either happy and victorious, or else somehow evil.  This one is just sad.  Even the events during the journey are sad... sweet and cute, but kind of sad too.
Note about the controls:
You "can" play this with a keyboard.  ASDF for big bro, arrows for little bro.  It's a bit difficult though, and some keyboards have trouble recognizing letter/arrow combos if pressed at the same time.  So, I recommend using a USB-wired XBox 360 controller.  I know it works because that's what I have.  Some people on the forums are reporting issues with the wireless version of the controller, others say they got theirs to work somehow.
Longer description:
It's a cute little platform-puzzler.  Story is very sweet, but also quite sad.  I won't spoil it for you though.  The graphics are very clean, very nice.  It's almost like playing a fairy tale right out of an old story-book.  There are even elements included just for eye-candy, such as the benches placed in good spots for the boys to sit and enjoy the scenery, or the fish pond where they can wash their face and scare the fish.  The gameplay is really simple, very easy to learn... but it challenges you by forcing you to use both hands, both sides of your brain, at the same time.  One hand controls each brother.  Left side stick and all purpose action button for big bro, right side for little bro.  Just one button and stick for each though so it really isn't very difficult.  The game is also pretty short, you might finish it up in about 6 hours if you're really in a hurry.  The game world is linear, too, without any significant paths that diverge from the main road.  And one other thing:  the characters speak a "fantasy" language in this game; it isn't a real language.  However, you can always tell what they want to say by watching their actions and following the camera during cut-scenes.  I should also mention that this is not a typical platformer game.  You don't have any weapons or armor or magic powers.  You don't actually fight hordes of enemies that stand in your way.  The two brothers simply work together to overcome various obstacles like activating switches to lower bridges, climbing up ropes and fences, and in rare instances even trapping "boss" type enemies so they don't kill you.  You're just two normal boys, not great warriors or wizards.  So use your smarts and your environment to get where you need to go... which brings me to my next point, the plot.  The boys' mother died at sea while with the little one, so the little bro is afraid of water now.  Their dad is very sick, but the doctor says there is medicine... but it is far away and hard to get to.  So of course the boys promise to go get it.  And so the journey through the village, over a mountain range, past a ruined castle, and through a ruined city commences.  The game saves automatically after every significant event, too, so you can quit any time and pick up right where you left off next time.

First Impression Review:
I played through the first mission and had some "Ok" performance on a gtx980ti and i7 6700k processor. I had to disable MSAA but didn't notice many jagged edges even at 1080p thanks to TAA. I also had to lower my shadow quality from Very High to High to help stablize framerates and get a consistent 60fps. The gameplay is very polished, though moving "Cover-to-cover" feels very clunky when compared to other games. The animations don't seem to flow very well making for an odd looking transition.
The real value in this game comes in the open-ended game design. I get the consistent feeling of freedom of choice, from a very deep HUD customization menu, to linear level designs that have several routes to choose from that lend themselves to different playstyles. It's very easy to find 2-3 alternate "Stealth" paths to use in every section just like Human Revolution offered. The story is deep and well written just like the last game. I get a strong "Metal Gear Solid" vibe from this and the last Deus Ex games with some western influence and it seems to work well.
I'll update this review when I get further into the game, but be sure to check my youtube channel to see some gameplay recorded at 1080p/60fps of each level if you're unsure of what this game looks/plays like.

Only get this if you're a fan of the show, the game is in Early Access and it shows. It has so many flaws there is no way I can cover them all. The good thing is, is that all of them can be fixed in time, so they have a strong base game with so many rough edges you'll probably get tetanus just from playing this, so on with the review.
The game only has 3 levels (takes a little less then a hour to  beat all of them, so a total of about maybe 4 hours playing with all four characters), the first is a okay looking forest the second is a boring gray ruined city and the third is a gray cave. While the levels are lacking in design, and visuals. There some unoriginal yet enjoyable moments to be had. They do have a fair bit if secrets to find for XP, but chances are your partners will just leave you if you try and find them. The monsters you fight and the girls you play as look great. Each monster is distinct and there are a good amount of them and they don't get old in the time it takes to beat that level.
The combat is good, but it shows that it's Early Access with a lack of polish. It is easy to pick up and play with a fair bit of depth with you being able to level up your skills and gain passive abilities, and do to how short the game is, it does add replayability which this needs. Also I think it would do the game some good to add more combat skills, and let you choose the ones you like, because they can get old and a number of them I just never use.
The four girls are all fun to play, and none feel too similar. Though the camera is lacking with no targeting and no way to focus it, meaning that you will get hit by something off screen more then you'd like. Over all the combat is rough but fun, and slicing your way though a horde of Grimm can be fun. But sadly the levels get old. So waiting may be best, for $15 there are many better games out there. But personally I don't regret spending that much as a fan of the show. But if you don't know the first thing about the show you will be lost. So at this point the game is really only for fans

Contrary to what many other reviews say, I believe that this game could be enjoyable to anyone, whether they are a fan of RWBY previous to playing the game or not. Of course, it's probable that one who was a fan would get an increased amount of enjoyment by seeing their favorite characters, but this by no means is equivalent to saying that someone who isn't a fan wouldn't enjoy the game.
That being said, the game is still in Early Access, and this should be taken into account when playing. Many of the mechanics that are implemented in the game are solid, but there is much that is still absent (for example, the only way to combo attacks is to just repeatedly spam the attack button). Additionally, the game is a very multiplayer-centered game, and is best played with some friends for the sake of coordination. playing with strangers or alone is all fine and dandy, but keep in mind that the level you are on can end up resetting inconveniently if the host of the server decides to leave.
There are also many small complaints, such as the fact that the Auto-Aim system for ranged attacks can target enemies that you don't mean to target, and the fact that multiple Beowulf-Type enemies can easily pin you into a corner and continually punch you until you die, but that's to be expected in an Early Access title.
Overall, it is a great game that I am sure many people would enjoy, whether they are RWBY fans or not.

OK, so this is a great old game.
If you are interested in good graphics and story driven gameplay then this game is not for you.
But if you like very good sandbox gameplay, with multiplayer mayem battles and sieges in e medieval era then keep reading to see what this game has to offer.
-Great singleplayer game with many options on how you choose to play.
-your and AI's choices are impactful.
-Every new game will be a different experience from the last.(replay value is infinite)
-There is no tutorial (there is a training level), so its a self learning process, like many old games
-Simple to learn combat mechanics but difficult to master.
-Good but derpy and fun combat AI (sometimes).
-Can be very easy and also very difficult depending on your settings.
-Epic large scale battles in different fields and castles (max number of Troops can be changed through some game files and it's very easy).
-Not a difficult game to run, although it is not optimised perfectly.
-No farming required to move on (although it is an option).
-Game flow and flow of battle are both very good and smooth if you have some experience in the game.
-Multiplayer is a very wierd and different but great experience, as there are many dedicated players that have mastered the combat system.
-No hacks in this game, just because the community is honourable.
-Some gamemodes including castle sieges where strategy and mayem both take place.
-Classes are balanced through the loadout system, and every faction has different loadouts as well.
-Plenty of mods you can choose from if you finish the game.
-Mods both enhance the native gameplay or create a completely new game for you.
-The modding community is creating new mods that come out almost every day, some of wich are months of team effort.
-The DLC for this game are just like paid mods from the devs of the game and are all very good and worth their price (the best being Napoleonic Wars).
Now there are some cons to this game as to every other:
-Character customization is very poor (but it doesn't affect the gameplay at all).
-Most weapons and weapon condition look the same although they act differently.
-Textures are old and bad (But a recent update turned them to HD).
-Gameplay can be quite repetitive sometimes when nothing huge is happening.
-Most servers are empty with a few exceptions (100/150 players or 47/50 players).
A tip for some new players, don't abandon the game from the first hours or minutes of gameplay. It's hard to begin with no tutorial and so many elements that can ruin your game if you don't play smart.
So if you are having trouble with anything you can simply watch some videos that explain every situation. (there are some dedicated youtubers that do videos regularly on the game).

A worthy sequel to the first two Brothers in Arms games. There's a very emotional story here that makes the events of the previous games come full circle, and one which the game flaunts with well choreographed cinematics. The gameplay feels like a next-gen evolution of Brothers in Arms in all the right ways. Cover, destructible levels, multi-squad command, air recon, the map replacing SA view, sprinting, and the kill-cam all fit right into Brothers in Arms and don't make the game lose its identity at all. The levels are bigger and better than anything seen before, and the enemy AI is as great as it ever was. The graphics, unlike the first two BiA games, actually stand the test of time thanks to vibrant, colorful levels and tasteful use of visual effects and bump mapping, unlike most early 7th gen video games. There are a few bugs, but not enough to ruin the experience. What does ruin the experience for players experiencing the game on Veteran is the fact that the player cannot use iron sights directly out of cover, which makes cover useless when the crosshair is disabled. Another issue is that weapon sway when aiming is not in this game, except for a second immediately after the player aims. Other than that, this game is an improvement over the originals in every way.

This is the ONLY game I've bought and owned on Steam. I bought and played this last summer having zero knowledge about Torchlight I. I loved this game so much after putting in many hours (and beating it the first time) that I wrote a two hour  review of this game on Amazon, that lists many many details about this game. I wrote that last July (July 2013). It's under the, "Torchlight 2 is so Good, RunicGames HAS TO Make Torchlight 3!" Very briefly, it's like World of Warcraft without the need for dependency on others to upgrade gear, weapons and trinkets in instances; it has, "common," "quest," "rare," "epic" and "legendary" items in the game. All of that is available for the individual player to obtain, which I love. There are four classes and each class has a pet. You can send your pet to town any time you want to sell off gear or buy things on the "shopping list," even if you're far away. You can give your pet spells, including a pet spell, meaning your pet can have a pet. You can enchant items (expensive), you can feed your pet some fish, which will transform your pet for 5-10 minutes with special attributes, store your equipment for later or even for your other characters when they meet the requirements to use those equipment, etc. I've never played Diablo, but I've read that the developers of Diablo 2 made this, and you can see that the interface between this game and Diablo 3 are similar. After you beat the game the first time, you're at around level 50-55. Original premise for a game... too bad the game itself is an unoriginal NES platformer.
As Mike, you must survive through Valley Lodge by leaving your family behind in order to jump, run and shoot snakes with a pistol. Sometimes you get a shotgun, which shoots a three-way projectile that won't hit anything else than whatever's in front of you. The first two levels of the game follow the movie, but everything is thrown out the window once you reach Level 3, which looks like Castlevania... as in it reuses the same graphics! Also, the boss of this level was supposedly so good it got reused in AVGN Adventures.
When Level 4 starts, your protagonist says "What a horrible night to have a missing wife and child!". Enough said.
As the game advances, the game stops bothering with Manos and becomes a Mystery Science Theater 3000 tribute. Tom Servo does a cameo in Level 2 and most levels involve enemies from other B-movies like Hobgoblins, Robot Monster and Plan 9 From Outer Space. Why call it Manos then? The setting fails because the writing is all centered on references, trying really hard to wink at you and say "Hey this happened in the movie, right?"
The game could have been good if the gameplay was interesting, but it isn't. You only shoot in a horizontal line and enemies just bounce back and forth forever, making fighting a joyless affair. Bosses are equally as mindless. The only challenge the game offers comes from occasionally unfair enemy and trap placement, where upon hitting them, you will bounce back in a pit and die. The game sometimes spice things up by making the whole screen dark around you, preventing you from anticipating obstacles and multiplying deaths where you fall in pits. Other levels are autoscrollers, which don't really have a reason for happening and forces you to progress at the game's pace. There's also a vertical autoscrolling level that rips off Castlevania 3.
Overall presentation is also weak. The graphics and sound are appropriately NES-styled, but they have no substance and fail at making an impression. The game also offers difficulty levels, but don't bother with them: all they do is remove health pickups, shotguns and checkpoints from levels. Yes, it makes the game harder, but it doesn't make it fun.
Manos will take you about 45 minutes to finish, maybe more if you want to get the full ending or finish the Torgo playthrough, which just switches sprites, makes you do lots of annoying noises and is slippery as all hell. The complete unoriginality is what mainly kills the game though; it doesn't attempt to add anything new to the old-school game formula, unlike games like Shovel Knight, Binding of Isaac or Axiom Verge. This game is about as faithful to its source material than a LJN game would be, so it's good at reminding you of LJN!

I bought Kingdoms of Amalur Reckoning on a 70% Sale and left the game while I played other things and wasn't feeling like giving it a try yet. I wasn't expecting anything spectacular, something Torchlight-Diablo-esque perhaps.
Turned out I was wrong.
Kingdoms of Amalur Reckoning has a moderately paced action packed battle where you can roll (or blink if you're a Sorcery user) to dodge and block or parry incoming attacks as long as you have the reflexes.
Every type of weapon feels unique and finding one that suits you the best might be a decisive point when you're aiming for a class (or rather, destiny). From swords to scepters, hammer to staves, bows to daggers and even chakrams, nothing is useless here. It may take some getting use to, but every weapon has its charm, its pros and cons. Every weapon has its gimmick and is impressive how different they feel, most of times a different type of weapon requires a different approach in combat.
The camera while fighting is somewhat weird, not unbearable but it can get more in your way than the enemies themselves sometimes. The game will focus on whatever hit you and sometimes if the enemy is past behind you the camera may follow him instead of keeping focus on the one you are trying to kill. This show how important is to have a lock-on option in games with such combat system.
One of the most memorable features of Kingdoms of Amalur is something introduced early for you: Fateshift. Fateshift is the usual "super mode" you activate once you gauge is completely filled.
Why is it so memorable? The finishing moves, oh dear, the finishing moves.
Few games make you feel so powerful like Kingdoms of Amalur does. When you see the first Fateshift finisher, which probably will be on a creature that is times bigger than you, you'll feel like you are unstoppable. And then you'll do it on a human sized enemy and it'll just scream OVERKILL. Nevertheless you probably won't be saving Fateshift too much because you'll want to see every last of the finisher moves, they are THAT awesome.
The game offers a lot of variety with classes and mix-ups every possible combination and you can build your character as you see fit, and if you don't like it you can re-spec as many times as you want. But keep in mind the re-specs WILL get pricey fairly quick (after the 4th re-spec you'll notice). While gold may be easy to come later on, at the beginning it surely isn't.
Want to get in the face of enemy and take everything head on with heavy armor and huge melee weapons? Might is your path.
Maybe you like to kill enemies at a safe distance with flashy spells? Sorcery it is then.
Or do you prefer backstabs and bows? Finesse is perfect for you.
However...
Really. Why should you become just a brutish Warrior? Why become a squishy Archer/Assassin? Why become a frail Wizard? Why when you can become a Warrior with magic, an Archer that's as deadly at long range as it is up close, or a Wizard that can use sneaky tricks if magic fails him.
Not satisfied? Mix EVERYTHING. Become an Universalist.
The best of Kingdoms of Amalur Reckoning is how it is possible to mix up EVERY class in the game. There are no boundaries in this game: you can mix Warrior, Thief and Wizard in any way you find better, nothing is stopping you. Doing this will often give you amusing results.
Of course that "pure breed" classes will have its unique advantages and some powers that only they can access, but mixed classes often have their own bonuses that, with the right gear, will more than make up for those last skills you can't afford.
One of the aspects I like the most in Kingdoms of Amalur: the complete LACK of status points. No Strenght, no Dexterity, no Intelligence to worry about, no "status puzzle" of sorts, just skill points that should be invested in the three skill three which will grant different amounts of HP and MP.
From simple quests like "Kill this" to "Bring me that" to "Deliver this" to "Keep me alive" to "Save the damn world", you'll have your hands full everywhere you go.
There are long questlines from specific factions that will grant you a special reward in the end. But with a twist: most of times you have the option to join the "hero" or the "villain" (opinions may vary) of said questline, and whoever you take the side will grant a different, permanent bonus. Some choices may have a deep impact in your game.
I normally avoid talking about graphics since opinions about it are arbitrary, but like Just Cause 2, Kingdoms of Amalur has incredible graphics and effects even on its lowest setting.
Spell effects are impressive and for once the often overlooked warriors and thieves gains extremely flashy and beautiful skills and attacks to watch, which I must say, is immensely refreshing to see.
First, look at any review from Kingdoms of Amalur Reckoning and you'll find out that everyone says the game is too easy even on Hard. They are not exaggerating, if you pick a Might class and become a tank it won't be long until you realize enemies are barely doing a scratch on you and only the most dangerous, most powerful enemies will pose a threat to you. On the other hand playing as Finesse and Sorcery characters will require care and proper dodge/parry skills as while they can dish, they can't take as well.
Indoor scenarios will seem repetitive after a while, especially cave and castle/fortresses ones, they may have different coloring, but that's about it. To make this worse the game has a tendency to grow quiet, musicless, on these areas.
Kingdoms of Amalur Reckoning has a decent repertory of enemies, but they are not enough. You'll encounter the same kind of enemies in several different areas from the start to the end of the game, some of the human opponents are mere re-skins of other enemies and there are even bosses who are simply overpowered enemies you'll find around, maybe with a gimmick or two, but that's about it.
The game also suffers with a problem that will show up for completionists: doing all sidequests will make you level up faster and you might end up reaching the level cap even before you travel to the last country (which is big on its own accord) which can easily frustrate people.
Another common complaint is how forgettable the main storyline is. Side quests are much more enjoyable and have many more noteworthy characters with more interesting back stories that most characters from the main story barely seems to have at all.
Even with its flaws and problems Kingdoms of Amalur Reckoning is a memorable game with a lot of nice characters, nice combat system and interesting quests with a maybe not-so-great main story, but it never fails to deliver what intends to.
In the end the saddest thing is that the developer (Big Huge Games) bankrupted and we will never get newer stuff for the game like spears or even bug fixes or a new level cap. And a sequel probably will never come to a light either.

Kingdoms of Amalur is at odds with itself.  On the one hand, it strives to be an epic fantasy along the lines of Skyrim or Oblivion (or even WoW).  On the other, it is an arcade action game.  The arcade part is fun.  The rest... not so much.  The backstory and the lore are dull, as are most of the voice actors.  Quests are generally interesting... many are simple fetch quests or kill monster X at location Y.  But many are multi-part with intriguing backstory.
The story has something to do with your character be exempt from fate because you were resurrected from the dead.  And other characters want to help or exploit you.  Or something like that.  But, as a whole, it just doesn't come together.  There's nothing compelling about the story.  The mini-games pale in comparison to their Bethesda counterparts.  I clicked through every dialog tree as quickly as possible.  There are stones scattered in the world which, when touched, divulge some of the lore via a voice-over.  I couldn't pay attention to a single one of them.
Now, on the combat side, it resembles more of a Darksiders flair.  You roll around to avoid enemy attacks and wait for the right moment to close and shred your opponent.  Some monsters just absorb hits until they die.  Others will take a few before striking back.  The only downside is that it becomes repetitive.  Each dungeon has the same types of monsters, reasonbly spread across the map.  But after my 5th encounter with kobolds, for instance, I was ready to move on.
Kingdoms of Amalur sports an RPG element.  Your character levels up and points can be allocated into different skill trees.  Some of them unlock cool moves that can be used in combat.  Others unlock world exploration skills like alchemy (dull), lockpicking (dull), finding hidden stashes (dull),  and the like.  And, you can re-roll your character at any time -- a feature that I haven't used yet, but appreciate that it is there.
The game is definitely on the easy side, especially if you avail yourself of the powerful weapons available at the start of the game.  Set the game on hard and pick less damaging weapons (like daggers) to make the game more exciting.
Nevertheless, with six hours into the game, I'm probably done with it.  It hasn't grabbed me.  And, as a gamer with limited time for gaming, I have to be engaged from the first moment.  The story needs to be compelling.  The characters (especially my character) need to be intriguing; their dialog something I listen to with rapt interest.  And if not that, then the action needs to be exciting.  Perhaps if it mixed the combat with some Prince of Persia like platforming elements, and downplayed the story/RPG stuff?
It feels too much like a couple of different incomplete games all squished together into a mostly ineffective whole.  It's not enough to keep my interest.

I'm fairly deep into the game so far.  It's very addicting.  There are some cons in terms of some of the graphics, but these honestly don't detract from the game at all.  It's very immersing and it's easy to play for hours without realizing it.  Unlike most RPGs with multiple races (Skyrim and the like, for example), whatever race you select at the beginning doesn't impact your development in the long run; they're all at an even playing field to start out.  None have any real strengths or obvious weaknesses; you can select whichever one of the four you want and not have to worry if they're going to be weaker in melee style or stealth style or whatever your preferred style is.  Using kb&m works just fine, so I have no comments as to whether a controller is any better or worse.  One other possible downside is that you need to keep a close eye on your weaponry and armor.  Depending on what you're fighting or how much fighting you're doing, your weapons (and armor to a lesser degree) will get damaged pretty quickly.  The system warns you when your weapon is close to breaking (permanently), so you'll have to use a repair kit or switch it out before it shatters.  Armor (including your shield, robes, etc) holds up pretty well.
There are a variety of destinites to choose from and you don't have to stay with one in particular; I actually recommend that you change around as more get unlocked as you level-up.  The game allows for a variety of styles without difficulty; you're not stuck with what you have and so you don't have to start over to change something.  You can see a Fateweaver to change your fate, but I've yet to see the necessity in doing that.
I will say this about the difficulty levels of the game: hard/difficult mode is the way to go.  I'll admit to having some trouble with the normal mode in most other RPGs, but even KOA's difficult mode isn't overly challenging.  I rarely fateshift unless I'm coming up against a foe I just can't figure out how to beat, or if I don't have enough health potions.  Levelling up is pretty easy compared to other games.  It's a very entertaining game and it being a little easier in terms of foes allows for better exploration, in my opinion.  I have been doing the side quests and faction quests as I go rather than coming back to them, but it doesn't seem to matter how you do it.  That being said, I'm sure I'm progressing slower than others might, and I've got a ways to go before actually completing the game (I've put the main quests on hold for the moment to do some exploring in areas I've not been to).

I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #30: Brutal Legend
Brutal Legend is an unapologetic love letter to hard rock and heavy metal music.  If you are a fan of this kind of music, that alone is enough for me to recommend this game.  But as it happens, Brutal Legend also happens to be pretty fun.
The story in Brutal Legend is pretty damn silly.  It's not meant to be taken seriously.  But if tongue-in-cheek humor is not what you are looking for, then you should look elsewhere because Brutal Legend brings it in spades.
The gameplay is a mix of combat and exploration.  The beginning is fairly combat heavy, but as I wrapped up my first hour of play I started to get a sense for more of an open world feel to the game.  Combat itself is fast paced.  You start with a huge axe for melee attacks, but you also get a guitar which shoots lightning (don't ask, just go with it).  But the game will also build on these basic attacks and unlock combination attacks and "guitar solos".
Along with the combat and exploration, the game also features vehicles.  It was a lot of fun the first time I hopped in a vehicle and started mowing over enemies.  I also did a boss fight entirely in vehicle, which offhand I can't remember ever doing that in a game before.
I didn't find the gameplay terribly difficult, at least at the beginning.  I played on normal difficulty and did not find it to be much of a challenge.  But it's always hard to judge from the first hour of the game, as it's not unusual for the difficulty to ramp up as the game goes along.
The art is pretty solid.  The environments were pretty varied, but it's the character design that really stands out.  And as you would expect for a game playing homage to rock and metal, the soundtrack is magnificent.  I love that Brutal Legend has a real soundtrack and not just some generic guitar riffs.  It's a great mix of rock and metal.
I had way too much fun with Brutal Legend not to recommend this.  Unless you just hate music, I don't think you'll be disappointed.

This is a very fun but simple game. I don't normally review games but for Portal Knights, I'll make an exception.
Pros:

Cons:
-The game is very simple in mechanics. Combat while fun for a while gets repeditive, mostly consisting of just holding down a button if you are a fighter or ranger.
-You can only go to level 30, which is ok I guess but once you hit that there really is little reason to do much of anything because about 90% of the special events that pop up or quests give you exp and sometimes some money.
-Loot is lack luster, like..really lack luster. Imagine hunting down a chest in a dungeon and getting some bricks. Yeah..
-There are only 3 bosses, 6 if you count hardmode which are just the same bosses just harder, loot from them is rather lack luster too, consisting of recipes, building material and sometimes a pet which does nothing but look cool.

-Storage, for a game that has you wanting to loot all building materials it sure has a lack of carry space.

You may look at this list of cons and wonder why I still gave it a thumbs up, its because despite them the game is still fun for a while and as far as I'm concerened still worth getting (though I'd wait for a sale). To be completely honest, I think this game is extremely monotonous, don't let my thumbs up fool you. I put over 100 hours into this game and I enjoyed it for what it was (thanks to the massive amount of patience I have), but the biggest problem with this game is that there isn't anything to do really, which is hindering this game from being a solid competitor to giants like Minecraft or Terraria. You jump from world to world trying to find the next portal and you quickly begin to realize that they all look the same and none of them have much to offer other than to mine, fight nearly the same enemies over and over, explore petty dungeons, and find the next portal. The game isn't as deep as a game like Terraria for example and honestly I wonder if this game is meant for kids or something. Let me make a simple pros/cons list.
Pros:
-  Game feels really well made, very polished, no bugs, no crashes.
-  Graphics are surprisingly amazing for such a simple game. Very pretty to look at.
-  Combat is simple, yet very fluid and fun.
-  The game has a leveling system (1-30), points to spend on stats and you get passives. Has a sense of progression.
-  Create your own character. Character customization.
-  Pretty cool crafting system, nothing deep but still fun.
-  You can build things of course.
-  Tons of loot.
-  Has little events you can complete for special rewards sometimes. Holiday events, etc.
-  The music is amazing.
-  Up to 3 friends can join your game anytime they want and play with you. Has local Co-op.
Cons:
-  Only 3 bosses (and 3 hard mode versions of those bosses I believe).
-  Needs more NPC's on each world, and they need to give more quests.
-  Needs a larger variety of enemies.
-  Needs more unique worlds, as the game seems to only have about 10 or more biomes with 47 worlds to explore, so you can imagine how that plays out.
-  Needs more classes, only has Warrior, Ranger, and Mage. It's not a big deal, but I think at least 2 more could've been thrown in there.
-  Get's repetitive really fast, biggest reason being because of lack of content.
The reason I gave this game a thumbs up are for 2 reasons. One, because it did keep me occupied for a solid 100+ hours so I think it'd be dumb to give it a thumbs down really. And Two, I really hope the developers are reading this and add a lot more things to do in this game, because I honestly feel that is one of the only things holding this game back in my opinion. Other than that the game is addicting. Don't go into this game expecting a ton of sh*t to do and you'll be fine.

Throw out your conventional narratives. Forget all you know about complex stories with plot-twists revelations, and words. And prepare yourself for some unique story telling I’ve ever had the pleasure to review.
Given the state of such a short indie game. I feel it is necessary to describe some things to take note of before venturing into Brothers. So SPOILERS! Because without them I can’t really make a review except maybe about a boring one of the feelings i experienced but then I still count that as a slight spoiler. Given this unique indie game I feel such spoilers is justified to be told.(Though I’ll still be limiting the amount of what you read, giving the absolute minimum to read, in order to not spoil any of the main story in itself).
For one the game is short. But, just because the game is short doesn’t deter any amount of enjoyment and satisfaction you’ll take into from this game.
Rather, to be quite blunt the story pulled me in. There were no narratives. No words to follow, no captions. Just two Brothers trying to save their father. A simple but enormous task for two young boys.
Only you, a controller, and two brothers to save their dying father.
It’s a simple objective, a simple journey to save their father, but do you expect things to be ever so simple?
No. It’s never that simple. The story telling for an indie game such as this diverges from traditional narratives who give you a dramatic voice in the background to flesh you into the world itself. For other games it works. But for Brothers it’s an entirely different story all together.
Brother’s goes back to the very roots of storytelling; what roots you may ask? Well, traditional story telling. You, the audience sits and listen to a story from a good book or a story-teller.
You could say that’s a bit boring, and yes I would be bored too! But, if you were a child you wouldn’t become bored. Rather you would become enraptured in it’s small details for each character and the ongoing story-telling unfolding. Brothers takes the traditional route of storytelling and gives it a twist by incorporating innovative mechanics to engage both young, new, traditional, old, players alike.
You are given control of two brothers in a world where no one makes any sense in English. Rather they have their own language to speak in. It’s un-needed in my opinion to know what they are saying most of the time because ‘actions speak louder than words’ and it is so true with Brothers. Their actions define who they are.

If you were dismayed that you were never able to play Journey because it was a Playstation exclusive, or played it and wanted more, look no further: Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is the Journey for the PC platform.
The characters are silent but expressive. The environments colorful and vibrant, yet at times dark and twisted. The path is straightforward, but full of hidden secrets along the way. This is not a game of reflexes and precision - there is no user interface to distract the player from everything that goes on. This is one of those fancy shmancy 'all about the experience' games; if you're not the type of player who likes a slower paced game, Brothers will not appeal to you. However, if an odyssey through gorgeous unknown lands with a silent storytelling scheme sounds like your kind of game, Brothers is the kind of game where you can get lost in.
The game is played from the perspective of the two Brothers, controlled simultaneously. Despite the label, you do not need a controller to play this game; keyboard alone will work fine, though a controller will feel more natural. The two brothers have only two actions: moving, and a context-sensitive action button. It may not seem complex, but when you coordinate the two brothers at once to navigate puzzles, a single action button per brother is plenty. The brothers may move in similar fashion, but you soon learn they have their own strengths, which I will not spoil as some of them are story-centric.
And did I mention the environment is astounding? There are countless hidden secrets and interactables, with the two brothers reacting differently to most of them. Everything in this game is hand-crafted and visually stunning. No lens-flare, no blood-on-the-camera, just luscious amounts of scenery porn. If you're packing a good graphics card, this is where you'll be happy to have it.
You would think a game where one controls two characters independently to be confusing, but it successfully creates a challenge rather than an annoying gimmick. Imaginative and inspiring, melding gameplay with adventure, Brothers is going to be a must-have for most people. If one wonders whether or not gameplay is art, wonder no longer - you'll be too engrossed in this game to care.
The only criticism is the stupid lever at the start of the game. God damn that lever.
The game is also pretty short; there's no doubt it's thorough, well-paced, and end at a good time, but it does leave one wanting to find more.
...
P.S.: As a side note, the game can also be crudely played with two people, one controlling each brother. While it may take away from the mechanical challenge of having to control two entities, it throws in a fun teamwork element and allows you to enjoy the game with a second person. We played with one person on keyboard and another on controller, but having two people on keyboard is also possible. Since the game is not 'meant' to be played this way, you may find some parts easier or more difficult than normal, but I can attest that the game will still be satisfying to play.

Contrary to what many other reviews say, I believe that this game could be enjoyable to anyone, whether they are a fan of RWBY previous to playing the game or not. Of course, it's probable that one who was a fan would get an increased amount of enjoyment by seeing their favorite characters, but this by no means is equivalent to saying that someone who isn't a fan wouldn't enjoy the game.
That being said, the game is still in Early Access, and this should be taken into account when playing. Many of the mechanics that are implemented in the game are solid, but there is much that is still absent (for example, the only way to combo attacks is to just repeatedly spam the attack button). Additionally, the game is a very multiplayer-centered game, and is best played with some friends for the sake of coordination. playing with strangers or alone is all fine and dandy, but keep in mind that the level you are on can end up resetting inconveniently if the host of the server decides to leave.
There are also many small complaints, such as the fact that the Auto-Aim system for ranged attacks can target enemies that you don't mean to target, and the fact that multiple Beowulf-Type enemies can easily pin you into a corner and continually punch you until you die, but that's to be expected in an Early Access title.
Overall, it is a great game that I am sure many people would enjoy, whether they are RWBY fans or not.

This is my only serious review because this game is on several of my friend's wishlist and I want to warn them.
This game is really horrid, it's basicly everything wrong with NES homage games. It looks ugly as hell, the game design seems intended to kill you instead of giving you a challenge to deal with. Even if this game was made bad in a ironic way, there is no actual fun to be derived from that. The only humor in it is "Did you see this MST3K episode? Well here's a reference to that". Which I wouldn't mind if I was speaking to my nerd friends, but just saying "look at these funnier people and what they joked about" does not constitute as a good joke for it's own premise.
About half the levels take place in the dark with only a small cone of light around you, which wouldn't be so bad if your cone of light wasn't barely bigger than your character. This creates a large amount of problems because the game just loves to throw enemies at you that knock you back into pits. You could potentially deal with this problem by just shooting what's coming up, but a lot of enemies home in on you from above, where you cannot shoot or are outright invincible. The final level is a auto-scrolling level that goes up, while you can't see what's actually appearing above. If you go too fast you will not notice the ball and chain that has just spawned that will knock you back all the way. There is a moment where they do this twice, one after another.
There is one level which is a plane level where you control a huge♥♥♥♥♥plane that covers atleast 1/6th of the screen. You die in one hit and it is nearly uncontrollable. The boss of that level is a giant chicken head and a plane which shoots small bullets you can barely see.
The game also just loves to cheat, early on there is a boss which changes your invincibility period to half a second, thus causing it to hit you multiple times if it so deems. This boss also is later reused in another game made by the same developer, so that tells you the effort put into it.
The music is decent, though. It's functional and does it's job well, never sounding unpleasant. However, not the same can be said of the sound effects. There is one enemy in the game that has a noise that can be accurately described as "Screamer midi as back in the dial up days". There is a UFO enemy that's spawned everywhere in one level that just the most painful noise known to man.
If you want to get a good homage to old NES games, I would suggest Shovel Knight. It is a better game than most NES games. If you want a funny bad game, just play Bad Rats, it's better than this is ever gonna get.
Oh also, the game outright didn't want to accept my DualShock 3 controller, no matter what program I used or input I set it at.
Update: As of this date, the dev has personally told me that they added a health bar to the plane level, this atleast negates my criticisms about that part. (Also 69% found this review helpful right now which is in fact Very Nice)
Update 2: The dev of this game tweetsearches himself and whined about this review for 3 days on his twitter. Got blocked when I told him in 3 different ways to stop tweetsearching himself. I have pretty much done what every game journalist sets out to do, so I now know what career I have perfected.
Update 3: He apologized, we all good.

A very boring rpg. Unless you have many free hours to kill, I recommend you stay away from this game. I was able to get 9 hours in before I made the decision to drop it for better games. Everything about the game was just too boring. The combat was super easy, the class system was average and the quests and story just didn’t have the right hook to get me interested.
The combat seems fun at first but then you quickly realize just how easy and frustrating it is. Enemies are generally dumb or cheesy. You can either face roll enemies or have no ability to dodge correctly, thanks to the wonderful camera and dodge system. You can try to dodge out of the way of an attack but occasionally the camera will be in such a spot that you instead dodge head first into the enemy, taking the damage and then some that you were trying to avoid. This happens more than enough to be frustrating.
The quests and story is what truly killed this game for me. The beginning of the story is very bland and almost feels unoriginal. You come back to life after being dropped onto hundreds of decaying corpses to find out now that you have come back, you now have no fate and can change destinies. It seems like a cool concept but it’s surrounded by so many mediocre and cliché rpg elements that it drowns itself. I looked up the ending to the game to see if it redeems itself but let me tell you no, it does not. I bought the game even though I've never even heard about it. It was on sale, I like RPGs so I thought I'd give it a shot.
The first thing I've noticed or rather heard were the familiar voices from other RPGs. It was great to hear Canderous Ordo from SW: Knights of the Old Republic who gave voice to Agarth. Also you can hear Cullen's voice from DA: Origins. I've figured out more names when I was playing it but I've forgotten most of them now, it was a nice surprise though.
I like the open world, and man it's huge! I've played ~100h and I still haven't discovered every location. Also, each location has different environment which is good because it doesn't get boring (well maybe except caves which are all similar).
The story isn't the best point in the game, the beginning is enough to get you intrigued about it but when I found out the truth I was a bit disappointed. However, a good thing was that I enjoyed every moment that led me to finishing the story. The gameplay is very good, I found it easier to play using controller, but sometimes I found it frustrating that you can only map 4 skills. However, if  you have a good feel of your character and combat it shouldn't be a big problem. Another thing that I absolutely loved about it is the possibility of mixing the skills from all trees which allows to make some interesting hybrids. It's a feature that isn't very common in RPGs.
I've found some things that were frustrating for me, for example sometimes when you have a boss fight the camera behaves weirdly, and you don't see the enemy. You just have to move your character to an open space but it's annoying if it happens often. Another things is that, you have to go everywhere on foot. Yes, there is fast travel, but the areas are pretty big and sometimes I wish they've added some mounts. Sometimes it seemed to me I've spent more time walking than fighting...And, one other thing - MORE ALYN SHIR!!! I mean seriously, she was the most interesting character out of all of them and you only interact with her a few times...such a shame. Don't get me wrong, Agarth was quite cool too but...ALYN SHIR!! What can I say, I just love her voice.
When it's on sale again, don't think twice about it, just buy it!
Edit (June 2015): I've just started to play this game again and man, the camera really sucks. You'll die more times because of it than because of your skill, it can get really annoying.

Gunz 2 tries to re-invent the original Gunz so many years ago, and succeeds,  in both good ways and bad. The Korean game developer has created a somewhat fun game to play, that is burdened with a few heavy problems, mostly related to the economy of the game.
The visuals, combat, and smoothness of the game have all been improved, but it still maintains some of the bigger problems most F2P games are trying to move out of these days.
The premium weapons and gear are simple much better than what you get without, and in a versus match, that is not exactly pleasant for those not spending the cash. Also, for those that do go and pay premium, items have time limits restrictions such as a day or two or hours.
The game also removes the versatiltiy of the original gunz, the ability to really make your own character and playstyle. Gunz 2 offers some very nice classes, that all play differently and have some nice voice actros backing them. The issue is you get one type of loadout, an example is one character has a sword, SMG, and a sniper rifle, and that is IT. You can upgrade them to various versions, however you cannot change your characters playstyle at all. There are 4 to choose from.
The grahpics are outdated to todays standards, but anyone who played the original gunz knows this is intentional as they want it to run on as many machines as possible.
There is one new feature that really makes this more enjoyable than the original in one way. They added skills. As you level up you will unlock a few different skills that can be used in battle, allowing you to roundhouse kick people, perform parry-attack counters, etc....
To sumamrize:
The Good:
-Improved visuals, gameplay performance
-Fluid combat, fun to use swords and guns
-More user friendly than original in some ways
-Addition of skills and mission modes with boses adds more variety than the original had
The Bad:
-Premium items are more powerful than their non premium counterparts
-Premium items have time limitations so you have to keep buying them.
-Time related items
-Heavy balance issues
-Hits and such do not feel very satisfying
-non premium users can upgrade their limited weapon selection, however they do not have many choices right now.
-They took away the custom playstyles of the original and force you into 1 of four catagories instead. You can no longer use the guns and melee weapons you like, you have to choose one of these 4 presets instead.
-The korean company has been known to ban people for silly reasons, AND I DEFEND MOST COMPANIES WHEN THEY BAN, but this company actually banned people because they got caught in bugs in early access and couldn't get out, like wall bugs and such. You fix them, you don't ban people unless they are openly exploiting...
-Early access game, but already has hacks out on the net.
-The game is simply an improved version of the old one, with better combat, but less of the things that made the original great.
-When characters die and such, there are only foru and they all seem to only have one voice line for thigns. So in a death match all you hear is like "UGHH I'm not done yet" CONSTANTLY lol.
-Melee combat is just a cluttered stun fest
-the game lags upon death
6/10, the game is good and playable and the new skills are cool, the power of premium, lack of custom playstyles, and few upgrade options make it not the best game on the market.

I've had this game since day 1 early access. What seems like a very promising game turns out to be just a little bland.
+ Building in this game is really fun and if I had tons of time, I'd be making huge castles and mansions. Even the most basic houses I've made look great. If there's anything to take away from this review, it's that I heavily enjoy the building aspect of this game. Unfortunately the game gives you 0 reason to build anything neat besides just for show.
- The combat is very slow and clunky. There also isn't much variety. I'd really like it reworked to be more active, so for now it's just a spam of left clicks with occasional dodging. Stats, skills, and gear customization are promising, but right now need to be improved.
- The core of the game gets pretty stale fast. Searching for portals and mining for materials can only take you so far. I'm a patient player so I don't mind the material grinding, but running through extremely similar islands over and over looking for portals gets old.
- The UI also really needs to be improved. Going through inventory and chests is a big pain. This normally wouldn't be a problem, but this game has a lot of loot so organization is a huge chore.
+ The devs in my experience are great. They offer a lot of community surveys and have a good idea of what the community wants. I've probably participated in all of them. They've updated the game with a lot of those wants in mind. My only issue is that content updates don't really come often enough and when they do they are rather small. I do hope they keep up the good work.
Overall I had fun with Portal Knights. I definitely got my money's worth, but at the time of this review I don't think it's something people need to get immediately. I think the game needs a good amount of tweaks and extra content before I can recommend it to my friends. Don't get me wrong though, this game has a great base, but when I think of sandbox games I think of playing and coming back anytime to mess around. Sadly I don't feel that way with Portal Knights with the current content that is available. More updates are to come however and I'll gladly change my recommendation if I think it deserves it.

has a very good reason for requiring you to use a controller; it is a single player game where you control two characters. The control scheme is very simple on paper: the older brother moves with the left analog stick and interacts with the left trigger, and the younger brother moves with the right analog stick and interacts with the right trigger. In reality it is very easy to get them mixed up, especially when the older brother ends up to the right of the younger brother. Luckily any time there is a puzzle element that requires each brother to be in a particular spot, the younger brother is almost always to the left of the older brother.
The puzzles almost always involve the two brothers working together, and more often than not they utilize each of their unique skill sets. For example older brother can pull heavy levers, and younger brother can slip through narrow bars. The puzzles are usually not very difficult to figure out, and very rarely are they a test of the player's finesse. This means that from a gameplay point of view,
is entirely counting on its unique core concept. Luckily it is a short game (about three hours) so the novelty does not have time to wear off.
The story is another strong point. Everyone in the game speaks a fictional language, which leaves only the character's body language and tone of voice to convey their message. The result is that you usually have a vague idea of what they are saying, but a very clear impression of the emotions they are feeling. The brothers' journey begins when their father falls ill and they have to travel to a presumably magical tree to retrieve an antidote. On the way they encounter many people and creatures both magical and mundane. A lot of time they need help of some sort, and the brothers come to their aid. Some of these are required to progress through the linear game, but others can be found just off the beaten path. It is worth noting that none of the achievements are awarded for progressing through the main story, but none of them are very difficult to get.
The writers attempted a few plot twists, but for the most part I saw them coming a long way away. There were some genuinely sweet moments, and some that took my breath away. My favorite was the hang glider flight, which was delightful. It felt like the cumulation of the wonder found in the world, and the musical crescendo was the most memorable in the game.
I encountered a couple of bugs that involved certain events not triggering properly or the enemy AI failing to react to the brothers properly. Both were solved by restarting the game. The most amusing bug was the fact that half the text in the credits was cut off my first time through. None of these were crippling issues.
takes a unique idea and uses its novelty to great effect. It also does not overstay its welcome, ending before things get stale. Reasonable price: $10.

First and foremost, I love and support Rooster Teeth. Their animations series of RWBY really inspired me into starting my own animation series. I hope you guys find this review to be helpful at least in some way.
Now before you read my review, take in consideration that this 'is' an early access game, meaning there will be bugs/glitches/game crashes that will happen.
Small details about the game to those new to it:
RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a hack and slash type game that has similar properties to Dynasty Warriors. However, I find Grimm Eclipse to be set at a faster pace. Each character has their own move sets and combos that can be difficult to land at first due to how fast paced this game can get, but it's not at all difficult to master in the long run.
Gameplay:
As I stated earlier, it is a rather fast paced game when it comes to attacking. Landing the full combos on the grimm were difficult at first, but it was better after practicing. You are able to easily control the direction you are attacking, and inputing the commands are very accurate to the point where you can expertly execute some skillful moves if you practice enough.
When you load into the game, you are limited to doing a certain amount of missions. Once you complete the entire campaign, you get the choice to restart it again, but your level will reset to one. The upside is, you can still complete the challenges for certain skills since they carry over. The downside is having to constantly level up who you play as every time. Of course, it is an early access game.
Scenary/graphics:
The environment looks beautiful, and the graphics are just like in the animation series.
PROS:
-The voice acting in this game is always enjoyable
-It's just simply amazing that a RWBY game came out. I encourage anyone who's a fan to play this
-Even if you solo the entire campaign, the difficulty setting is just right
-The controls are easy to use and master
-The gameplay is enjoyable; especially it being co-op
CONS:
Once again, this game is in early access. I'm sure a lot of improvements will be made in the future. These are just my personal CONS of the game.
-There are several spots in certain areas where the invisible walls shouldn't be. It takes away from the "exploration" part of the level in my opinion.
-The missions are currently very liniar, and do not involve much of area exploration(yes, finding the artifacts involved 'some' level of exploration, but even the artifacts seemed to be located at obvious dead ends)
-The game does crash occasionally in its early access stage. However, I've noticed it crashing only after performing the same move several times too fast or when another player does something similar
-The connection to other players severely lags the grimm creatures, and finishing combos on them becomes more difficult
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone; especially those of you who are fans of RWBY.
