As the game is now, I cannot categorically recommend it. However, this is mostly due to the simple fact that it is an Early Access game, and as such is not yet finished. As such, this IS a positive review with the caveat of EA, aimed at both potential buyers and providing feedback for the devs.
As it stands, the game has a lot of promise and I think it will be highly enjoyable once it is complete. As a spectacle fighter it's definitely enjoyable, but it does get old quite quickly at the moment. The combat system plays well and feels decently broad, albeit a little shallow. I haven't tried out all the RWBY girls yet, but they seem sufficiently distinct in playstyle. The enemies are good, though lacking variety at this point.
In short, there's a laundry list of things I hope and expect to see once the game reaches full release, and I will note a few of the most impactful here so nobody is misled:
- A full campaign. This one's a no-brainer, it should just be a matter of time. As of now, the game does not go anywhere much.
- A more responsive camera and/or a targeting system. I played with an Xbox controller, meaning I had to use the right analog stick to direct my camera, and it felt awfully clunky. Similarly, some way to snap to a target like most 3D/iso brawler games have would not go amiss.
- Depth of customisation. Each character has three special moves with two linear upgrades each, plus long-term 'achievement'-like unlocks and a small number of generic upgrades. I would love to see some more options for customising loadout as the game progresses.
- Optimisation. It's no secret that my computer is low-end, but I expect to play most games in fullscreen mode without dropping below 24 fps (gasp). This is not the case with RWBY as it stands. I am currently forced to play in 640x400 resolution in order to achieve reasonable framerates, and that's not cool -- especially for a game with relatively simple graphics. Just Cause 3, this is not.
In short, I can recommend the game as it stands only to other RWBY fans. I think some context is required to appreciate the content we have so far, as the show - and by extension, the game - relies a lot on the characters to drive it and make it interesting. I would compare it to the Legend of Korra game in this regard -- you can play it without watching the show, but you likely won't enjoy it a lot.
As a final aside, do note that a number of 'Features' listed on the store page have not yet made it into the game as of the current moment: the storyline, locations and enemies are all very bare-bones right now, I've yet to see tangible evidence of this new villain, and there are no achievements or rewards that I am able to see (with the possible exception of the 'kill 300 Grimm with this skill to unlock a bonus upgrade' thing).

Keep in mind that this review covers the game in Early Access, and does not reflect a finished product.
The Good:
-Multiplayer funtimes
-Characters feel faithful to the series
-Gameplay is solid and feels fluid
-Challenges to unlock new variations to skills and traits, and progress to unlocking new traits is saved between games
-Art style is faithful, and the game itself looks great
The Bad:
-Every character has at least two Chargeable traits for their skills, which feels like lazy design
-Characters don't quite seem to be very well balanced, but this just might be my interpretation. Ruby felt way too strong early on compared to the rest of the characters.
-There doesn't seem to be a camera reset fuction, although I just might not be seeing it.
-Enemy variety is somewhat lacking, and their attack patterns are very restricted - granted, the show itself hasn't introduced a huge variety of monsters, but the game could take advantage and make new ones.
The Ideas:
Ruby - Increase dodge distance and speed, but give her longer recovery in return. Damage seems to be extremly high in comparison to the rest of the cast as well.
Weiss - Would love to see more done with her glyphs, as she could be a potential support character. Glyphs could be used to speed up allies, slow enemies, etc. As of now, she seems to have only one support trait
Blake - Blake seems fine for now, although there doesn't seem to be anything done with the ribbon on her weapon, so she could potentially use that to get around the map more, or use it in conjunction with a teammate for combo-attacks.
Yang - Yang seems to be the tankier of the characters, but not by much. From my experience, she doesn't seem to have her Semblance, where she gets stronger the less health she has (Although it might just be locked and I haven't unlocked it yet) If it's not in the game, this would be the main thing to add in.
Special Perk Diversity - As of now, almost every special has one 'Hold Button to Charge' perk. I personally would rather have a more diverse selection of perks that amplify the specials in some capacity. Examples might be elemental affinity, cancel points to combo afterwards, self buffs, enemy debuffs, delayed activation, launching or stronger knockback, etc.
Combos - Most of the combat feels like 'Mash X to Win', although some do seem to be able to use their ranged attack mid-combo. I'd like to see a bit more diversity in the combo system, such as X X delay XXX to launch a rapid, multi-hitting combo, or XXY for a quick knockback combo, something to give the player more diversity and options when fighting, and to feel more involved in the fights.
Camera Reset - When playing on controller, being able to press a button and reset the character behind my player character would be an amazing option to have. PC controls might not really need one, but it would still be nice and make things much easier for bigger, more hectic fights.
Roster - Right now, the crew of Team RWBY is fine and fun, but later on down the line, I would love to see other teams added into the game. Not something major to focus on, but it would be cool.
Overall, the game is fun to play, either by yourself or with friends. There is definitely plenty of love put into the game, and it has lots of potential once it's finished. If you enjoy RWBY, you can't go wrong with this.

The game also has a strange and clunky cheap feeling to it. The cities are filled with guards who have strange psychic powers and can sense wrong doing from half a mile away. You're allowed to play good or evil and make choices in a Mass Effect like style. This is fun until you realize that your choices really don't matter much. While many seem to think Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning as a poor game (Just google its name and prepare for the hate!) it has a great storyline with a lot of action, quite a few twists and a truly unique setting.
In the world of Amalur, all living thing has a destiny, a fate. And all follow it, even if they don't know they do. Fateweavers, people who study fate for years, can see its threads and as such can tell someone else's, or their own, fate. Wether anouncing to a prisoner his imminent and unexpected release or telling a young man he will die in his prime due to an accident, what a fateweaver sees always holds true. For no one is above fate itself.
No one but you. Yep, you read that right! The player character in Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a recently diseased person brought back to life through certain experiments and their recent return to the land of the living makes them fateless. Supposed to be dead, fate holds nothing more for you. Soon, and without knowing this, you are sent to see a fateweaver. Not remembering your past life, you hope he can bring you answers. What a shock when you get there to discover that not only does fate not affect you, but YOU in fact affect fate itself! Your actions, as they are fateless, are purely up to you, and nobody can predict them. Because of this, you can change anything: Kill someone and the fate of their whole family, or even of the whole land, might change. Bought this one on a whim when it went on sale and was positively surprised by it. Some might describe it as a poor man's Dark souls mixed with MMO-like open world game where you do side-quests and events while following the main plot. And the world is big, some might even call it huge, with lots of towns, dungeons and forgotten ruins to visit, there is also lots of backstory to the world and you get a feeling of being in a magical world that is undergoing a conflit between various factions of fae, men and possibly gods. You can also just kill stuff and take their loot if exploring the world and its multitude of personal stories isnt your cup of tea.
That brings up the combat which makes up a big part of the gameplay (i suggest gamepad over m/kb) or at least so far about the only gameplay ive encountered as this game is really puzzle-lite. Not that its a bad thing as the combat is smooth and enjoyable. There have been couple of challenging fights so far, nothing impossibly frustrating, but most of the encounters resemble one-sided beatdown much more than an grueling conflict of two equally matched forces. Changing your build and gear does bring variation to the game and after trying both the mage and warrior builds i ended up with plate-wielding warrioress using spells to support her combat capabilities.
Even with its faults and simplistic gameplay Kingdoms of Amalur is an enjoyable and fun experience for those times when you need to just sit back and relax. Get it but dont expect anything too deep or revolutionary from its gameplay even if its world had potential for future (shame the developer went bankrupt).

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is the third game in the Brothers in Arms series and, in my opinion, the best. It has taken the good and the bad from the previous 2 games and vastly improved them. Better level design, the tactical map is more immersive, 2 knew additional teams to control (MG and Bazooka teams), and another amazing story told from the perspective of, now, Staff Sergeant Matthew Baker (again).
The Good:
The Hell's Highway's graphics were quite good when the game was first released and has held up reasonably well over time. The reinvisioned tactical map is incredibly immersive, and is authentic to what the Reconnaissance troops of the 101st Airborne Division would have. Killroy's are new to the series and are an interesting addition to the game, making me want to go back through each level and find all of them. Which brings up my next point: The replayability.
Hell's Highway is incredibly replayable. Before I purchased it on Steam I used to own it for my PS3 and I would play the hell out of it. Still, after many hours of playing it on the console, I continue to return to play through a few missions in the game. I continue to find new ways how to pin down German troops and outflank them either by myself or with my assault team.
The cover system is new to the series, and is a very good addition. From my experiance with Hell's Highway, and past titles in the series, the cover system has allowed me to better assess a situation and direct my troops, as well as improving my ability to engage German troops. It's always nice to get a slow motion action cam of a round from my M1 Garand going in to the skull of a Nazi.
The characters and the story of Hell's Highway are incredibly well done, with healthy amounts of character development and definition, and well done story arch with a cliffhangar of an ending. While the main theme of the story is Operation Market Garden, the actual story is about Baker dealing with PTSD from his experiances in Normandy. Baker also seems to be loosing his grip on his mind, as he contiues to see hallucinations of men that were killed in Normandy.
The Bad:
The lip syncing in the cinematic cutscenes could have be improved on, but they're not that much of an issue for me.
There's a few bugs with the AI's pathfinding abilities, and this will sometimes cause your own men to get killed, or get stuck on an object for a few seconds. It is really unimmersive and a bit of hassel, especially when you're in a firefight with huge amounts of lead going back and forth.
A few people have made complaints about the FOV, however I don't have an issue with it. But that's just me. I'm sure there are quite a few people who would have a serious problem with the FOV. Although there is a few ways to fix the FOV if you do have a problem with it, and you can easily find tutorials of this fix on the Steam community page or through a quick google search.
Overall:
Overall, I'd say this is probably one of the best damn WW2 shooters you can get. It's authentic, immersive, with great, replayable gameplay and an incredible story. The only downsides to the game would be the bugs with the AI.
So in the end I'm giving Hell's Highway a 9/10, and I would highly recommend it to anyone with an interest in WW2 shooters or squad based infantry tactics.

Simply put, this game has terrible netcode and even worse balancing.
As someone who has played the first GunZ more than any game in this generation, I was initially sad to see K-styling go, but I knew it was necessary to appeal to a new audience. I had hoped GunZ 2 had the same action packed combat even without the fancy moves of a kstyler.
It turns out I was wrong.
Not only does this game lock you into weapons depending on the character you use, some characters are so powerful you might as well not even use anyone else. Take into account the powerhouse of the game, Elena the Gunslinger. She has an assault rifle as well as a grenade launcher. The grenade launcher has a mechanic if you hit one, your target is stunned for half a second. In that time, if you shot another, it would explode right next to them - essentially being able to lock you until death. Not only that, the assault rifle has a very small cone of fire, such that you are able to shoot and dash at the same time without much repercussions. However, I had the unfortunate luck of choosing Ivan (I like scarves), and to my disdain, he uses a sniper rifle.
A sniper rifle. In a game where you're always dashing. What's worse is that his SMG is completely horrible at anything longer than twenty feet due to its ridiculous cone of fire. It requires Ivan to move in close, and even then the dashing makes it quite difficult to land consistent shots. Why would I choose Ivan's SMG when I would rather use Elena's rifle? I would love to switch it out but I can't because weapons are locked to characters. This is a shooter, not an RPG game, Maiet has done a very poor job in allowing people to play a shooter as it's fundemental core. Locking guns to a character not only creates a disparity between them, it also forces people to adopt a playstyle they may not like and have to endure insufferable games in order to afford a new one.
If that doesn't convince you not to play, then the netcode will. The most pathetic thing is that the first GunZ had a BETTER netcode than this one. Sure, you had to lead your shots - but the character models were smooth and did not teleport. In this game, it assigns a host that people connect to. If any game does this as a shooter, they are bound to fail. This is not 2007, the only viable way to design shooters is having all players use CLIENT-SIDE netcode. If the host is bad, everyone suffers EXCEPT THE HOST. This game doesn't even have dedicated servers. Players rubber band, I end up hitting ghosted targets and the host gets away with having fifteen kills while I can barely hit anything with the latency and my cruddy SMG.
For those who would argue this is an Early Access... the game has been out in Korea and EU for nearly a year. Even if they fix the netcode, the balance will be still absolutely horrible. I search up videos of GunZ 2 in korea and I barely see any Ivans. If its taken them this long and nothing has happened to the game, you can expect it to happen again here on Steam. Any balance done to the game has to go through Korea first, and from my experience with past games they have a very poor track record in doing balance patches.
I am really disappointed in Maiet, and I hope this gets taken off of Steam. I rarely get frustrated to the point I uninstall a video game, and its incredibly saddening I have to do so with my childhood game. Pathetic. Just absolutely pathetic. Do yourself a favour and do not play this game. It's charm of running on walls and chaining sword and gunstrikes loses it's charm very quickly... unless you play Elena.
This game has much potential. Looking forward to growing with this game and learning new styles. Although I wish the dash was how they showed it in EU servers. Makes it look way more responsive.

You know what? As a person who generally doesn't really "do" visual novels, once I got past some of the more fan-servicy bits and the occasional sloppy translation ("huts like hell..."), I think that this actually has a really engrossing story. So here I am, giving it a positive review. I know, I'm shocked, too.
Edit: Finished the game and liked it enough to make a mini-review video (no spoilers):

I had heard of visual novels and how fun some of them could be, but I was blown away at how epic the story was. I had run into the original story of the 47 Ronin during a research project for an English class, and I really liked how this game took the story and made it where the characters and their personalities could be related to. The main game with the Chamberlain route was fun, and gave a great preview of the full story, but if you want to get the most enjoymentof out this game, I highly recommend getting the DLCs for Chapters 2&3, as well for Chapters 4&5. The story's twists and turns will keep you on your toes for what will happen next (like it did for me!). The story is nice and linear, but there is one instance in Ch. 3 (spoiler alert!) where you make a choice. Once again, I HIGHLY recommend this game to both people who have played visual novels, and to people like me who have heard of them, but never played one.

I was expecting a game more like Terraria or Creativerse or any other block builder, but Portal Knight is a bit different in that you don't actually need to build stuff and dig deep. At the beggining you create a "Universe" composed of 42 worlds, and your goal is to find a portal on each world and activate it ( you need to craft specific cubes for this ) to progress. You don't spend much time on each world, don't really need to build stuff ( there are empty houses everytwhere anyway ).
Ressources seem to be widely available on or near the surface, and the worlds are just floating islands so you really can't dig deep. Caves and dungeons are mostly copy-pasted, empty and repetitive, so exploring the worlds seem boring after the first few hours.
Crafting seem nice but you either have to keep the multiple crafting stations in you backpack to put them down when you need them ( taking a lot of space ) or you'll have to create new ones each time you want to craft something.
Another thing is that everything is kinda handed to you. For example the map gives you a list of every ressource available on the world you are on, making exploration and discovery pointless. And you can craft a compass giving you the direction of the next portal to activate. And you can find coal and iron on the surface, even gems just there growing like fruits on a tree.
The classes are totally unbalanced, at least from I've seen. The mage feel weak and requires rare stuff to craft gear that you can't find on the forst worlds. The warrior uses melee weapons with a really short range and seem to miss often. The ranger on the other hand is totally OP, killing everything at range with ease.
As an example, my level 6 mage had a fireball ( you don't have it at the beginning you have to craft the spell ) dealing 44 damage. With several seconds of cooldown. And it takes like 1/4 of your mana. So that's not really powerful and mostly useless in combat. On the other hand, the first bow you can craft for the archer deals 41 damage per arrow, and shoots like two arrows per second, so that's 82 constant dps, plus the crit hits, with no need to reload, no cooldown, and no need for ammo ( infinite arrows ). How is that even remotely balanced ? The mage has to rely on weak weapons and long cooldown spells while the archer can just shoot arrows from afar and destroy everything.
To sum it up, the game might have a really cool art style, but it kinda seem to lack anything that makes other games of the genre interesting. Short and sweet. That's how I would describe this game. It had unexpected twists with satisfying pay-offs and didn't cross into the realm of predictable, Disney-esque storylines. The music is enthralling, especially when paired with the cutscenes showing off vast stretches of places you're going to and later, the places you came from.
I praise whoever worked on the cinematography and camera, as well as the director. From beginning to end, it is easy to see that a lot of care went into the details, especially with regards to the vistas you can view from benches and the angles around which the story unfolds. Everything you need to see is shown exactly the way the creators intended you to see it.
If you want to see how powerful a game can be as a storytelling medium, give this game a go.

Never Alone, and Journey.
The two boy's mother died drowning which made the little brother afraid of water and unable to swim. Now the father of the two brothers is deathly ill with... something. You must go off on an adventure to go fetch something from a giant tree (possibly tree of life) which will heal your father. Team work is everything. Each anologue stick and trigger on the controller will control a brother and his actions.
The puzzle solving is very intuitive. The graphics create a truly breath taking environment at nearly every junction of the game. The brothers truly depend on one another during your travels.
Without voice acting and a larger variety of music I found it very difficult to feel the emotional impact of the journey that they were clearly aiming for. You can't help but feel it is a waste to have such great scenes and no real reason to stick around them other then to look from a bench that is provided for you...? Side quests for NPCs you meet along the way would have given you the time to enjoy  the view while engaging in the world.
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a highly atmospheric and unique game that falls short by missing out on a few features that would have allowed you to engage more in the world. Even when this game ended and appeared all emotional i was left not caring because I never felt like I was part of it. Still the game is quite beautiful and the puzzles are simple yet clever.
The game itself doesn't really have replay value and it is only three hours long. I suggest the value to be about $3.50 for it sadly.

After that I could best describe the game as a whirlwind of adventure meets beauty as you traverse multiple areas in search of a specific place to save your father.
Storyline, characters, and design. I give it all 2 enthusiastic thumbs up and highly recommend to everyone to play. It is worth the time and money.
This game punched me in the feels. 10/10 would feel again.
If you are a gamer who is upset about the state of video games because they no longer move you, then you should play Brothers.

The War of 1812 was a military conflict that lasted from June 18, 1812 to February 18, 1815, fought by the United States of America against Great Britain, its North American colonies, and its North American Indian allies. Historians in the United States and Canada see it as a war in its own right, but Europeans sometimes see it as a minor theatre of the Napoleonic Wars, as it was caused by issues related to that war (especially the Continental System). By the war's end in early 1815 the key issues had been resolved and peace came with no boundary changes.
The United States declared war for several reasons, including trade restrictions brought about by the British war with France, the impressment of as many as 10,000 American merchant sailors into the Royal Navy,[5] British support for Native American tribes fighting American settlers on the frontier, outrage over insults to national honor during the Chesapeake–Leopard Affair, and possible American interest in annexing British territory.[6] The primary British war goal was to defend their North American colonies, although they also hoped to set up a neutral Indian buffer state in the Midwest.
The war was fought in three theatres. First, at sea, warships and privateers of each side attacked the other's merchant ships, while the British blockaded the Atlantic coast of the United States and mounted large raids in the later stages of the war. Second, land and naval battles were fought on the U.S.–Canadian frontier. Third, large-scale battles were fought in the Southern United States and Gulf Coast. At the end of the war, both sides signed and ratified the Treaty of Ghent and, in accordance with the treaty, returned occupied land, prisoners of war and captured ships (though neither side returned the other's warships due to frequent re-commissioning upon capture) to its pre-war owner and resumed friendly trade relations without restriction.
With the majority of its land and naval forces tied down in Europe fighting the Napoleonic Wars, the British used a predominantly defensive strategy in the Provinces of Upper and Lower Canada. Early victories over poorly-led U.S. armies, such as in the Battle of Queenston Heights, demonstrated that the conquest of the Canadas would prove more difficult than anticipated. Despite this, the U.S. was able to inflict serious defeats on Britain's Native American allies, ending the prospect of an Indian confederacy and an independent Native American state in the Midwest under British sponsorship. U.S. forces were also able to make several gains and score victories on the Canadian frontier; taking control of Lake Erie in 1813, seizing western parts of Upper Canada. However, a large-scale U.S. attempt to capture Montreal was repulsed in November 1813. Despite the major U.S. victory at Chippawa on July 5, 1814, serious U.S. attempts to fully conquer Upper Canada were ultimately abandoned following the bloody Battle of Lundy's Lane on July 25, 1814. The U.S. then fell back roughly 30 km (19 mi) from Lundy's Lane to Fort Erie, where they withstood a siege for several months. The British eventually withdrew, but as winter set in, the Americans demolished the fort and fell back across the Niagara.
In April 1814, with the defeat of Napoleon, the British adopted a more aggressive strategy, sending larger invasion armies and tightening their naval blockade. However, with the end of the Napoleonic Wars in Europe, both governments were eager for a return to normality and peace negotiations began in Ghent in August 1814. In the Deep South, General Andrew Jackson destroyed the military strength of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend. In September 1814, the British won the Battle of Hampden, allowing them to occupy eastern Maine, and the British victory at the Battle of Bladensburg in August 1814 allowed them to capture and burn Washington, D.C. They were repulsed, however, in an attempt to take Baltimore and Fort Bowyer, and during their assault at Fayal. An American victory in September 1814 at the Battle of Plattsburgh repulsed the British invasions of New York, which, along with pressure from merchants on the British government, prompted British diplomats to drop their demands at Ghent for an independent native buffer state and territorial claims that London previously sought. Given that it took six weeks for ships to cross the Atlantic, news of the peace treaty did not arrive before the British suffered a major defeat at New Orleans in January 1815.[7]
In the United States, late victories over invading British armies at the battles of Plattsburg, Baltimore (inspiring the United States national anthem, "The Star-Spangled Banner") and New Orleans produced a sense of euphoria over a "second war of independence" against Britain.[8][9] The war ended on a high note for Americans, winning the final engagements of the war and bringing an "Era of Good Feelings" in which partisan animosity nearly vanished in the face of strengthened American nationalism. The war was also a major turning point in the development of the U.S. military. The poor performance of several U.S. militia units, particularly during the 1812–13 invasions of Canada and the 1814 defence of Washington, convinced the U.S. government of the need to move away from its Revolutionary-era reliance on militia and focus on creating a more professional regular force. Spain was involved in fighting in Florida but was not an official belligerent; some Spanish forces fought alongside the British during the Occupation of Pensacola. The U.S. took permanent ownership of Spain's Mobile District.
In Upper and Lower Canada, British and local Canadian militia victories over invading U.S. armies became iconic and promoted the development of a distinct Canadian identity, which included strong loyalty to Britain. Today, particularly in Ontario, memory of the war retains its significance, because the defeat of the invasions ensured that the Canadas would remain part of the British Empire, rather than be annexed by the United States. In Canada, numerous ceremonies took place in 2012 to commemorate the war, offer historical lessons and celebrate 200 years of peace across the border.[10] The conflict has not been commemorated on nearly the same level in the modern-day United States, though it is still taught as an important part of early American history,[11] and Dolley Madison's and Andrew Jackson's respective roles in the war are especially emphasized.[12][13] The war is scarcely remembered in Britain, being heavily overshadowed by the much larger Napoleonic Wars occurring in Europe.

Havn't felt compelled to write a Steam review until this game. Most games don't surprise me too much anymore. We know about their release usually as soon as they're announced at E3. So any game i want I'm usually following its development and ready for it to come out or go on sale. However this one snuck up on me.
I've been a fan of fighting games since MvC2. Got into Street Fighter after that then that eventually spiraled into Mortal Kombat and Injustice when Street Fighter took a nose dive. Well this is by far the best out of them all. At least when it comes to fighting. I think that Neatherealm has them beat on the campaign aspect. However the actual gameplay of this game is near perfection.
It starts with the Netcode and FPS near flawless most every match after they did the update rollback. The mechanics for every fighter are unque. Sure theres a few OP Tekken players or people that take advanage of King but they are few and far between. Because the community is awesome. Already. Which is also a feat.
The developers showed they cared when they made this game. They showed they still care and listen when they did that update rollback 9 hours later. With all that being said I think this game and Tekken in general have avery bright future. We have a knew King of Fighting Games (At least until that DBZ fighters game releases).

Such a surprising amount of fun.
I had a grand time roaming this game world; makes me sad that it did not win over more people. This could have been the start of a new, worthwhile franchise.
And that is probably what the developers were banking on. The troubles of 38 Studios is a tale of big ambitions that did not work out.
But about the game: This is very much an action-RPG. Your choices  along the way do not drastically reshape the overall end result. Mostly your are improving your gear, gaining new skills, grabbing loot.
And that can be enough for some. If you want a game that dynamically branches based on your choices, this is not the game. Because this game was not trying to be the next Mass Effect, Fallout, or Witcher.
Dare I say this is more casual fun than a hardcore game?
Yes, you can spend hundreds of hours playing in this world, as I have, pursuing all the side quests (and there are LOTS) before advancing the main plot. But the level of detail is not as refined as certain other games. This is not Skyrim.
Yet, not being Skyrim is also a good thing. I would have stopped playing early on if it was just a rehash if what Skyrim was. Amalur gave me a fresh landscape to enjoy.
I will miss certain quirky characters, one in particular who made me laugh every time she spoke. Maybe if they had embraced more of that humor, this could have sold better when it was released.
So what are the downsides? What are the problems?
Weird camaera angle shifts. If you are fighting on an incline such as a hill, you may suddenly see the perspective change and no longer can see what you are doing. Same thing may happen when you come to a corner in a hallway. It's sporadic and exposes some of the flaws in the coding.
In some dialogue scenes, the camera angle is effected again. You might end up looking at grass or a hedge that obscures the person you are talking to. Yeah...
The environment can feel really sparse and vacant. There are HUGE rooms, caverns, and fields that seem deviod of life. I understand, it's a trade off for sake of game performance, but you may wish some of the environments were scaled smaller so they were not so empty.
As your character gets closer to max level (40), the battles become extremely easy. Like god mode easy. Once I crafted armor with the best possible material within the game, I barely took any damage from my enemies. Your weapons and powers become so deadly most enemies drop within one or two strikes. As I got to the end game, I just ran straight at groups of enemies just to amuse myself. They could still knock me back, but the damage was nil.
Definitely buy this whenever there is a Steam sale. Get the complete version with all the DLC.

Okay now that I can actually get into the game, it's time to give it a fair review.
GunZ 2: The Second Duel is the successor to the fast-paced third person shooter GunZ, which was by far one of the best experiences I've had with shooters. GunZ is a very unique game which requires good positioning, dodging, and accuracy. Now with GunZ 2, there are many changes from the first game, both good and bad.
Before I begin, I am neutral on the removal of K-Style, I believe that it both helped and killed the game, creating elitism where people were making "smurfs" and just completely obliterating the new players. I believe it is what killed the community, and it was a decent idea by Maiet to remove this ability. However, one of the best parts of K-style was the incredible pace that your character was able to move at. It was absolutely amazing to be able to slash shot from wall to wall while shooting people. It gave such an "epic pro" feeling. Also, it made sword fights and 1v1s amazingly fun, where it was a competition of whoever could position themselves best, and making one single mistake lead to your demise. In the end, I believe that Maiet's decision to get rid of Kstyle certainly does improve the community and help new players ease in, while also reducing the speed and pacing of fights. Now time to carry onto what I believe they did well and didn't do well in.
What I believe they did well with.
1, The gun play and accuracy is much, much, MUCH better and smoother than GunZ was, where in GunZ  it was only viable to use shotguns and SOMETIMES pistols due to the difficulties with aiming with other weapons (Renards cough).
2. Sort of branching off of the first point, the amazing amount of diversity in weapon choice. With the new class system that Maiet created, you can now choose certain weapon kits that fit your playstyle. For example, if you feel that you want to be a tank initiator, Shield Trooper is your man. I feel this is one of the redeeming features for why GunZ 2 is amazing, since in the predecessor, everyone was using the exact same weapon kits with little variety (Maybe someone will use a breaker 7 instead of 8 or something...)
3. The pace of the game. In addition with GunZ 2's new lobby match making system, you're going to be able to join and finish a game within 5 to 10 minutes no problem due to the extremely fast pace that it moves in, which I believe is what makes GunZ amazing. Who wants to play a slow game anyways?
4. The leveling system. I don't know if I'm remembering correctly or not, but it felt like MILLENIUMS to level up in GunZ, it surely took me a while to be able to wear my sexy brown trench coat..
5. The Interface and lobby. It feels that one of Maiet's focuses was to make some quality of life changes to social aspects of the game, where now you can have tabs to chat with friends and your clan, with a public lobby where you can chat up and meet new people!
6. PvE! I wasn't much of a PvE'er in GunZ, but from what I remember it was pretty decent, but needed those materials in order to increase the difficulty, which I personally did not enjoy. With GunZ 2 now, we have an entire campaign mode for PvE, which includes difficult bosses and hordes of enemies. I'm currently on season 1 (I don't know if it goes further?) but I'm assuming that there are more seasons to come :)
7. Tumbling. Nobody, and I mean nobody, liked tumbling. Theres always that moment where you trying to slash shot while dashing and accidently tumble into 3 people just waiting for you with rocket launchers. The removal of tumbling is definitely a good move by Maiet, it improves the viability of using ranged weapons and sets melee weapons down a peg. But maybe by too much.
What I feel they didn't do as well in
1. One of the parts of the game that I am most disappointed with personally is the dashing. The speed of dashing is worlds different compared to the first game. In GunZ, you were able to dash like crazy, moving at an extremely fast pace which increased the difficulty of getting hit, and hitting your target. This is what made GunZ so much fun for me, the fast paced action where you need spot on accuracy in order to win, while also managing your character's location and trying to dodge according to where they shoot.
2. The synergy between your weapons! Where is it?! GunZ is meant to be a fast pace shooter, which means that it is essential to be able to synergize your attacks and be able to react quickly to the situation. In the predecessor GunZ, you were able to switch weapons at extreme speeds, where people often used two shotguns, two pistols, or a mix of the two, to switch between the guns to achieve a faster firing rate. I think that it was what made it so important to choose which weapons you want to use. Now in GunZ 2, when you're in a fire fight, you're basically stuck to using one weapon until the enemy needs to reload or you are able to run and hide. This is extremely offputting to me, and it gives off the "Spray and Pray" kind of play style that I personally hate.
3. Stagger, stagger, stagger, stagger. I am Ivan. But seriously, the stagger given off from melee weapons is just ridiculous. It now makes it so that you are screwed once somebody is within melee range of you because of the extremely slow weapon swap speed, and how it cuts out your attack animation completely. I feel that it should let you continue shooting, but making your screen shake so they don't just get nuked in the face once they get near you.
4. Wall climbing. I personally enjoyed the epicness of running against the wall and shooting at somebody down the hallway in Mansion. However, with the removal of slashing the wall to climb, it seems now you're in such a vulnerable situation if you ever want to climb the walls. It certainly screams out "SHOOT ME IN THE♥♥♥♥♥quot; while you climb to the next floor in Mansion. I believe the system of dashing + slashing up the wall should have stayed.
5. Lobbies. I personally HATE the CoD matching making system where you are simply randomly placed with other players with no choice. This is limiting the freedom that us players have by not allowing us to have our own rules and what not (Attack and Defend anybody?). It also means that... gulp... random host. I'm sure that if any of you have been playing for at least an hour or two, you have run into that one extremely laggy host who uses it to their advantage. I'm talking about that time where everyone is at 999 ping, teleporting everywhere, while the host is racking up kills faster than an AC-130 in CoD.

6. Last but not least, the lacking of character customization. By this I mean different character faces, facial features, body types, etc. I expected a greater amount of customization out of GunZ 2, where you can change your features similar to how most MMORPGs do it. This is probably not one of their highest priorities, but it would certainly be nice to look different than the thousands of the other people playing Rena.
To wrap this up, I think that overall GunZ 2 is an improvement from GunZ, and it feels that it will stay alive for much longer, as long as Maiet continues to update the game with new game modes. I'm really hoping they bring back a swords only game mode, and introduce a community workshop to allow new costumes to be introduced :)

This game, upon its release, was shabby and I was eager to give it lots of breathing time to update and polish. After a couple of years now, it's clear Rockstar decided to take a very poor direction. This game is anti-consumer.

I finished the story with one character, and didn't like it as much as I had hoped I would. If you are into these games more than I am you'll probably have a blast with it, as it is solid enough. I had no bad time with it, but it could have been better. I thought it was a real Diablo killer or something, as I had heard people glorify it this way, but in the end I had a mixed feeling of "Yeah, ok, cool" and "Meh...". If you like looting a lot you'll love this game since enemies usually drop a whole lot of stuff to wade through, and there is a fair amount of item variations to go through. There are some interestingly designed creatures in this game which may strike one similarily impressive as for example Tyrael in Diablo would, but you don't really get to know too much about them (or the world itself) and the story as well as the level/area progression is far from being creative and innovative. It's your typical good vs. evil-stuff drawn long enough to make you go through some rather typical "forest - desert - ice/tundra (?) - volcano" level scheme. I don't remember 100 %, but they sure were following Diablo very closely when they made this game.
What sort of ruined the experience to me was the sheer visual overkill on the screen. I was playing alone mostly, with a character class called "Outlander" (dealing ranged damage with guns), and at least with the skill and weapon combo I was using there were explosions all over my screen when I was fighting mobs. If I want to get headaches while gaming this may be great, but I just didn't see the need or appeal in this. I had hard times knowing where mobs where left and what was going on. Luckily I played on an average difficulty where it didn't really matter too much but where spamming gunshots roughly at the direction the mobs were coming from proved to be enough for most times. I don't want to imagine the overkill had I played with more people online even.
And I want to mention this too, though I usually refrain from commenting graphics as such: This game looks a bit... awful technically. It has a rather coherent style, but this style incorporates low-res textures from what a layman like me can tell. It's World of Warcraft in the shoes of Diablo visually-wise. Nothing to write home about, really, though there were some nice pre-game lobby screens showing that you can still give a hint of good ambiance without high-res FPS graphics. But in the end this doesn't really go over into the game as it is a top-down ARPG with whole lots of mobs to slay, loot to swim in, stats to calculate and effects to look at but nothing really all-too-unique.
If I have the choice I would still go with Path of Exile. PoE is a Diablo clone too, but has more unique and impressive aspects, an overall better and more creative story, bombards my screen with less effects and is even free-to-play. The only thing that someone may rate higher with TL2 is that it apparently allows for extensive modding. But I've never tried any mods and don't like the idea of taking community-created content into reviews as I believe games should be rated initially by how they look in their "vanilla"/"stock" state (an engaging, creative fanbase should not make up for the lack of what developers do).

Hell's Highway is a game with a solid gameplay experience, an interesting narrative, and some glaring faults.
As a direct sequel to the first game in the Brothers in Arms series Hell's Highway follows newly-promoted Staff Sergeant Matt Baker and his unit  through the Netherlands during Operation Market Garden. Baker's sanity wanes due to the contention of his men, rumors of a haunted pistol, and the memories of friends lost.
The combat in HH holds to the tradition of the earlier titles in the series, while adding additional squads and features. Flanking and diversionary tactics are vital, as running into the open while an enemy fires upon Baker or his squad will result in a quick death.
However, Hell's Highway is a game that needs some fixing to enjoy. For anyone like myself who gets headaches or feels sick at a lower field of view, here's different methods of how to counter the horrid default setting.
--------------
Method 1:
A simple binding to toggle the fov. This will change the fov when pressed, but will zoom out cutscenes, break sniper scopes, and disable zooming in when aiming.
Go to your "Documents\My Games\BIA Hells Highway\SumacGame\Config" folder and open "SumacInput.ini" in a text editor.
under the"[Engine.PlayerInput]" section add the following.
Bindings=(Name="KEY",Command="fov DESIREDFOV",Control=False,Shift=False,Alt=False)
Method 2:
Changing the action of the zoom hold command to change the fov. The fov will lower when aiming to zoom in, then zoom out to your desired standard fov on release. This will also zoom out cutscenes and break sniper scopes. I suggest a zoom fov of 60, and a standard fov of 100.
Under "[Engine.InputActionDefinition]" in SumacInput.ini look for the line that starts with "Actions=(Id=IA_ZoomHold,Alias...".
Change the line to, "Actions=(Id=IA_ZoomHold,Alias=".ZOOMHOLD",Names=("Zoom"),Command="ZoomIn | fov DESIREDZOOMFOV | OnRelease ZoomOut | OnRelease DESIRED DEFAULT FOV")"
Other tips:
Creating a bind similar to the bind shown in method 1 set to "fov 63" will set cutscenes close to what they look like normally.
In the "[SystemSettings]" section of "SumacEngine.ini" you can pump up the graphics. I suggest setting "EnableHighPolyChars=False" to "True" and fiddling around with the MSAA.
-------------
Like Far Cry 2, Syndicate, and Rage a good game is held back by stupid issues that can be solved with a few simple tweaks. I enjoy fixing issues in PC ports, so I may be biased, but Hell's Highway is one of my favorite games of the last eight years.

Torchlight II, in my opinion, is the pinnacle of the hack'n'slash ARPG genre. The graphics are great, with a colorful but still dark feel to them, and are pretty hi-res. The class system is completely innovative; instead of being stuck wielding one or two types of weapons, every class can wield every weapon in the game. (There are some unique-level class specific armors, though.) The skill tree is solid, with balanced abilities and special attacks that can be a whole lot of fun to unleash. Sending pools of flame rippling across the floor while casting down bolts of hypercharged lightning feels pretty epic. The difficulty is pretty balanced, unless you go for the highest difficulty setting on Hardcore mode. You might rage a few times with that. The story is intriguing; the Alchemist, portrayed as the "Big Bad Guy" , has a good amount of depth. As you uncover his journals, he doesn't seem malevolent, and you almost feel sorry for him. He never seems to do anything unnecessarily cruel, and he just seems misguided. In his plan for healing himself of the Ember Blight, he even apologizes to the Guardians when taking their power. (Note that I'm not all the way through the game; some other plot element may be revealed that shows a darker side of him.) For the cons, I'm really nitpicking; some bosses have obnoxious levels of health (I'm talking to you, Eldrayn), and when the game forces you to grind, you have to really go out of your way; enemies don't respawn. But for this caliber of game, $19.99 is really a steal. This is certainly one of the best, if not the best, ARPG currenly on the market

A fantastic arcade game that handles, looks and sounds just right.
The premise is very simple: crates with weapons appear on the screen, and you must collect as many as you can. Whenever you pick up a crate, you are forced to use the weapon from it to fend off hordes enemies until you lay your hands on another crate. Some weapons are overpowered, some are goofy NERF guns, some are suicidal.
At first, it feels overwhelming and nearly impossible to collect more than a few crates. But as you learn all the quirks of each weapon, enemy spawns and movement patterns, you can survive for much longer without breaking a sweat.
Every death feels "fair" in the sense that you always know how it could've been avoided.
Every attempt (which usually lasts for less than a minute as you start) you become better at the game, and the realisation of that is very satisfying.
If you're into anything arcady, by all means give it a go. It's free and just 30 Mb in size. You could've installed it and died a buncha times by the time you've reached this paragraph.

Will I say that this game is good?
Yes, yes I will.
Spelunky is definitely not for the faint of heart (For guaranteed depression, play Spelunky with the Frozlunky mod).
Spelunky is one of the hardest games I've ever played.... I can guarantee that through the enormous amounts of deaths I have...
Spelunky is heavily polished, like a Ferrari fresh out of a factory.... So no doubt is there a lack of problems to list...
Spelunky is a fun game once you understand the mechanics, once you start checking for blue frogs (Most OP enemy in the game, more than Yama), once you start realising that stealing that jetpack proably wasn't the best idea, when you start realising that dark levels are the most realistic representation of Satan in this game, when you start realising that the Damsel generally doesn't like landing on spike pits or next to tiki traps..
All of which are concepts which one will learn, over time that is....
Don't just expect to pick this game up, plug your controller in and have a fun time...
Admittidly, when I first played, I was close to throwing my controller out the window... I still am sometimes... But, after each run, I just got better and better, as I started becoming more aware of the environment (Sometimes I just became angrier and angrier). This game is plentiful in ways it wants to kill you.. Whether it be a shop keeper that you didn't anger but is angry, or a spider Tom Cruising/ Grappelling down on top of you, it is bound to happen.
Deaths are inevitable... Guaranteed... A good time is inevitable (Not guarnateed).
Long story short... It's pretty good...
I'd actually call this game one of the best indie-platformers I've played... Because it's just so.... Perfect....
P.S The only issue I could find was an issue with controllers where they start acting up. EG: My character flicks to the right every once in a while (Even if I'm holding left), but I'm sure it's just a glitch that could be easily fixed with some simple cache clearing ETC
P.P.S A personal issue I had was a weird "motion blur" effect. I'm not saying the game started becoming a Picaso of motion blurs..... What I actually mean is that the movement can actually be an eye strain, especially up close. I often find that I'm distancing myself further and further from my TV/Laptop Screen due to this strange effect. I'm not sure what actually causes it, and maybe my eyes are just stuffed or maybe it's the game messing with me....

I played a bit of this on Xbox when it came out and enjoyed it quite a bit. While it would be better for the PC if you have a controller the keyboard/mouse combo is pretty simple to use and get used to. The game itself is a little buggy on occasion but it's nothing bad (definitely not Skyrim status buggy). The storyline is fun and it's an exciting game but it doesn't have much replay value to it, even if you choose a different race. Character customization is limited but not bad. Character classes are enjoyable throughout the game, and there's a decent variety of weaponry and skills. The fateshift thing is pretty cool. You can basically dual spec. as well. The crafting skills are great. Cinematics and character/NPC interactions are entertaining. Overall I feel it would be a better game if there were different story paths, or if it were more in-depth in general to go with the amount of time it takes to complete all of the side quests + the main quest, but for the type of game it is and how it plays it's about an 8.5/10 for me.

This game is really fun, however, the real issue I have with it is that if you do most or all the side quests this game becomes too easy. You become OP on almost any difficulty and nothing is challenging which, in my opinion, is boring. So, if you get this awesome game I recommend that you only do the main quest and a few of the Guild's quests. (Warsworn, Ballads, Scholia Arcana, Travelers, etc.)

Chapter 4 however left me asleep because of everyone talking back and forth all the time. I know thats how it is in the other chapters, but in those chapters the characters talked about subjects that progressed the story. There are quite a few "Minecraft but x" games out there now, and Portal Knights is (with some caveats) probably the only one that I would recommend. As with all games of this nature, it's best with friends - I wouldn't recommend it as a single-player experience at all.
In our "Minecraft but X" template, Portal Knights adds RPG elements - 3 classes with different talents/skills and attributes. While they don't play hugely differently, it adds a bit more variety and specialisation that I like. It also breaks out the Minecraft style "biomes" into different worlds, which is a neat idea. Having to explore a world to find the exit is pretty fun. The big con with this is that it can be infuriatingly hard to find the portals because of where they can spawn, making the compass nearly a required item.
There is also a concern with performance. Even with a pretty solid computer, I was getting some tough lag. It appears as though once you visit a world, it's entirely stored in memory until you end the session. This is fine if you're spending your time on 1-2 worlds, but if you're jumping between 6-8 of them for farming, even on medium-sized worlds it can get costly on your machine. I suspect this is the reason that multiple players cannot be on different worlds, and must travel together.
The crafting system is really solid and fun, controller support is great, and combat is relatively fun / interesting (though as a mage, the wide aggro range of things like maggots can become infuriating). I'm not sure how long it'll keep me interested, but if it's on sale and you have a few friends and enjoy exploring / crafting, it can be a fun little game.

Let me get this out of the way. Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is one of the best WW2 shooters I've ever played. There, I said it. Why is that you ask? It takes everything good about the first two and amps them up times ten. While the sound design, voice acting and ability to control your fire teams are the same (and still very good), graphics, level design, gunplay, and story are all much MUCH improved. The battlefield moves from France to Holland as your crew including Matt Baker and Joe Hartsock and boy, does it show. Instead of the same boring grassy humps, you'll fight in, around and through beautifully detailed farms, churches and bombed out cities. The fire fights are intense and the guns aim much better. A third person cover mechanic was also added giving you greater flexibility to kill the enemy and command your troops. Is it perfedtion? No. The cut scenes run a little long and the last mission is somewhat anticlimactic compared to some of the buzzsaws you run through earlier in the game. Since a recap of the first two games is included I would actually skip the first two BiA games because Hell's Highway is such a quantum leap for the series. I cannot recommend this game enough. I got the whole series for around $13 (it's been as low as $10) and this one alone was worth the price of admission.

I know, I know I've barely played the game and yet I'm giving it a negative review. But I'm exercising my right to protest the excessive use of one time use microtransactions in a single player game.
It's bad enough that companies like Overkill and Tripwire are trying to milk multi-player gamers dry at every possible opportunity, so to see it happening to the same ruthless degree with a single player game is utterly tragic and shameful.
The game already has £32.97 worth of DLC available for it, and it has only been out for a few hours!
At the time of writing this the pre-order bonuses are one time use items, which is shamefully cheap. I assume they will all appear in the in-game shop very soon.
If we don't protest against being treated like cash cows - via negative reviews - then we'll just see even more of this, until games are broken up in pieces and sold bit by bit as overpriced DLC and MTs.
If you care at all about the future of gaming, you should protest this kind of money obsessed treatment, not mindlessly accept it.

If you dont run around out of cover, and know how to work in a squad, you'll have a good time playing this. People who get irritated with multiple spawning, because you ARE going to die, should rather stick to a single player game.
You start off with an infantry unit after choosing your faction from United States, Germany or Soviet Union. As you learn the first small map named an Encounter, you will level your initial weapon up while earning in game credits that allow you to modify and upgrade it with sniper scopes or
vs
bullets and suchlike.
Eventually you will be able to become a walking arsenal combat medic with a scoped MG and anti tank sticky nades along with a package of bandages and some good drugs in your pocket. They must be good as I've healed people from 2% health to full instantly.
Once you clear a few of the mid sized Skirmish maps, and finally Assault maps you can look at buying a Paratrooper infantry and leap out of planes into combat instead of relying on one of your own or squadmates vehicles to get into combat, or even try your hand at being a tank commander starting with light tanks moving through medium and heavy to tank destroyers. Or become an annoyance in the sky with 3 ranks of planes to pilot.
This is all the
portion of the game, the
aspect is a relatively simplistic RTS implementation, where units you own as well as fellow members of your faction are shuffled around the WW2 arena. Once sufficient time has passed battles start at key points on the supply lines and you can shift from the
mode into the
mode and actually control your own reserves.
There is a lot of depth and fun in both modes, but as with all PvP shooters you have your spawn campers, one shot snipers and general buffoonery of team killing lunatics and suchlike. This is mostly avoidable through careful gameplay and pretty much entirely alleviated if you run with a good tight squad.
The entry level weapon is perfectly fine even unmodded if you use it in one of two ways. Careful aiming while in cover, or hip fire and move like a mexican jumping bean. Although dont jump too much, as you can't shoot while you do that!
The 3 factions USSR, German and US are mostly balanced, but you'll find it boils down to play style more than anything else.
Give it a go! Its free and fun and if you can find 2 friends to play with, REALLY good fun! ;)))

Let me start with my minor gripes with the game, just to get them out of the way. If they ever remake this game or create a 2nd one, they need to clean up the loot system a bit and add less, but stronger dialogue. That being said...
Everything about this game is pretty damn good. The graphics are solid and unique, enemy AI is responsive, and the enemies themselves are also a lot of fun to kill. There are a variety of character builds, and the farther you go into the game, you can either specialize deeper or become a hybrid (personally went warrior-mage, you get a blink teleport). The story is interesting, with the meat of it coming from the characters around you rather than the storyline itself. The DLC is pretty solid and worth it if you really enjoyed the game, and would like to play more.
The main selling point of this game that I have left for last is just how humongous the game world is. There are around 4 or 5 continents if I remember, each with up to 15 or so subzones, with different environments, quests, etc. It is reminiscent of WoW in the way that they created the map (in a very good way).
One could say this game took elements from many different games and combined them, to which I would agree. But this is not a negative thing... the end result is that this game really doesn't have a weakness. It definitely has replay value (though I passed on that, too many games to still play...) For $19... cmon, you really can't go wrong with this one

You absolutely should give this game a try. It does so many things very well, and is a lot of fun to play. I have played most of the popular, recent MMOs and RPGs, and Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning holds its own, and ranks among the best.
Story
The story is very well written, and wonderfully intertwined throughout the game. The authors did a great job of telling an epic tale, and keeping the story interesting and engaging for its entirety.
Graphics
The graphics are just as good as any AAA game out there today. The maps, scenery, characters, and animations all look great. The interior spaces such as houses, castles, and dungeons are very detailed and finely crafted.
Setting
The setting is more of a fantasy setting, as opposed to a realistic setting as in Elder Scrolls. It feels like its filled with magic with a lot of graphical touches that look magical.
Quests
Quests are given by voice acted interactions with NPCs. The quests are story driven, and closely related to the overall story and background of the world. Every quest you do seems to have meaning, and is important in some aspect of the game. There are no junk “kill ten rats” quests. Instead the quests either further the main story, or provide interesting background to the characters or world.
NPCs
The NPCs have interest, character, and look great. I think every single NPC has a different look - not like the cookie-cutter clones in so many games today. The faces in particular are very detailed and show character.
Voice Acting
This has got to be the best voice acting of any game I have ever played. It is outstanding, and gives the quests that extra ambiance.
Classes
You can mix and match your class trees as freely as you wish between magic, melee, and stealth skills.
Combat
Combat is a blast. There are dodge, block, and combo mechanics. You can cast spells, use ranged weapons, and melee weapons. If you play on hard mode, then fights can be a good challenge, and you have to be alert in order to survive. The combat is easy to learn, but takes practice to master.
Leveling
I took my time, and had so much fun doing everything, that leveling happened naturally at a good progression. There are 40 levels total.
Crafting
Crafting is pretty simple and basic. The good thing is that you can craft some of the best items in the game yourself.
Character Models
The character models are actually better than many games out today. The faces are very detailed, and there are many varieties of armor.
Music
Like everything else in the game, the music is top notch.
Length
It is a big world with lots of stuff to do, and will take a good while to get through everything.
The game is awesome, and I highly recommend it.

The UI is somewhat bearable, but tends to use just a click too much for most simplest tasks (like junking the loot you want to sell later).
The biggest downside to this game is the story, a cliche setting that tends to contradict itself quite often, bunch of forgetable characters and hero that on one side has to fulfill the insertplayerhere role, as well as having a background of his own that hardly makes sense in big picture.
Still, I had my fun with this game - if you are looking for a way to drown yourself in escapism and explore a huge world, this is a perfect game for you. If you rather want a story driven RPG that makes sense, stay away!

ChuSingura 46+1 S is a visual novel developed by Inre. For those new to this concept, visual novels are interactive games that have very few choices if any at all. The concept might seem boring, but those interested in books ChuSingura is a jewel among VNs. It is also one of the games that will make you think of your own life and wonder what would you do different if you could travel back in time?
The main protagonist is Fukami Suguha, an average Japanese student that ends up transported back in time during the Genroku era in 1701 CE. The story essentially deals with the 47 Ronins and their plans to avenge their lord unjustly while also restoring the family’s honor. It is a story of courage, bravery, romance, mystery, magic and duty.
The game is excellent when it comes to provoking emotions in the player thanks to the amazing special effects used when the samurai are fighting with their swords, the music and the imagery. Some moments will be so touching that the player will shed tears.
I personally did not encounter any bugs with the game, but there were some minor translation errors, although nothing major.
Each chapter of ChuSingura is excellent and so far I played the 3 released. I think it is worth giving a try considering the fact chapter 1 is free for everyone and chapter 2 and 3 are bundled for 20$. Each chapter deals with the same story but someone else’s perspective as well as different events.
Overall, I think ChuSingura is one of the best visual novels I’ve read and I would gladly recommend it to anyone (heck, first chapter is free, so why not?). I give the game overall with its dlc a 9.5 (lost 0.5 for the minor translation errors). It is a must have in your collection.

Hell's Highway is the 3rd in the series and the upgrade to the Unreal engine shows.  If you can, definitely play all three but if you're only going to start with one, I suggest Hell's Highway.

I must tell before anything else, I have been a fan of the Mortal Kombat franchise since its beginning in the '90s so my review might miss a bit of objectivity! Almost all negative reviews out there are talking about business practices and technical issues, with little bearing on actual gameplay. So here's something for you peeps who still want to venture into this game despite all that.
TECHNICAL
- 4 hours in, no crashes or anything, I'm on default high settings without MSAA, and it runs fine for me and I only have a GTX980M. So I have no idea what's with others' performance issues.
- Minor bugs yes, it is to be expected, nothing game-breaking.
VISUAL
- I don't care much about how gorgeous a game must be, so currently the look of this game sits fine with me, especially aesthetic-wise, it's pretty much the same with DXHR.
- I needed some time to adjust to the UI, I often feel there's way too much information in the HUD and  seems a bit clunky.
GAMEPLAY
- Controls are fine for me. Although the mouse acceleration problem mentioned by many is quite annoying, I set it to ~15% and I could live with it. But I'm not experiencing problems with taking covers and stuffs like others suggested, no idea with this either.
- Gameplay mechanics are very standard if you played DXHR, you should be able to get right into the action. I like sneaking around without causing all-out conflict, so I can say the stealth approach is as the same as DXHR. If you are more trigger-happy, guess you have to test out the FPS approach yourself.
- My favorite minigame from DXHR, hacking doors, controls, pcs, safes is back! I don't know why I just love it. Even when I have the code to bypass it, I would still hack it for fun.
- The Breach is quite fun at the first glance. The gameplay is like the score-attack mode in Tomb Raider, but Deus Ex appropriate.
STORY
- Usually this part is most important to me for any RPG games, but since I'm only 4 hours in, I can't say much about it. But I'm not having any high hopes for the plot. Any plot contains conspiracy in games these days provides literally nothing new, it's all the same trope.
And finally, the god awful, greedy, BUSINESS PRACTICE.
- Yes it has microtransactions, but it didn't impact my gameplay at all. Hell, I didn't even know there IS microtransactions in-game until I've seen the reviews. I preordered the deluxe version, and the preorder bonuses (guns, credits, etc.) are still in my storage (not in play), and I play just fine, let alone buy more stuffs that are easily accessible in-game. Ammos and credits are plenty to grab, so I don't see why it suddenly becomes an issue.
- BUT, if the DLCs are actually restricted to one save like other reviews claimed, then yeah this is some BS pulled by SE. If this problem is not addressed by SE within a week, I will switch this review to negative because I cannot condone this kind of practice.
TL;DR
Game plays fine, like you would expect from a DXHR sequel.
If you just cannot stand the idea of microtransactions in a single-player game (albeit it has no real impact on your playthrough), then there are other fish in the sea.

Okay before this whole review starts let me say one thing. I am a super nerd of RWBY and when I saw this game I freaked out and was super excited so my opinion will most likely be super biased. Moving on from that I love this game. This game has amazing art and the witty remarks that the characters say throughout it just bring a smile to my face. The enemies in the game can get very frustrating at times due to their invincibility frames and how easily they can swarm you. That doesn't make this game bad in any way however as the combat feels nice and you can have a more "tactical" team if you have a group of friends to play with. This game brings elements from RWBY that I absolutely adore and if you're like me and like the show, you like fighting games, and you wanna support this project then buy it! <3

Started playing it post release and...I still find it unimpressive.  If you are a RWBY fan, you've bought it and no amount of convincing will tell you otherwise but otherwise, I'd suggest finding something else.  If you are a fan of the beat-em-up genre you may give this a go since there are few PC offerings in the genre but otherwise, no.
The gameplay is a simple beat-em-up game you pick one of the four protagonists from RWBY or JNPR (if you have the DLC) and run them through a series of levels spaced across several chapters fighting grimm.  The gameplay is standard beat-em-up fare ranged/melee attacks, jumping, combos, blocks, co-op attacks and specials.  Generally you'll pick the same set of combo attacks which are useful, abandon ranged attacks, kite when your shield is down until it recharges and repeat.  The combat feels repetitive (like many things in this game) and the most positive I can say about it is that it does its job without breaking anything.
Each character has some differences in how they handle.  Yang is melee focused with slower attacks, Weiss is tough to aim at things and has a good mix of range and melee,, Blake is fast-hitting and fast moving, and Ruby is overpowered.
Defeating the enemies gives you experience and with experience you can buy new skills and side-grades to your attacks and abilities.  You should be able to level cap a character per play through and there are unlockable requirements you have to do before you can purchase some skills, "kill 100 grimm with ranged attacks," for example.
Most of the gameplay is focused on multiplayer, and the enemies all scale up with more players.  You can take on the chapters with one player if you are good, but you'll manage a lot easier with friends as you can't revive yourself.  Multiplayer also gives you co-op attacks.  Unfortunately, it's a multiplayer focused game with mostly dead servers you would be lucky to find a party of two at any time.  Enough still play it you may be able to find someone else, but you should bring friends with you.
The far more significant problem with this game is its repeditiveness and lack of content which makes everything you do in the game feel even more boring and repetitive.  A single play through does not take all that much time - you may be able to manage it in a single sitting.  There is nothing noteworthy about the story which will invest you or make you want to stick around.  After that, the only reason to replay the game is to play with a different character or get achievements.  There is something of a prestige ranking system in this game to help pad content.  But, in order to manage that you have to replay and replay and replay the game across several characters in order to manage it, this provides no in-game incentive other than bragging points in a game where you have to force yourself to stick around.  Even after they made the DLC you can use four new characters in the same levels where what this game desperately needed was more levels and more ground to play in.

This game is not the best i have played, but not the worst.  It starts out okay, especially when playing with friends.  It started out enjoyable, but as time progressed got more and more tedious as well as boring.  It became a grind to get better gear and level up, and the enemies would sometimes get ridiculously difficult, but after crafting one new weapon, they became mince meat.  The random events in this game are also a bit weak. Enemies that spawn during the events scale to your level or even higher (though sometimes lower, that may be due to how far you have progressed in the game), but the experience points that they drop scale with the level of the area, meaning you will only get about 100 experience points for killing a level 30-35 enemy.  Some events also have you finding treasure the the enemies have that contain rare materials for crafting late game items, but those kinds of events don't pop up very often and it is already difficult to acquire the amount needed to craft late game items.  The game also only has 3 bosses at base, which once you learn their attack patterns, become as easy as the enemies, not to mention the 3 end-game bosses that require you to use hard to acquire materials to craft the items just to access the areas they are located at, but once you have defeated them, you must craft the item again, which requires you to get more rare materials, and even then some of the loot they can drop is very lackluster.  The game does have an easy to use crafting system and also has you upgrading your stations, which is not hard and allows you to play the game at an enjoyable pace.  Exploration across the islands can get a bit annoying since you have to grind for materials from the enemies in the area, but each one will only drop 1 shard, and as the game progesses, you need to acquire more shards just to craft 1 portal block, not to mention the fact that enemies take a bit of time to spawn after you kill them.  The class system is good with each class having it own unique talents, weapons, and abilities.  Overall, I don't recommend getting the game with the current state it is in, maybe as more updates are released, it may become something worth purchasing, but right now, it is not recommended.

Polished, but incredibly boring after a short time. Because it's NOT Minecraft, no matter how often this comparison comes up and is presented as a fact. This game describes the image of german engineering like no other: extremely solid in its mechanics, but void of any creativity. 1+1 = 2.
While Minecraft has to offer crazy setups with its endless worlds (yo, never dig down directly - it might happen that you fall through a cave 50 blocks in height that stretches over 2 parsecs in length and the floor is lava by the way. Oh and look, there's a mineshaft over there - I wonder where THAT lead...oh, there's a light at the end of the tunnel! AND I hit bedrock! By Grabthar's hammer!), Portal Knights always follows the same boring formula: every world is a small island. Somewhere on this island is an entrance to a dungeon.
At the bottom of the dungeon there's a chest with stuff. Otherwise find enough material to craft the portal stones necessary to get to the next all-the-same world with a different texture set. Oh and there's a monolith standing in the landscape. Why don't you go over there to find a treasure?
Portal Knights is an interesting idea, but isn't able to provide a scope that would make it remarkable in any shape or form. The mechanics it provides are polished, but are lost in one - despite its graphical fidelity - of the most unremarkable video game worlds I have ever stumbled upon.

Not too big into VNs usually since I don't see the appeal. I saw the first chapter of this one up for free and was impressed by the production quality of the CGs and was kinda bored so I gave it a try not knowing what to expect.
Ended up binging through all of it during the course of a few weeks. I think the reason is that this VN is less about choices (there's a grand total of 1 so far which just bad ends you) and romancing. It's just a straight story.
The pacing, world / character building and atmosphere in the VN totally hooked me in. Each chapter is essentially a new loop through the same basic set of events, but you get to genuinley experience it all from a different prespective and tone each time which was really cool. You can tell that the writer wanted to make the most out of the ground hog day premise to make sure that it didn't get too boring or perdictable. Each chapter does a very good job building up the stakes anew which culminates in very powerful scenes near each ending. And the really cool thing with the writing in my opinion is that even with only 3 of the 5 chapters, you still get what would be a pretty strong conclusion to the story by chapter 3, so I definitley feel like I got my money's worth here. The last two chapters feel like they'll just be tying up a few loose ends so I don't mind the wait.
The only sore spots with this VN mainly lie in the translation quality. I could mostly look past it and just fill in the gaps myself but there's a decent number of grammer errors and typos that indicate that chapter 2 and 3 were rushed to meet the deadline. If waiting longer means we get a more refined translation for the next 2 chapters then again, I don't mind.
Overall I definitley recommend giving the first free chapter a try to see if this might be your thing, and I am looking forward to the last 2 chapters!
