Not recommended, at least not in its current state.
There are a multitude of problems with the game currently and these being the biggest ones in my opinion:
In almost every match I've been in that I wasn't host I've had 100-200 ping and shots were really delayed in both firing and hitting. Melee had really wonky hit detection where I'm either clearly hitting the person and doesn't register or I'm hit from almost double their normal range. Yet when I'm hosting shots are instantaneous and melee works like it should, giving a fairly big advantage simply because I'm not delayed.
From what I've played, Shadow Dancer (Rena) is next to useless when compared to Silent Avenger (Ivan), so by picking the SD you're essentially gimping yourself, not to mention they're heavily countered by Shield Trooper, so the reasons to pick that class is next to non-existant. Gunslinger (Elena) seems pretty fair in balance, she's pretty bad in melee combat but makes up for it with fairly powerful ranged weapons, one of which, the grenade launcher, can't be used effectively in close range without hurting herself but is very powerful otherwise. Then you have Shield Trooper (Max) who if played right is hard to kill one on one if you're skilled enough since he can block all attacks from the front of him (other blocking can still be hit in the lower leg area) and can't be knocked back/stunned by melee when using one of his ranged weapons (I think this might be changed?). Silent Avenger (Ivan) is probably the only class I feel is too powerful simply because he's good at just about every range, he has a very hard hitting sniper rifle, a side SMG good for close to mid range, and a katana which is arguably the best melee in the game.
This could probably be put under the first point, but I decided to make it a separate one. There is absolutely no dedicated server support, meaning the current host system is what we're stuck with. A lot of people have pointed out that this system probably works well with countries that are smaller and have better infrastructure, but it doesn't work at all for NA and such, with games usually averaging at about the 130 ping mark.
I'm sure a lot of you have seen or at least heard of those systems in some games where there's a low chance to get something really good? Well in Gunz 2 the guns that are in the Tesla shop are direct upgrades and currently there's no real way to get the premium crystals, which is the only way it stops it from being Pay to Win, but as it is, you have to be really lucky to get one of these weapons, and if you do, you'll be enjoying a fairly nice advantage over other players forever.
All of that being said the game is okay, it's a fun little shooter and while it's debateable if it holds up to GunZ 1, I think it's okay, but like I said, it's not recommended in its current state until some if not all of these issues are addressed.

Let me tell you something about this game. This game is the best game I've ever laid eyes on, even when I play singleplayer. It has 4-5 difficulty options, which makes it great for gamers of any skill level. The unique Gem Socketting system is really fun to toy with, where if your weapon has enough slots, you can put a venom ember and a flame ember on it to give it a certain boost against two types of enemies without having to switch do a different elemental weapon. The randomized loot system reminds me of Borderlands, since it has prefixes, stat changes and even rarities, going from White, Lavender, and Orange from what i've seen so far. There is also a skill tree system that is JUST PERFECT, because if you unlocked a skill that is above in the tree from a skill you don't have, you can still get it without making the other a prequisite. If you're looking to buy this game, get ready to face millions of minibosses. The miniboss fights are the best part of the game in my opinion, since they are literally around every corner, providing you more loot. The games areas are unique, where to the south there is the Undead, and the lore rich Strumbeon, to the north is the frostbitten spiders and goblins, and some bandits, and to the east you ride to a desert area filled with high level basilisks and creatures. All in all, this game is my favorite thing ever and I can safely say that without a doubt I will encourage others to play it with me.

is a small step up, and acceptable for less-choosy players, but still not entirely choiceworthy.

titles, the core "vertical Zuma" gameplay is still there, but 3 goes far beyond 2 in adding extras.  There's a puzzle mode, a hectic timed-defense mode, an "Onslaught" mode where you try to play Luxor while simultaneously shooting down pop-up barriers that shorten the track, a river-crossing mode that blends
mechanics with
level design.  There are plenty of powerups, and by collecting coins, you can purchase upgrades for your favourites.  Other targets appearing from time to time grant score and coin bonuses or unlock bonus levels.
Even with all I've mentioned
still isn't the most feature-laden casual game on the market in 2017, but there's enough content and variety there that it doesn't feel barren, outdated or too limited.  For the action-casual player,
will still be quite satisfactory, all the more so if you catch it on a good sale.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This one is a lot more traditional at its core.  There are main quests that advance you through the maps and local side quests for each area.  I honestly haven't tested if maps beyond my current exploration are leveled higher, of it it's all matched to my level.  I'll have to look at that later.

From the fate system, it looks like it's designed for you to be able to mix and match fairly effectively, so you could do a fighter/mage/thief and not completely suck.

None of the other quests seem at all tied to it.  People mention a faraway war a lot and there are some quests relating to that, but it doesn't seem to have anything to do with your character's story.  You mention the Tuatha, and the only response people give is, "That's weird, the war is far away from here."

I have never played a visual novel before this one.  I've been mildly curious about them, but never enough to shell out any actual money.  So when this one popped up on my radar as being FREE, well hey, I'm willing to risk that kind of money.

And it turns out that it's pretty good.
I thought I was getting "Baywatch Nights", but set in Edo-era Japan.  I figured I'd watch it for 30 minutes, maybe an hour, and roll my eyes a lot.  Instead, I got "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon", plus cleavage.

What an absolutely stunning experience. Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a testament to what video games as a medium are capable of. Despite the inherent length of the game; ~2.5-3 hours if your capable of quickly solving puzzles, the game is incredibly fun. If there ever were a perfect time to say something was short and sweet it would be for this game. You'll find yourself taking control of two brothers during their quest to save their ill father. The controls seemed a bit tedious at first but after a few minutes of playing they began to feel pretty natural for me. The puzzles are simple yet satisfying to solve and if you're experienced gamer you'll probably only lose a handful of times. Even if you fail more the checkpoints are pretty forgiving. During the game You travel through numerous, incredible, beautiful landscapes, experience hardships and make allies to aid your in you quest. I didn't think I'd be a willing to accept (let alone; embrace) the emotional core of the game that I'd had heard about. But after a couple hours of playing I began to grow attached to the heroes and people you met. I won't even lie I even shed a tear or two.
Another thing to mention is the graphics, although the first few cut-scenes didn't grab me, the beautiful spanning vistas you come across did. A few times I even considered taking a screenshot for a new wallpaper. At a couple locations in the game you climb much higher up from a puzzle you solved earlier and it really lets you feel the grand scale of the game. Another few scenes (which I won't spoil) really impart the feeling of an epic journey to the player.
In closing my thoughts I would definitely play this game through again and I might even be inclined to purchase it again on another system if it were released *cough* Wii U *cough* I will add however that $16.99 CDN seems a little steep. I picked it up for a $2.49 CDN during the holiday sale and got A LOT more than expected out of this game. Though I feel people who shrug most games off as "just a video game" should experience this one. Very few games actually manage to portray a beautiful and emotional story in the way that Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons does.

Everything a good sequel should be. It's all here, the South Park trademark humor intact, and a story that I thoroughly enjoyed from start to finish. Biggest difference there from the Stick of Truth is a somewhat darker edge to some parts, though I wish they had bigger consequences in the long run.
Compared to Stick of Truth, the combat is actually fairly well balanced this time, though admittedly still fairly easy. Playing on Mastermind difficulty, there were only three fights in the game that I actually had to make multiple attempts at, and all of them were late-game bosses.
In addition, the collect-a-thon has also been toned down in favor of more character-focused side-quests. There are still a few things to collect, though not in near the number as the Stick of Truth used to pad itself.
My final save came in at just over 16 hours, finishing everything except a couple of the collections, and that's still double the length of my first play Stick of Truth, so definitely more time for your money as well.
Main downside is the season pass isn't really worth it, at least not yet. A few Stick of Truth themed costumes and Towlie butting in at random times to point out the obvious don't justify paying for. They should have just been part of the game. We'll see if this changes when the bigger DLC that's been promised does arrive.

Runic Games, w/ some former members of Blizzard and Travis Baldress of Fate, have once returned with Torchlight II. If Torchlight 1 felt a lot like Diablo 1 to you (in its ARPG gameplay department + with the constant direction of going further down the dungeons w/ each level), then Torchlight II should then feel like Diablo II. Torchlight II improves so much over the original TL, I don't even know where to begin - just like how Diablo II improved immensely over the original Diablo. Granted, TL2 has its own spin on the ARPG genre, in some ways: you have a pet by your side (who you can send back to town to sell items; who can help you in battle; etc); the graphics are much brighter + more colorful than Diablo series; and it has a steampunk-inspired setting.
No longer are you confined to go down, down, and down the dungeons some more like Diablo. The game is now a bit more open and epic than that. TL2 sports multiple towns - just like Diablo II. Also, the side-quests here - they also can be found when you're out an about in the game-world, which likely will have their own areas and dungeons for you to crawl through.
Combat is as awesome and as action-packed as ever, with the game constantly chucking out tons of new and unique loot to the player to modify and upgrade; and there's tons of skills to learn. Leveling-up allows the player to sink points into the player's base-stats for numbers how they see fit, unlike some other major ARPG (Diablo III) - allowing the player's builds even within the same class to possibly be different from another player's build.
While the story + characters are nothing truly special here - like in many of these ARPG's - it's still certainly better than the previous game. The graphics are nothing truly remarkable in terms of technical quality, but the art direction is fantastic, quirky, and colorful. TL2 sports SIngle Player support (for online play or offline play); Online support for Co-Op via Runic's servers; and also LAN support - unlike another ARPG that has currently forced "online always" gameplay (Diablo III). If a gamer is looking for numerous different ways to play this game - it's certainly here.
Once finished with the Campaign, fans can come back and explore some other Randomized Dungeons and even enter New Game Plus Mode. Given that, and that this game offers a lot of value for those not just who do one playthrough (took me around 27 hours, all by myself - SIngle Player style) - but also to those who want to replay the game. When it debuted at its budget-price ($20), it offers plenty of value and "bang for the buck" when compared to its competitors that were charging $50-60. Even now, when it's on sale dirt-cheap - it's pretty much a steal. And this all, this isn't even counting that the game also does have Mods out there, which further can extend the life of the game - since this game comes with The Game's Editor (GUTS) and also supports The Steam Workshop.
If you love ARPG's, this one's pretty much a no-brainer: Torchlight II is an excellent ARPG that just cannot be recommended enough. Simply put: it's one of the best of these loot-crazy, action-packed ARPG's around.
Final Grade = A.

Giving this game the benefit of the doubt and thus a positive review. Its a hollow shell of a game, a beautifull shell nonetheless. It offers a stunning open world with absolute bunker graphics and visuals. It is very well optimised for a game that released on console too, I had well over 75 fps all the time (on ultra settings) with a GTX 970. I found no bugs either.
Now the downside of this game comes to the 'indepth part'. To start with: No story, its just not there. You teleport from world to world onto shattered islands, and you find some random NPC's from time to time who say nothing more than 3 or 4 words. The resources you find are determined by the level of island you teleport to. That means that if you have five level 10 islands there is no reason to explore the other 4, because you won't find anything new there that you didn't already found on the first one. All the enemies are the same, so are the treasures and objects you can find.
Resources come in tiers, from stone to iron to gold etc. You know how it goes. There is nothing to explore there either. Where you make a metal chair on lvl 10 you make a golden chair on lvl 20. It just goes on like that. You grind for better gear so you can use that to grind for better gear. A mistake that many games make.
After all, I have been playing this with a friend I also played Terraria, Factorio, Minecraft etc. with. So I guess we can call ourselves veterans in this genre. Eventually its good fun co-op and overall a fun game in the end, my conclusion is just what I started this review with: A hollow shell of a game. And it's a shame because this has so much more potential.

A Global strategy game that gives the player control over many facets of the country they choose to play as.
The various campaigns and scenarios provide an interesting goal-driven experience and a few "what if" situations covering various actual and hypothetical conflicts.
The sandboxes each have a wide array of customisable settings and an immense selection of countries to play as - from the largest world power, to smallest having little more than a single city.
Once in control of your country you have full control over just about everything.  Land, Air, and Naval forces are present letting you conduct everything from static-front wars of attrition to amphibious assaults, bombing campaigns, artillery duels, and more.
On the economic front you have budget choices, goods production, goods import / export, military production, research, and more to manage directly or step back and assign some (or all) of the responsibilities to the generally useful AI assistants.
Diplomacy is a bit of a weak point as whilst alliances and spheres (essentially large alliances) exist, as do various pacts, nothing really binds the player to a given path of action nor is the AI required to act in response to the pacts being invoked (e.g. if someone declares war on your, your allies may not do anything and similarly, if someone declares war on your allies you don't have to do anything).  There are penalties for inaction however they do not have much of an impact outside of diplomacy.
The ultimate version of Supreme Ruler builds on years of development of previous editions (2020, Cold War, 1936) resulting in an extensive tech tree, unit selection (including country specific and generic units) and maps that reflect fairly well the state of development of the world at their given points in time.  This allows you to play fairly far in to the future regardless of when you start.
There still remain some rough edges however the developers have shown a long term commitment to providing updates, fixes, and minor improvements as well as an interest in using the ultimate version as a platform for building future editions on, such as the Great War standalone / DLC product.
Finally whilst the military and country development aspects are fairly easy to understand the economic side can be somewhat obscure even on the medium (normal) difficulty.
I recommend anyone who experiences frustration with the economics impeding your desire to blow things up to turn the economic difficulty down one step at a time until you find a nice balance between needing to consider economic development and its impact on your plans and not having the economy hold you back.

I'm going to compare this game to Witcher 2 and Skyrim because they are my two favourite RPGs and many people have played them.
Secondly, if you're going to buy this game, it goes on sale fairly often so I would suggest waiting for a sale
KoA does a lot of things right but a lot is sincerely average:
KoA has the option to completely change your character's style and perks at any point meaning that you can change the type of character you have whenever you want to try something new. This is cool but it made me feel like a second playthrough would be fairly pointless as I have already tried all the character builds in one playthrough.
Playing through the whole game the environments are beautiful and varied.
The look of the game is more animated than Skyrim or the Witcher and this gives it a "friendlier" look, this is either good or bad depending on your preference.
The fighting mechanic is fun and fairly reactive, being more like the Witcher than Skyrim. You can dodge and mix spells and abilities seamlessly in with melee or ranged combat.
I found the game too easy, playing the whole thing on hard and never really struggling, eventually you become so powerful that you cannot be beaten and fighting creatures becomes tedious even though the fighting mechanic is fun
The main story line is decent and has some originality but is definitely not on the level of the Witcher (but few games are in my opinion)
The faction storylines are fun and to the point but fairly predictable
But the side quests have some cool little twists and original little stories.
The soundtrack is terribly repetitive and NPCs like talking during battles which results in you missing half of what they are saying because the background noise is so loud
Some reviewers found the voice acting sketchy but I did not notice any problems
There is a lot of lore to be discovered which is nice for people into that and it isn't thrown in your face so you can ignore it if you want
Lastly, you can sell any item to any merchant and they all have unlimited funds (because running around trying to sell things in Skyrim is pretty annoying)
Pros:
Beautiful environments
Great fighting mechanic
Lots of lore
Decent storyline
Recustomising your character at any point
Cons:
Too easy (for a Dark Souls person)
Predictable
Repetitive soundtrack and some difficulty hearing NPCs explain key story points (which they don't repeat)
No point in a second playthrough
So in conclusion
KoA is a fun game that I would recommend to any RPG fan, but I personally would not rank it above either Skyrim or the Witcher 2

Tekken's legacy culminates into one defining release that encapsulates the initial draw of the series and meshes it with tons of improvements, undoubtedly granting this game a long lifespan. Tekken 7 for the PC is the definitive version of the long-running 3D fighting game series. I own both console/PC and have played through all the modes extensively; needless to say, to be able to play smoothly without input or frame delays is splendid. It had been years since a fighter this polished rose to challenge modern competition. Tekken 7 completely washes away the nightmare that was Tekken Tag 2 and provides a lasting experience, one that stands on even--if not higher, footing compared to current fighters like Street Fighter 5, KI, BBCF, KOF14, and others. Tekken 7 on the PC only holds one glaring flaw in that it lacks the jukebox mode which I have used endlessly to customize my training music on the console, hence why I opt to train using the ps4. Beyond that disappointment, this version as far as gamplay, optimization options, and graphics, is the one to own.
Graphics do not make or break a fighting game, but Tekken 7 decided to build an aesthetic of confident allure. From the surface filter that covers even the background to the sparks that fly when nailing a crush move, there is eye candy with every passing frame. The PC version also does away with the noticeable console delay as well as doing significantly better on the latency department. I believe that only 1 out of every 10 matches on the PC have been laggy for me, and even then, those were matches that I could've won. The difference is noticeable, especially if you have played at least fifty console games. Some might scoff at minor things like input delays, but please try to consistently block seeable lows like ss3 (Ling) or db 4 (Leo) on the console before regarding this improvement on the PC version as insignificant. You will rarely lose on the PC version from a low that you could not react to, and that in itself is worth fifty dollars. But beyond that, punishing 10-13 frame moves feels natural, because what you see on screen is pretty much what you can react to due to the optimization of the PC version.
Tekken 7 tweaked the overall combo system. No longer do some moves put opponents in bound (B!), rather now, tailspin/screw (S!) is what keeps the combo flowing. This changes many things from okizeme to wall combo potential. The most important, however, is the effect it has on scaling. Sure you can still get a form of bound during okizeme tactics through counters ie Lili df 3 ch will put the opponent in a launch state, but counter properties are necessary. This spurs adaptation and a divergence from long-trusted Tekken strategies. Because of this, old combos or strategies may yield significantly less damage or fail to even provide guaranteed follow-ups due to this one change in mechanic. Was it a good change? Yes.
Combos now flow seamlessly and have upped their visual style thanks to the the S! mechanic which is conducive to creativity. This affected every character, although some benefited more in either damage or style departments. For example, Leo now gets better wall carry than before, Ling can virtually connect everything as an S! state opponent can fall pray to her dance, oki, empty jumps that much more. Beyond the visuals, S! truly revived Tekken.
Additional changes were implemented to rage. Now you can use a super called rage art or a special property move ie (with rage df3+4~3 by Lili will give her move blockstun and armor allowing for an added mixup). This changes the end-game thought process for both sides. Now I find myself dropping combos that will activate my opponent's rage in favor of relaunching them just to prevent giving added options. Nothing is more satisfying than seeing two rage-enabled combatants backdash cancelling every which way, trying to just get one natural combo in or whiff. It is both frightening and exhilarating. Lastly on mechanics, crush moves/armor moves, were added to alleviate silly spam as well provide an approach against seemingly insurmountable moves. They're fantastic against newcomers or low-level mashers as they provide a pierce through their natural strings ie df 3 by Ling will negate any 112 by a Mishima who is punishing air. They all differ, some hit high while some hit mid making others better, but it is a great tool nonetheless.
The new characters added to the Tekken family can all be classified as enjoyable, unique, and occasionally head-scratching. While not my favorite set of newcomers, this group stands strong not only in viability but also in impression. Some of the characters were re-imagined versions of past fighters like Josie (Bruce) and Master Raven (Raven). Josie sports new moves like b3+4 and her butterfly flip which I think is one of the best moves in Tekken 7. She also got a lot of moves from Bruce's arsenal that helps her stun and craft amazing counterhit combos. Despite the prevalence of old, these characters play differently in the presence of memorable moves like uf 3+4 (Josie) and are still so much fun. Others introduce gameplay mechanics that stand apart from tradition like Claudio whose starburst gives him additional mixups and launchers that lead to north of 70 damage one at a time. Katarina runs on 50-50 mixups after her command dash which can also be derived from normals making her one risky woman to both sides of the ring. There are also characters that provide a challenge to play and fight like Lucky Chloe who can be the root of depression for opponents who fail to check her command list; add in her "one-two" chants and we can see why she causes rage even to opponents above red health. From my little time with Gigas, Akuma, Revolution add-on Eliza, I can say that Gigas is fairly difficult to win with, however, he does have mechanics that remind me of Iron Tager from Blazblue which I find to be a welcome addition. Eliza and Akuma can combo using traditional 2D commands and even possess jump-in options that are consistently viable: unlike awkwardly animated uf*n*4 by pretty much everyone in Tekken. They are fast, fun, and intuitive given their traditional 2D inputs which most of us have grown up with. Overall, the new characters bring fresh and fleshed out mechanics that alter Tekken's notion of inputs, gameplay, and aesthetic.
This soundtrack is masterful. The ost is an important feature in fighting games as they are titles that require hours and hours of grind. To listen to something mundane or worst, annoying, can often lead to more frustration than necessary. Thankfully Tekken 7 will remind us many years from now of those first weeks and months of our time spent with our favorite characters thanks to a memorable barrage of melodic trance and vocal orchestrals. This by far has the best training stage music, assuming you are using Infinite Azure as your go to stage for non-wall combos. Even stages like Geometric Plane which we see in other fighters have this laid back, I-can-come-back feel sprinkling from both sides of my headphones. Volcano and Duomo stand out as some of the best vocal tracks in the game. It is no coincidence that I do best in those stages.
The gap between Tekken 6 and Tekken 7 in terms of presentation and gameplay reminds us how this franchise has remained the zenith of 3D fighters. Its willingness to depart from conventions is nothing new to Tekken. Bound mechanics were introduced and changed how combos and wall scenarios played out. Now enter Tailspin, and that changes again, and with it a new era. Whether we see Tekken 8 at all is not important. Tekken 7 is balanced, diverse, and it is the definitive Tekken experience to date, reviving the series from the ashes of TekkenTag2. It has reminded me of why I loved Tekken then, and moreso now. Thank you, Harada san.

Pros -
Fast paced, 3d fighter action. Matches don't feel long.
Variety in the roster. Quick, tricky characters. Heavy hitting brawlers. Your traditional shotos.. and Akuma!
Story mode is very good for a fighting game. The story isn't anything to go home about, but it's not awful.

Custimizable items make characters feel unique! Lots of items to get in both treasure mode, and tournament mode.
Graphically very impressive for a fighting game.
Optimized incredibly well! Actually runs better than the console version!
Easy to pick up
50 bucks for a AAA title! Pretty solid, imo.
Rematches in ranked mode!
Cons-
Denuvo title
Treasure mode gets incredibly repetitive, with input reading AI upon higher difficulties.
No true arcade mode.
Very hard game to master. If you jump online while being new to this game, you're gonna get blown up real quick.
Tons of movesets for each character. Can be intimidating to learn multiple characters in this game
Tournament mode bugs. Encountered a bug where the game put me into losers bracket because my opponent desync'd with me, despite actually winning the majority of the match by 2 rounds.
Certain custimizables are locked by treasure, and can be a pain to try to unlock if you're unlucky.
Treasure mode bosses are B.S
Not cross play, but this is the fault of sony and not the devs. However, this means the likelyhood of the pc community dwindling is somewhat high.
Deluxe edition isn't really worth the money
Film grain is annoying, but you can change this with a simple config mod.
Ranked is best of 2.. Meaning you'll very likely see a 1-1 with no 3rd match happening. Kinda lame how that works.
Overall, Tekken 7 is great. Some minor issues with the game, but they're, again, minor. The pros heavily make this game one of my favorite fighting games to play currently. I recommend getting this! It's a lot of fun :]

This game is honestly not that bad.
Did it have a wretched launch? Oh, oh yes it did.
Does it have stupid day one DLC that is already on the disc/virtual copy of the game you bought? Yes.
Does it have a good story? Eh.
Mortal Kombat X is without a doubt my new favourite fighting game. It's awesome. However, it is not without its flaws. Its release was absolute complete and total trash, and was unacceptable. However, once you get past it's "background installation" bull it's not that bad of a game.
Is it good looking? Why yes, yes it is. This is one of the nicest looking games I've seen in awhile, especially the backgrounds, and is a huge improvement (graphically) from MK9. Blood is still lacking but eh, not everything can be perfect. And besides, who cares when I can impale someone's eye with their frozen stomach juices? This game has a lot going for it in the graphics department though, the backgrounds/stages look better than ever with tons of tiny details here and there for you to notice throughout playing (like the soldiers shooting demons from the netherrealm), and the characters you play look pretty nice, too. However, the cutscenes look better now than they ever have, and the only thing holding them back is a little thing called "30FPS," which not only affects cutscenes, but gameplay too. Graphics for me get a 8.5/10 because of the framerate drops.
Gameplay, or in the case of this game, "playability," is alright. The game has very smooth combos and amazing fluidity in fights, but that doesn't do much when the fights can be riddled with lag or even slo-motion. This is especially a serious issue in online where seemingly everyone has a ping of 1k+ and is running the game on a computer from the 90's. In other words, online this game lags. BAD. However, in single player it runs fairly smoothly until the before mentioned 30FPS invades your game. This can ruin an entire game, and has ended up being the deciding factor in whether I win or lose several times. Aside from those problems when the game works, it works amazingly. It runs smooth, it looks very cinematic and is impressive to watch, and the fights are just plain awesome. Gameplay gets an 8/10 because of all the issues, but keep in mind how much fun it is when it does work.
Story. I haven't beaten it yet, but so far the story is... mediocre. I didn't expect it to be as good as MK9 but this is just... eh. It seems to be based around Johnny Cage's green kick ability becoming super powers. Because why not. The main villain is okay I guess, but he could be better. Then again, no story is without it's flaws, so I'll try to remember and update this review once I've beaten the game. So far I'd rate it 6.5/10 for being kinda dumb and boring.
Music. The same as every Mortal Kombat game, just a few dramatic build-ups and some background noise, so because of this I won't rate it. Just don't go in and expect an amazing soundtrack, be happy the music exists in the first place. Or don't. I don't care, I'm not you.
Overall I'd say after going through all the bull it puts you through in the first few hours of owning it, this is definitely worth a buy. Whether you'd pay for full price or on sale is up to you, but I personally would buy it during the summer sale since it's so close, however you do whatever you want it's your money.
Overall I would rate MK10 as a 7.5/10, it would be an 8 or an 8.5/10, but the framerate and story keep it down. Wait a little bit, and I'd definitely recommend you get it. Hope this review helped.

I do love the game and played long ago before i even began playing on Steam when i bought Supreme Ruler Gold 2020 on CD. As computers upgrade, i am please to get it on Steam. The possible battles to play is overwhelming, espeically if you tech develop beyond what your neighboring nations (AI) can develop within their time, allowing you to overwhelm and crush them. The option to colonize defeated enemy is a nice touch, as some times to much territory without proper support, leaves you dealing with support the people of your newly absorb territory, and this can kill you capability.
Problems:
In the WWII mission, basically when i play Germany from the beginning and is busy upgrading and preparing to for the next invasion, i find myself force to jump thanks to Italy (AI) jumps the gun and begin sieging territory (France first) that would have been mine to absorb. Also i noticed when i do not control Japan in WWII, somehow they get overwhelmed by China's military production capablity. The simple jeap troop vehicle, only 10 days to produce, by the time Japan (AI) attacks they are normally overhwhelmed by number of jeap troops, as Engineers and Tanks take from 40 to 60 days. There is also the Special Forces units with high killing ratings getting into the mix.  I often find myself force to sale off all my units for free to Japan, to give them the numbers to overwhelm China. Other times Soviet Russia is overwhelmed by German production in WWII setting. I call this an off balance problem.
When rival nations conqure an enemy nation, they do not seem to get the problem i find facing when i absorb enemy nations. Their production is normal, while mine suffers.
Lastly as the years pass during gameplay. I often find the speed of play slowing down. Once where the fastest rate allow a day to pass within mere seconds, is slowing down to the point it taking longer as you keep playing. This is a heavy problem, when you need to build new units, new resource supplies on conqured lands, and even new bases to allow units to resupply instead of reteating all the way back to your own territory. I beleive this is likely to do with the game AI, producing more and more units for other nations, while you can not see them, the AI is control and tracking them, and thus its causing the game to slow down.
Yet overall i do enjoy the game. And often time to time play the game, when the urge comes back. And playing WWI is bringing up that urge. The idea of appearing on WWI battlefields with WWII tanks and fighters, along with bombers is going to be fun. With enough research stations, i find often within two years, long before Germany begin its war in Europe, i set off with units from 1942 era instead of units of 1938 era, and often that is overwhelming firepower.

Mortal Kombat is easily my favorite fighting game franchise and so far I've picked up Netherrealm fighting games since the release of Mortal Kombat (2011) on release in April of 2011. With that said here is a  review of Mortal Kombat X.
Story Mode:
I really like it. The story mode in all Netherrealm games is always entertaining. The writing in Mortal Kombat X (will be referred to as MKX from now on) is better than what was seen in MK9 and Injustice. However, it is brief. I completed it in one sitting and I estimate it only took me around 4/5 hours to see to its conclusion.
I believe the art style and themes of the game are somewhat inspired by the live action series Mortal Kombat Legacy and as a result I was expecting a rounded out focus on what 25 years in the future for the characters could hold. I was disappointed. For the most part the story centers heavily on the Cage family as well as a focus on Special Forces and the descendants of existing characters like Takeda, Cassie Cage and so on. The new characters for the most part are pretty interesting. My particular favorites being Erron Black and Kotal Kahn (concept and design but not gameplay.)
That is where the story falls a little short. Because of the focus on the children and off-spring of existing characters we never really get any payoff (what happens next?) with the fan favourite characters. Without any heavy spoilers I will give you an example in the form of the relationship between Scorpion and Sub-Zero.
------------
POTENTIAL SPOILERS, SKIP THIS SECTION IF YOU WANT A FRESH STORY EXPERIENCE
----------------------------
In the opening of the game you see Scorpion, donning his Mortal Kombat (2011) skin, and an aged or grey version of Sub-Zero and they are working together. It is revealed later on that Quan Chi is controlling a series of characters in the Mortal Kombat universe. Once these two are freed Scorpion returns to human form, taking his real name of Hanzo Hasashi back. The blank pupil less eyes are gone and now he is normal.
You would expect a decent payoff and resolve between Hanzo and Kuai Liang, either resulting in anger or an ultimate understanding and acceptance. We do not really get this. There are glimpses of a payoff but it is thrust to the bottom of the pile when compared to the story of Cassie Cage against Shinnock.
----------------
POTENTIAL SPOILERS OVER
-------------
Returning from Mortal Kombat 4, Shinnock makes his revival debut. In short, he is not a good villain. He is no Shao Kahn and seems to just be a push over with no plan. In terms of gameplay, once you reach the top of a ten man tower, he is a fairly easy, if cheap, boss fight who then turns into what seems to be a smaller, weaker and earlier form of Onega from Armageddon. He does not have a plan, the only real thing that happens with him is that he makes areas red... So scary.
Graphics:
Absolutely stunning. This game, on higher settings, can be beautiful at times. Every character model has a rich detailed flare. Clothing and armour are realistically bound to the kombatants with shiny, solid metal texturing. Particle effects are fantastic too. Fireballs, ice shards and the assorted selection of coloured magical abilities stick out against the background crisp and clear as day. The backgrounds too are phenomenal. Particular densely populated stages like Outworld Marketplace, the gorgeous and hypnotic warping glow of the Jinsei Chamber or the pure "to the death" feeling that dwells within Dead Woods is truly haunting.
However, each stage seems to be cut down in comparison to what we have seen in previous Netherrealm fighting titles.
By this I mean there are NO stage fatalities of any kind, gone are the days of knocking an opponent into a swamp marsh, lava pit or sentient tree. MKX borrows from 2013's Injustice: Gods Among Us with the items scattered across the stage that can be interacted with. There are multiple purposes to each type; some like cars or vines will allow a fighter to dash across the screen quickly providing potential damage to an enemy or smaller items like vehicle engines, stones and bystanders to be thrown like projectiles into the oncoming direction of a rival. There are ways to escape corners in most stages by flipping off a wall. These prove not very effective against veteran players of corner guarding but the option is still there. I believe however these stage items and smaller less iconic stages do not hold up quite as well against the Flesh Pits for example from MK9 but it is trying to establish itself as something new and they have good qualities.
Gameplay:
Here's where it all counts. How the fights are. In one word, awesome. MK9 was sluggish and slow in places and resulted in a slower pace than competitors, much unlike earlier Mortal Kombat titles. Injustice speed the formula up where it was a lot faster but a lot more simplified ditching High Kick, Low Kick and Front Punch, Back Punch for Light, Medium and High. MKX is the fastest fighter Netherrealm has put out there. Kombat flows far better in this game than any before it. Kombo chains, mixed with special moves are more accessible to newcomers and are more rewarding to more seasoned players.
A couple of hours with a character one likes the look of in training mode and they will be pulling off 8/10 hit kombos in no time. X-ray moves have become far more dynamic too, and far more brutal thanks to next generation technology. Bones shatter and muscles are torn from their source in a way that could make the most unfeeling, insensitive person breathe in air through their teeth. The kombat is fantastic, and rewarding too. Landing a punch has impact just the same as breaking an opponent's arm or shattering their spinal column. Sound design is completely on point.

It is sad that the first negative review I write is on one of the only fighting series I've ever loved, Mortal Kombat. This is probably the greatest iteration in the series, being flexible, full of personality, and introducing fresh faces that blend into the universe easily.
However, DO NOT BUY THIS ON PC! This is probably one of the worst ports I've played in a decade. My system is far overqualified for this game and it lags consistently. The game has a horrid memory leak that makes it perform even worse the longer you play it until you have to shut it down. I also find it amusing that this is the only game I've ever played that doesn't even shut down correctly; At least 3/4 times I have to go into the task manager and end the game process after closing it. On maps where it rains or snows (which is visually beautiful) the game plays in slow motion and drops frames.
Online is also, for all intents and purposes, unplayable. Matchmaking is slow because so many people are turned off from the horrid performance issues and the netcode is so sloppy you are almost guaranteed to disconnect within the first 10 seconds of a game.
And the nail in the coffin is the one who did this; High Voltage Studios. They ported Mortal Kombat 9 and Injustice: Gods Among Us. Both made by Netherrealm as well, both were never fixed to playability. Both studios have routinely deleted complaints about the game and refuse to acknowledge the broken product they are selling. IN CONCLUSION: If you love Mortal Kombat, buy this game. Just never, ever on PC.

*EDIT* Don't bother with this game. They aren't supporting it for PC any more and future DLC is going to be console-exclusive. I will no longer be buying or supporting NRS as long as they are affiliated with Warner Bros. /end edit.
Maybe I have a little more tolerance and patience than others, and that's fine. I can't speak for those who have reviewed this game in a negative manner, which happens to be due to several issues having to do with online play.
I myself do not play online, so I personally haven't run into any of these issues.
Graphics- this is, in my opinion, the best looking Mortal Kombat game made. The art direction is phenomenal and the stages are top notch. Every character has had some true love paid to it and it shows. Characters of which I've had no interest before have snagged my interest, and even old favorites have gotten a facelift that make them stand out.
Sound- This is the best sounding Mortal Kombat made. Lots of time and effort has been spent making the right sounds fit, and it is top-notch.
Gameplay- I don't have the skills that other gamers do, but I've had fun fighting while using different characters. I love that each character has 3 variations- I think it adds variety and spice to the replay factor.
Story- kinda short. There was potential here, and this is about the only place where NRS may have dropped the ball a little bit. There was a good chance to develop characters here, and the development is minimal.  But it still is satisfying, in my opinion.
There is a lot here in this game, and in my opinion it's a worthwhile buy. I would, however, suggest that if you were going to get this for only multiplayer, to perhaps wait until NRS/WB and the studio working on the PC port get the online portion fixed.

The game currently only has one campaign which on average lasts for 45 minutes to 1 Hour, depending if you playing solo or with friends but recently, I have only been playing the campaign to either complete character specific challenges, play with friends or since it's the only campaign you can currently play right now.
The combat is kind of hack 'n' slash, with three abilities, a dodging system which proves helpful in maintaining the combo to regen SPECIAL points in order to use those abilities.
However, I can't help but make suggestions for the developers to consider in their game. I don't know if other fans would appreciate this but I know I would love these additions if they are not already being thought about.
• The enemies in the game currently kind of weak currently, with them being only 200 HP, 400 HP, 1000 HP and so on and so forth. I would also like if the campaign had levels of difficulty in them, longer levels or more levels (Basically missions) and bosses would be a great addition to the game aswell (Cause every game needs a boss fight, come on!).

• The current characters are obviously the main characters of the show (Ruby, Weiss, Blake & Yang) but if other characters or teams (JNPR, CRDL, CFVY, SSSN, ABRN, NDGO, BRNZ) were added, I have no doubt they would make the game a nice variation and also if certain characters had abilities that could only be performed with other characters.

• This was suggested by a friend of mine and I thought this would be awesome to have, which is a character customization system, where you can create your character with the choice of customizing appearances, style of fighting and weaponry.

• While in game, I noticed you can't check your teammate' health bars or special bars and would prove helpful to have them on the screen while fighting in case a team needs a quick revive or help with some enemies.
• There is a leveling system in game but maybe a profile level wouldn't be so bad if other character do come out. That way, you can show off how much a character you have played, your best charater, best stats, etc.

It's hard to find the right voxel game to play, but I think this comes quite close.
I was interested in Portal Knights for a while but since it was in Early Access, I didn't want to invest. Now I have it because it was on sale, and it turns out to be a pretty fun game. It looks like your standard voxel game, and there is harvesting and crafting, but there are also RPG elements that give you a sense of progression.
You start by customizing your character's look and picking one of three classes: Warrior, Ranger or Mage. The world you enter is made up of about 40+ islands that were broken apart in some ancient explosion. Each island has at least one portal leading to another island (some have more than one). The islands are also crawling with enemies that drop loot and xp you can use to better your character, which you'll need to do in order to cross the world and defeat its bosses.
The main focus of the world seems to be getting from one island to the next, but crafting is essential, as you'll need to create better gear to handle more difficult enemies, and build your own home to store your stuff. But crafting and fighting enemies aren't the only things to do in the game. There are NPCs that can give you quests, as well as buy/sell things. Events pop up randomly on different islands, which give you a chance at better rewards or rare ingredients. There are also dungeons on practically every island, with large treasure chests hidden inside. Many useful recipes only drop from enemies and bosses, too, so you'll want to get out there and fight so you don't miss anything.
Multiplayer is pretty fun and interesting. Unlike other voxel games, it's not done with a dedicated server; instead, one player will start a play session and the other(s) will join in. XP is shared, but items are not; however, item sharing shouldn't be a big deal since you're playing co-op. The only thing I don't like about multiplayer is how "stuck together" you and your party are. The game will only allow you to be on one island at a time, so if one party member decides to jump through a portal, all party members get dragged along. No one's allowed to leave the group to rush back to the home island and craft/store something.
I recommend Portal Knights to anyone who loves open world survival/crafting games. With the presence of level-based monsters and the random shape of each island, this game can easily hold my attention for longer than others in the same genre. It has the one thing that most open world crafting/survival games are missing: A sense of progression and accomplishment.

Very rarely can a game be regarded as a masterpiece - this is one of them.
From its stunning, attentively detailed, beautiful art style and graphics, to its innovative gameplay mechanics, this game has it all. The story is extremely powerful and made me cry a well of tears. I laughed, cried, 'aww'ed, felt hope, fear, agony, strength, trust, love, and just about every other emotion on the spectrum.
Without an understandable English word spoken once, you still comprehend and appreciate the entire story, what is being said, and the emotions being felt, simply due to the excellent animations, symbolism and direction. I feel it is better this way without English being spoken, since you get fully immersed in the environment and truly focus on every other aspect to contribute to your understand of what is happening, versus just letting potentially dull exposition tell it to you directly. It is so much more fun, unique and driving to infer these things on your own; this approach also leaves some things up for interpretation by each individual player.
This game is really, really short, possibly the shortest full game I've ever played - it took only 3 hours to complete (yes, even shorter than Modern Warfare 3's campaign :P), and an extra hour to finish unlocking all achievements. Even so, in those few hours, its story is so effective and efficient that you become so utterly, dearly attached to the characters. Their personalities are so deftly displayed and understood in such a short time - even for all the side characters, which just comes to show how amazing this game is. It truly understands human nature, what it means to be human, and all the faults that come along with it. Rarely have I encountered a game which so accurately depicts realistic human behavior and psyche.
Its art and animaiton are unparalleled, and all the more impressive that it is pulled off with zero graphics settings available - this game is so well optimized it can seemingly run well and this beautifully on most PCs. The devs did an astounding job in making this game as polished and realistic as can be - it has some of the best and most realistic water physics and visuals I have seen in a game, even beating Bioshock's water simulation, when it comes to standing bodies of water.
The puzzles are simple and at times very easy, but they are still fun, unique, and clever implementations of the game mechanics and controls, making for great scenarios that can only be exclusive to a game like this. The satisfaction that comes after completing many of the puzzles is enough to make something like this not that big a concern. If anything, it is better for it not to be too difficult, so as not to distract from the pacing and the main aspects of the game, primarily its story and world.
The animation is incredible and extremely fluid - everything is animated just as it should be, with an excellent eye for detail - from the reflections on the water, to particles in the air, the devs made sure to keep everything as spot-on as could be. I had been continuously wowed throughout the game with its visuals, vistas, colorful, lively, realistic environments, and unparalleled use of shadows and highlights, which all make for a gorgeously toned, unforgettable game and experience.
The soundtrack is also something very compelling and emotional - it is one of the better OSTs I have been witness to in a game. It perfectly complements the emotional ride and tone of the game, making for a unified experience that hits you on all fronts. The music is so good and at times so epic, that I will be downloading its soundtrack, and will revel in the memories that get recalled each time I hear the songs, both the sad ones and beautiful ones.
There is very little this game does wrong. Only one time did I encounter a bug which left the younger brother stuck in place unable to move (so I had to restart from checkpoint), and at times the controls can get wonky and confusing (due to lack of control instructions or the ambidextrous nature of its movmenets), but faulting it on things like this would be an utter crime. This piece of art so aptly demonstrates how powerful, emotional, meaningful, and beautiful video games can be, and the unique experience that only something of this genre and medium can offer. This is one of those few games which I very much feel represent how gaming is an art form and this is one of the games I would give to a newcomer or critic of gaming to experience, to truly understand what video games are about and what they have to offer.
You MUST play this game. For the emotional ride, for the unique experience - every aspect of this game is worth your while. You couldn't spend 3 hours any better way.

A review for this game may be pointless now. But I feel I need to praise this game for the immense enjoyment I got out of it since purchase. I will say three very positive things about this game.
1 Combat balance: While it is true this game is super easy past level 20 or so, the "balance" I am talking about here is the balance between warrior/mage/rogue play styles. Unlike many other fantasy type games I've played, where your mage character usually gets much less choice in equipment compared to warrior/rogue types, here in this game, mages have the equal amount of variety in both weapon and armor selection, and some of the mage weapons are the most interesting ones I have ever played in any game. Reversely, in many other fantasy games, while warrior and rogue characters got more choices in equipment, they got shafted in spells they can use, this is again not true for this game. The rogue and warrior have a lot of interesting abilities they can cast around just like mages. This balanced playing style makes all three schools and any combination of the three feel refreshed and extremely fun for the majority of the game. And if you are like me who feel mages should have as much choice in equipment as other characters you are certainly going to love this game.
2 Art style: Kingdoms of Amalur is probably the most gorgeous game I have seen for a very long time. While many mordern games may have better "graphics", they don't necessarily look any prettier. I am in the camp that firmly believes a good art design and style is more important than graphics and constantly find games from 1990s look better than games released in the past 10 years. And while the very particular bright and colorful art style of this game may not be for everyone, it is definitely the preferred style for me. And the game maps is carefully designed so you end up in many majestic positions in game to appreciate the view. Each major city in the game is grand and elegantly beautiful, each region has its own unique charm while all look amazingly appeasing all the time. In summary I think the art style is perfect in this game, if you love it at first sight you will love it for the remainder of the game.
3 Sound track: While not many of the soundtracks stand out on their own, the magic thing here is that each of them goes along perfectly with the scenary. Good soundtrack in video games enhances the atmosphere and by that standard each music piece in this game is considered superb. Whether if it is charm, grandeur, danger or mystery the music in this game brings the mood out perfectly.
To sum up, this is one of the most fun and beautiful game I have played in a long time. I hope whoever read this review can enjoy it as much as I do with this piece of epic gem.

Game Name: Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning
Developer: 38 Studios / Big Huge Games
Genre: Role Playing / RPG
History: I first played Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning on the xbox 360 2 years ago about 6 months after it's debute. I loved it! I saw it on sale on here and picked it up. I had a blast playing though it a second time.
Story: You are the "Fateless One" you start the game off as a dead body. You are dumped down onto a pile of bodies in what seems to be an incinerator room. Shortly after you wake up and find the place you are at under attack. As you progress though the story you find out how you came to be, and that you have no "fate" and are able to change the fates of those around you. This leads you on a quest to stop the evil  Tuatha Deohn, their King Gadflow and  their God  Tirnoch all of whom want you dead a second time.
Game play: This is where is game shines and also falls short. You can chose from any combination of three classes Warrior, Rogue, or Mage. You have many skills and a very well done progession tree. You can also redo your toon anytime you want at a fatewaver for a price. This is very well done to me it allows us the players never to be tired down to one class. If you want to be a mage and use a greatsword as your main weapon do it!! You also have a unique power to fateshift enemies. This grats an experience bonus and each enemy has a different fateshift death all of them are really cool. The monsters in the games quests level with you but, on the open world map they have set levels. This ensures that you can't get too far ahead as enemies will start to one shot you before too long. As for the games difficulty it's a very easy game. They made it way to easy to make your toon unkillable ( Unlike in skyrim where there is an armor cap making heary armor useless accpet for looks as you can never get past 80% damage reduction ) In this game there is no cap at all on armor or resistance. I had made my toon almost unkillable by about 20 hours into the game. That's where is falls short the first time. You should never have a "no cap on armor or resistance" always cap them at least 80%. This also made to me all the sets of armor pretty useless. None of them could come close to what I could make just by socketing a few gems into dropped armors. This also sets the game up for you to have a lot of fun making your perfect unkillable toon though. By the end of the game when you have access to flawless blacksmithing you can in fact make a toon that cannot be killed. I had a great time making my unkillable mage with -100% mana costs. I had a blast just slinging spells left and right completely obliterating all that opposed my demigod powers!
Where is game really falls short is making the people and stories interesting. After the first few hours of gameplay I found myself skipping all the dialogue and just following the yellow circles on the map. The people are boring and the way they talk in that monotone voice set put me to sleep. Only a few of the main assist charactors have thier own unique models it. Everyone else in the entire game pretty much looks the same. I found this to be very boring. They could have used more soundbites as well... I hated running though adessa every single gnome says "What!!" as you walk past and all the humans say "yes, aye" just one trip made me mute the sound till I left the city. If they had made the toons more unique and added more soundbites it would have been so much better.

The whole squad control thing didnt interest me at first, but the way you control your 1-3 units is just a two button execution. One to toggle between the teams and one to execute a order which are dynamic depending on what you are looking at. If you aim at cover, they move there, if you aim at enemies they shoot and if they are close enough they will use hand granades as well.
Suppress, advance, flank and kill is the most common tactic. Every enemy has a icon over their general location which makes giving orders easy. While the enemy icon is red, they are a threat and can easly shoot you. If the icon are gray, they are supressed and you have a easier time advancing... and so on.
The gameplay is great, fun and works fine. The story is trying to be like the HBO series Band of Brothers, but considering the shorter time a game has to tell such a story it becomes very cheesy.
I would recommend it if it goes on sale again.

I've played for barely an hour so I'm not really sure what all to say about it. It's early access, so it's still pretty rough. But it's come a long way from the pre-alpha demo that RT Sponsors got early this year, and I have a feeling we're only seeing the tip of the iceberg here.
Pros
+ It's RWBY! In video game form! Any fans of the series are going to enjoy the game just for that fact alone.
+ The playable characters (So far, just Ruby, Weiss, Blake, and Yang) have movesets that you'd expect them to use in the show.
+ The music and scenery are all fitting for the world that it is supposed to be set in.
+ The character models, both playable and nonplayable, are spot on. If you told me they were ripped straight from the show, I'd believe it.
+ Lindsay Jones (Ruby), Kara Eberle (Weiss), Arryn Zech (Blake), and Barbara Dunkelman (Yang) all reprise their roles from the show, as well as Ryan Haywood (Professor Port) and Joel Heyman (Professor Oobleck) providing commentary and mission objective updates.
+ Patches! It seems that the development team is working hard to make sure everything is working the way it's supposed to, and their first patch came out within a few days of release.
Cons (Because this is early access, some of these can be taken with a grain of salt, as they will probably be fixed later)
- While the controls are pretty pick-up-and-play, there is no tutorial or controller map, so you're left guessing what buttons do what.
- No offline mode. You absolutely HAVE to play online.
- No matchmaking. Players are matched up entirely at random, and you can't even choose to start a room on your own. If you want to host a match, you have to hope to get lucky.
- No lock on mechanic. There's no way (as far as I can tell) to lock on to a single enemy. You're basically left to swing away until you hit something, and during heavy fighting, you can end up switching targets multiple times.
- Might just be personal, but I experienced delays in animation when characters start to run, resulting in a motionless glide across the ground.
- Minimum requirements are fairly hefty. I play some pretty intensive games on this computer, even online, but this game gets quite a bit of lag when multiple enemies and players are on screen.

This is a very interesting and deep global conflict game. Perhaps my favorite one out of the competition, due to the fact that the research system is actually pretty deep. The best selling point for me was, though, that any country can develop its economy system as much as it wants, limited only by the amount of land hexes it has. Indeed, the resources are not all available everywhere, especially uranium (several places on the map), yet one can decide to specialize in industrial (building) and consumer goods and be flush with cash even if the raw materials are not available in the country. Just develop a good relationship with a country that has the raw materials and get "discounts" on the goods through manual trading.
The game teaches one very important aspect of real life: A country is only as powerful as its industrial base allows it to be. Armies do not win wars, economies do. In other words: Germany was not a winner in either world wars for a reason. The best armies and equipment in the world in the beginning of those conflicts inevitably proved to be lacking as the industrial/resource base just wasn't enough to take on an extended fight.
So: get the game, choose a country, develop a good relationship with a resource "donor", use its raw resources to build up your industrial/military might, then take over the neighboring losers who were not smart enough ot do the same (AI lol). Flush and repeat. A month later (real time) - you have the world conquered and ready for another go with a smaller/poorer country.
Yes, the game will take a LOOONG TIME.
Worth it if you are young and have time to kill.

Highly recommended if you're into strategy.

I've played the Supreme Ruler series since SW2020 now 10 years ago.  SRU is an excellent game if you understand how to play it.  There is a learning curve.
DIPLOMACY: There isn't much feedback ingame regarding the diplomacy system, which is rather streamlined compared to 4X games (you won't see a leader come to you and have specific personal responses to specific in game actions such as putting troops on their border), but if you trade actively and support the regimes of whatever nation you are seeking to woo, you will see diplomatic relations steadily improve. Otherwise, the diplomatic relations seem mostly random, simulating various diplomatic accomplishments or crises going on behind the scenes and outside of direct view to you as the Supreme Ruler. On higher volatility levels you can see relations improve or deteriorate quickly on their own.  There is supposed to be a reason for changes in diplomatic relations, but it is often not directly clear. Increasing your military cap is one way relations will deteriorate (per the SR wiki). If your volatility is set to "None" diplomatic relations hardly change at all without your direct input. If you use "support the ruling regime" option for a particular country the relations will improve with the government you are targeting, apparently simulating diplomatic efforts to increase ties with that nation. If you select "support opposition" the relations will deteriorate with that government somewhat quickly without explanation, soon giving you a pretext on which to declare war. Trading often and generously (on terms more favorable to the other side) will increase your relations slowly with the common people of the country (as opposed to its government/ruling elite) over time. That's essentially it as far as the diplomacy system goes. The diplomacy has dramatically improved with recent patches, and the AI now actively creates alliances and declares war and peace, something it did not do very often before.
MILITARY: The military simulation is extremely well detailed and modeled, with precise unit description by both nation and era, everything is simulated from infantry unit types, to mobile infantry, to air and sea down to specific small patrol boats. Unit movement is real time (units will move as fast as you'd expect them to in one game day) and very realistic. Land features and geography are hex based and each hex is meticulously modeled and based on the real world geographical data, and the game also includes a dynamic weather simulation that can affect combat. As of July 2017, AI is still a little sloppy on naval warfare but hardly worse than most games out there. The AI will not form fleets or conduct extremely organized naval campaigns using aircraft carriers, but it will randomly send ships over to whoever it is declaring war on, hoping at some point to land some troops on the continent in question. Land combat is more realistic with AI units moving back and forth, resupplying, and gaining position slowly and strategically.
ECONOMY: The economic simulation is realistic and accurate, as long as you understand that the game makes no distinction between the private economy and the public economy.  The economy responds, in my experience, very realistically to changes in inputs and outputs.  For example, substantial state increase in infrastructure spending will result in a good year of 40% GDP growth, curtailing slowly quarter over quarter until it is back to normal.  The economy responds slightly less resiliently to tax cuts than to spending changes.  You are considered the "Supreme Ruler" of both the public and private economic sectors.  The game doesn't care if the health care sector for example is run privately or publicly.  If you increase health care spending GDP will start to rise as will inflation.  The more you spend, and the more you cut taxes/prices, the faster the GDP will grow, but be careful you don't overheat your economy and cause high inflation or the prices of buildings, goods, and services and resources will rise dramatically.  Impatient management of your economy and large fluctuations in stimulus will lower your economic score. I recommend running numerical reports quarter over quarter so you have data from which to compare changes over the next quarter- write down all the values including production and consumption values for each commodity.  To have more control over your commodities and to drive up prices in your favor I recommend bulk trading only, when market conditions are favorable.
This game is an excellent game and is constantly improving.  The developers are VERY responsive to any issues that arise, and have recently reopened the studio full time to once again work on future SRU titles.  If you're interested in the genre of detailed and realistic world strategy this game is definitely for you.

Portal Knights is an exploration RPG with a plethora of crafting mechanics. The game went through an early access period, and from what I read, the developers listened to the community rather often to help shape the game. At the time of official release there are 3 classes to play, Warrior, Ranger, and Mage. In order of mention, they are your archetypal melee, ranged, and magic classes of any RPG. Each class has their own unique talents that can shape your playstyle that you can also, to my great relief, change whenever you want. You also get specific character skills like strength for extra melee damage, but these can only be changed with a rather rare potion. After that is where the real player uniqueness comes in. Some items can only be used by certain classes, but there is room to mix up your playstyle, such as a melee-based Ranger with a high strength build.
Where this can kind of hit a brick wall is the intentional scaling of different tiers of ores and materials in the game. You are also required to grind out quite a few recipes, which unless you run across them or read a guide, you won’t know they exist for the most part. The problem this brings is that some of these recipes may be required to continue doing your playstyle without getting your♥♥♥♥♥beat by random enemies in the world. For me, this is both fun and very tedious because you must adapt to what items are available. The game is continuously updating and becoming more complex so things may change and this can become less of a “problem,” but there’s always room for you to adapt. For now, the tedium is there of feeling underpowered because you’re forced to make do with a mediocre weapon. Sometimes I felt like I was searching more for a better weapon than exploring and enjoying the world I was on.
The worlds of Portal Knights are the shining redeemer for me though in what is chiefly an exploration game. There are various biomes that a planet can be and its filled with enemies that are relevant to that biome. What makes the worlds special though, is that each one feels truly unique even though they are randomly created. There’s houses, forts, and other buildings that can dot the landscape, or it can be a barren wasteland. The various flora and enemies complete the package and really flesh out the worlds. Enemies can be recycled, but may have different abilities, and the color pattern for biomes can get repetitive, but there’s only so much they can do with that. They do have plans to introduce new enemy types and such though, so something to look forward to.
There are also friendly NPC’s you can run into, most of whom I immediately attempted to kill on sight. You can’t kill them, at least not yet. Most say a few one-liners and stand around. A few can be traders or quest givers. The trading and quest system works fine, but there’s no marker for the NPC on the map. So, after you went halfway across the world to kill X or craft X for the quest, there’s no indicator of where to return to. Add in the fact that you’re mining and/or fighting your way across the world, it’s pretty damn easy to get turned around. Same thing applies for the trader. You have limited inventory, so say you went back to your base for something to sell, you better have remembered where that NPC was. All part of the exploration aspect I guess, but the first quest giver I ran into was standing in the middle of a jungle. The entire world was jungle, so after a few minutes of wandering around and fighting for my life, I gave up trying to find him.
My Two Cents
The final sale price is $19.99 on Steam and some people set their expectations of a game solely on that price. I’ve learned to use it as a good buffer but always step into something with some optimism.  I found some things that annoyed me like the recipe grinding, but that’s honestly nit-picking. The game has a great premise and executes exactly what it set out to do. I truly had fun exploring the different worlds and beating up on bad guys. I never reached that dreaded point of asking myself “what now?” or why I was still playing. If you’re looking for a colorful exploration RPG with crafting/building, definitely pick this game up. The developers are still avidly working on it and that’s always a great sign, that developers care about what they created rather than thinking of it as just a paycheck.

I've been a Blizzard fan boy for quite sometime and needless to say, with the lackluster delivery of Diablo III, I was searching for yet another aRPG franchise to take up the slack.  Without prior knowledge of who created the Torchlight series I quite obviously and understandably turned to Path of Exile.  PoE was free and well received.  Although it was "fun" it left me wanting more still.  Fast forward to this years Steam Winter Sale and Torchlight II for 5.00$ seems like the deal of the century for me.  As quickly as Runic Games won my heart they crushed it equally quick with the departure of co-founders Erich Schaefer and Travis Baldree.   My hopes lie with the rest of the team though to come up with another great sequel in Torchlight III (fingers crossed).
Anyways, on to the actual game.  Torchlight II is a hack and slash RPG that changes minimally from its predecessors so that it is different but so familiar it seems like you've been with it for years.  The character classes are a welcome departure from our normal warrior,mage,rogue and add a more colorful cartoony element to the game.  The story telling although sometimes minimal is enjoyable and a break from large cinematics with more narration and cartoon style cut scenes.  Outside of these changes it is a tried and true hack 'n slash with multiple acts (3) - lots of challenging creatures & dungeons - and new and sometimes interesting NPCs as you travel from town to town.
Overall Torchlight II is an amazing game that has all of mechanics you love in a hack and slash game with just enough of a difference to make it stand out from the rest. If hack and slash is your genre then Torchlight II is a must own & play.
