TL;DR at the bottom
The core of the game mechanics are there. It really does feel like a Hack n' Slash just like Dynasty Warriors, except there isn't thousands of grimm to slaughter. You get to play as team RWBY, each has a basic attack, long range attack and 3 specials. The combat is smooth except for the long range attacks and specials, with thes you can end up shooting the ground instead of hitting the grimm rying to eat you. I believe some sort of lock-on mechanic would be able to fix this.
The upgrade system is.....well functional. You need to do earn certain achievements to unlock certain skills and bonuses that increases your special damage, your aura(HP), aura recharge rate and special bar(used to activate specials). But due to the current short nature of the game, you'll only be able to get a small amount of these upgrades (I managed lvl 10 by the end of the 3rd mission).
The game features a fluid difficulty, the more players, the harder it is. Soloing it is childs play while a full party of 4 people is still childs play. I feel the game is lacking difficulty, I find it that the presence of the grimm is not menancing enough and really easy to clear out, soloing or in a full party.
The glismp of the story we get  is interesting which adds a little bit more lore to the RWBY universe and does not require the show to understand it (would be helpful to get to know the characters). Would like to see how the full story plays out.
Graphics wise, would be similar to a JRPG, and has 3 settings, Potato ( can't believe this was actually a setting), Normal and Ultra. I also find no difference between Normal and Ultra. There's multiple  resolution options to chose from.
I do find people are disconnecting a lot in parties, which the hosts are usuaslly are blamed, but I find it unlikely that every host has bad connection. So the server seems to need some tweaking for proper multi-player experience.
TL;DR
Bare bones of the game, fighting mechanics are there, barely any story. Only recommend if you're a massive fan of the show and want to support this game production.

Long winded review
Gunz: The Duel was an all time favourite of mine in terms of Online gaming. It had three things that would attract any testosterone filled young male to its seductive grasp: Guns, Swords, and acrobatically combining them along with flexible coats and scarves for extra Flair. I spent months grinding to level 20, relishing every battle and every lesson I learned to get that flexi coat. Naturally I felt inclined to play the long awaited sequel/reboot to theis all time high speed Third person shoot-em-up.
To specify a number of things the Original game had: there was a character customization system, with a wide array of weaponry and outfits each with attributes to suit different play styles, an incredibly high speed parkour system that required both skill to use and to shoot at, very reasonable ping games due to popularity and localization, as well as compatibility with most graphics cards due to the 2006-era appearance. On top of all this, Gunz' main draw was that it seamlessly (for its time) integrated the use of firearms and swords as weapons in battle, no fight was just a firefight or just a swordfight, each weapon type had strenghts and weaknesses to comabt each other, and players were required to use guile to use this to their advantage.
What does New GunZ2 has? Does it back this up, Does it immprove on this? does it have an even better system?
No.
character customization? enjoy having a selection of one of four racial sterotype, cookie cutter, CLASS BASED, "Actors", bear in mind you have to pay micro transactions if you blindly make the wrong decision, as you cannot test each class out.
Wide array of gear? ♥♥♥♥ that, have a choice of three aesthetic costumes and barely a handful of Class based guns that have only slightly varied stats
Parkour system?I have no idea how they managed it, but they seem to have made parkour the single slowest part of the game, not to mention painfully user unfriendly. It seems like they were catering to americlap babies who couldnt keep up with experienced koreans. In fact, it seems that the parkour only remains as a tribute to its predecessor for which it was so revered. I could easily see that GunZ 2 was designed, and then some chaep system was thrown in at the end for parkour. its insulting
What about ping and graphics lag? welcome to APB Reloaded, only you live in australia, and the servers are still in the US. no matter what your ping is, you're gonna get shot through walls or have that random asian cat magically teleport behind you and stunlock you with their swords.
on the topic of APB reloaded, the new GunZ shares the same, miserably colourful art design. the old game had an art style of muted colors gothic hallways and an all-in-all grim and gritty feel. the new one simply looks like they took a level of street fighter (and characters) mashed it to fit a basic CS:S layout and called it good art.
Finally, gun-to-sword combat. This is what GunZ is famous for, right? this must be what's coming through to prevail for the new game?
NOPE, NO DICE.
Gun. always. trumps. sword.
Discarding the fact that the game designers ignored the existence of assault rifles, you can pretty much bet that the nly reason people run into one another with blades is either to depserately try and scarpe any of the old exhiliration from the old game, or they're simply trying to stunlock the other guy until he dies (which is a thing. a very bad thing. That I exploited and won every match with).
There is no tension, no risk that someone on the enemy team might have a knife making you wish you picked kodachi. the worst you have to worry about is "oh, someone was stupid enough to pic shieldguy? nvm I flanked him he's dead now"
Should you play GunZ2?
If you want to see how maiet have successfully managed to cripple the name of an amazing game by producing the exact opposite, and you have no concerns wasting your time which is better spent playing an actual game.
even then No. go play an actual game. this is one of the worst pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥I have ever played. Uninstall it from your computer and use that memory space on a game worth playing, such as the Original Gunz: The Duel

Your 'mana' does not recharge outside battle, why? 12 hit combo required to charge 1 mana for special attacks which cost 1 or 2. Either make it easier for special attacks to be used or don't make them useless by making them stronger.

If these suggestions can be addressed then that'll be great.

Without prior knowledge of who created the Torchlight series I quite obviously and understandably turned to Path of Exile.  PoE was free and well received.  Although it was "fun" it left me wanting more still.  Fast forward to this years Steam Winter Sale and Torchlight II for 5.00$ seems like the deal of the century for me.  As quickly as Runic Games won my heart they crushed it equally quick with the departure of co-founders Erich Schaefer and Travis Baldree.   My hopes lie with the rest of the team though to come up with another great sequel in Torchlight III (fingers crossed).
Anyways, on to the actual game.  Torchlight II is a hack and slash RPG that changes minimally from its predecessors so that it is different but so familiar it seems like you've been with it for years.  The character classes are a welcome departure from our normal warrior,mage,rogue and add a more colorful cartoony element to the game.  The story telling although sometimes minimal is enjoyable and a break from large cinematics with more narration and cartoon style cut scenes.  Outside of these changes it is a tried and true hack 'n slash with multiple acts (3) - lots of challenging creatures & dungeons - and new and sometimes interesting NPCs as you travel from town to town.
Overall Torchlight II is an amazing game that has all of mechanics you love in a hack and slash game with just enough of a difference to make it stand out from the rest. If hack and slash is your genre then Torchlight II is a must own & play.

I like the game. I do. I enjoy playing the singleplayer. I enjoy the story. The writing is decent and the gameplay is fun. However, there are two reasons why I can't recommend the game in its current state.
One is the stupidly heavy monetization push in the game. You can just straight up buy credits/praxis points for the singleplayer game. That's unacceptible. Even EA doesn't really pull shenanigans like that. Breach mode is also adversely affected, because the economy of the game is such that repeating missions to get higher scores or complete missions is a waste, since you won't recoup your ammo expenditures. Also, the preorder bonuses are one time use, so if you grab them on a file and then choose to do something else, they're gone forever. There is no way that this in any way resembles a good idea, not only from a monetization perspective (which is moot because it's not like you can buy them again) but also from a technical perspective.
Second is apparent design oversights or lack of cares. Some of the breach mission objectives, for example, are things like "Complete the mission in seven seconds" for a mission where you have to defeat a powerful enemy. By the time you hit the door, even if you one shot the enemy somehow you'd still be at like two seconds used. Some of the levels, just downloading data from terminals takes as long. Unless you're hacking, these objectives are basically unobtainable at the point in time you would first hit the mission unless you have insane augs, and might actually be impossible, meaning that there are gates in areas that will *never* be breached. I've also encountered a few bugs, such as clipping through an elevator after interacting with the button while moving and issues with getting stuck interacting with objects like the safe in Jensen's apartment.
Ultimately, because half the game's content (Breach mode in pretty much its entirety) is a cash grab and the other half feels like it's lacking in polish, at this point I *cannot* recommend the game to others. I'm still enjoying it, and I got it 40% off so I don't feel ripped off, but it's aggravating to buy a game that expects me to pay to play half the game meaningfully or to accelerate my singleplayer experience.

First off, the 6 hours on record would constitute my second time attempting to like this game, after about 15 spent a year of so back. Sadly, it's another failed attempt.
The game has a lot of quests, loot, crafting, decent combat and a very rich world, with extensive lore. Then why do I always feel bored 30 minutes into a play session? Mostly because it feels like someone took a generic MMORPG and tried to make a single player game out of it.
- The crafting feels useless, just a time sink.
- The abilities, skills also feel useless, since your character grows in strength mostly due to changing equipment.
- The open world feels empty - I felt like looking at one of those driving scenes in old movies with bad background work. The images change but you know they're not real. At some point pretending to use the steering wheel becomes pointless.
- The rich world filled with lore I mentioned above? Completely boring and bland. For all the dialog available, I found myself skipping through it, realizing that I would forget it anyway 2 minutes after the conversation ended.
- There was some thought put into enemy design, you will encounter very different types. Too bad the AI is truly poor, and you can literally go through them by button mashing away.
The only slightly redeeming quality is the combat, as it offers you plenty of options in killing those forgettable enemies I mentioned.
Overall, you might enjoy this to pass a bit of time, but it's definitely not worth going through the whole story. It's only the illusion of a fully realized RPG, and it's all downhill once that becomes apparent.

Often after completing an RPG I feel the need to immediately start again with a new character to explore alternative paths or skills. That did not happen with this game. It’s pretty good but not great. There were good parts and bad parts and overall the good won out. The world is interesting and the graphics are nice enough. After a while though you start to notice caves repeating themselves. But this was nowhere near as bad as Dragon Age 2, there were a lot more combinations. The combat flows well and feels like you’re in control although it took a little getting used to after hours of Skyrim.  I was playing as a warrior/rogue combo so I don’t have much experience with the spell system. For the size of the world there was not quite enough enemy variety. At higher levels you just fought the same foes but with more strength and armour. Also by the time I’d reached the max level (way before I was close to the end of the story thanks to DLC areas) I was way overpowered. Combat no longer had any risk. The main quest was great but it felt very spread out. In order to fill the large world there were just so many side quests. At times it felt endless and the problem was they were very generic compared to the main storyline. Go here, kill this. Save this person. Bring me 10 things. By the end I wasn’t really listening to what people were saying anymore, just waiting for the map marker to show up letting me know what I needed to kill. I’m glad I played through it but once was enough. If you’re an RPG fan with a gap to fill it might be worth a look.

Occasionally I play a fighting game at the arcade, but I haven't purchased one since Soul Edge for PS1. I played a decent amount of Mortal Kombat 2/3, Street Fighter 2, and One Must Fall as a wee lad. I say this because I think a lot of people like me have gotten tired of grinding CCGs, memorizing RTS build orders, and keeping up with MOBA meta builds,
I have to be honest, the fear of Tekken (and every fighting game) dying off within a few months almost scared me off. I played the game for just under 2 hours and seriously considered refunding it because of all of the doom and gloom. That's right - I actually enjoyed the experience, and I still thought about refunding it. I looked through my multiplayer options one more time, and couldn't have cared less about any of them. So I kept Tekken 7, played a couple more hours, and I'm happy to report that good decisions were made.
+ Noob friendly. This game isn't about learning a complicated set of Shorukens, Hurricane Kicks, and Hadokens (unless you're Akuma I guess). This game is about positioning, reading your opponent, and slowly learning what counters what. Yes, there are combos that are vital to learn for top tier play. It's just that these combos are a small piece of the puzzle compared to games like Street Fighter. Basically, when I lose in Tekken 7, I learn something. When I lose in Street Fighter I usually have no idea what happened.
+ Online netcode is fantastic. I've played about 20 onlines games, with 1 desync, no lag, and waiting an average time of under 30 seconds for each match.
+ Bandai Namco seems serious about listening to the players and my experience with them in Dark Souls III has been generally good.
+ Customization options are on point. There are tons of things to unlock/purchase without paying any real cash.
+ Music and stage backgrounds are varied and immersive.
+ Weak like on the number of characters. It's cool to have so many options, but it's also unrealistic to main more than 1-2 of them that it just adds more work to learning their counters.
+ Story mode is appealing for a fighting game. I care more about what's going on than I expected (which was to be none at all). I see some complaints about it - maybe Tekken used to have better stories? I don't know. As a Tekken noob though I am digging it after 1 chapter.
+ It's actually an enjoyable spectator game and the Twitch scene surrounding it seems pretty strong right now.
+ I hated rage arts/dives at first but realizing they aren't THAT hard to counter, they add another dynamic element to the gameplay.
- Tournament mode is unplayable right now. I'm really happy one exists and the rewards are really good when it actually works. Unfortunately, if the host drops then the entire tournament folds. If anyone leaves (like after losing, which is totally reasonable) then the rewards lessen. Spectator mode for tournament fails to ever sync. This should be an easy fix. If it's still broke in say, September, I'll start worrying about Bandai Namco a bit more.
- Treasure hunt mode feels like grinding. It's not that worst thing cause I can still practice moves against the AI, but the rewards growing for streaky play ruins the "jump in, jump out" nature of a fighting game. It's worsened by the fact that tournament mode is currently unplayable due to the above issues as these are the only two ways to unlock the more rare customization options.
- Weak dislike, but I'd like some more single player modes. It would probably lower the online community though which is, and should be, where the bulk of gameplay is focused.
- Mentioned above, but the doom and gloom player base. "Tekken 7 is dying OMG", "Should I play Tekken 7 or wait til XYZ", "Is there enough value here?", etc. The fact is: Tekken 7 is the biggest fighting game launched in the PC's history. Maybe it doesn't last as long as it deserves, but if I get a year of great play out of this then it'll easily be worth it.
I'm someone who wants to be rewarded for playing well, punished for playing poorly, and play a game that's easy to learn and hard to master. Tekken 7 is the epitome of these desires.
If you want an awesome fighting game and you've never played one then buy Tekken 7. It's worth it, you'll get tons of hours of gameplay, and you'll help overrun the Negative Nancys and Kevin Killjoys of the world. And if for some reason you aren't finding matches make sure you check your Steam region matches your Tekken region.

Divided We Fall takes the good old classic style of RTS from games such as Call of Combat and tries to bring it to the more modern design in regards to graphics and gameplay. Sadly however it feels like they were on the right track but gave up.
=========
The Good
=========
1. Gameplay - The General feel of gameplay is rather nice, you have cover system where your forces will take cover to objects that you would know give you some sort of cover. You have a small squad of units that require you to work with other players to make the best out of your team and overall you have a decent of weapons to use/pick up such as sniper rifles, sub machine guns and etc. Overall everything felt nice.
2. Map Designs - The map designs are nicely done with a lot of terrian to use and allows forces to flank each other or use a lot of cover to advance forward.
3. Fog of War - A very nice feeling to the fog of war, you can't see either of your forces or enemies but you can hear the directional gun fire allowing you to  create a general area to flank or support.
==========
The bad
==========
1. Buggy - Sadly the coop is broken, many times the game would crash at the end of the match or we be stuck in the game forever until trying to close the game. Many times I found randomly my forces either spawn with no weapons or have weapons but would just stand still without taking cover or firing back.
2. low or no playerbase - Sadly with no enough to keep players, it felt many times lacking in regards to player count. I found most of my companionship through playing with a close friend but looking for outside players seems unlikely.
3. Lack of gameplay - There isn't really much modes to enjoy, there isn't any special objective mode but mainly capture points or deathmatch. There is also a lack of variety in regards to units/equipment and etc.
4. A.Is from Hell - The A.I in this game is just evil...i found about 99% of games it would grenade spam me to hell...yeah it would literally be a game of toss as many grenades at the player to see how long he can dodge them...it was completely crazy.
================
What can be improved
================
1. Objective/story mode - Have a mode where players are given an objectives or an assault mode, objective mode could be like having one team defend a special objective such as an flak 88 while the other team must destroy it. The assault mode can be a large map where players have frontlines and must play a game of tug of war pushing their front lines closer to the enemy base, both teams can build bunkers, tank traps and etc to halt or slow down enemy player advancements.
2. Customization - Allow a more open squad customization adding classes and more equipment. For example have a medic class that can heal wounded players, have heavy support that can carry the heavy machine guns that require the unit to "set up" before use, have snipers/scouts that can see more of the map. Add Airborne that allows the squad to pick a random spawn throughout the map. Allow players to customize their uniform to better reflect their Squad making it feel more like their own. Allow a "X-Com" type squad system where your unit can level up but if killed (dies in combat too many times), they will be killed losing their level  and forcing the player to retrain a new unit, this would allow a deeper connection between squads as they would move more carefully and plan more instead of "run and grenade" tactics.
3. More factions - Add more factions for players to enjoy. Like Japanese, Russians and etc
4. Add destruction - Allow grenades to destory cover forcing players to rethink.
Overall I have to say the game has a good chance but a lot needs to be changed/improved to bring more interest. At the moment I recommend avoiding as there isn't much to do to keep you going. The player base is rather low or dead and you can find other war games out there to give you a better experience.

Well surely I am a RWBY otaku, bought this game in Day 2, and thought it was worth each and every bucks. But if you are a normal 'gamer', keep away, this doesn't worth $15 in a gaming standard, not yet. If it's ready, which I'm sure it will be, I'll tell you guys then.

Initially, Spelunky can be very difficult. There are many ways to die in Spelunky. Fortunately, there are many ways to avoid death. I think this is the core of why I find it so satisfying.
There are many ways to play Spelunky. You can be cautious or reckless. You can collect gold or ignore it. You can learn to use all the items or avoid the ones that you don't trust. You can try to rescue every damsel or ignore them. You can wantonly kill enemies or just try to avoid them. You can attempt special side-levels or stick to the regular ones. No matter how you choose to play, you can probably beat the game (with enough practice).
Spelunky is a game of skill. At first, you may have trouble getting out of the mines. When you start to reach the jungles, the ice caves, the temple or beyond, you can know that you, personally, have become a better player, because the game isn't doing anything to help you out. Every new game starts at the same place and follows the same rules, no matter how many times you've won or died.
The world of Spelunky is complex and rewards close attention. As you play, you may discover new levels, new interations or new ways to challenge yourself. These discoveries are not "unlocked" by the game. They have always been there, waiting for you to notice them. Even after you can defeat Olmec consistentlly, you will probably keep making new discoveries. (Of course, you can also read everything there is to know online instead. There are many things that I probably still wouldn't know if I hadn't learned them from a friend or seen them on the internet. But, discovering some things for yourself is also very satisfying.)
Of course, the mechanics are very good also. The controls are consistent and responsive (although I find that wired controllers and "less fancy" TVs work best). The graphics are attractive. The music and sound is effective (and can be subtly crucial sometimes).
I was part of the beta, and I admit, I bought this the SECOND it was available, so expect me to continue to help make it better. :)

Brothers: A tale of Two sons
Review
There are games that exist merely with the intent of making us feel like the ultimate bad♥♥♥♥♥ there are games that test our reflexes and our minds, and then there are games like Brothers: a tale of two sons. An emotional adventure that has sealed a place in my hearts with its brilliant sets and memorable characters. Let’s take a look at this little masterpiece.
Story.
Brothers: a tale of two sons is a story about you guessed it brothers and their quest to a magical tree that holds the antidote to their father’s illness. Armed with nothing but a map and each other, these boys set off on a magical adventure that takes them to a strange land where it becomes clear that they don’t quite belong. You can go ahead and argue until your blue in the face about silent protagonists and how they are old fashioned and how you can’t get an emotional connection with the characters if they have nothing to say but that’s just untrue. These two boys show more emotion and character in a few hours than most triple A protagonists do across an entire series. The amount of emotion expressed in each movement and each grunt and nonsensical language they speak, speaks volumes to their personalities and thoughts. I can’t overstate enough about the emotional impact and will delve deeper in my story review but the tale of these two sons is one story I won’t be forgetting anytime soon.
Gameplay.
As far as the Gameplay goes there’s not much to be said here. It’s your typical puzzle solving gameplay where two protagonists each with their own unique abilites help each other through varies situations. The catch this time is that each of the brothers is controlled by an opposing analog stick on your controller. Being the uncoordinated ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that I am I did find the control scheme to be quite bothersome at times. Having the wrong brother running ahead while his younger sibling is plowing into a wall can be frustrating at times but luckily there isn’t any platforming that needs to be so precise that this becomes to much of an issue. As far as the actual puzzles go there isn’t anything too complex but I will give credit to the section of the game where you are roped together with your sibling as easily the highlight in the gameplay category. All in all the game is fun to play even if it is annoying at times.
Presentation
The world that Starbreeze Studio created for this game is emaculate. The amount of mystery and wonder behind each section was breathtaking. I kept wondering to myself as I was playing, what’s going on here, what are these guys doing, what kind of creature lives here?” the entire time I was playing. The art direction is fantastic even having spots where your character can sit down and enjoy the beautiful scenery. From great mountain views to creepy castles all the way to terrifying caves. The diversity in presentation is something to admire in this title.
Brothers a tale of two sons is an experience very little games these past few years that I have played have been able to accomplish. The amount of emotion put into these characters and the journey these boys go on is a one of a kind experience that no one should miss out on. Tale of two sons is a crowning achievement in the study of how games can offer a one of kind story telling experience that can not be matched in any other genre.

This visual novel is basically about a talented protagonist that has lost his will to nurture his own talent, then coincidentally gets transported back in time to a time where pride and honor is the most important. He is forced to go through many hardships, but then tragedy strikes and he was given another chance to literally redo his life in the new world through time traveling. A journey where his personality constantly changes depending on the new knowledge he continues to learn, while looking for a way back home.

It's pretty fun and casual.  The world is not like open world, it's more like you explore closed sections (size you can change when creating a new "universe") with each section being varied biomes (ie one area is snow, while another is voclanic).  Aesthetically I do find it charming.
The combat is not super impressive but I enjoy it more than some other games like this.  The skills needs to be more worked on as you don't really have many choices.  Don't expect like rangers to use like "rain arrows" or a charged snipe shot.  You craft spells, which some of them are "shouts" that can be used by warriors.  Spells aren't locked to mage class so any other classes can use them (ie if you want to make a paladin or a swordsman/archer that can cast spells).  You can craft bombs for archers once you get their recipes, and there is a spec that can boost bomb damage.
Both magic/"skills" and armor are not class locked so you can kind of build the classes freeformish.  If only weapons were not locked, and deciding which class to choose would mostly be based on the talents, but this is just my opinion.
Even though they changed the stat system, all but one seem useful to me.  It is clear which stats belongs to which class but there is some flexibility as some stats are unviersal.  There are 6 stats: CON, STR, AGI, DEX, WIS and INT.  CON can be used with all classes as you can get more health.  INT/WIs can be used for other classes than mage if you wanna mix some magic.  Agility is the only stat I have issues with as it only boosts your movespeed.  I personally cannot tell any difference as most mosnters keep pace with me and the speed penalty you get when you attack (slows down when you start attacking) doesn't seem to speed up enough either.
The bosses aren't super difficult but I really love them, they can be fun for a casual player like me.  At least in my opinion, they are kind of reminiscent of bosses in calssic platform games like crash or spyro.  It's not super tactical but you have to do extra stuff to beat them and not like just pure attacking.  Again it's not really difficult once you learn the bosses' mechanics, but it's (imo) funner to grind lowbies with rather than having to grind as it is possible to beat them without taking much damage, it'll just take a while to beat them.
Multiplayer is kind of wierd and I honestly can't tell you if you'll like it or not.  It is fun to play coop but your party cannot play on seperate zones--if one ports, everyone has to join.  It is kind of a hindrance if you like wanna work on a plot of land but also want to contribute by farming materials from other regions but you cannot.  This really doesn't bother me as much, but can't say same for you.  Despite that, if you can plan it out with your fellow knights then it can still be a fun time.
This game feels (at least imo) like it's more focused on adventuring.  I think it is kinda fun unlocking new sectinos of the world, but the loading times may annoy you.  They aren't super long but you'll have to go through them frequently.  The length of time depends on the region size you are loading into.
I don't think the price is that bad, but game could definately get more things as well as improvements to the combat system (both fighting and skills/talents.)  I hope they bring more content and updates in the future, like maybe more weapons.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a puzzle platformer, made by the Swedish developer Starbreeze. You play two brothers on a quest to help their sick father.
I played this game on PC using an XBox controller, which I highly recommend. It can be played using a keyboard as well but I am convinced that you will have a much better game experience using a controller. You will rotate cranks, jump, climb, and experience controller vibrations as things get heated. I can’t see this working at all with a keyboard and you may even miss some very important story elements without a controller.
Much of the charm in this game lies in the game controls: What makes Brothers an interesting game is that you control both brothers simultaneously. It’s like playing a co-op with yourself: One hand will be rotating a crank, the other one will be climbing chains. Distract monsters with one brother while you attack with the other. It’s a game experience I haven’t experienced in my 20 years of gaming, and it works very well.
The surroundings look great and sometimes I took a moment to just look at the view. Magnificent sunsents, massive mountains, green fields… it’s just one picture perfect view after another. The game also has a lot of fun easter eggs that encourage you to explore side paths (even though most of the game consist of a one-way railroad).
Brothers also manages to tell a quite beautiful story, even though the characters speak nothing but Simlish.
The puzzles are pretty good, but I found the game a bit too easy. There were no real brainteasers: The solutions were always clear and there was only one way to go. There were no especially challenging jumps or other kinds of technically challenging passages either.
Playing the game a second time, picking up some achievements and easter eggs I had missed the first, I was also frustrated when I realized that all cutscenes were unskippable. For me, the game was very relaxing and would have a high replayability value, but having to wait for NPCs to move or cutscenes to finish took away from the fun when I had already seen the story once.
But, all in all, Brothers is a great game and gives a whole new gaming experience.

Initially, Spelunky can be very difficult. There are many ways to die in Spelunky. Fortunately, there are many ways to avoid death. I think this is the core of why I find it so satisfying.
There are many ways to play Spelunky. You can be cautious or reckless. You can collect gold or ignore it. You can learn to use all the items or avoid the ones that you don't trust. You can try to rescue every damsel or ignore them. You can wantonly kill enemies or just try to avoid them. You can attempt special side-levels or stick to the regular ones. No matter how you choose to play, you can probably beat the game (with enough practice).
Spelunky is a game of skill. At first, you may have trouble getting out of the mines. When you start to reach the jungles, the ice caves, the temple or beyond, you can know that you, personally, have become a better player, because the game isn't doing anything to help you out. Every new game starts at the same place and follows the same rules, no matter how many times you've won or died.
The world of Spelunky is complex and rewards close attention. As you play, you may discover new levels, new interations or new ways to challenge yourself. These discoveries are not "unlocked" by the game. They have always been there, waiting for you to notice them. Even after you can defeat Olmec consistentlly, you will probably keep making new discoveries. (Of course, you can also read everything there is to know online instead. There are many things that I probably still wouldn't know if I hadn't learned them from a friend or seen them on the internet. But, discovering some things for yourself is also very satisfying.)
Of course, the mechanics are very good also. The controls are consistent and responsive (although I find that wired controllers and "less fancy" TVs work best). The graphics are attractive. The music and sound is effective (and can be subtly crucial sometimes).

I like the game.  Though I cannot recommend it to friends.  I am a Supreme Ruler junky.  I have clocked hundreds of hours on the old 2020 DvD rom copy, and I have bought the game from multiple online vendors and even hard copies.  None of my friends have ever taken a liking to this title, but I am a strategy junky, and I love geo-politic sims.  Though, this game is more world domination, as politics doesn't really get you anywhere unless you want to tech trade.  I bought Coldwar and 1936, and bought ultimate because I really wanted to see the battle goats shine by optimizing this game and allowing me to play in all eras of SR in one neat package.
So in a nutshell, it's a real time strategy game that has moveable units like command & conquer, but nation and diplomatic elements like...well, watered down Civ.  It's base on real earth and real nations, and you can pick any nation you want, from any supported era of your choice, WW2, Coldwar, future.  You can build unit construction buildings, and resource collection buildings on resource tiles.  Create battle groups, and give orders via very clunky and unintuitive UI.  There is a resource economy, and money is time.  Your debt, or ability to acrue debt, inflation, or even positive treasury effects how fast you can build things and muster units.  Moving large amounts of units is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ and planning invasions is a chore.  It's easier to just take a beach head and turn on AI manager and let him zerg the enemy for you.  Though I still enjoy the game from time to time, because it is a neat world domination game and not a lot of games like it.  It is very niche.
So why can't I recommend it?  Well, it runs slow for one.  The AI isn't very good, and once you learn how to play, you can pick just about any country and take over the world, in time.  The economy is confusing for new comers, though is so simple once you get it down.  In fact, once you learn it, it is essentially cookie cutter, but dependent on what resources are available to you.  Basically, if you are a good player, conquering the earth is just a time factor depending on the nation you are starting as.  If you suck at the game, you will get ganged up on by unforgiving AI.
Biggest gripe on the whole series is the game slowing down because of AI bloat.  The game is still unfinished in that regard.
How is the game unfinished?  Well, 2020 came out in 2008, and I bought the original CD-ROM from in the base exchange.  I had a new computer for 2008 standards, and after a while, the game would slow down because the AI keeps building units and the game slows down to a crawl.  Flash forward to 2011, SR Coldwar, I bought that in digital copy from stardock or something.  Same thing, AI unit spam, slow game.  Then SR 1936 came out on Steam...same thing...  Before 1936 was even officially declared "finished", Ultimate was put up in the steam store.  Because I am an SR junky, I bought it.  SAME THING, slows down...
To this day, SR Ultimate, regardless of game era, will slow to a crawl after a couple of decades.  Again, I have a brand new PC 64GB RAM DDR4 Intel core I7 nVidia GTX970 and SSD.  Slow game.  Almost 10 years have gone by and the devs cannot prevent AI bloat.  The engine is largely unchanged between each version, so I have a feeling that the programmer wrote the core game in 2007 and gave everyone the finger after that.  There are also problems with the tech tree.  Ultimate never fixed the path from Future -> Coldwar -> WW2.  They did however, add all techs and designs into the entirety of SR, so if you start in WW2, you can go properly all the way up to future.  However, if you start in the future, you have to spend years researching WW2 stuff because the devs forgot to include old techs and era techs from WW2 and CW in the future era version....this means even if you are Japan or Germany with maglev trains, GPS satellites, and internet, you have to research bi-planes and refrigerators to unlock some cold war era infrastructure techs to get the new 1990's era techs.  You have to download mods to fix the base game because it was never completed.
If you are a diplo-game / world domination junky feeling risky, then try this game out.  Otherwise, you will probably hate it.

This game has a lot of potential but unfortunately I must count it as broken. AI is laughable, especially when it comes to naval warfare and diplomacy. There are MANY bugs, which won't cause CTD but will break your game if you want it to make any logical sense. Economy doesn't really resemble real one and GDP will rise and fall very unrealistically. I will say it clearly and in capital letters - DON'T BUY. Buy Hearts of Iron instead.
1936 sandbox and campaign are particularly broken and quite frankly unplayable. There is no Spanish Civil War, technologies are not great by any standards, Japan will declare war against USSR no matter what, and get squashed like a bug, China is way OP - it smashes Japan in months, naval warfare is really bad (AI has no idea what to do) and generally it is really bad when compared to Hearts of Iron games or ones by Matrix Games. War in Ethiopia is a nice touch. AI will immediately move most of its forces to mainland Italy and attack Ethiopians with several thousand men only to be predictably slaughtered. Ethiopia was still alive and well throughout the entire war. Diplomacy is great and both Bulgaria and Finland, German allies during the war, are hostile towards you since the beginning. Why? Your guesses are as good as mine.
Maginot line is really easy to pass through so there is no need to go through Belgium.
I really love pathfinding in this one. Panama army ends up in Austria, Ethopian in Denmark, French and Turkish in Poland, and more. Good job.
Cold War sandbox is much better, but even then, barely good. AI is rather poor, there are many historical units missing, and again, a lot of bugs. Pathfinding is terrible too. Thousands of French and British ships carrying troops going to Vietnam will try to move through Leningrad and Ladoga Lake and get slaughtered. Problem will end if you will win the Vietnam War and they won't need to transport them anymore.
Alignment mechanics are broken too. Switzerland will immediately become Warsaw Pact aligned despite being allied with me, and generally alliances seemingly don't count when the game calculates alignment, only diplomatic deals related to trade do so the only way to sway it during the Cold War is to give them money and very favorable deals.
Perhaps the least broken, but all of the above applies. Economy is still broken, AI is laughable, and setting is blah when compared to previously mentioned ones.

Tekken 7 is one of the most exciting fighters i've ever tried in a long time. It's a welcomed addition to the long series and hopefully won't be the last. Being the first time for a Tekken to be introduced to the PC universe, the port was well done and smooth with no problems encountered whatsoever. Which Is what many games seem to fail at launch.
Some things I liked about Tekken 7 was...
1) The fighting style - Never have I seen a fighter quite like this, It's different to most of the classic styled fighters including the Street Fighter series. The overall feel is smooth and exciting. All characters have a unique move set fun to learn!
2) The graphics - The graphics are spectacular and give an immersive feeling.
3) Story - The story may seem a bit clunky at first, but once you've finished it you're left thrilled and waiting for the next Tekken to come out! It's been well thought out and put together quite nicely, which is a key componant many fighters fail to give, story.
4) Character customization - From creating weeb outfits or your favourite characters outfit from a movie or game. Tekken 7 offers a huge selection on chatacter customization and will let you have fun doing so!
5) Sound - The sound in Tekken 7 is truely satisfying and the developers didn't lay out a single drop on it! All characters have unique voices and dialogs along with that sound that gets everyone going when you lay a hit into your opponent.
In overall, this game is really fun. And I recommend It to anyone who may be thinking about buying this game.

Pros:
-Very well optimized
-Graphics are extremely polished, great level of detail
-Netcode. Even on yellow bar, theres hardly any lag
-Content. A lot of customization was placed for each character which adds a very unique trait to the community.
Cons:
-No tutorials outside of a basic movement lesson in Story mode
-No trials
-Arcade is very, very short, and each character only has ONE story chapter.
Overall, I love Tekken 7. Being the first game I actually invest time into learning, I could see myself placing this as one of my favorite fighting games of 2017.

The story mode feels like a cop out. Akuma was meant to be a big part of the story but it feels like he was squeezed in mid way through development because he has no purpose in the story other than to add a few more fights. They don't bother to explain why he is in the Tekken universe or how he knew Kasumi or why he would even help her. The narrator also feels like they came to the end of the story and realized it was too short, so they put in this half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥journalist narrative that no one cares about because his voice is void of any emotion. The premise for the story was also overblown as it was meant to be the end of the Mishima saga, which I interpreted to mean that this would also be the end of the devil gene storyline which started with the Mishimas, but no, it's actually just a fight between Kazuya and Heihachi that may or may not be to the death. Jin is conviently unconcious for most of the story, probably so the writers didn't have to add any sort of depth to their story.
It's not even worth playing through arcade mode anymore because there are no vignettes at the beginning and end of a character's journey, apparently because it was too expensive, but I feel like they could have just done some drawings with narration - like Tekken 4 did - and it would've been satisfying.

Portal Knights, oh how i adore you.
Portal Knights is a funny little game, with cute graphics, which adds something fun for everyone.
It's a Minecraft meets Terraria meets Zelda type game. It reminded me of Sky Saga, before they ruined everything. Portal Knights does everything right, and is worth a check.
Portal Knights is a Minecraft-esque game created by 505 games, the same guys who handle Terraria on Consoles. where you can explore, build, mine, dig and craft. They also have alot of cute vanity pets that follow you around, and amazing armor and vanity sets, so you can dress yourself as a bad♥♥♥♥♥viking, or a cute little miner. Just like terraria, the game offers slots for armor -AND- slots for vanity sets. There are 3 types of worlds, Small, Medium and Large, offering everything for everyone.
You start on a easy and lush island, which teach you the ropes, how to attack, dodge, gather and everything you need to know to get the game started. Each island has it's own materials, trees and enemies and a portal which allows you to teleport to different, harder islands, again with their own materials and enemies, But before you can do so, you need to collect Portal shards to craft portal blocks you need to open the next portal. These shards drop from enemies, pots, chests, and even, rarely, drop while mining. It's a quirky little game, with a lot of Pro's and barely any Cons.
the game recently left Early Access and was release on PC, PS and Xbox, showing a bright future for this cute little game.
The updates so far have been free, and the only DLC items so far are vanity gear, robot suits and some emoji helmets.
I give this game a solid 9 out of 10. Totally worth it.

I never write lengthy reviews for any game, but I feel like I need to write this just to call out this horrible piece of software the developers call a game.
Like others pointed out before me, this game is just a gimmick- You buy it, say "haha I'm performing surgery", and then you probably move on; you won't get your money's worth if you intend to just♥♥♥♥♥♥around like this, so if this is you, you're probably better off watching videos or something.

I don't mind putting in a lot of work in order to beat hard games but this isn't NES megaman difficulty or anything, this is just a studio trying to pass off a bad game with a bad physics engine as a challenge. The developers have the audacity to claim in their FAQ that this game is hard because they wanted people to feel "rewarded" for being able to put up with something they didn't even have to program. Even if you're into goofy stuff, you're better off playing the game where you shower with your dad and a bunch of naked guys than this.
PS: It also seems like there's an issue with mouses for this game- if you plan on playing this on a laptop or with certain types of mouses, you won't be able to grab an item and lower the hand at the same time which is pretty necessary to complete ANY of the operations, so be ready to potentially have to buy a wired mouse because of this one game.

Spelunky is a roguelike exploration game where you dive into a dungeon looking for treasure, save damsels (or pugs) and die. A lot. Aside from the spiders, snakes, skeletons and other baddies inhabiting the world there are plenty of instant death traps and a shopkeeper with a shotgun who doesn't like getting ripped off. You never know if Spelunky is going to throw you a softball level or make you pull some Kaizo Mario nonsense to survive the first room but you get some bombs and ropes to help blow through stubborn floors or get around levels more easily. If you get to the end of it all, great treasure awaits but is guarded by the mighty Olmec.
This game can be tough as nails but only occasionally felt unfair, a tough balance to keep in a roguelike. The controls are solid (aside from the fact that you grab ledges at the most inopportune times) and they have to be because the game requires some precise maneuvering at times to keep from taking damage or outright dying. It's fun and challenging and doesn't take itself all that seriously, all qualities I like in my games. Also, Tunnel Man has a sick afro. A+ would play again

This game has a very unique grenade system, which have been called by many names in steam reviews. I must say, it is not one trying to simulate realism. Grenades only kill occasionally. For the most part they stun you, and when players clash they are all over the place. This may look weird and unbalanced to new players expecting a more strictly “tactical” game. However, this grenade system is what, in my opinion, makes the game. It makes the game intense, where skills matter as well.
They included AI bots in the release. However, I think the PvP part is where this game shine, and I would say bots are only for practicing controls (Have only tried a couple of games against the AI). Because of the high skill cap, out-multitasking is a valid strategy (albeit a risky one, as mistakes occur more frequently when you (I) try to), and this gets lost when playing the AI.
A must buy if you like fast played multiplayer teamwork (PvP) and can handle a game that requires some skills besides your thinking.

I want more games with such immersive and fun themes as this. Every moment of this game is straight out of a heavy metal album cover, and it's always great to look at. While the graphical fidelity isn't the best, the aesthetic more than makes up for that, along with the good sound design and AMAZING soundtrack. The gameplay, on the other hand, is not always the best. The most fun I had with this game was at the beginning, before the RTS elements get introduced. The simple brawling mechanics and the fun driving missions and free-roaming are where the game really shines, but trying to implement an RTS with stage battles just didn't work.
The stage battles are clumsy and awkward to control and direct, since you also are in direct control of Eddie the entire time while trying to direct mobs of your own forces with an incredibly unintuitive interface based around very simple "follow, defend, attack" commands rather than a traditional overhead point and click interface. (yes this game was originally on consoles, but still) In my opinion, the stage battle RTS sections should have either been converted to a more traditional working RTS format, or removed entirely.
Aside from the Stage Battles, which comprise maybe a third of the game (and definitely aren't AWFUL, just clunky), this game is very, very good. It features tons of heavy metal icons as voice actors, a blistering soundtrack, amazing aesthetic, and good zelda-esque fighting mechanics and visceral driving segments tied together with a large open map and many side objectives.
Plus, there's Manowar-inspired scantily clad amazonian ladies riding massive fire-breathing beasts of destruction that you can recruit for your cause. If that doesn't sell you, I don't know what will.

This game... is incredible!! I went in skeptical, having heard this game was a decent RPG but was no where near amazing. It might just be personal preference, but I had an absolute blast playing this game! I played as a sorcerer the entire way through, and whilst the Main Quest only took me approximately 12 hours, there is so much to see and do in the lands of Amalur. I may revisit this game some day, seeing as though there is so much left for me to do (in the form of side-quests and more exploration), but I was very satisfied with the Main Quest.
The combat system I found was quite enjoyable to use. Often you have to juggle between certain spells (well, at least I did being a sorcerer) whilst using your main weapons (mine being a staff and chakrams, which are awesome!) in conjunction to fight most effectively. You can also go down the path of Might (swords, hammers, etc.) or Finesse (bows, daggers, etc.), but like I said, I went down the Sorcery path (staffs, sceptres, etc.) which I found to be a LOT of fun! As you can tell, I found no issues with the combat in this game!!
I also found the ability to roll (or dodge, or in my case (being a sorcerer in later levels), blink) quite useful. When you feel like you are getting swarmed by many enemies, you can simply dodge to get out of there! Or, if you're smart, you roll behind a troll as he brings his log down on you, allowing you to hit him from behind until he recovers.
That brings me to the enemies in the game. There is just so much variety! You will come to hate certain creatures in the world as they can be quite a nuisance, but some you will greatly enjoy beating the snot out of!! I myself found the Niskaru to be an absolute pain to deal with, but facing off with a troll was quite a delight as you felt a great deal of satisfaction when destroying it.
I only had a few issues with the camera angles, though. I believe twice this happened: after performing a fate-shift, the camera was pretty much on the ground, looking up at my legs... meaning for about 10-15 seconds before it recovered, I couldn't see anything! This was a very minor issues and only happened twice, but it's an issue nonetheless. When the camera did work, however, it worked wonderfully! It zooms out when there are more enemies on the screen, allowing you to see everything that's happening around you. And when the action is over? Well, it just goes back to 'normal', which was nice.
The storyline of this game I also found to be intriguing. Whilst it's not the bragging point of the game, it sees your character defying fate itself, being able to perform a 'fate shift' whereby you change the order of how things are meant to be in the world (it basically makes you really strong for a short period of time, giving you the option to perform a sort of quick-time event during this period to shift the fate). The MAIN characters you meet along the way are also quite good, and (for the most part) their voice-acting is well done too.
The presentation of the game is just beautiful as well. It's got a sort of fantasy-charm to it that makes you feel like you're exploring a really lovely world, taking you out of the reality that there are all sorts of dangers around you. It's a well optimized game that will run well on most low-medium computers, so there are no worries there! (Though I did run into some trouble where the game was just completely black, still with audio and all, that could only be fixed by turning off post-fx. I believe this is an issue that only occurs for users that have AMD GPU cards...)
The sound in this game was also really well done! At times I just had to take a moment to appreciate how great the music accompanied the current setting, or how it subtly dropped off as you reached your location, as if it was perfectly timed (or was it?...). I had no issues with the rest of the sound, either, which is a positive!
As I didn't do many side-quests, I can't offer my opinion on them, but what I can say is that if you are looking for a fantastic third-person action RPG that you can play for an excessive amount of time before putting it down, this game is for you! If you're like me and would prefer to just focus on the main storyline, this game is also for you! I hope my review has helped you in your decision to purchase this game, so enjoy! :D

I realize that I played through this entire game and its DLCs and even went so far as to get 100% of the achievements, but I just cannot recommend it. It's not all negative, it's just... boring.
And it shouldn't be. The environments should be mind blowing. The character design should be good. The weapons and armor designs should be interesting. But, they just... aren't. They are by themselves out of context. The screenshots and such for this game make it look really interesting and captivating. But when you are playing, everything is really bland text-book fantasy cliche and so all these things that look really nice out of context become dull and boring when put together as a whole in the context of the game.
Also, the crafting system sucks and doesn't seem to make any weapons or armor better than what you can find in the game. Also, the random loot system sucks: you find a piece of a named armor set, but by the time you randomly get all of the pieces or even enough for it's cumulative effects to be useful, you've leveled up way beyond it and have found generic armor beyond its capabilities. And, I'm not sure if it is possible to make sidequests any more generic, boring, and repetitive.
The gameplay itself and combat are fine, I guess.
So, bad crafting, bad loot, extremely meh gameplay, nothing special combat, and incredibly dull cliche story and characters make this game just plain boring. If you are looking for a fantasy world to explore, you'd be much better of going and wandering around Skyrim again.

Kind of a blend between Skyrim and Darksiders. Clearly the intent of the game was that of combining the free roaming experience of the former and the excitement provided by the flashy combat system of the latter. It works in the beginning, but the over all low level difficulty of the game devoids the combat system of its appeal soon enough, and the plot does not hold to the pressure. The level of involvement in the story- which is not that bad to be honest, but fairly standard nevertheless - is in the average simply not enough.
In my personal experience it proves once more that in this particular genre the gameplay should not be the main focus of the gamedesign process. If you look at Planescape Torment or Morrowind you can see how plot, characterisation and context provide the core of the best gaming RPG experience.
KoA is fine if you are looking for a more casual experience or you are not that much into the genre. It's by no means a bad game, but I would not recommend it to an experienced gamer.

I played this game with an xbox controller so this is how I am reviewing it. It was really interesting and challenging to control both of the brothers at the same time. One half of the control controlled the younger brother and the other half controlled the older brother. The controls, however, weren't difficult to understand since only the 2 scroll buttons and the triggers are used.
Past the controllers, there was absolutely no dialogue which kind of threw me off at first, but once I played a bit more, I realized the game didn't need dialogue. The story was pretty straight forward, however twisty it DOES get at the end, and it gives you exactly what you need as you go through it.
The graphics and artwork in this game are absolutely astounding. I'd play this game over and over again just so I could get a look at the scenery. There are little benches all over so if you see them, PLEASE sit down and scroll around you really will not regret it, it's amazing.
The story isn't very long, but it still makes you feel very attached to the characters. This is much more like a visual story game than anything, even though you control the brothers, because there is only one ending but the story is so interesting that it's worth it.
I didn't really find anything I disliked about the game. I mean, yes, it was a bit difficult to control both of the brothers at the same time, but I think that added to the interest level. I feel like if I was only playing one of the brothers, it wouldn't have been so imersive. This also made me feel connected to the two brothers because I was able to see how most of the things you needed to do, came with the reliance of the two brothers. You wouldn't have been able to finish the story if you didn't have both of them...

Spelunky is a roguelike exploration game where you dive into a dungeon looking for treasure, save damsels (or pugs) and die. A lot. Aside from the spiders, snakes, skeletons and other baddies inhabiting the world there are plenty of instant death traps and a shopkeeper with a shotgun who doesn't like getting ripped off. You never know if Spelunky is going to throw you a softball level or make you pull some Kaizo Mario nonsense to survive the first room but you get some bombs and ropes to help blow through stubborn floors or get around levels more easily. If you get to the end of it all, great treasure awaits but is guarded by the mighty Olmec.
This game can be tough as nails but only occasionally felt unfair, a tough balance to keep in a roguelike. The controls are solid (aside from the fact that you grab ledges at the most inopportune times) and they have to be because the game requires some precise maneuvering at times to keep from taking damage or outright dying. It's fun and challenging and doesn't take itself all that seriously, all qualities I like in my games. Also, Tunnel Man has a sick afro. A+ would play again
Yes it is not easy that you will die hundred or thousand of times, but practice makes perfect, and I high recommend it!

I've been playing this series since Supreme Ruler 2020. Since that time I have had 5 aggravating problems with these games.
1. The difficulty of moving infantry to other continents or islands.
2. An inability to decide how to generally tweak the AI behavior.
3. An inability to change the name of my country.
4. Performance issues affecting the late game (like queueing military builds or the whole map slowing down when there are more than 2-3k total units in the map).
5. Engagement behavior (usually resulting on England being at war with everyone but being untouchable by everyone but the player).
Now after all the series releases and now all of the patches applied here's what they did with each one.
1. Move the troops to a port and give them the sea transport command and they will turn into merchant marine ships and go where you want them to go. If the troops are amphibious, they will land wherever you want.
2. One of the most recent patches allows you to choose AI behaviors such as "Unpredictable", "Aggressive", and "Defensive". Aggressive mode exactly what I always wanted.
3. You can do this now.
4. While this problem isn't fixed, it may be unrealistic to expect anything but a faster CPU to solve this. That being said, running a lean and mean military is usually the best way to go economically speaking.
5. Engagement behavior is now improved enough that I generally trust the AI to run my military for me in most situations. It's also advanced enough that the AI countries fighting among themselves is interesting to watch. While the England issue is still somewhat the case, I do see that sometimes the right conditions are met for an aggressor to "chase" across the chunnel. I do think that AI sea invasions could be improved, but they work a considerable amount better than they used to. The only flaw I'm still seeing, is that in aggression a neighboring island is not considered a neighbor enough to trigger a war declaration.
As for the game in general, the main selling feature of this title is its Dynamic Border/Supply System. Borders fluctuate in war based on who is providing the stronger supply to a specific hex in the game. Supply being fed by transportation routes and supply spouts (air fields, supply depots, industry, cities, ports). Troops may capture territory but it is lost if there is no supply to it. The troops themselves rely on supplies and will become immobile without it.
It doesn't sound like much but this concept is what has attracted me to this series for years and its only real downside is that it sometimes results in border gore (whose only fix is to declare war on the country in the other side of the border gore).
The Economic system is not simple, but also not particularly hard to get used to. Certain goods are for industrial demand, certain others are for domestic (some for both). The tax system and the societal spending system affect all of the economy in several different ways (this is the part of the economic system that can be difficult to grasp). Though the game, manual, and website try to explain how these factors affect things, some of the explanations are lacking. So some guess work is in order.
The game has an Espionage system, though I honestly rarely use it. When I do use it, it is simple and straightforward. You give the spies a mission and priority and place them on the enemy hex you want them to do their stuff. They will either succeed or get captured.
The military system is simple on the surface. You fill your production slots with whatever you want built, and it gets built when it's production run ends. However, there are a lot of specific details which are good to learn quickly. For example, which infantry are amphibious, what the fuel range is on a transport plane, and whether one tank type is likelier to survive anti-tank than another. The game can be forgiving in this respect. There's also a manpower mechanic in the way of "reserve troops" that puts both a foundation and a cap on the maximum war power you can field.
There's also a weather system, but I never quite got what the deal is with that.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to strategy/grand strategy fans with decently powerful CPUs (Sandy Bridge and later on Intel side and the new Ryzen chips on the AMD side).

Long story short, Tekken 7 is probably the best fighting game on PC. It corrects the mistakes of Tekken 6 and offers a rich, complex combat system for players to explore. The game allows for hundreds of approaches to a situation, keeping matches fresh and dynamic. There are no “abilities” to spam or complicated button inputs to memorize. Tekken operates under simple mechanics that harbor amazing depth beneath the surface. When Tekken 7 gets something right, it nails it. The combat is the most balanced of any fighting franchise on the planet. Online matches have zero input lag. Framerates are rock solid on almost any rig. Even my modest PC build can handle the graphics in full 1080p with maximum settings. Without doubt,  Tekken’s core mechanics are tuned to perfection. If you’re a fan of the franchise, you’ll love this game. That said, there are some serious issues to consider before making a purchase. Firstly, Tekken 7’s netcode is the worst I’ve ever seen. Once you join a match, things usually run without a hitch. But the game constantly fails to connect you with other players. Make friends with error screens, because you’ll be seeing a lot of them. (As I’m writing this review, a new patch was released that attempts to correct the issues with matchmaking. Too bad it now takes an eternity to find a game. New problems replace old ones.) To put it bluntly, Tekken 7’s online is a hot, sticky mess that wasn’t ready for release. On top of that, the graphics are a downgrade from Tekken Tag 2. Some of the characters look pretty good; but others (like Asuka) look plastic and unfinished. Some of the details like hair also fit awkwardly on the character and appear two-dimensional.  The settings and particle effects are top-notch, so why do the characters look worse than last gen? The music, too, is far from “quality.” If you like obnoxious dubstep, you’re in luck. If your eardrums are accustomed to something less ghastly, you might want to hit the mute button.  Combine that with occasional glitches, no team battle or time attack, and no character endings in arcade mode, and you have an experience that’s far from perfect. But considering the competition is doing things like implementing pay-to-play models on full-priced games and having barely-functional online battles, Tekken 7 sits comfortably at the top of the pile. It’s a good Tekken game; not the  best, but good. Just make sure to weigh out the positives and negatives before you buy it. 8/10

I'm upset with myself for one reason: I hesitated to buy this game.  On sale for $5 and with an 82 Metascore, I was still a bit iffy on the game, even though it happends to be an RPG, of which I love.  I shouldn't have wasted the time thinking about whether to buy it.
To start, if the game is ever on sale for 5 dollars and you like RPGs to any degree, add to cart.
About the game, you are the reanimation of a fallen soilder from a battle against a new-found enemy awoken from the chaos created by a new Emporer.  You first see yourself as a dead body being dropped into a pit, but soon enough you awake atop hundreds of dead who where like you.  The story then takes off, introducing you to what will become an exponentially more intense battle style and to a wide system of freedom and choice.
You choose what to say in a ring of different phrases you may speak.  These phrases can start quests or make enemies depending on how you choose them, a feature I enjoy.
The system of battle is intense and never gets old.  Dodging, shield parrying, and combos all mix to create a battle style I hate to stop playing.  You choose, through unlocking powers, active and passive, in one, two, or all three trees of skills.  Melee, Sorcery, and Finesse are your three skill trees, with different powers and skills for different playstyles.  You can also mix the three trees' skills to create your own style.  This customization is wonderful and fun to explore, and I've only scratched the surface.
All in all, 9/10 at least, I am very happy with where my 5 dollars gave me, and the full price is fairly reasonable for such a game.  As I said earlier, if you enjoy or respect RPG games in any way, this is most definatly a game to try out.

Welp, I've been pushed over the edge into writing this review in lieu of recent events which can be read in any other review posted recently. This review will cover actual issues the game has instead of chewing out take2 (though they do deserve to be chewed out, but, at this point I feel anything I'd say has already been said).
I will begin by saying this game was entertaining for a short while. It has nice graphics, pretty fluid gameplay, and they like to keep online updated which they've done for free instead of having you pay for dlc so I commend them for doing that. Unfortunately that's all the praise I have for this game.
I will begin ripping this thing apart with single-player mode. Unlike other GTA games I've played (mostly Vice City and San Andreas, which are arguably the best 2 in the series) the game is a cakewalk. When I play GTA I want to be challenged to the point of rage-quitting then coming back to it a short while later (anyone remember Demolition Man from VC? or what about the damn RC plane mission in SA?). Not to mention this game feels smaller than SA with only 1 city and the countryside. The story is decent, some of the characters are great, but all of that is overshadowed by how easily one breezes through the story. This isn't a GTA game, it's got the look and some of the humor of a GTA game, but it lacks the soul-crushingly difficult mission(s) that gives each of the other GTA's I've played their unique charm.
Now on to the real killer for me: online mode. Online mode is a great concept, but, horribly executed. It's nice to be able to play with others and progress from having your first vehicle you stole to having a few houses, a business, multiple full garages full of customized cars, etc. It would also be nice if that were possible in a reasonable amount of time. Unfortunately, it's not. If you're like me and refuse to do any microtransactions so you end up grinding the resourses, online takes eons. They price things so exorbitantly high that most players just end up buying the shark cards, making it one of the cardinal sins of gaming: pay-to-win. Online, at this point has become just a money grab. Additionally, online mode is riddled with players who bend the rules. Some of these people are nice, but most I've come across are just trolls. Then there's the seemingly endless supply of rule-abiding trolls. Those who don't circumvent the rules with additional tools, but rather use their equipment to wreak havoc on honest players. I understand that some of this is fine, fun even, but when it's every server then it makes it unbearable. Also, you can forget about acomplishing anything in your own private server, the freeroam events are disabled, thus forcing you to play in a troll-riddled hellhole of a place just trying to accomplish anything to make some decent cash so you don't have to spend real money on those damn shark cards. As far as running the MC or CEO stuff, most people don't want to bother with it unless they get the highest cut, so everyone runs their own stuff rather than working together. So many of the practices with online mode are very anti-cooperative play, which is in direct contrast to the real world of crime where you have people working together to achieve things. So even as a crime simulator this game fails.
Now to break my own rule I gave myself at the beginning of this... talking about the Take 2 legal action against a certain modding tool.
Mods are what made single-player mode bearable. You could make it difficult, quirky, grimey, and downright weird. But that's the beauty of mods in games. Companies like Take 2 think of mods as ways to break rules and ruin their games, but that's not what modding, real modding, is. Modding, for all intents and purposes, is a way for people to enjoy the product that the company has released long past its vanilla playability allows. Furthermore, it's a form of creative expression allowing people to view the game as a wonderfully built canvas to unleash their creative desires and share with others. Modding brings me back to the good 'ol days of gaming; before all the extreme budgets, corporate buyouts, playing it safe with releases (which this game is... dumbed down to appeal to the widest audience). All gaming is nowadays, seems like it's about making the most money rather than providing quality entertainment. I remember a time when games used to be innovative, groundbreaking even, people used to push the limits, take risks, succeed and fail. But that was the beauty of it. If a game failed it was because it was a bad game, not because they didn't spend enough on marketing (in the beginning anyway... this did eventually become the reason many games do fail). Modding allows people to do what those crazy fools did back in the day: push the limits, cause paradigm shifts, and create quality entertainment. Many of the games which have brought massive loads of cash in for some of these companies began as mods for other games, so it's sickening to see companies doing things like Take2 has done to the modding community. Basically what they're saying is: "Your ideas are trash, allow us to give you what we say you want" rather than being a decent company and providing us with what we actually want. We get the same 15 games every year because it reaches the widest audience, mods are there to make the more nuanced alterations that fit smaller segments within the market, allowing us to turn the game into what we want. Some may claim that it sullies the original work, my response to them is to wake up and realize that it's just a money game now when it comes to the big companies.
Back on topic a bit: Take2's legal action against a certain modding tool is appalling. They claim it's to prevent modders online, which would be fine since it's their servers, people may have conflicting mods, there's no way to manage them all, among other issues. However, this particular tool doesn't allow for any sort of online modding (not to mention the modders who are online are rarely punished anyway). So why is it they claim it's to prevent online modding when clearly it's not? The answer is simple, long ago they said that they'll allow modding in offline mode, it's your game so you should be able to turn it into something you enjoy playing. They say it's to prevent online modding so they don't have to go back on their original promise, though actions speak louder than words and it's clear they have indeed gone back on their word. Why do they want to eliminate offline modding? Well that's a simple question to answer. As stated earlier, mods allow players to enjoy games long past their original playability value. In the case of GTA5 once you beat the story and quests there's nothing left to do so naturally you head online. Mods allowed peole to continue to play offline long after the story ended which was no good for Take2. Once you remove the Mods, the playability factor is gone thus forcing people to play online. Once online, they realize the exorbitant prices for most things and either quit playing the game altogether, attempt to grind it out, or in the case of most people, buy the shark cards.
This kind of anti-consumer behavior cannot stand. Not to mention the game isn't even that spectacular and is riddled with issues that they don't appear to care enough about to fix. So no, I do not recommend this game.

Spelunky is the kind of the people who enjoy solving 8 by 8 rubix cubes would like.
You don't play Spelunky so much as learn it. It's not hard so much as it is punishing. A single mistake can and will kill you, forcing you back to the beginning of what could be a half an hour plus run depending on how long you take for each level. So you learn the game, learn its every move, learn everything it could possible throw at you, learn until you can get past the point you were stuck at. Then the game throws something new at you in the next level, killing you instantly. Better start learning again.
Eventually, if you are determined enough, you will beat it. Get to the end and see the credits roll. But there's still more to do, you havn't reached 100% completion yet. If you leave any stone unturned then you havn't beat the game, the game beat you. It's a contest of wills and endurence between the player and the program that was designed to break you.
If you are really masochistic you will try to get onto the leaderboards, but there are people competeing on the daily challenges there that having been playing the game since the free version came out 8 years ago.
It's also a good game that you would probably like if you like good games that are hard.
