I held off playing this game for a long time because it claims to require a controller, which I can't stand using most of the time, and because it was published by 505, who published Payday 2 and How to Survive - neither of which I enjoyed.  This game was quite the pleasant surprise, though.  First off, a controller is not required; using a keyboard can be a bit awkward at times, but will work just fine.  Second, unlike How to Survive, there were no game-breaking bugs, meaning I actually got to finish the game, and I'm glad for it.  This was an amazingly innovative platformer with beautiful artistic design and a well-told story.  It's brief, but it doesn't need to be any longer than it is - in fact, trying to stretch things out to pad the length would have hurt the overall experience.  The puzzles aren't too complicated, and are all very logical - the challenge comes in controlling 2 characters at the same time, who need to work together to solve the puzzle.  It's one thing to play a game like Portal 2, where you and a friend have to work together, but having to work both brothers at once takes some getting used to.  It's a completely unique mechanic I don't recall ever seeing before now, and it was a fascinating way to play the game.  The entire story is told without a single line of dialog - there is a language being spoken, but it's gibberish and you're not meant to understand it.  Everything is conveyed via gesture and inflection, the mood is set through the music, and it's all done very well.  It helps that the story is very simple and straigtforward - this game is about the journey, the bonding and the loss, and the spectacle of it all, and to that end it was very well crafted.  I'd say it's definitely worth a playthrough.

Multiplayer issues are still broken as of March, 2014.  If anyone in the party has a bad connection the entire game is unplayable because it uses P2P and shared user hosting to create the games in the lobby.  I got this game solely to play multiplayer with my friends and I can't do that so thumbs down.  Game is absolutely not DSL friendly.  Packet loss builds up until massive de-synchs happen, and eventual disconnection.  Hosting is "shared" between all players in a multiplayer game, so whomever is chosen as "host" is decided by in game actions, such as who enters a zone first.  If anyone in your multiplayer game has a poor ISP then the entire game suffers.  Don't take my word for it, go read the forums in Steam.  Don't buy this game.

Behind the complexity hides an economy that is completely irrational and spins out of control for all countries - AI and human - within years of game start. The complex economy formulas are so horribly unbalanced, that you can switch off all production in the country, cut all social spending, and still end up with a "not enough workers" problem, bringing inflation, and prices for everything you can build skyrocketing as a result.
Behind the wealth of units is completely and utterly incompetent AI - both friendly and enemy; ships run out of fuel and get stuck in the middle of the ocean, planes fly out of range and crash, land units of all sorts behave like a plague of locust, brainlessly advancing at top speed with no regard for tactics or strategy, positioning or defensive terrain. You can micromanage your own units to not do that, but the AI never will, resulting in wars that feel idiotic and unsatisfying.
Behind a reasonable diplomacy screen is an absurd diplo system where you have to pay 10 years worth of your country's GDP to EACH of the NATO countries if you want to be friends with them, where an alliance does not mean an actual alliance, where the rest of NATO stands by while USSR does an amphybious invasion of France for some odd reason, and where West Germany and France go to war with each other at the height of the Cold War.
And if you are thinking of treating this deep and detailed world as a sandbox and using cheats and mod tools to work around the inherent absurdity of the game, you are out of luck. The cheats are few and limited, notably absent is the ability to force an AI to agree to a diplomatic offer. The modding support is somewhat reasonable, but requires a confusing and time-consuming cache regeneration process that looks like it hangs your game for a good five or ten minutes and finishes without any indication as to success or failure, following which you have to manually move and rename certain files and restart the game. It's very easy to mess up and will take some time to get the hang of.
Overall, as much as I'd love a game of this type and depth, I cannot recommend this one.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse (Beta) is a good game so far! It's not as good as you would like it to be and rough around the edges as a hack & slash type game. The game is in beta or Early access so don't expect too much out of it except for fanboy/fangirl characters you wanted to play as or fighting along side.
-PROS:
*The lag is barely noticeable & get to play with people
*The Controls are nice for an Early Access and hope they improve it
*The Whole RWBY team is avalible for play and have their different attacks based on their style
*The voice acting for english is actually very well done! Keep up the good work!
*Style & Graphics maybe rough but it'll grow on you like part of the world during gameplay
-CONS
*No single player: Seriously, there is none whatsoever and you're always online which kinda sucks
*No Character Creation: Not really a con but it'll be great to fight along side the RWBY team or have your own attacks
*Many people can be the same character: I literally had 3 yangs on one team. Funny though but so much yellow ...
*No control Mapping: It's actually hack & slash friendly but no option to change for other people
*No other characters besides team RWBY: I would like to see more characters besides the main team.
*Graphics: a Small problem but you look like you're walking on air and the style needs to be flourished more (to me).
*The biggest problem I have with the game is the attacks and Leveling. once you comeplete 3 stages you beat the early access game story line. Once you start again you go back to level 1 no matter what and some of the perks are locked due to challenge you have to complete. Not having a save feature for this level is much to be desired but it's early access so probably in due time
-SUMMARY:
Even though it may have a ton of cons in this review but the pros outweigh it by light years if only the game wasn't $15. I wish this was a bigger project so you can be another character or be one in the series. The Combat needs to be improved along side the stats so you can feel like you're actually getting better. Though as it's a beta it's fine! Just wish there was more and hope it doesn't catch the early access cold where this is the game as most like H1Z1 did to other people.Other than that, Most cof the cons can be a Pro which is a very big plus on this game and wish they follow up with it.

A much better game than Minecraft. When sandbox meets rpg, it is a great experience.
Pros:
-Create a customized character.
-Choose one of three classes with unique passives.
-Various spells and shouts to take control of the battle.
-Usable combat Items like throwning knives and bombs.
-Various blocks and decorations.
-Simple and Easy Crafting system; just need the items without having to place them in certain shapes like minecraft.
-Sharpening tools repair all damaged items on action bar.
-Fun Tactical combat.
-Events occur often.
Cons:
-Too many maps with the same Biome.
-Maps might be a bit smaller than desired, but there are many of them.
-The game might be a bit difficult at the beginning for solo players.
-Items like throwing knives are expensive to make in the same tier as other weapons.
-Seeds that require a certain Biome don't tell you which one they will grow in.
Tips:
-Grow a lot of Cotton for torches.
-Replant what you harvest.
-Thrown weapons and bombs can allow a melee to damage out of range enemies.
-Shouts scale to strength and will cause flying monsters to fall to the ground.
-Healing isn't based on attributes and can effectively be used by any class so long as you have the mana.
-Healing Scrolls do not share a cooldown with the healing spell or with potions.
-When looking at the world map you can see if a location has the monsters or resources you are looking for.
-Events occur often and can reward you with items and resources that you can't find with your current progression.
-When mining underground you can use the ledges at the end of the area as a source of light.
-You can wear the miners cap as a vanity item and it will provide light for you.
-Most monsters have a weakness; Fire is weak to Water, Water is weak to Lightning, Lightning is weak to Nature, Nature is weak to Fire, Light is weak to Dark, and Dark is weak to Light.

I wish to give this game a good review, but it just ain't possible. The game suffer with so many multiplayer problems, that make it pretty much impossible to have good experience playing with friends:
- 2 players can't be in different islands, that doesn't make sense, it completely break the building experience, I want to keep puting blocks up while someone else go hunt materials.
- long time spend loadscreens,  and in multiplayer everybody must teleport together, and if you're not the host, expect double or tripple time, so you better get A LOT of extra resources when teleport to an island, cause the teleport time is just no worthy at all just to get 4 or 5 of anything.
- desync, desync, desync all the way, even staying in the same island as everybody alse at some point someone will desync and be stuck in a chest or crafting station, and if someone is stuck - team work - everybody will be stuck too,  on whatever they are doing.
- game use sooooo much machine power, I have a pretty end computer for video editing with way much more memory, gpu and cpu power than the game recommends, and it eats up all everything,  still experience a lot of fps drop, often my fps goes from 60 to 15 out of nothing and i have to wait around 30 seconds to normalize. If multiplayer it gets crazy.
Now, the game offer a nice experience single player, not a fun game do play by yourself, but if you like to play alone the game works, mostly. Even single player the game uses too much of your computer, fps drops frequently and you still get to restar the game sometimes cause you got stuck in a crafting station, other than that, it works way better than multiplayer.
Talking about game mechanics, it is a simple game, simple to understand, not a lot to think, gear you equip doesn't really matter cause the game is as easy as a kids game can be. Even been a challenge cause you can't miss a dodge, the mechanics are simple and in a couple tries you understand the patern and now is just repeat it to kill them hoping that a fps drop doesn't kill you.
As many people said around the web, the game tries to mix rpg and building aspects, but just tries, cause both experiences feels too simple and too easy.

I want more games with such immersive and fun themes as this. Every moment of this game is straight out of a heavy metal album cover, and it's always great to look at. While the graphical fidelity isn't the best, the aesthetic more than makes up for that, along with the good sound design and AMAZING soundtrack. The gameplay, on the other hand, is not always the best. The most fun I had with this game was at the beginning, before the RTS elements get introduced. The simple brawling mechanics and the fun driving missions and free-roaming are where the game really shines, but trying to implement an RTS with stage battles just didn't work.
The stage battles are clumsy and awkward to control and direct, since you also are in direct control of Eddie the entire time while trying to direct mobs of your own forces with an incredibly unintuitive interface based around very simple "follow, defend, attack" commands rather than a traditional overhead point and click interface. (yes this game was originally on consoles, but still) In my opinion, the stage battle RTS sections should have either been converted to a more traditional working RTS format, or removed entirely.
Aside from the Stage Battles, which comprise maybe a third of the game (and definitely aren't AWFUL, just clunky), this game is very, very good. It features tons of heavy metal icons as voice actors, a blistering soundtrack, amazing aesthetic, and good zelda-esque fighting mechanics and visceral driving segments tied together with a large open map and many side objectives.
Plus, there's Manowar-inspired scantily clad amazonian ladies riding massive fire-breathing beasts of destruction that you can recruit for your cause. If that doesn't sell you, I don't know what will.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding lemon bars recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

Allow me to review one of the greatest games ever created.
Spelunky is a random-gen, side-scrolling, platforming dungeon crawler that seems tame enough from the trailers and such. Realistically, this game is brutal. It pushes your skill, knowledge and reaction speeds to the limit as you dodge traps, evade the myriad of enemies and elude the embrace of the ghost whilst you collect gold, gems and useful items that allow you to climb walls, throw farther, jump higher or kill some enemies in one shot (and damage others which were once immune to your feet).
The controls of the game are amazing. You can control your speed and momentum in air, which just makes the game easier to play with. The art style is really good too. It's a cute cartoon style that's not too hard on the eyes but not so vibrant either that it becomes distracting.
The music is also really fitting and easy to listen to. In the beginning levels it's fun and carefree, but as you get further into the game the music starts becoming a little bit more serious.
The replay-ability on this game is pretty good. I always come back to this game, even when I get far, die and rage quit. This is one game that will probably never be uninstalled from my machine. I just love it too much.
One thing I'd like to emphasise is the difficulty of this game. Newer players will undoubtedly have a tough time. You will probably die 200+ times before you get to Olmec. This game takes some getting used to. For reference sake, I've beaten the game countless times, yet I still die a lot in the first few levels.

Now I had a little bit of an edge going into this game as I had watched LPers play this game beforehand. This means I spoiled a lot of the games later levels and enemies and secrets to myself. So when I bought this game, I went in with a good idea on how to play around the levels. I still died a lot though. I'm up to about 1200-1500 deaths now I think.
One thing about Spelunky that keeps this game unforgivably difficult for experienced players is the secrets. If you've beaten Olmec before, congrats, but you're not done. There's still plenty more, including the 'secret' boss; Yama. To get to Yama you'll need to get a bunch of items that might appear on one specific level i.e. the Udjet Eye can spawn on 1-2, 1-3 and 1-4. You only get one chance at getting these items so keep an eye out. You thought getting to Olmec was hard, good luck on your Yama run. You'll need it. Seriously, you will.
Beaten Yama yet? If you have then you can move on to the daily challenges where you compete with others to get the highest score of the day on a set seed. You'll need to dig deep, use bombs strategically and possibly discover what 'Ghosting' is.
How about those achievements though?! Funny enough, you can get them all by yourself but they all present their own challenges that will drive you insane. No gold? That's a lot more difficult that it sounds.
But wait, there's more! If you see a present/package in the shop, buy it, don't break it open, place it on the sacrificial altar and look up on the wiki why in Kali's name did you just get an
. (This challenge is really difficult, even I'm too scared to do it D: )
Done? Well you can look up more challenges to see what tickles your fancy but at then end of the day, you can just go back to the dailies. Or look into Frozlunky, which is a community modded Spelunky.

A beautiful game.  A Narnia-esque world accompanied by a musical score that accents all the emotional moments, as well as utilizing silence in some of the best ways I have seen in video games.  A modern twist on a side-scrolling platformer, 'Brothers' has you controlling two separate characters with each joystick (or opposite sides of the keyboard), and I recommend keeping each brother on the side of the screen that corresponds to his control side.  This control scheme works brilliantly and I am sure will be copied for years to come.
All I will say about this game is that it is a must play.  The collision detection can be off, some pop-in may occur and your character might not do exactly what you want on occasion, but to let any of these minor flaws deter you from playing this game would be a shame.  It manages to bring together ideas from games like Uncharted, God of War, Journey and Heavy Rain all into a 3 hour storytelling masterpiece.
Worth it at full price, easy, and the biggest steal ever when it goes on sale (80% off on occasion!). Do yourself a favor, buy this game.  Take your time.  Explore off the beaten path, when you can, and just enjoy it.  Do your best to avoid spoilers and you will be handsomely rewarded.

Truly, this game has many things going for it - but sadly, just as many things speaking against it.
Portal Knights makes a bold attempt at combining the sandbox building of minecraft, the colorful combat of Zelda and the procedurally generated worlds of "No Mans Sky", yet It both hits and misses on all three accounts.
It has mine-crafty mechanics okay - but it's grindy work.
It has Zelda-like combat.... every five seconds, and repetition soon sets in.
It randomizes the location of key elements, which adds replayability to the game. But it also places the all-important
portals in places where you, literally, have to excavate the entire planet to find them.
It's a hairline balance between being an attractive, joyful exploration and an exercise in frustrating, boring, repetitive grinding, all depending on the roll of a die.
The game is slick and graphically beautiful, and the developers deserve kudos for trying out a bold new direction, but in its current state,   it's simply too easy to get stuck in an hour-long, unrewarding hunt for something to do,
or - in lieu of that, locating the next portal, jumping and hoping for a more interesting island.
As much as I want, I cannot  wholeheartedly recommend investing the time and money in this game, when other games accomplish the same goal much more painlessly. Portal Knights shows great promise, but there is work to be done, before it lives up to its ambitious premise.

While I like the game, there are quite a few things you should know going into it before you decide whether to buy it.  Just read pros/bizarre/cons and the bolded text for the short version.
What their advertisements don't tell you:
1.
Each world is essentially a series of floating islands that come in various sizes. Some islands can be large-ish, while others are barely bigger than your character. Every world is like this.
2.
That is probably a seasonal event-only thing.
3.
If you like owls, cats, rats, or frogs, you will probably find enough of each that you will find something you like. Otherwise, good luck. There are other exotic pets, but they are event-only. For example, a blue parrot is sometimes a reward for an event that may trigger a couple of times a week. Others are seasonal, I hear.
4.
You can farm these items, but your most common solution to heights and gaps will probably be laying down dirt bridges.
5.
The split screen feature does nothing to help this. If one player goes to a different world, everyone else goes with them without warning. Plants are also biome specific, so you cannot have a friend farm silk while you look for gold resin. This kills the experience for many people. It is still possible to have a good time in multiplayer, but your goals need to match each other pretty well. You should want to build a base in the same world and agree to farm the same materials at the same time.
6.
And you see them all in the ads. It's actually a pretty short game if you are just here for the plot, so I hope you also like combat, mining, and building as well.
Now, that I have talked about how the ads differ from the actual experience, I am going to briefly cover pros and cons:
Pros:
--Attractive aesthetics
--A fun, non-Eldritch Minecraft/Terraria baby, if you don't mind smaller worlds
--Three different fun classes to choose from
--Pretty fun dodge-and-attack combat system
Bizarre:
--Can switch all talents in the talent tree at anytime
--Only the best armor is class-restricted, while all weapons are now class-restricted
Cons:
--Not enough pets. A blue frog ceases to be exciting the sixth time you find one. Harder dungeons should introduce more pets.
--XP is dropped in yellow cubes, and can fall off of platforms
--Warrior does not currently have access to holy weapons, and one enemy needs a holy weapon to be defeated
--Poor coding optimization. Frequent loading screens and slow-down.
--Baroque furniture recipes don't come with drafting table upgrades
--Spell cooldown + mana bar is excessive
And the far biggest con that demands attention:
I have seen this product referred to as "polished" in some reviews. In looks, I will agree. There are shiny materials, and they look great. In gameplay, however, I disagree. I feel like this game left Early Access way too soon. Most of the bugs are small, thankfully, but it does feel unprofessional to frequently encounter them in a final product. Note how I said "most" of the bugs are not that serious. There are at least two serious bugs, one of which I have encountered:
--
This happened to me at Farpoint. This doesn't happen often, but I literally cannot get to the final boss in one of my universes. I am not trying to use a compass in a world where I have found all of the portals, either. At first, I was hoping my compass was just glitching, but it worked in other space biomes.  Additionally, I did a very exhaustive search of the area. The portal just isn't there. I have contacted support about this, and requested that they fix it. I have spent hours of work in other worlds in that broken universe. At least the support staff was kind enough to let me know that the bug has received the developer's attention. They haven't fixed my universe yet, but I will be sure to update this review if they do.
--
This seems to happen largely through random disconnects in multiplayer play. Thankfully, this bug has never happened to me. You might want to keep a backup of your saves, though, just in case.
Those are the major bugs. The minor bugs I have encountered, which don't hurt anything but can be very annoying, are as follows:
--
Whenever I turn on the game and first enter either of my worlds, my character's pack inventory will be completely blank. No square slots even show up; it's just a blank white screen. This is true regardless of whether there are items in the pack. Don't panic, the items should still be there. Just quit to the title screen and re-enter the world. This is annoying, however, because I am forced to endure two loading screens just to play.
--
I think this happens because I open/close a chest too quickly? All I know is that, sometimes, when I leave the chest screen, the chest stays open and I cannot move my character. I find bringing up the pack items briefly will let me move again.
--
This happens mainly with the flying eyeball enemies in the dungeons. They'll get stuck where you can still see them, but they cannot attack you and you cannot attack them. You cannot dig them out, either, because it does not let you mine near enemies or other foreign mobs like birds. But it's not vital to kill everything.
--
Sometimes, if you are outside of a certain range, enemies just instantly restore the damage you do to them. There are no sparkly effects or anything when this happens, which makes me believe that this is a bug. It's weird, and I do not know what exactly causes it, because, as a ranger, I often have no problems nailing them from further than lock-on distance, and effectively taking them down. It's annoying when it occurs, though. If it happens to you, getting closer to the enemy seems to stop the problem.
--
Let's say that you have stairs that are just two blocks that are directly diagonal from each other, with no block connecting them vertically or horizontally. A block, gem, or ore can fall through this crack, even though they really should not be able to. So, watch out for that when you mine on the edges of cliffs and such. On the more humorous side of this bug, some blocks fly unnaturally up a little before immediately falling back down.
--
The animation will not always trigger, and you may not warp in a timely manner. Just hit the "return to the landing pad" button in the map menu again if you want to make sure the warp itself triggered. This can be problematic if you are warping to get away from enemies.
--
From what I hear, the devs are already aware of this problem. Just don't be fooled when they are maxed out.
This is probably not an exhaustive list. I haven't bothered to report the smaller bugs, because I have already bothered the devs with a large one, and they don't inhibit gameplay that much. However, all of them combined communicate why I personally think the game does still lack polish. And, at $19.99 and advertised as being out of Early Access, I feel like it should be better. But if that doesn't scare you off, there are still hours of fun here.

Pros:
— Awesome universe, beautifully crafted and immersive
— Pretty good graphics
— Killer soundtrack
— Great scenario, with depth and twists
— Delicious cameos from Lemmy, Ozzy, etc.
Cons:
— Frustrating controls (no jumping, no strafing, and worse: not enough responsivity...)

— Too much (useless) cutscenes, especially in the beginning

— Way too often the game threw me into the domain of I DON'T KNOW WHAT THE HELL IS GOING ON AND I HAVE NO IDEA WHAT I'M DOING. That is not a good thing.

— The fact that there is nothing on the screen (no health meter, no map... nothing) may be "arty" but it doesn't help and makes the game even more confusing.
Conclusion: What would have made an absolutely awesome movie makes a game that is okay at best. The fact that the gameplay is a blend of various genres is nice, but not well done. The artistic part is AMAZING, but the gameplay is just not good.

Supreme Ruler is a strange game. In a way it's seriously ambitious, with an in-depth tech tree spanning from 1936 into the 21st century, but unfortunately the game suffers from so many flaws overall that it's just never going to live up to any ambition it has.
The biggest issues are optimization (Big battles, wars between continents, etc will cause insane slowdown even on the best CPUs), then a lot of overall game mechanics, such as there being a massive lack of diplomacy options (You can't ask for parts of a country, no peacedeals, AI is currently so hyperaggressive that Germany often declares on Poland, France, UK and Czechoslovakia all by Late 1936).
The in-game economy upscales horrendously too, with oil demands upscaling in such absurd volumes that it's genuinely quite impossible to play a 20-year game, never mind getting through the century, simply because there isn't going to be enough oil in the world to cope with Europe, nevermind anyone else.
It's a shame because had this been more polished and properly balanced out, this game could be great. Unfortunately the closest you can get is alternative grand-strategy games like EUIV or HoI4.

Animated Puzzles is an enjoyable game for all levels- ranging from an easy puzzle with only a few pieces to 800+ pieces.  Each puzzle has a "pull out" tray which stores the unplaced pieces but it still allows you to lay pieces onto the puzzle "board" without placing them, which is similar to a real jigsaw puzzle.
This game allows the player to choose from many included puzzles (several levels of difficulty), plus the workshop has even more high quality, user created puzzles to download for free.
You can make your own puzzles from photographs, and choose the shape of the individual pieces for all of the puzzles (traditional jigsaw shape to completely square).    Animated Puzzles has several included puzzles with an interesting animated effect on the pieces, though most workshop puzzles are traditional static photos or drawings.
This game allows you to have numerous puzzles that are "in progress" so you aren't required to finish one before beginning another.   This is a great feature if you have several people that use your computer to access the game, but want to choose a different puzzle.
Animated Puzzles offers benefits that a traditional jigsaw puzzle can't :  I don't have to find a place to store a large puzzle in progress, pieces don't get lost, and my cat can't destroy my puzzle.  I was a little unsure  about the concept of an electronic jigsaw puzzle until I tried it.  I have truly enjoyed this game and I am very glad that I purchased it .  If you enjoy jigsaw puzzles then this game is well worth the money.  A+

From Spilsbury to Ravensburger, I used to do a lot of jigsaw puzzles.  Heck, I've got a 15,000 piece puzzle sitting here in a box right now.  It will stay there though, as these days, my vision and my cats would both make putting that together well nigh impossible.  Perhaps I'll never get to do another jigsaw puzzle again.
What's that you say?  Animated Puzzles is a jigsaw puzzle game that lets you choose the number of pieces in the puzzles, and also allows you to pan and zoom as you assemble it?  Well sign me up!
Actually, I already did get the game, but I guess you knew that since I'm, you know, writing about it now.  Despite having lost the dramatic tension, I'll press on to elucidate the salient points without sesquipedalian obfuscation.  Oops, ♥♥♥♥ed that up already.  Anwyay.
Animated puzzles offers pretty much everything I would hope for in a jigsaw game.  As I mentioned, the pan and zoom ability does a lot to make the game easier on the eyes, and while the selection of pictures in the game is a bit slim, Steam workshop support ensures that you can just keep adding pictures of your choice.  Heck, upload an old wedding photo and as you assemble it you can pretend that you are putting back together a failed relationship.  The possibilities are endless!
Also worth noting is the animation, since thats what the game is called.  The animations in the puzzles are pretty low key.  Things like clouds passing by, or dandelion seeds floating around.  It adds a nice touch without causing performance issues.
Finally, if you want a more challenging experience, you can choose different shapes for the pieces, do the daily challenges, or even go for the leaderboards in time attack.  Honestly, this game is so accomodating to however you might like to play, that as long as you actually want to do jigsaw puzzles in the first place, you can be happy with Animated Puzzles.

Just to preface this review, my Internet crashed right when I was posting this review, so it should say something that I've bothered to retype all of it (and even expand it a little bit!).
There are many things that I like about the game and the UI, so I'll bulletpoint my findings:
- The pieces are neatly sorted on the right side of the screen, thus avoiding any clutter.
- The board itself is grid-based. When you drop a piece, it will be placed into one of the pre-defined spots. This doesn't mean the puzzle auto-solves itself; the pieces won't be locked even if you put them in the right spot. It is simply a way to avoid clutter and to better figure out where a given piece fits.
- The pieces themselves are automatically connected if you have two matching pieces next to each other and with the correct orientation. I only wish the game would automatically connect matching pieces regardless of the orientation, for example if both pieces are upside down and placed correctly relative to each other.
- The music is lovely. I wonder if it's possible for users to expand the playlist however they like?
- You can zoom in and out.
- You can preview the picture whenever you want.
- The puzzles go up to 150 pieces, but perhaps the limit is higher. I hope in the future the game will support puzzles with arbitrary number of pieces, e.g. 500 or even 1000 pieces, especially since the game's UI is so convenient.
- The game offers three difficulty levels for each puzzle (the higher the difficulty, the more pieces there are) and you can choose four types of pieces for each difficulty level. Time is recorded for each individual piece type at each difficulty level.
- The game has Steam Workshop support, so you can add static images as puzzles (a Miku puzzle is already available). Hopefully, you'll be able to create animated puzzles in the future. Perhaps there could be some cross-promotion with other games.
- You can compete with other players online in head-to-head battles. I haven't tested this feature, so I can't say much about it for now, but it is neat it's there.
- There are daily challenges, but they are unique. Instead of just putting together another puzzle, you have to play various modes. For example, there is one mode where a single piece is placed on the board and you have to figure out where the single provided piece goes. As you continue to place more pieces, you have to consider more possible spots. It's a nice twist on the usual jigsawing.
- Don't worry about missing a daily, since you can always go back to any days you've missed whenever you like.
To sum up, this is THE jigsaw game on Steam right now. It is laser-focused on providing you a pure, clean and crisp jigsaw experience with non-distracting modern conveniences. If you hate how Pixel Puzzles does things, this game will be a breath of fresh air.
If you are a casual or hardcore jigsaw lover, this game is worth your attention. And if you've managed to read this far, why haven't you already bought the game?
This game is absolutely worth it in its current state and at the current asking price.
I look forward to seeing it grow!

As usual, I'll give you both a written review and a link to my First Look video, for those that want to see some of the gameplay.
There's two parts to this game, the map, where you move your barbarian, and the battles.
Let me explain how the map works.  You start off with your Barbarian, and then slowly start to explore the map, gathering troops from nearby villages or castles.  As you grow in power you will be able to take on enemy forts, and if you are able to defeat them, they switch to your side.  Each time you move is a turn.  The different towns and castles you control have a current number of troops and a maximum number of troops, they slowly replenish as you take your turns until capping out.  In addition, you have gold you find during your exploration that allows you to up the maximum number of troops you can hold in your army, as well as, how many dragons you have.  There's a balance you must find between exploring too far too fast and wasting turns doubling back to build up your army, and just building up without exploiting all of the map.  You have a maximum number of turns (days) before the apocalypse.  Your goal is to defeat all enemy forts and gather enough strength to slay the demons once the apocalypse takes place.
The battles are fairly simplistic in nature and you have little direct control at first.  Later on into the game, you get a little bit more.  First few battles will have you watching your crazy army of rabble (peasants) charge straight ahead and try to zerg the enemy.  Then you'll add knights and archers to the mix, who tank better and fire arrows, respectively.  Still, they all charge forward with no rhyme nor reason, just bloodlust and anger!  (I have to admit, I love watching the fights, it just makes me grin)  Eventually you'll defeat a dragon guarding a fort and then it will join your army.  You can click on the battlefield where you want the dragon to attack and it will spit a fireball out to murder enemies (or friends if they are too close) in a small aoe.  It's really nice to pick off clusters of archers hiding behind walls.  The next tactical unit you get is the cavalry.  You can position them anywhere on your side of the battlefield and resize their deployment box.  Then you choose two waypoints for them to charge for, allowing you to bypass enemy troops or walls.  They are quite tanky and do a great job of tearing archers apart.  In some maps you get giant walking trees of doom.  They are super tanky, do a very small aoe and are quite a problem for your normal troops, or the enemy's.  You can also unlock a banner in a temple which allows you a bit more direct control over all of your army.  It allows you to click and drag on your army, to redirect them to where you feel they'd be better suited.
Over all the combat is fairly simplistic, yet still quite fun.  Finding the right balance of troops, the right amount of exploring to building up your army, and utilizing your money properly all add to the strategy side of the game.  Is this the most advanced, complex, deep, or difficult strategy game ever made?  Nope.  The game is designed to play each map quickly and still offer strategy, fun, and a sense of accomplishment.  Don't sell it short, it's still quite enjoyable and I'm looking forward to whatever comes next from Wolff Dobson & Studio Puffer.

This game's a fun, simplified take on the "build an army and conquer the map" genre of strategy game. Instead of spending hours micromanaging production queues and battle formations, in 10 Minute Barbarian, you get to find out if a disorganized rabble of peasants can storm a castle held by a handful of archers. And when you find out the answer is no, you start over and try again 5 minutes later, this time with twice as many pitchfork-bearing farmers.
Your tactical options in battle are a bit limited, but you are a barbarian, after all, not Rommel. Most of the units act on their own, but some can be given simple marching orders at the beginning of the battle. You also get controllable artillery in the form of dragons, but their fireballs lay waste to foe and friend alike. At least their aim is pixel-perfect, so if you suffer any friendly-fire casualties, you know whose fault it is.
The 10 maps in the game may seem like a small number, but the scenarios get pretty varied after the first 3 or so levels. Each map has a theme, but the exact layout seems to vary with each game. You also get introduced to new units regularly, and some scenarios play out like little puzzles, requiring you to vary your tactics a bit.
It's a fun, little game. Just go in expecting a light strategy snack that takes tens of minutes at a time.

The game is pretty simple, you are a barbarian that runs across villages and castles to gather men, and then you use your army to conquer other villages and castles to gain more men (and unite the kingdom against the demons). That's about 85% of the gameplay.
Later on in the game you'll find a dragon among the enemy that shoots fireballs at your men. Kill the dragon and you can recruit them for yourself and use them to shoot at the enemy. That's another 10%.
Even further in the game you'll find cavalry that you need to tell what to do, meaning you need to tell them to charge at point 1 and then point 2 before the battle starts. This leads to them running past the enemies to point 2, unless they are blocked. Then they attack the closest enemy, which can be a wall or an actual enemy. You also get a banner that you can use in battle to guide your men, kind of anyways. Both of these are generally useless and when you can find a for use it, it won't make much of a difference. This is the last 5%.
You can finish this game in about three hours on standard difficulty and honestly you only need to finish the first map, out of a total of ten, to experience the entire game.
The time played compared to the price paid (€9) and the gameplay itself aren't sufficient to justify a purchase.
During a sale it might be worth to check it out if your looking for a casual strategy game.

The hour or so I've spent with 10 Minutes Barbarian has been enjoyable. It's a pretty simple little game where you have a limited amount of turns to explore an over world, raising an army, and conquering kingdoms. The combat is mostly AI driven, so power in numbers takes precedence.
The strategy involved is mostly micromanaging your turns. Do you use your limited amount of time to explore and conquer, or do you double back to previous bases to raise a larger army? It's simple to jump in, but thoughtful enough to be enjoyable.
The graphics and sounds won't win any awards. Though the sprites aren't ugly by any means, the overall presentation takes a more utilitarian approach to it's graphics than artistic.
Overall 10 Minute Barbarian was a simple, but enjoyable little game.

If you are up for a challenge and/or into modern rogue-likes, this is required playing.  The core mechanics are simple but it's challenging and deep with a lot of replay-ability.  It is possible to play in short doses if you are short on time but it's also hard to put down and can be played for hours on end.  The randomized levels keep things fresh and require skill, you can't just memorize it through repetition.
Even though the game is extremely difficult and has randomization, it's  well balanced and the controls are excellent so it never feels frustrating.  You will die a lot but if you stick with it, the game forces you to learn and improve (not just in the game but in real life too).  It's highly rewarding when you finally start to do well, even if you never beat the game.
The daily challenge is an excellent way to keep you coming back for more, especially if you compete with some friends. Local co-op & vs. is a nice addition just to mess around with but it's not how the game was meant to be played.  Spelunky is one of my favorite games of all time.

"Just one more go". With its procedurally generated caves, its polished graphics, its fluid animations, its Rouge-esque "light" roleplaying elements and it's unforgiving mechanics,
is a platformer you are bound to keep coming back to - it's a game that awards quick reflexes and the occasional improvised move, but relentlessly punishes careless stunts.
Loosly based on Brøderbund's 1980s arcade hit
(ported to Commodore 64 and other 8-bit platforms), Spelunky tells the tale of a lonely cave explorer venturing deeper and deeper into the depths of a randomly created dungeon (or, in local multiplayer, a band of cartoon like characters). Not only do the denizens of the caves themselves present a challenge - and your fellow players, if you're unlucky - but so do the scoreboards; every day at 01:00 CET, the game server creates a new, global "Daily Challenge" - every single player gets one go at beating the dungeon, which identical for all Spelunky players. It's reminicent of having your own arcade cabinet at home, with just one quarter to use every day - which adds further more to a platformer that's already ahead of its competition.
The regular asking price (€14,99) is more than justified, but sales prices south of €3 are simply put nothing short of a steal!

I own a great deal of fighting games over Steam.  I regularly scan the store for new releases or ports of older games being brought over to the front of the scene on PC.  I've watched Capcom slaughter the Street Fighter franchise with poorly implemented DLC and horrific netcode; I watched DOA5 drop their idea of online play after nude mods hit the scene -yet again-; then watched the terribly poor implementation of the Guilty Gear XRD debacle just to get additional characters. Unbelievable day one execution; so far the netcode is holding great, the graphics are seamless... If you're considering this as your next fighting game purchase, get on it immediately.  Get the season pass.  Then invite your friends over and bust some heads.

I wanted to wait to write a review until I beat the game.
in KoA.  This is with Both DLC's, Teeth of Naros, and the Legend of Dead Kel.  Not all the side quests were done so there is still a lot of content out there that I haven't even completed yet.
Pros:  The combat is amazing.  It can require a bit of timing, a bit of planning.  It can be unforgiving on a higher difficulty.  It’s as fast paced as you like it to be.  You can fight more conservatively or you can go more aggressively.  Want to go stealthy and backstab everything, go with stealth!! The world is beautiful.  All the NPC's are voice acted.  There are TONS of things to do, you are also awarded for doing these things, see Lorestones.  You get a bonus for finding all of the Lorestones in each Zone.  The side quests do a great job walking you through the world, introducing you to new zones.  Also these quests will normally lead you right to the next main area that you will be going to anyway.  In the 61 hours I have not had a crash, the game is very stable, there are few bugs I'll touch on those however I haven't found any that were game breaking.   You can create your own potions (alchemy skill), weapons & armor (Blacksmith skill).  Your character is flexible.  At any time you can reset your skills (for a price), if you want to venture into other things.  You are not locked down at any point in any class.  Flexibility is amazing.  The lore!! The lore is amazing and it’s everywhere.  Its in books you can find, citizens you can talk to, letters you find lying around.  If you ever wanted to be completely immersed into the game world definitely read these.  They will give you a history from the religion to the way of life of all the different races.  Good good stuff.
Cons:  Even though the world is beautiful, your walk/run speed can be frustrating.  There have been several times I thought to myself, Is there a potion to make me faster?  You can fast travel which makes things much quicker.  You just have to get there first.  Difficulty... I played on Hard to start.  Honestly I didn't find it that difficult.  The enemies are more aggressive in Hard, however in the end its not that difficult.  The Blacksmith skill can be an absolutely game breaking, making things way to easy.  About halfway through I noticed this, I re-spec'd my character out of blacksmithing salvaged my weapons/armor I created, and just when with things I found in game.   While there isn't many bugs there are a few that are really inconvenient.  There are items you can get that will just stick into your inventory with no way to get rid of them without the external help of a hex editor on your save file :|.
Closing:  All in all I really enjoyed my time with it.  I would definitely recommend this to anyone seeking to play a game that has a rich story.   I would recommend playing with a controller as opposed to a keyboard your mileage may vary.  Just stay away from Blacksmithing unless you want easy mode :D

Update since finishing the game:
Wonderful stealth game with pacing and narrative issues that are extremely hard to reconcile. Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is by far the closest any game has gotten to nailing the level design of the first game in the series; the complexity of some of the levels here is mind-blowing, the amount of ways to get to your objective gets ridiculous at times. My biggest complaint about Human Revolution was the size and simplicity of its levels, they followed the spirit of the original, but refused to let you off your leash until the last few hours and even then, it never met the scope of Deus Ex. Mankind Divided doesn't just improve on this, it's more than I ever could have imagined.
Sadly, it's made extremely clear that the rumors of restructuring in Square Enix were true, because this is effectively the villiage idiot of the series, writing-wise. The components of a good story are there, but they're just splattered all over the floor like a bowl of mom's spaghetti. It feels like this is the first act of a proper Deus Ex game slowed to a crawl with some hints of a failed attempt to give it a traditional narrative structure. This will step on some toes, but it sort of reminds me of The Fellowship of The Ring; it's not really an independent work and if you try to consume it that way, it feels extremely flawed, it's relying on the reader caring more about finding out what happens next than the fact that they just read 450 pages of exposition and nothing else. About 90% of what you'll take away from this game's story are unresolved questions, which is disappointing considering that we know Eidos Montreal's writing staff is talented, it can even be seen in this game's side missions. Something obviously went wrong here and I'm feeling like it's on the business side of things.
Currently this game gets an honorary Best/Worst Game I've Ever Liked award.
Original Review: Everything is in place...
Very fun, plays like a smoother version of the last game. Level design is fantastic, the first level is larger than Omega Ranch from the last game. Many things from the original Deus Ex make a return, like Biocells, Multi-Tools, and multiple ammo types. In short if you want more Human Revolution, play this, if you haven't played Human Revolution, play that, then play this. UPDATE: Interesting how Human Revolution matched New York and Hong Kong in the original one and Mankind Divided is almost entirely based on the France section of the original. It includes the large portions in the sewers.
There are apparently microtransactions, but I haven't actually encountered them in my time with the game. If I hadn't seen them on Reddit, I probably wouldn't know they existed.
Performance is good, but the game is very demanding. You'll need to tune settings for your machine and unless you're running a top of the line PC, you probably won't be playing with things like MSAA and Tesselation. Don't buy this and get pissy because you can't just hit ultra and start playing. Several people are complaining about black screens, but I haven't experienced this personally. UPDATE: New patch has given me 2 crashes in 4 or so hours.

Brothers -  A Tale of Two Sons can be both described as art and game in one, though to call it as a game by itself would be injustice in a sense. An experience would be more befitting considering through how the narrative is told. However, like some tales - it's best having heard once or after being forgotten in narration in my opinion.
This is a game that blends showing the essence of what it's about with the gameplay and telling you what it is with its world.
From a small village, this tale is told through gestures and a Simlish-like language that can be understood as easy as though you've learnt it all your life, the brothers Naiee and Naia set off on a journey that is both grandiose in scale and meaning. It will take you from warmth of civilisation and community to the cold isolation and loneliness, from beneath the earth, deep valleys and into the mountains piercing the sky leaving the clouds and lights of the normal world below. I will not spoil the locations and areas of the game but it can certainly be said that the none of the effort to put the player into the world goes unnoticed.
Being a game that revolves around the two brothers, the mechanics are all playing with about four buttons, six if you want to include the camera movement keys. I found it easy to coordinate the brothers, each having a side of the PS3 controller I was using - big brother on the left stick and trigger and little brother on the right stick and trigger. Symbolic in nature and in the game itself especially near the epilogue.
As for someone like myself who adores lore in games, this is one that is best left to the imagination like Dark Souls. The story behind this world is certainly bright at first but taken through each one carefully one must wonder about the world the brothers live in. The scale and design of the creatures while familiar are just different in some way to make it unique in the world.
But it certainly is not a happy game, I say here that it's quite dark, you'll know when I mention the word - Ice.
It most definitely is a beautiful game though, even the developers know that, since they conveniently place benches for the two to sit on while the camera pans to whatever panoramic view it wonderfully wants to show. Which does kind of bring me out of the game every once in a while when its in a very questionable location, but hey, its good to take a break from adventuring is it not?
I just have to say that I didn't feel the massive experience or the feelings supposedly other people have playing the game. Even playing with headphones, screen in front, controller in hand and 2AM in the morning to play uninterrupted. It is by no fault of the game though, I just simply was able to guess what was happen, the game does a good job of foreshadowing things whether intentional or not.
I did experience some odd bugs in the game that took me out of the experience at times - black figures of characters would appear next to the actual character that would show something.
All in all -  play it, it's cheap and an experience that might change how you see how arts and games and game mechanics can be made to be one.

Possibly one of my favorite games, this action-RPG is Diablo-like as people say, but has its own taste.

The amount of weapons and armor you can have is endless, although after a while it can make you crave for more powerful weapons.
Another key point to this game is the multiplayer/co-op portion of this game, it allows all the players to get their own loot. It allows offline and LAN multiplayer, and allows VPN programs like Hamachi or Tunngle.
The only complain I have is that you can't respec in this game, you can refund your last 3 skill points invested, and can screw up some characters.
For the insanely low price of $19.99, its more "refined" compared to Diablo for the price, and in the future they will hopefully continue this series.

I'd recommend this game to any looking for a quick and fun "pick up and go" game, especially fans of strategy games (Risk comes to mind).
A Nifty little game that does a pretty good job of mixing enjoyable, satisfying combat with simple, and almost "hands-off" controls. Mid-game you get some units that you can control more, but the battles are more or less autonomous. The controllable units inject a bit of strategy to tip the odds in your favor, namely the dragons that function like mortars, and the calvalry, whom you can direct, but they are relatively few in numbers. Late game, you can get things like the banner which allows you to command a small patch of units - very useful for navigating around walls.
The majority of the player's strategy comes not on the battlefield, but rather on the overworld map, where the player must balance the decisions of who to fight when, when to collect more troops, and when to face down the odds for a much needed special unit (the necromancers are basically amazing. Pinch your pennies - they cost 5k!)
The later levels, I found to be a bit closer to "15 minute barbarian", but the title nonetheless sums up the experience nicely; The player is able to pick up the game, play for a relatively few minutes, and get a fix of both strategic play, and watching satisfied as the battles onfold.
Great work!
For those that would like to see the game in action, here's my videos on steam:
or my playlist on YouTube:

Once you settle on your preferred tactics, you can usually just roll with it through all nine campaigns. There’s a Hard difficulty setting if you want the experience to demand more of you, and even a hidden six-star rating that can be tricky to acquire (I have it, of course), but the campaign's brevity is what does the most to keep a player coming back to slay invading demons and put the boot into those pesky necromancers. In theory, the game is the ideal way to kill a quarter-hour of dead time. Just be wary: it has a habit of eating up significantly more of your life than that.

Spelunky is, quite simply, one of the best games ever made.
I spent about half a year (most of which on xbox 360 when it originally came out, hence the low hour total on Steam) making a couple of runs a morning. It started out as a perfect "podcast game," something to play while drinking a morning coffee and listening to a podcast. It's not exactly mindless -- on the contrary, its movement requires grace and precision. But for whatever reason my ADD brain can totally twitch reflex its way through Spelunky while also listening to a conversation.
At first I sucked, but over time I started developing skills. Knowing how to properly kill bats, or look ahead for arrow traps. Over time it becomes a game about risk management -- are the rewards worth the risk? Depends on the difficulty of the task ahead of you. It drips little bits of randomness at you every time, and for a game with such a limited set of sprites and textures, it always finds a way to surprise you. There's a complex and interesting meta if you want to engage with it, but most of the time I took the levels at face value.
There's something hypnotic about a Spelunky run that makes it almost remind me of meditation. That's how good this game is -- its harmony of visuals, sound, design and challenge are reminiscent of feelings most associated with religious trances (at least according to me).
If you've somehow never played it, you should fix that right away.

I should've written this game a review a long time ago. But, right before I was going to write a review, the developers always add something new. So, I have to go test it out to see if I like it or don't like it. I've found the reviews to be "Mixed", which just doesn't seem right for my taste.
Heroes & Generals is a free to play WWII FPS game. Entirely multiplayer, you have three factions that you can play as (USA, Germany, and USSR). Using historical weaponry, you dispatch other factions and take capture points for your own faction. The other side of the battle is from a RTS perspective, involving moving resources around to win the war for your faction.
Purchasing new weapons, vehicles, and upgrades using credits, you can enhance your gameplay. After every match, you must repair said equipment before using it again. You can also buy new soldiers to play as, most notably Infantry, Pilots, Tank Crewmen, Paratroopers, and Recons. You can also purchase a General, if you don't mind the extra credits. Once you purchase a soldier, they're locked in that career (which is tough luck if you find you don't like it).
The #1 deal for me is that the game is actually FREE TO PLAY. You don't HAVE to spend real-life cash to get in-game upgrades, credits, etc. You can get it all by simply playing. Everything can be obtained by playing.
What I like about this game is the replayability that comes with it, as well as extremely limited in-game voice communications. You can play strategically with friends (using your favorite communication software, mine is Discord), or you can just type out whatever you can to benefit your team (such as spotting tanks and snipers). There is also a whistle feature, which'll allow for getting team members (or even an enemy's!) attention. These limited communications really cut down on obnoxious in-chat behavior. With the strategy comes to the replayability. Every single encounter is new, and involves different combinations of soldiers and vehicles.
What I don't like about the game would be that very new players are left in the dust sometimes. Other players have some upgrades on their weapon, which gives them a slight advantage on damage, range, or speed of their bullets. In the beginning you'll die a lot if you don't play smart. After you get a hang of the weapons, you'll get the upgrades to give yourself an advantage. And once you decide you want another soldier, you'll find it easier to obtain better weapons (because you're more skilled with the starter rifle).
If there is one thing that I can't give a thorough review on, it's the RTS part of the war. I haven't experienced that quite yet. (I think I'm kind of scared to experience it)
Now, for a simple list of pros and cons...
PROS:
- Strategic gameplay (mostly)

- Historical weapons/vehicles
- Active development team
- Colorful maps (limited, but colorful)

CONS:

(Disclaimer: This is a completely un-ironic and non-satirical review. Most of my other reviews are silly and are supposed to be funny, but this is a 100% true account of this video game.)
I know that at the time of me writing this review, it says that I have barely any hours put into this game. This is true for the PC, as I just bought it on sale. However, already having 150+ hours on console, I feel that I can effectively write a review of this game. Brutal Legend has been, since I bought it in early 2010, one of my favorite video games of all time. I do not say this lightly; this game has touched me personally and changed me. This game introduced me largely to what i am today.
First, a little backstory. I was blessed with a very musical family. Me, my brother, and my father all play instruments, and I have been around guitars and hard rock ranging from ACDC to Metallica from a young age. My parents are both fans of metal, and so from a young age, I listened to music like Iron Maiden, Motley Crue, and Dragonforce, just to name a few. One of the earliest band shirts I ever remember wearing was an Iron Maiden shirt in first grade.
Video game have also been a medium for my family for years; we've had consoles ranging from the Saturn to the Dreamcast to the N64 to the PS1 to the original Xbox, and we still have a plethora of consoles to this day. I have always been a fan of video games, and luckily my parents don't mind what kind I play; in fact, some of my fondest memories were of playing Halo 2 system link with my parents in their room and me and my older brother in the living room (my father drilled a hole in our wall to make this possible).
Anyways, shortly after the game came out (about February 2010) we went to Best Buy. I had some money left over from my birthday in January (I believe I just turned 11, and was in fifth grade), and I wanted to get a video game. The choice came down to Red Faction: Guerrilla or Brutal Legend. After carefully reading the backs, I decided I had to choose: destruction, or heavy metal? I ended up buying Brutal Legend; however, I did buy Red Faction a few months later.
So I went home, and it being a weekend, I played the game for hours. I beat the game in a few days, but continued to play it for much longer. I believe that the last time I've played, I had every tab, and I know I had every upgrade. I beat the game on Brutal at one point. I believed this game was pure perfection. When I was younger, as I've said, I only really listened to some baby metal; this game showed me the wonders of different subgenres. I've come a long way over the years, all thanks to this game. I started out with bands like Dethklok, and now I listen to all different types of metal, with my favorite being Atmospheric Black Metal along the lines of Summoning and Drudkh. This game was the reason for all of this.
Another amazing aspect of the game was simply the detail in the characters and the world. I found the game mesmerizing as a child, and believed it was hilarious; not just in the dialogue, but the depiction of the stereotypes. I remember laughing with my father as he expressed amazement at the fact that Lemmy, Ozzy, and Halford were in the game. I remember thinking it was the funniest thing as I reamed goth people in a car while blaring speed metal. I remember the depictions of Hair Metal kids as sellouts, and loving it. Understanding the references may not be hard, but for a fifth grader, it was liberating, finally being able to understand comedy.
As for the gameplay itself, the game isn't that amazing. Basic combat and the clunky RTS elements make it a bit awkward, but the game more than makes up for it in sentimental value and world design. I eagerly, and relatively naively await the day that Double Fine announces Brutal Legend 2, despite the fact that it probably won't even happen. When it does, it will be among one of the games that I have preordered, a list that as of now only consists of Bioshock 2 (a severe disappointment in my eyes) and Dark Souls 2.
In conclusion, Brutal Legend is an amazing game that has a special place in my heart. This review may not be too helpful, as I recognize the fact that it's all sweaty fanboy-ism, but I felt that I had to let other people in on a personal experience I've had with the game. If you are a fan of heavy metal, play this game. If you aren't a fan of heavy metal, still play this game, because the amount of detail and the humor are still enjoyable. Plus, maybe it could broaden your musical tastes and FORCE you to like metal! In any case, I cannot recommend this game enough. I have had more enjoyment with this game and hold it in higher esteem than any other, except perhaps Dark Souls. This game changed me as a human being, for better or for worse, and while it may not touch you in the same way that it touched a cringy antisocial preteen (THAT SENTENCE SHOULD NEVER COME OUT OF ANYONE'S MOUTH), you may still find some enjoyment in it. Hell, if you buy it on sale, you pretty much just spent three bucks on "Drive Around and Kill♥♥♥♥♥♥While Metal Plays Simulator". If you can't find enjoyment in that, I feel sorry for you.

This review will definitely be subject to change as things go on, but as of now, I personally on my rig, which is far from top tier, have enjoyed the game both on and offline, especially after the most recent patch solving the majority of issues I have had with the game so far. However, I will admit, the game online currently does have a ways to go, even with decent connections there is still some input lag which is relatively annoying, but still can be easily adjusted to. Perhaps the most annoying thing about the online as of now is the fact that sometimes you will get a ping of 2 bars who runs absolutely horrid, while at other times I can get people with red or one bar to no bars at all who run perfectly and what you would expect from 3 bars. Now, for the actual game itself and in offline use, it is very fluid, and the kombo system is easy to pick up on, but difficult to master. It is fairly balanced, though some characters with high-low combos easily manage to find themselves being abused slightly. And all the variations feel fresh and unique, though some are quite underwhelming in comparison to others. The story is well made, and despite being shorter than the last story in MK9 or MK 2011, it definitely gives the character some emotion and feelings, with my only real gripe is that it left some rather big questions unanswered. Overall, in its current state with how it runs for me, I would say personally that you buy it on sale, or find a cheaper venue to buy it like I did, or wait for some more patches to come through if you'd like to devote large amounts of time online. If you simply wish to enjoy the game for what it is with the towers and story, I say it is definitely worth it, and even on lower end rigs it should be relatively playable now with the frame smoothing option and general lowering of requirements for the game.

I guess in light of the reviews the game has been getting I will write this as more of a performance review than of a review of the game (I love it so far).
My system:
i5 3570k at 4.5Ghz
16GB GDDR3
SLI EVGA 970 SSC
First off I want to say that I have had great performance with the game so far. I have textures at "very high", TAA on, Contat Shadows "off", shadows set to "high" and everything else is set to "Ultra" (yes even volumetric lighting). I am currently getting between 50-60 fps (no MSAA, turn off "sharpening" to significantly reduce jaggies). It is worth noting that despite getting decent scaling on my cards I did turn SLI off for the time being as the frametimes did take a hit and my performance was not much better than it was with a single card (about 10fps higher). I was expecting the poor SLI performance as it has been the norm for a long time that SLI does not work well on launch (I'll give it two months and if it is still broken I will come back and change this review).
I have noticed that some people with V-sync "on" did not notice that the default is a "double-buffered" V-Sync, which will cripple frame rates. Setting this to "triple-buffered" should smooth things out. The settings that seem to crush cards are the "Volumetric Lighting", "Hardened Contact Shadows" and "Screen-Space Reflections".
Volumetric lighting from Ultra to "on" gave me between 5-15 fps average with almost no loss in quality (I kept it on because I am mostly at 60fps, though I will drop it if I get worse perforamnce)
Hardened contact shadows are more difficult to notice in the game and by turning them off I gained 10-15fps.
I have not played around with Screen Space Reflections much as my framerate is fine now. Though I am willing to do a much more comprehensive breakdown of the settings and their FPS impacts if enough people would like me to.
Cannot say much for mouse acceleration. I guess it does not bother me very much (I realize it is a huge deal to some and that it really should be patched in as an option ASAP).
I do not want this review to come off as me stating there is nothing going on for some people. For those of you that are truly having difficulties I am sorry that the game is not working for you. However I do see some people whos bad performance is due to them being too stubborn to turn down one or two crazy settings and for them I have no cure.

I wrote a negative review on release day because the game was unplayable for most. It was one of the worst PC releases of all time and that's saying a lot. I promised to revise my review when they fixed the crashes, poor performance, stuttering, launch failures, and bugs. Most of those have now been resolved and what's left is an extremely satisfying addition to the Deus Ex series.
Some reviews have criticized the short main story. You should consider that there are dozens of hours of interesting side quests and plenty of ways to play the game. It's meant to be played through multiple times and I guarantee you will see new things each time around.
The game plays exactly like Human Revolution plus beautiful yet demanding graphics and a more engrossing story. That's the best way I can put it. If you enjoyed Human Revolution and you have a high end PC, you will love this game. It is still incredibly demanding so if you have anything less than a mid-range, recent generation GPU you may consider looking up some benchmarks before buying. This is by far the most hardwawre demanding game I've ever played.
Some remaining issues to consider: DX12 offers no performance improvements and in some cases decreases performance, crashes still occur though less frequently, multi-GPU support is nonexistent in this game. If you have SLI or Crossfire consider turning off your second GPU and your performance may actually improve.

an updated pros and cons, most of which appear in just about every other review for this game..
Pros:

- much improved gameplay mechanics regarding movement, cover/shoot, inventory
Cons:
- ugh, where to begin.... the port was initially unplayable, crashed often, terrible stuttering, though this has since been patched to a playable degree; still not great
- the whole dang story is BARELY half a game, no doubt to charge players another few times for what should have been one game
- the "villian" quickly shifts from the interesting actions of the illuminati to a pawn that is hard to care about at all; an insult to what made the predecessors so deep and enticing
- the only hub, Prague, is far too small to warrant the horrible need to constantly be going back and forth through the different districts via an incredibly annoying loading sequence; it seriously ruined many of the otherwise interesting side missions. This becomes even more bothersome with all of the unecessary cutscenes of the police checking your papers and insulting you about your augs. - with this being the first game in the series that features the return of a main character, it's wasted due to the fact that none of the significant characters that we grew to care about in the prior game join Jennsen; likely a way to appeal to the larger audiance rather than the returning fans of the series
- micro transactions and day one DLC (which was used to mislead players into preordering) appear, meaning Square Enix prioritized this above all of the glaring issues in the port, as if paying at least $60 for barely half a game wasn't enough
I could go on, but I'd like to forget about such wasted potential as soon as possible.
Bottom line: if they want to sell you a buggy half of a game, don't let them charge you for a full, finished game

So far this is setting out to be Human Revolution 2.0, which is not a bad thing at all. A lot of people are expecting this game to "do what HR did in 2011" which was essentially resurrect Deus Ex as a series, but HR already did that... So here's a better version of that 2011 game with really cool new Augments and a new story, which a fresh graphical coat of paint.
Excellent PC port, but unless you have at least 1070 even @ 1080p do not expect a STABLE 60fps with everything maxed out (Do NOT use MSAA, TAA is great).
To be a bit more specific, the big hitters are:
-MSAA (lol just don't)
-Volumetric Lighting (set this to "ON" rather than "Ultra")
-Shadows. As always for any detailed game world, shadows is almost a sure promise that your frames will tank.
"But muh microtransactions"
I personally see no need for microtransactions in a AAA single player game being sold at $60, its pay-to-cheat anyways and anti-consumer. But then I think "wait, if I don't want them, then I guess I won't buy them!". Honestly, how much money is SE thinking they're gonna make off of this? Maybe $100 total in a few years. Then again, one could argue "well if they don't make any money, why are they here?" I have no idea, maybe SE thinks they could make a quick buck. The Microtransactions situation is unfortunate, but I feel like the best way to protest this is to simply not participate with the Store (or just buy the game on sale). At the very least, the store itself keeps to itself and will not interfere with your gameplay. Its a menu icon that sticks to itself (Really though, shouldn't be there in the first place). its also affecting the Steam user ratings harshly so it might get their attention. However, given that everything else this game is (so far) doing right, I cannot make a review to not suggest purchasing this on microtransactions alone. Its a stain on a white velvet bed.
I've also read people complaining that the season pass is only per playthrough (as far as drops, and this also applies to things bought via the store)? There really is no excuse from that... just sad... (but then again, I'd ask why you paid for a season pass no knowing the quality of the content you'll eventually be getting... at full price. Thats on you homeboy).
Unless you're a Deus Ex fan or want that HR craving satisifed, then sure, wait until a sale.

Despite contending with ridiculous unlock delays and pre-load issues I eventually entered Mankind Divided with high hopes. Unfortunately those first two hours have not been a pleasant experience
[System: 4770K/16gb/980Ti - Nvidia Driver: 372.54]
- The mouse acceleration is unbearable, configuration files are not user accessible.
- The maximum FOV is uncomfortably narrow.
- Changing LOD settings in-game causes basic objects to disappear resulting in floating objects. You can also enter 'restricted' areas as the collision detection is mapped to many of these surfaces.
- Increasing screen resolution causes severe frame rate issues. At 1440p I can play with most settings on high/max at 60fps+. At 2160p I can barely maintain 30fps with all settings on low.
- Visuals are distinctly soft and low resolution at a moderate distance, despite disabling effects such as motion blur, depth of field and temporal AA. There appears to be further post-processing effects which cannot be disabled.
- The mouse and keyboard controls are not very intuitive, Jensen frequently jumps when attempting to move between cover. I will have to explore this further via custom key bindings.
- Excessive and unskippable splash screens, plus the usual nonsense regarding the game's auto-save 'feature'.
Many of these issues should be an easy fix but the tyranical approach to the file system means we will be left waiting for patches or perhaps a savy programmer to release tools to modify the files.
There are currently too many issues to even consider recommending this game, if I had purchased direct from the Steam Store I would strongly consider a refund. Bitterly disappointed.
