When I downloaded Super Crate Box, I had a lot of hopes. While I have quite a bit of experience with action platformers and side-scrollers, I had very little experience with arcade-style games. As such, I was expecting a game that drew players in with a concept that was easy to pick up and learn, but far more difficult to master, offering a simple, addictive design with a high, yet fair, difficulty.
As you can see from my time played in this game, Super Crate Box falls far short of these expectations.
To the game's credit, it does a few things correct. The objective of Super Crate Box is to collect crates while fighting and avoiding enemies in a single screen stage with a predetermined layout. The trick here is that each crate grants a different weapon. This means that, in order to truly excel at this game, one needs to master all weapons in the game in order to succeed in the long run. The idea of developing proficiency in using multiple different methods of attack is one that could be commended as very creative and pleasantly challenging (if it were implemented well). Furthermore, with the exception of the title screen music, the game displays a fairly nice soundtrack. It isn't anything incredible for those acquainted with the soundtracks of famous 8-bit or 16-bit games, but I have no complaints with the sound presentation of this game.
Unfortunately, this is where the positive aspects of the game end. For starters, I was very disappointed to find that it was impossible to rebind the keys for this game. This is an immense black mark on any modern video game, especially one so simple that most players would not consider getting an external controller for it. There is no reason the game could have not included an option for key bindings, especially since the game is extremely simple and requires very few keys.
Furthermore, as previously stated, I would have commended the idea of developing proficiency with multiple weapons throughout the course of the game as good if it were implemented well. The problem is... well, it isn't. Certain weapons like the bazooka and revolver are able to dispatch enemies with ease, while the dual pistols cut your damage output massively in exchange for being able to fire in both directions, a utility that is both rarely useful during the game and frankly unnecessary in the hands of a more skilled player. While it is certainly possible to obtain proficiency with all weapons, the severe imbalance between the weapons renders this struggle rather unnecessary, as one's success in the game honestly depends more on being lucky enough to gain strong weapons from crates than any form of skill.
The issue of weapon imbalance is exacerbated by the excessive simplicity of the game clouding just how strong the weapons are. I understand that the goal of this game was to create an old-fashioned arcade-style game, but completely hiding damage values and hit points from the player just leads to excessive confusion. I remember a few times in which a large enemy was charging towards me and I thought I could bring it down before it reached me, only to have it survive my attacks and still hit me. Had the HP of the enemy been displayed over its head and the damage done by each shot showed in small numbers nearby the enemy, I doubt that I would have had much trouble doing some basic mental arithmetic and determining that it was a better option to retreat and fight the enemy from a distance. Refusing to show such figures to the player causes one to rely more heavily on intuition than knowledge, further distancing one’s success at this game from any skill.
But all of these problems are nothing compared to what is easily the biggest issue of Super Crate Box: it doesn't work. No, I don't mean that the difficulty is too high or the control is excessively loose. I mean that the game literally cannot run for longer than five minutes without crashing. First off, it is extremely deterring to a first time player if, within an hour of starting the game, the game unexpectedly crashes, but when this occurs frequently within the first time playing the game, what reason does the player have to continue playing? Even if the other flaws in the gameplay did not exist, this issue is still absolutely unacceptable, because it means that the game was released in an unfinished form. After reading some articles online, I found that apparently, this issue is exclusive to Windows 8 and, while the makers of this game have acknowledged the problem, they have failed to offer a solution. I was stunned when I heard that, not only were the makers of this game aware that their game was released in an unfinished and barely functional state, but that they were in no rush to fix the game. After a little more searching online, I found numerous sources providing patches for the game to allow it to run smoothly on Windows 8, but by that point, I was too disappointed with the core gameplay and astounded that the makers of the game would leave other gamers to finish what was honestly their own work that I turned away immediately.
In conclusion, I do not recommend this game, because I simply cannot recommend something so unpolished. While many aspects of the game fall short of expectations, I may have been able to persist through the problems and find some redeeming qualities after spending a few hours on the game. It is not uncommon for a gamer to dislike a game at first, only to develop a liking for it later on and I have no doubt that this game may have been one such case for me; however, when the game fails to achieve that most fundamental expectation any gamer has of a video game (i.e. to be able to play the game.), then the game is frankly not even worth picking up in the first place. Super Crate Box may lure you in with its free-to-play tag, but the money you may have saved selecting a free Steam game will be more than nullified by the time you will waste trying to play a game that simply does not work.

I've said it time and time again; developers should have perfected 2D shooters decades ago. Instead we have another fairly recent title that misses the mark. Now before I go any further, let me mention that this also applies to modern beatemup developers.
I believe that some game developers have a nasty habit of... underestimating the genre they're working on. 2D shooters, shmups, STGs, or however you call them are supposedly very simple to design. There's a spaceship, or an airplane, or a psychic teenager. They have to fight off an alien armada, an evil army, or an old psychic lady. You put these opposing forces into a blender, sprinkle in a few hundred million bullets, and like magic, a shmup is made.
But is it a good shmup? Well, that's where things get complicated. There is a lot that goes into these games, but it's never really obvious. You have to pay attention to how the game plays, the way it flows, the motion of the ocean, and so on and so forth. If you slap stuff together without a semblance of care, then you're left with something that's not any fun. This goes double for everyone out there who thinks it's easy to make games about punching people.
Sky Mercenaries could have been decent. In my mind, 2D shooters where players can upgrade their ships and boost stats are a tough sell, but I can still understand their appeal. The problem is that SM trips right at the start by having an awful frame-rate. I mean, what's the FPS in this game? 30?
? Because it's nowhere near 60. I play a LOT of arcade STGs, and while I'm not very good at them, I can at least recognize that they average between 54 and 60 FPS. That should be standard, but
can't even get that right. So when I started up SM for the first time, and was greeted with a laughable frame-rate, a thought appeared in the back of my mind. It's like a fortune cookie cracked open and the message inside said: "You don't have to take this game seriously."
I'm a reasonable reviewer, or at least I think I am. I perservered, despite the gargantuan red flag. Unfortunately, this game is continually problematic, and that can be attributed to its sloppy design. The stages don't really have a theme beyond "enemies & bullets". The weapon system is half-baked, so most of the time you're going to feel underpowered. Even the tinest turrets and flying junkheaps can take several hits to destroy. It's not uncommon to find the screen flooded with bullets, simply because you can't destroy anything. Frequently you'll camp in front of enemy ships for an inordinant amount of time, but sometimes it's just not enough.
The player-ship can switch between red and blue to absorb like-colored bullets, but it's also a half-baked and messy system. It would have been better to simply drop it entirely, and just focus on the basics. What we get instead is a lame excuse to add a bunch of unnecessary bullets.
This is also yet another 2D shooter that has way-too-large hit-boxes. While the player-ship has a shield and restoration drops are common, there's no excuse for how much damage occurs, especially because it dramatically affects the score. Sometimes lasers can fire from off-screen, and those can result in BS deaths. Losing isn't a huge punishment (aside from having to restart the stage) but... I guess it doesn't really matter.
After a certain amount of time with this game, I just stopped caring. I developed a sense of complacency, and allowed myself to be lulled into a barely concious stupor. I'd move the ugly ship around eye-searing environments, shoot the far too durable enemies, and get bamboozled by the impossible bonus rounds. It all goes back to the frame-rate. It's so bad that it brings down the entirety of the game. Then again, if the frame-rate was better, my expectations would also be higher, and the resulting disappointment would be that much greater. So in a roundabout way, maybe that's a plus?

Ah, portal knights. An MMO minecraft game, that's actually fun, may I add.
From what I've played with friends, while slacking off and watching eachother die by destroying the block underneath eachother's feet and then watching eachother fall into the void, the game is quiet fun. It adds minecraft elements of placing blocks with MMO and RPG aspects. You can level up by gaining xp, which is obtained through enemies, mining, and breaking pots, and with leveling you can upgrade your character as you choose. Have an archer, but want close range damage instead of building onto your ranged attacks? The stats aren't locked to specific classes, so ♥♥♥♥ it! Make your archer an warrior(If you want..even though you can't wear their gear..) The game has so many different worlds/portals that it's insane. The enemies that you kill also respawn when you leave the world you were just in, making grinding for levels easy. Every now and then while leveling you get to choose from a skill tree(which is customizable even after picking a skill you want)with these skills you can make your archer into an immobile turrent, or into a fast moving rouge. (if you can't tell, I picked archer as my class of choice)
Would I recommened this game at the stage it's at, at this moment? Hell yeah, it's worth picking up. Even for the original $15 price. Just make sure you have friends to play with every now and then, or it's content will seem boring at times.

Portal Knights is a very cute game. For sure thumbs up! Deserves a recommendation.
The game is so lively, so fresh, so eye-candy, so full of color and action! It catches your attention right off the bat. It's like opening a flask of perfumes and feeling the fragrance in the air! You enter a magnificent land of magic, green fields, gorgeous skyline, magnificent views, nice music and sounds...
It's a blend of minecraft, lego and rpg. You can say it's an rpg version of minecraft with high-res bricks, graphics and characters. Minecraft, just better. Same as in Minecraft, the world is "chunky", built of bricks of different types and textures. You can manipulate them: delete, add, move around to mold the surroundings according to your desire. Yes, you can build some interesting structures in Portal Knights. Structures like houses, castles, dungeons... whatever comes to mind. I must stress the better quality of bricks compared to minecraft, which makes a whole lot of difference.
It's also lego, as the main character's face looks 100% lego-like, as well as the characters body gird.
Portal Knights is an RPG. You fight mobs, gain exp, level up, craft items. You have an inventory, stats and talents. You create a character, choose from 3 classes, customize the look. You can plow fields and grow vegetables and trees.
The game reminds me of Wizard101 (cartoon manifestation of Harry Potter), if you've ever played it. Some may say Portal Knights is a game for kids, but that really depends how you look at it. As Portal Knights is probably mostly addressed for the younger audience, it can as well be played and enjoyed by adults.
You enter a universe consisting of, currently, 44 worlds and 3 Bosses. There are approx. 5-6 different types of worlds: springs, frost, desert, moon-like. The world types repeat in different configurations. The worlds are generated randomly per account, but once they are generated, you live with the outcome.
Exploration is an important factor. Vast terrain, cleaning out mobs, checking out the deep caverns, climbing mountains and gathering resources while you're at it... In order to travel between the worlds, you need to find portals, which must be activated using portal stones (gained via mobs). Once every 10-15 worlds you get a unique Boss to fight.
That doesn't mean that the game is bug-free. Far from it. There are numerous ones and you notice them as you progress. When fighting mobs you sometimes run into situations, when you can't hit them and you need to relocate in order to "make it work again". Questing is somewhat weak. There are occassional NPCs, which give you quests, but the NPCs are scarse and the quests are somewhat erratic. You have a feeling that the devs were in a hurry when they added the quests. The game requires some serious balancing when it comes to the classes, abilities and mobs. And you only have 3 classes to pick.
The game lacks the end-game content. Once you hit level 30 (which is a cap), once you defeat the 3rd Boss, once you craft everything, there is really little else you can do. For now.
When I first started the game, I couldn't really play it. I had to spend a long time tuning the options, in order for the game to run smooth. I read in the forums, there many people had the exact same issue. Some even reported multiple crashes, which -fortunatly- I didn't experience.
Portal Knights is officially an "Early Access Game" and to be honest it's unfinished or should I say it requires more content. In the last world you find a big red portal, which you cannot activate. What is it?... Probably a portal to the next expansion yet to come.
Interesting thing is where will the devs take the game. What will be the direction. What will be the future of Portal Knights. So far the saves are stored on your local disc with some parameters stored in the Cloud. You can co-op in Portal Knights, play with friends, but it's not really an MMO per se. Will it go full MMO? Or will it remain a single player game? According to the announcement the devs now focus on a playstation version of the game.
Strangly enough, I didn't find much resources on the web regarding Portal Knights. Very few guides and articles here and there. Some of them old with the outdated worlds and mobs names, which was confusing. When you have a specific question or problem, chances are you won't find a solution online. And I'm sure you will have questions as you play, as some things are not that intuitive. I don't really know why the forums are not that crowded, the game is great and it deserves to have more resources available.
It was made by the Germans. If that matters to anyone.
Lots of small things people ask for, like the ability to lock the blocks from moving or protect the chest from robbing by others who enter your universe, changing how the Events work, changing the way the crops work etc.
All in all, Portal Knights is a beautiful, cute and stunning journey. It should definiately be recommended. Hopefully the devs will add more content, rebalance the gameplay and eventually launch it as a final product. Preferably as an MMO.

Decent game but very unbalanced.  As the description said, it's a co-op hack'n'slash and I think therein is its problem: the repetitive predictability of hacking and slashing.  It reminds me of Dynasty Warriors (although minion enemies are way more active/aggressive) where the gameplay emphasis is overwhelmingly on button-mashing melee with the occasional spice of abilities thrown in.  In fact, the (only?) fastest way to recharge your resource to activate those abilities is to score sequential basic weapon hits without taking a hit in return.  In no way does this game feel like the spirit of the online show RWBY.  In the show, teammates constantly display new and inventive tactics where cooperative synergy is the dominant force and the finishing moves are mind-blowing uber powerful one-off abilities.  In Grimm Eclipse, however, the abilities play a minor role versus the efficacy of basic melee, are embarrassingly underpowered compared to the "real" characters' inventive potency, don't recharge fast enough, are prone to missing or having suboptimal effect if the enemies aren't lined up 'just so', and one player's abilities have no beneficial synergistic effect with any other player's.  The only coop effect I could perceive was that when my character was fighting (in melee of course) near to another, our individual melee hits seemed to do a lot more damage, much like, again, Dynasty Warriors coop mode.  If this game is to do proper homage to the show, the abilities need a massive beefing up with greater complexity, frequency of availability, ease of use, and team-oriented effects.
Some good things:
1, the music.  (Thank you for adding a sound fx volume slider after I wrote this review, but why are character fighting voices applied to sound fx instead of, um... Voices slider?)
2, Although the mayhem of melee feels like button mashing, there is a bit of strategy in it in that you can and should use jump and dodge and, by throwing those into your rotations, your chain attacks change up a little bit.  (I'd like to see more of that.)
3, Every character has their niche and feels distinct, even when doing basic melee animations.  For instance, Yang is great at keeping enemies occupied by kiting them with right-click cone effects, compared to Weiss who can pick off enemies with long range attacks.
4, The MOBA style levelling up works.  Personally, I'd prefer a persistent character whom I could take back to the starting chapter with a friend and power through.  (Think 'The Legend of Korra'.)  But with the MOBA style you're encouraged to stick with your team and help each other keep leveling up and progressing.  You quickly become attached to the power/improvements your character gains.
5, It's a great coop game.  Very easy to pick up and play, no team killing shenanigans, no server/lobby lag, people can drop and join at any point, and the enemy difficulty scales to how many players are in the party.  Oh, and a party can consist of four Blakes, if you really all want to have kitty ears.
Some little things I'd recommend improving:
1, I already said the abilities.
2, Please do balance the volumes.
3, I think it only makes sense to have the crate experience spheres contribute to group xp just like the artifact chess pieces.  No point in making people fight over crates or prioritize them over enemies.
4, Wave fights are good and all, but I sincerely hope later levels will include more coop based mechanics, like simultaneous activation puzzles, or needs to separate enemies and tackle them away from each other, or enemies who are especially vulnerable to flanking maneuvers.
5, I know it's a hack'n'slash MOBAish thing, but please let there be some way to save progress.  This game has the potential to be virtually unending in its maps/chapters, but that'd be ridiculously infuriating to have to leave suddenly or have internet hiccup and disconnect a player when they're 20 chapters in and are forced to start over from Ch 1.
6, There should be a lot more evidence of semblance power.  Ruby should become faster as she gains more sequential hits or by capitalizing upon the recoil from Crescent Rose's sniper fire (as is canon).  Would also be nice if she had an ability to sprint across the map to help teammates.  Weiss should have more glyphs, like being able to freeze at a distance, teleport, speed up teammates while slowing enemies, imbue teammates with power, etc.  Blake should do a lot more teleporting and should be able to deploy a distraction dummy of herself, turning invisible or at least dumping aggro until it's destroyed.  Yang should be able to absorb hits and channel that energy back as extra melee damage.
Overall, a fun game, wonderfully reminscent of the world of Remnant, beautiful canon aesthetics, cute little quips from the characters, smart level design, etc.  Good game.  But can be much better.

This is a follow-up review for Hexen. If you haven't read it I'd recommend doing so to get the gist of what it's all about in order to get the most out of this one. Thank you!
Hexen: Deathkings of the Dark Citadel is the only official expansion pack for Hexen and developed once again by Raven Software, released a year after the base game. Unlike most expansions released for shooters around this time period Raven don't outsource theirs to third parties but prefer to create their own. As such the quality of the expansion is more or less on par with the original title, which will either be a good or a bad thing depending on how much you enjoyed or loathed Hexen overall.
Deathkings continues the story of Hexen, shortly after the defeat of Korax, the three heroes come upon the source of Korax's power: the Chaos Sphere, an ancient artifact that can create new worlds or destroy them, and appears to be kept inside its own pocket dimension. During the ending sequence of the original game the player is poised to take the Chaos Sphere for their own use, but is warned that there still exists other beings more powerful than them, foreshadowing Hexen II. However in Deathkings it's revealed that when the player takes the Chaos Sphere they are whisked away to the Realm of the Dead, which is occupied by Korax's broken armies, and the heroes must find their way back home. This is very similar to what happens to Corvus in Heretic when D'Sparil dies but not before uttering a curse to condemn Corvus to a similar fate in the game's fourth and fifth episodes. It's never mentioned whether this was a result of the Chaos Sphere's own power or a curse laid by Korax in Deathkings' scenario, but according to the game box description the Chaos Sphere is powerless in the Realm of the Dead and the heroes must overcome the Deathkings, the rulers of this forsaken place who reside in the Dark Citadel.
Whereas Hexen had five hubs to complete Deathkings has roughly half that at three (technically there's four but the latter's reserved for deathmatch only and cannot be visited in single player) at around twenty levels and contain pretty much every theme visited in the original game, like swamps and wilderness areas, castle and seminary themed locations, only re-envisioned and mixed up. Even all the puzzle items and keys used in the base game are back and recycled but handled in a different order. It's almost as if the Realm of the Dead mocks all your efforts to get to this point and makes you do them all over again, only in traditional expansion pack fashion: it's going to be a lot harder now. I'd argue that the first hub Blight is the most difficult to endure and definitely the most confusing to navigate, with the remaining hubs Constable's Gate and Nave being less of a headache and a bit more streamlined.
Combat was never a huge focus in Hexen like it was in Heretic (unless you were on the highest difficulties) due to the stronger emphasis on puzzle solving and exploration, but here you'll be doing a lot more fighting, as it appears that every foe you've slain in Hexen has come back to get even with you plus more and they're more heavily concentrated and in greater numbers. You will not be afforded a single breather this time around, and the occasional Ettin spawning into the level was replaced by practically an entire battalion of monsters spawning in after a while if you take too long to get things done. The Death Wyvern, a pitiful boss in Hexen was brought back and now there's four of them flying around in a level early on and each one must be killed in order to progress the hub. This is very difficult to pull off with the Fighter and Cleric until you find their third weapon and even then the Fighter is guaranteed to have the hardest time as none of his weapons have hitscan properties like the Cleric and Mage have access to. You'll also be dealing with a couple Heresiarchs later on again just the same as in Hexen but if you've developed a good strategy against them they won't be any harder.
As for the final encounter the 'Deathkings' are your former Masters again, as Korax's gift of Unlife has allowed them to continue their reign of power in the Realm of the Dead, and they must be slain once again in order to return to the world of the living. Heretic's extra episodes also recycled the Iron Lich and Maulotaur boss fights as it wouldn't make sense to see the Serpent Riders alive again. Still a lazy ending and makes me wish Raven would've considered adding actual new content beyond just another set of levels.
That's really the biggest flaw with this expansion is that it's nothing you haven't already seen before and exists solely to sate appetites for diehard fans of the original. There's no new textures, no new music, no new enemies, no new weapons, no new items, nothing new to really talk about in this review, just a collection of maps that as a whole I think is a weaker campaign than the original's, but ultimately they're not too awful. The levels are for the most part fairly well designed and there can be some pretty cool moments and if you really enjoyed Hexen and want more this is essentially the most you'll ever get again as there's very little user made content available for it. Another issue I can cite is the strange lack of music, while it re-uses Hexen's the soundtrack in version 1.0 of Deathkings is still associated with the levels of the original game, not those of the expansion. There's a small patch (dkpatch.zip) that was released and updates HexDD.wad re-enabling the music and upgrades it to version 1.1.
Once again if you're a diehard fan of Hexen I'll still recommend it but if not then there's nothing to see here.

Pros:
"Brothers" is a exemplary example of how a game can be entertaining, innovative, artistic, and emotionally gripping, and does it all without a single line of real dialog. Despite their sim-lish, the characters are expressive, and you can quickly glean personalities and emotions from tone of voice and body language. The environments are colorful and gorgeously designed, ranging in style from Disney-esque to downright creepy and disturbing (wait until you see the Valley of Giants).
The controls may take a little getting used to. I've heard it described as "Single-player co-op", and I find that to be extremely apt; each thumbstick and trigger controls one brother, forcing you to split your concentration between both of them. While this is tricky at first, you'll get used to this two-braining fairly quickly. The challenge of the game lies in discovering how to the brothers can work together to solve the various puzzles that block your way forward. That said, there aren't too many head-scratchers, so you should be able to find your way along without too much frustration.
The basic premise of the Brothers' quest is to find a magic healing elixir to cure their dying father. I'll leave it at that: exploring the story is the whole point of this fairy tale. "Life is a journey, not a destination."
Cons:
First, it requires a dual-analog controller (I am reading now that it has keyboard controls as an option. Your mileage may vary, good luck). Second, it is very short. I beat the game straight through, and later went back for all achievements, and have logged a mere 4.1 hours.
But damn, it was worth it.
Conclusion:
I don't know if I can recomment it at the full $15 price-tag, but on sale, it is a no brainer - Picking it up! As I said above, "Brothers" is a journey that should not simply be explained, but rather, it should be experienced. I hope enjoy!

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning succeeds in some important ways, but in my opinion inevitably falls flat on its face for anyone who has played RPGs before. It really depends on why you play RPGs.
KoA has a story that is at times refreshing and inspired, like with almost everything surrounding the Fae and their interactions with your character.  At other times, it is cliche and groan-inducing; just about anything having to do with the "Fate" concept in the game was at best predictable and at worst actually insulting in its lameness. The dialogue outside of story missions was also trite and felt written around a quest that had already been programmed into the game without a justification. This is extra egregious in a game that advertises how a famous fantasy author developed the story.
It has an art style that screams in vivid colors and exaggerated animations, which I personally love as a longtime ex-player of World of Warcraft. However, if you're a fan of dark and gritty, you won't really find it here.
And honestly, most problematically, the game has a huge difficulty curve problem: it's way too easy. By halfway through the game, I had broken it even on "hard" difficulty. My warrior character, built in an extremely obvious fashion (and avoiding the bugged Last Stand talent), was nigh-invincible and two-shotting everything except bosses, and that's before stacking over 100% damage and several layers of mitigation in potions. The fundamental axis of interaction in KoA is combat; when it becomes so trivial as to be boring, the game falls apart unless you were happy playing on easy anyway.
Overall, I really, really wish I could recommend KoA. . . but I think for most people that would read a Steam review, it's just not going to be the right choice.

I don't know if this game is supposed to be an homage to old school shmups because it sure as heck doesn't tell you so.. or anything else which possibly could be of use to the player for that matter. It almost seems like this game tries to bite off more than it can chew, resulting in what feels like a watered down shooter that doesn't excel at anything.
I don't write negative reviews lightly (this being my second). I generally just don't bother with 'mediocre' or lower game but in some cases I do care. So from an almost 3 hour play session (which is more than lenient for this type of game) this is what I got from it.
- Damage Numbers: By default, this setting is enabled which may be 'fun' in the beginning but later on just serves as more crap and distraction on the screen and doesn't really add anything useful whatsoever.
- RPG Element: I usually enjoy RPG elements in games when it's done right.. but it does absolutely nothing for me here. It feels like a boring linear treadmill which almost seems required to progress which is pretty absurd for a shmup.
- Color/Absorb/Polarity: A nice mechanic popularized by Ikaruga but falls a bit short here. Players unfamiliar with Ikaruga will either have to stumble upon it, get it from the subtle one-time 'hint' in the game or read it from the achievement you get for switching colors.
To cut things short, I'll speed it up a bit.. The UI is unpleasant to navigate; in-game HUD is very bland; Hitpoints for the player's ship are localized to separate ship parts/drones which is useless because it's not like you have any real control of it; enemies often seems to have too much HP regardless if you 'specialized' for damage; and the bonus level seems to be bugged unless you're not supposed to move and tank sporadic rockets that sway towards your ship until you die because I can't imagine shooting all of them down whilst also trying to wittle down the 'boss' of it's seemingly infinite HP.
There's probably more minor grievances that I have with this game but despite of everything I just wrote, I would be okay with this game if it wasn't for the dreadful sound effects. I have never played a shmup that felt less satisfying than this one does. The sound effects are very bland to the point that there's no sense of impact when you shoot or kill an enemy ship.. not only is it unsatisfying to shoot and kill, it makes it somewhat difficult to tell where and when you actually kill an enemy. For a game that revolves around wrecking swarms of enemy ships and crafts, this makes for a very dull and boring experience.
But that's not all unfortunately because the horribleness of sound effects stretches even further.. Now I am not a rookie at these types of games but in certain levels it throws so much crap at you that I'd be surprised if you can come out of it unscathed. Calling it bullet hell feels degrading towards other actual bullet hell games so I usually like to call it 'bs hell' as that's what it is. In other words, you will sometimes get hit quite a bit. ..and when you're in the middle of taking all of those hits in a bullet infestation, it really.. really doesn't help that taking damage sounds like you're being smacked on the the side by a muppet.. or stung by a swarm of muppets for that matter. Because that's not a sound that makes you think you're in trouble or may be about to die. If it wasn't clear.. by muppet I mean a little puppet that makes a squeeky sound when you squeeze it. ..it's horrible. But on the flipside, after an hour playing listening to it your ears become immune and you'll start thinking that colliding with enemy spaceships only tickles you and you're immortal.. ..well, until you see your ship crashing down that is.
And with that, I think I have said enough. Honestly, I do think this game has/had potential but it just seems that it tries too much whilst the most essential parts of the game fall behind unfortunately. One thing I did enjoy was the music.. but for some reason it's random as heck which doesn't distinguish the stages/tilesets from each other and makes each level as forgettable as the last.. which sadly is also true for the game as a whole.
As a fan of this genre in general, I can not by the life of me recommend this game at it's full asking price. Perhaps the multiplayer/co-op could be fun, but alas like most of these games it's local only. And even then, I would advice just getting it on a sale because there's far better out there for your money's worth.

5min of gameplay
A Ikaruga like shmup
You pick 1 of 3 pilots that have 5 unlockable skills: Bills good with drones, John does shields, & Lea does more damage when red.
Then you pick between 3 ships with 22 up grades: the attacker with lower defense, the defender with lower damage, or the one that's ok at both.
In combat you can switch between red & blue, where your attacks change a bit but you can absorb like color bullets.
Absorbed bullets will charge a bar that when full will discharge a large beam forward.
Watch for bullets with a hue of both colors as you can not absorb these.
You can see your hp in the upper left and various power ups in the bottom right.
In all there are 8 Worlds, with 3 levels each, and a boss fight at the end of the 3rd level with a chase mode after the boss.
In chase mode you don't control your ship but are firing backward at a boss as you try to take out drones before they hit you while also trying to take out the boss.
There is also a edit mode so you can make or your own levels.

This game is amazing! I'd love to see this game continue progressing and gain more content. So for starters, I started playing Portal Knights because I've been looking for a multiplayer adventure/sandbox game to play with my fiance. We've played games like minecraft and terraria, so this game was right up our alley. The following are my opinion of the pros and cons of this game:
Pros:
- Supports multiplayer
- Graphics are visually pleasing. The graphics are very pretty and the art is stylized and quirky.
- Music is great. It reminded me of music from Banjo-Kazooie. The music suits the environment and always gives you a sense of wonder and adventure.
- Combat style is engaging, making every fight that much more fun.  Each boss is unique and calls for a unique way of defeating it. I can tell the developers put a lot of love and effort into creating the boss fights. ( I can't wait to see what other creative ways they can develop more bosses)
- Characters can level up and progress. Like an RPG, characters can level up and gain new class unique skills. This adds to the play time and makes you want to level up and see your character grow strong.
- Plenty of dungeons to explore. Each island has dungeons with treasure chests in it.
- Questing system. Unlike Minecraft and terraria, Portal Knights offers various quests to complete. This gives players more to do.
- Random island events. This adds to your environment changing and again provides more things to do.
- Building. Like Minecraft and Terraria, you can also let your creative side loose and build anything your heart desires.
Cons:
- Combat is a little clunky. When you auto lock enemies you can no longer jump. To do so, you have to unlock on the enemie and jump. It's inconvenient that I have to take that extra step to use a basic function. Additionally, when you need to tumble and you're attacking an enemy, you have to physically stop attacking before you can tumble. This means I can't hold left click down and press shift to tumble at the same time. I have to physically let go of the left click button and then press shift to tumble.
- When tumbling you can't tumble up a single block, only on flat surfaces or down  blocks. I got stuck so many times trying to dodge because of this.
- All non boss enemies look the same but with different colors. I'd like to see more variety and have the ability to fight more unique enemies.
- Craftable weapons are just stronger recolors. A little bit of variety wouldn't hurt.
- Random events are too rare. I don't know about other players, but I only get random events maybe once a day irl. With 47 different islands, I'd like to see more events going on.
- Character customization is limited. I know the game is still in early access, but as of now, I'd like to see more vanity items and potentially female versions of armor.
- All dungeons are the same. I lost the sense of adventure with the dungeons because of this.
- Torches held by other players do not emit light for you.
- Some items are too hard to get. (Ex: Sun diamonds. Theres only one island that had it in my world and only had a little bit of it. This forced me to make a new world just to get enough to complete an armor set.)
- Not much to do after you unlock all islands.
TL;DR
The game is great and has a lot of potential. It's worth playing, but definitely needs more variety and needs to work out some kinks.

Mortal Kombat X is the 10th installment in the legendary fighting-game franchise, Mortal Kombat. Coming after Mortal Kombat 9, which undoubtedly delivers one of the best fighting-game experiences of all time, my expectations were pretty high. I was not disappointed; they've done it again!
Mortal Kombat X is basically a reconfiguration of the traditional Mortal Kombat formula with a large host of tweaks and configurations. Firstly, the story mode; clocking in at about 6 hours, the campaign is significantly shorter than the previous game, and the character variety throughout is fairly limited. Most of the story mode focuses on the dull, new special forces characters as opposed to some of the more interesting characters. By far, the most interesting segments of the game have you fighting the civil war in Outworld as awesome characters such as Kotal Kahn and D'vorah. Unfortunately, the campaign is quite short and doesn't get as entertaining or substantial as the excellent story mode in MK9. With that said though, there are a lot of great moments and it was a great way to get familiar with many of the characters (many of Takeda's and Kung Jin's moments are pretty fantastic).
Speaking of characters, this game includes 25 fighters (I think that's correct, but feel free to correct me), each with one with three variant fighting styles. An incredible amount of love and care has been put into designing these characters and their fighting styles, and I can honestly say not a single one of these characters feels underbaked or half formed. It is a shame that Goro, an iconic Mortal Kombat character, is locked behind a paywall (or free if you preordered).
Once you finish the story mode, there's a wealth of other play modes to muck around in. You have single fight, which lets you choose your fighter/variant and face off against a number of fighters in a stage of your choice. You always have the excellent tower modes, including the awesome Living Tower mode, which lets you run through a list of opponents as a fighter of your choice while a random event will change the fight unexpectedly (for example, the 'sloth' sends orbs into the stage that force you into slow motion if they collide with your character). This was an excellent addition, as it helps vary the gameplay even after you've played for a considerable number of hours. There's plenty of content for offline-only players here, making Mortal Kombat X worth the price purely for the single-player content.
The online modes are also a hell of a lot of fun, and remain pretty addictive after investing a significant amount of hours into the game. You can choose your Faction, meaning you and other players in the same Faction will earn XP towards their Faction goal, and the winning faction for that week will allocate Krypt coins to the members of the winning team. While the online modes are excellent fun and are very substantial, the netcode is currently rather shaky and players may have trouble connecting to and remaining in a stable online game. Hopefully further patches can improve this issue.
Overall, Mortal Kombat X is an excellent fighting game; the wealth of content and sheer polish put into this title makes it worthy of purchase for long-time newcomers and even for newcomers of the franchise. So here it is -- the anime web seris that looks like a hack-n-slash video game now really is a hack-n-slash video game. (Which is one of the things I liked about RWBY. Keep your pants on.)
While I fully appreciate that Grimm Eclipse is effectively a WIP, we clearly have a long way to go.
There's no tutorial right now, much less the option to bind keys or anything in the way of story beyond, "go here and complete an objective straight out fo TF2" (one level literaly has you pushing a bomb cart down a mineshaft) but the gameplay is simple enough not to need one and  you can count the number of actions you can perform on one hand: movement is WASP, space makes you jump, shift makes you dash a short distance, M1 is your basic melee combo, M2 is your ranged attack, and you get three special moves bound to numericals 1,2, and 3 respectively, all of which are slightly different for each memeber of team RWBY. It's as awkward as it sounds, so best take full advantage of this game's controller support.
Combat shows some promise, but has a lot of basic features appear to be missing: there's no pointer or lock-on system, so when there's a slew of enimes in front of you and you want to interrupt the big nasty grimm while he's still telegraphing his attack instead of, say, one of the small harmless grimm, there's no way of telling which enemy Weiss will attack until she's already hit the wrong one and is bleeding out on the ground.
Reviving allies in the middle of combat is almost impossible. Nine times out of ten, the fight will already be over by the time you get your allies back on thier feet because standing still for even ten seconds to revive them is a great way to get curb stomped by a mob of grimm. Contrast to, Dragonball Xenoverse, which let's you block while reviving someone and made it clear how close you needed to stand to them with a ring graphic. If there's a way to block in this game, I've not found it.
Character progression is handled by a surpisingly convoluted set of skill trees. Each time you level up, you gain a point you can spend boosting your attributes or upgrading your special attacks, with some options being locked out untill you kill X number of grimm with the fandango attack, revive an ally, grind the fandango attack X number of times whilst balenceing a boiled egg on your nose, etc. with branches at the end.
The game doesn't pause while you're upgrading, so make sure your teammates aren't sprint ahead to get a lead on you -- which brings me to another problem.
For a game that's clearly tryignt to emphasize teamwork, there's a lot of intra-team competition going on here. One of the chief ways the game pits you against your friends is the score system, which is displayed at the end of a level showing how many times you killed an enemy, died, and how many points you scored. I'm not even sure how this works, since I killed more enmies than Yang and died the same number of times, but still got a lower score.
'Must of bribed the scorekeeper...Just where does she get off wearing that revealing outfit anyway, the cantankerous litte wh--

Anyway, what really got my snow-white knickers in a twist was the level system. You gain exp. from killing enemies, finding things, completeing objectives, and vandalizing crates (property of the Snee corperation, I'll have you know) like you're Crash Bandicoot in a dress.
Now for the first two of thouse, fair is fair. If someones can kill more grimm than me they deserve more points, and when the control point is held, the whoule team gets the full share. Problems arise when a certain black-haired silver-eyed hedgehog is able to horde solo exp.s from the exploration bonuses singing "Gotta go fast!" all the merry while because she appears to have higher movements speed and better dash range; made worse by the fact that Weiss appears to be slower than the other characters, with a slower projectile weapon to boot. (Having said that it's almost appropriate given how infuriating Weiss finds Ruby in the show.)
How bad is it when a Snee has to rely on riff-raff to break her own 6ft styrofoam crates? (I don't know how I'm going to explain these shortcomings to Winter.)
It would have been fine if everyone benefited from smashing crates because it would encourage specilization and teamwork: you go break my boxes until wumpa fruit comes out, me and Blake will take care of these

grimm while Yang fashions her Ember Cecilia into a make-shift defibulator incase things get hairy.
Joking aside, the lead characters get from smashing crates is marginal at higher levels (which makes me question why they exist) but I still find it odd that players are pitted against each other at all. If I see that this game can make personal success feel irrelevant next to the success of the team, I will feel content that everything will fall into place.
Visually, everything in the game looks exactly as it should, since most of the models and possibly even the environments, have already been made in the series (one advantage of having your game based off of a
3D animated web-series) and while it certainly looks great, it's yet to surpass my expectations in that regard, so I'll hold off singing it's praises.
Overall though I feel the project is going in the right direction with a game that has every oppertunity to thrill fans of the show with little nuggets of character moments and lore without intruding upon a simple pick-up-and-play hack-and-slasho-button-masho extravoganza that you can play with all of your friends and marvel at how the members of team RWBY don't tear out each other's hair constantly.
So, bottom line: is Grimm Eclipse worth the price of submission as a gaming experiance? In it's current state, frankly, no. It's just not done yet. What's avalible is analogous to a demo. If you want to by this game, understand that what you're buying is your say in how this game grows, and promises of what may be. For many a fan, this will be enough, and if you like this game as a concept, then you should definatly throw your money down now. The project can't be a success without your support.

For those who played Hexen: Beyond Heretic and wanted to play more, Hexen: Deathkings of the Dark Citadel is right up your alley.
Deathkings of the Dark Citadel is an expansion pack that contains 3 new sizable hub worlds and increased challenge compared to that of Hexen: Beyond Heretic.
Much else can't really be said than what I already said about Hexen: Beyond Heretic.
You can use GZDoom to play this expansion pack, although before doing so, it would be wise to read one of the guides that tell you how to fix the "no music" issue through a patch. Other than that, you should have no huge problems.
I thoroughly enjoyed this expansion pack and, as I previously mentioned, would recommend it to people who enjoyed Hexen: Beyond Heretic.

HeXen: Deathkings of the Dark Citadel is an expansion pack for Hexen, released in 1996. It doesn't feature any new gameplay elements, instead it adds more hard levels for single player and adds more levels and improvements for Multiplayer and Deathmatch. But since everybody uses Zandronum for multiplayer in Doom engine games anyway, it's only just more levels.
Now, if you will try to play the game right as it was installed by Steam you will be met by disaster. It really got to be the worst out of all games that id software published here.
Most importantly, the game is unpatched. It's original release. A flawed original release, where develoeprs somehow forgot to link music of Hexen to new levels. So, unless you download and patch the game up, you will have to enjoy some silence. Amazing. Check community guides on how to do that.
Then, as usual, DosBox isn't configured good. It lags and so you have to go to game's directory, open the needed .conf file and edit "ddraw" output to "opengl" one.
And then if you want to choose your control and music device, then you will have to go to game's folder again and drag "setup" file over "dosbox" to launch it.
Expansion pack pulls quite an excuse plot twist to justify action: The evil or the sphere teleported you away into land of the dead where you have to defeat Deathkings before being able to return. Who are they anwyay. Ah, right, they just reuse end bosses from Hexen.
So, game adds three new hubs to conquer.  Which totals in around 30 levels. They don't use any new textures. Though there are some interesting inviroments anyway. But it's more of Hexen but harder.
The thing is, Hexen was already too dragged. It didn't had enough of variety in combat and weapons for each class. It had tedious part. And bringing even more levels that are also harder and bring no new gameplay elements, well, it's not a good idea. At all.
Yes, it has a sin of using bosses of Hexen as tough enemy. You fight big mage demon at the first level of the second hub already.
It doesn't help that I had glitch two different glitches on the first hub. First, there weren't enough of fire masks, key items, in the first world. Yes, I checked with walkthrough on all spots. Somehow, there wasn't. Somehow. And then on another level magic bridge just didn't appear either. And wyverns, bosses of Hexen, got stuck in walls too. So, watch out on first hub.
And main problem and difference in difficulty is monster respawn.
Original Hexen would spawn Ettins, common melee weak enemies, after each 10 minutes. Or at least it feels so. It was there just so player will not get lonely while being lost.
Dark Citadel rushes you down and beats you up. It can spawn hordes of any kind of enemy more often. And shielding centaurs that are incredibly annoying or flying imps that shoot fireballs at you aren't good enemies to respawn.
What it means is that you will have to rush levels down, having to solve "puzzles", saving/loading and doing other things while being rushed down and under constant heavy pressure. Killing enemies in this game doesn't bring any benefit, there is no leveling or such. You only waste mana and time. A lot of them. So you will have to try not to pay attention to them as you have to rush rush rush your way. And if you get lost, like everybody does in Hexen, then it will not be pretty.
It gets really bad on the main level of the last hub, Citadel itself. It's pretty much a hall with teleporters and switches. With water pools for no reason. And enemies not only respawn all time there, they also teleport around when reaching water pools for some reason, with without any special effect. You will be telefragged at least once.
Actually, perhaps it's easier to play as Mage here. His basic weapon, that don't require mana, is a ranged one.
So, Deathkings isn't good expansion pack It feels like it just milks on Hexen more. It's hard not in a good way, it's buggy, it brings nothing new outside of levels and it just makes Hexen outstay it's welcome. You miss nothing.

Oh Hexen, how I love thee. Bar none, my favorite FPS. How its expansion pack fails to live up to the original. Long story short, the balancing issues are obnoxious and it really takes away from the enjoyment of the game; for the sake of cranking up the difficulty, now ALL monsters respawn instead of just Ettins, which as pointed out by another user, renders much of the game an unbalanced pain in the @$$ instead of making it more challenging due to constantly draining you of ammo and supplies. Imagine having to play Doom with constantly respawning Cacodemons and Mancubi, that's how it feels to have respawning Chaos Serpents when your Fighter is low on green mana (trying to do Brackenwood as the Fighter, without even your Hammer of Retribution yet while FOUR Death Wyverns are flying around, is tantamount to only having your fists and chainsaw while being hounded by 4 Cyberdemons). By comparison, the expansion to Heretic (Shadow of the Serpent Riders) manages to up the difficulty while not making it seem far too cheap. And speaking of Shadow of the Serpent Riders, it comes packaged with the vanilla Heretic when you buy it, why couldn't they simply add Deathkings to the original Hexen port? Then it would make sense to buy them both as one package deal. So that being said, only pay money for this if you're buying it as part of a Heretic/Hexen bundle, if not, save your money for Hexen 2 instead. At least it provdes some novelty instead of an underwhelming rehash of a classic.

The mechanics are novel (controlling two plaftormer-type character simultaneously), but it goes far deeper than that. The mechanics aren't merely special for the challenge they present. They are part of the narrative structure of the game. This is as much a storytelling experience (without words, mind you!) as it is an interactive one.
The environment is beautiful and hides many subtle touches and ways to interact. Although I finished the game (& all acheivements) in under 5 hours, I have no doubt I will return to it time and again to immerse myself in this beautiful world and to be swept up again in the grand adventure.
Anecdote: At one point my son started watching me play and initially he thought we were watching an animated show. I started narrating as if I was inside the brother's minds and he sat right down next to me for almost two hours, just as engaged by watching the experience as I was playing it.
You owe it to yourself to check out this game. Don't be discouraged by the ~4 hour length. This is 4 hours dense with adventure, wonder, delight, and surprise.

This is an Ikaruga-like vert-scolling shmup.  You can absorb bullets depending on what color your ship is curretly flipped to.    However Sky Mercs also adds in a bit of class/ship progression, by allowing you to replay missions at different difficulty levels for credits.  You can then purchase ship upgrades.  Your pilot also levels up (5 levels total) and you get to choose a skill at each new level.  Overall the skills and ship upgrades passively make your ship better.  This lets you do better and get further in the missions.  This kind of system is a bit of a deviation from standard shmups that rely a lot more on pure player skill and bullet dodging.
Some things to note:  The game is marginally buggy and still suffers from infrequent crashes, generally this only happens right when I'm launching a mission, and the missions are short enough that it doesn't bother me too much.
Sky Mercs just becomes a grind-fest for levels/credits once you finish the main levels as there are many more ship levels and items to unlock than the game provides progression for.
You can play with the mouse or keys, but the mouse is ideal as it provides instant-movement to wherever the cursor is on the screen.
It's hard to tell what enemies are vulnerable to, and how to dispatch them quickly.  Sometimes, lack of enemy appearance makes it impossible to chain multiplier bonus due to poor level design.
End result: If you like vert-scrolling shmups you might find this enjoyable for a few hours.  Otherwise, if you're new to the genre or want something more polished, I'd suggest sticking with classics like Ikaruga and Raiden.

This is a very fun shmup game, that is good for just about anyone interested in the genre -- from people just giving the genre a try to hardened veterans.
People have made the argument that the game is generic, and for that reason passable.  I disagree, and will explain why.  First off, it would largely be a generic shmup if not for the polarization / bullet-absorption mechanic a la "Ikaruga" or the latter "eXceed" games.  It's well-implemented here, for a fun and satisfying level of challenge -- and the 'Overloads' take the mechanic to its (super fun) logical conclusion IMO.
Additionally, the music is absolutely fantastic.  With a nearly album-length soundtrack of original compositions made specifically for THIS game, it sets the mood perfectly and is absolutely perfect for getting into that "Matrix zone" trance and blast some motherf*ckers!!  It's a nice electronic soundtrack that reminds me of classic arcade shmups but with a kind of dubsteppy feeling (but without its by-the-numbers drops, and nothing obnoxious or distracting).  A HUGE thing, just added in one of the most recent updates, is Steam Workshop functionality -- you can make and d/l levels for the game, meaning ENDLESS replayability.  The RPG elements also add a lot of value, and customization to the game -- instead of purely collecting coins for score, you are able to use them for a number of upgrade systems.  NO, it's NOT an RPG... but they said "elements"!  There's a difference.  Lastly, the developers have been GREAT so far -- diligently listening to, working with, and participating in the community; even releasing same-day hot-fixes for the problems we report!
That brings me to my next point.  Almost every issue people have brought up in the negative reviews has been addressed by the dev team.  This game is great fun, and is getting consistently better.  In an environment where LOTS of games get released horribly broken, you can't really fault a small independent team for having some problems at release.  But..  I really have a lot of faith that one day this game will be VERY close to "perfect".

I bought a copy of this for my 5 year old who was getting bored of his current collection of games.  This is a great title for kids who already play stuff like Minecraft and Lego Worlds.   After helping him play a bit, I ended up getting a copy for my 8 year old and myself.   This game bridges many gaps - from Minecraft to Torchlight to Zelda.   It even reminds me a bit of Fable in it's simplicity, combat, and mystical feeling to it.
It's a fairly seamless game with an easy building system, great day/night cycle and colorful art style and quick setup for multiplayer games either on the LAN or from Friends on steam.  It's a fairly kids safe game and easy enough for my 5 year old to explore and level up in, but has some more complex tasks that leave me and my 8 year old "grinding".
The game is not without issues, but it is an early access game.   Audio cuts out sometimes, and I've had some CTD's on the client.   I don't see a server option, so if the client that's acting as a server dies, the rest of the party goes with it.  Luckily it autosaves and you can restart in the world you were last in fairly quick.   But the CTD's and Audio cut outs need to be fixed.
The other instance where the game's early access moniker is apparent is in the disparate stories.  Character interaction is way better than something then Minecraft, but still fairly limited and the "quests" need some improvement in scripting and direction.   But, you can tell they have a great, great base to work on, and this is a game that can grow into something very special over the years.
Microsoft/Mojang could really learn a thing or two from this.  I think most parents fume over the expensive "paint jobs" that Microsoft offers with limited functionality improvements.  So much so that I took the windows 10 editions of Minecraft off my kids computers and installed The Forge with some great mods.   But here is a game that's taking the block building systems and not just adding to it, but redefining it.   Great job - look forward to seeing my kids grow up with a game like this.

This game is really good for an early access game. But you know like every other early access game they could use some improvement... here's a little list of thing I really want to see in the future.
- improvement to the classes: we currently have 3 classes mage, melee and ranged. I think a healer would be cool... but then if you're solo what would be the point then? Well maybe it would be awesome if we had some more pets and that those pets actually had a health bar and could help you with fighting... if they die they would have like a 1 minute cooldown before respawning again.
- NPC improvement: We can find some npcs doing their own stuff on some islands... I've seen some people build amazing looking towns and it would be great if random npcs could move in a house you made. further npcs just stand still and do nothing really... I think that npcs should have a free movement is safe areas and for the guard/hunter nps, they should attack enemies close to them.
- Enemies : Enemies are pretty cool but when I'm in a dungeon there is not really a challenge... maybe a mini boss could spice everything up in dungeons and they could drop some unqiue stuff.
- Weapons: instead of crafting all your weapons it would be cool if there is a low chance to get weapons or other rare drops from enemies or mini bosses. I would like it too if you could also "customize"your gear a bit more by allowing to chance collors on weapons. And why can't a melee class not use a dagger at full power?

Okay so I've beaten this game with the warrior so I think I am qualified to give this a review.
This game plays just like it sounds, Minecraft with better combat and more RPG elements, like attributes and classes. The 3 classes are archer, warrior and mage. I can't say much about archer and mage as I haven't played them much, I will update this review when I have. The warrior is okay, but not particularly spectacular. The shouts in particular felt really lack luster. 505, give warrior some interesting shouts. Make one of them a fear or something. The weapon triangle was cool, but I would have liked more elemental weapons so I could counter enemies' elements. Giving each weapon type a special strength was a good move though, and I would like to see more types added to the game. Maybe remove the lv 2 talents and remove them, as it felt like they were more of a hassle to change when I changed weapon types rather than actually adding anything to the game. Armor felt like there was one good choice each time, but maybe that was only me. Overall though, a very fun game, all of these problems felt fairly minor in comparison to the game as a whole.
The worlds felt varied and interesting. Water felt more like a hinderance than a feature, but it was easy enough to mine through the ground and have it all drain out to into the nether. On a side note, I'm fairly sure a good 3+ hours was just me trying to drain all the water. I kind of want a version of this game where everything is underwater and you have to drain it all. But, I digress. I will say that many of the lunar levels gave my video card a work out, dropping it to 20 or less frames until I turned down the settings. And my GPU isn't weak, the game just needs to optimize better.
I will say the game felt sort of grindy with making armor and such, especially towards the end. 20 titanium for one bar felt excessive, especially when I needed like 40 bars to finish all the stuff I wanted to. Dropping that to around 15 would have made it felt like I was really working towards it without feeling excessive.
Dispite all the bad things I say about the game, I didn't have much of a problem with the rest of the game and there is a lot of content here. Easily 30+ hours per class.

As of now I've only played 20mins of this game but I do plan on playing more.  To my understanding this game was made by a very small group at Rooster Teeth (last i heard it was about 4 people), also this is the company's first video game ever.  For a first time game it runs a bit better than expected.  The graphics look great and the controls are fairly straight foward on a plug in controller (I perfer not to use the mouse and keyboard).  The sound, voice acting, and music are great.  To my understanding this game uses the concept of Dynasty Warriors, fighting large groups of enemies with the occasional boss fight, in a smallish map area.  But there are some problems I've encountered.  It is difficult to maintain the camera angle with the character flying all over the screen rapidly switching from one target to the next.  There are two combo buttons that can be used to fight enemies, short range melee and long range projectile, that can be pushed in a sequence that damages the enemies in different and creative ways.  While using these combos it is difficult to tell if you actually did the combo with the speed the characters are fighting and flying around hitting every single enemy.
To me it seems like a solid start to this game but it does need some big improvments.  My thought would be to get rid of auto-targeting and allow the player to control which enemy he/she wants to target (maybe a specific button to lock on to a single enemy) and when not in lock on mode the just attack the direction the character is facing.  Slow down the speed of combat slightly so the player can actually see how the character attacks and the enemies attack and recieve damage.  Also maybe if possible include a sprint button that maybe has a conjoined attack of sorts?
I like the game so far and would reccomend it for anyone that is a fan of the show it's based on at this point.

Sky Mercenaries is a sh-mup that has an interesting play mechanism: polarity / color. Otherwise, it's a fast-paced sh-mup like Raptor where enemies comes from left, right, but mostly up/front.
Your fighter can swap between 'red mode' and 'blue mode'. In red mode, you absorb red bullets and gets damage by blue bullets, and vice versa. Obviously you have to switch based on your tactical situation: sky too crowded? Switch colors to absorb the shot. Remember though, enemy will adapt with you. You can be accompanied by up to 4 drones and depending on which powerup you nabbed you can be joined by wingmen and more. As you fly through debris of enemies you pick up dropped "coins" and whatnot which you can spend on upgrades.
One thing that sets this game apart somewhat is location-based damage, as the ship can take damage in 4 different locations, and the drones have their own individual life meter.
There are three different fighters, with different default strengths (heavy defense, heavy offence, average). There are over a dozen upgrade options, and three pilots each with different skill tree (there are only 5 skills each though). One pilot is mostly offense, one's mostly defense, and one's a drone expert.
Game itself is simple. Fight your way through various planets and moons against baddies, enough said. If you finish a particular world (3 levels), you get to play "escape stage" where you are running away from a boss and you use your rear guns against it and the missiles it shoots at you, and if you get away you get a lot of bonus bucks you can use for upgrades.
The sh-mup is an very old genre, and the "polarity" system had been done before, but the skill tree, pilot, fighter, and upgradeable parts makes the game seem rather fresh. other than the game looks a "little" low-res on a 1680x1050 screen, I see no downside to this game. Sound is average with a proper adrenaline sound-track.
Worth a try if you like the genre.  But read the manual before you start. There is no help within the game that explains the color system.

Sadly windowed mode will simply use the same resolution, windowed. There doesn't appear to be an option for it so I have to disable Surround to play.
Still, for the  current sale price (-75%) I can recommend it for fans of the genre. It falls short of living up to the full €10 though.

NRS fighting games are easy to recommend, especially to newcomers to the format. Meanwhile, the story modes in NRS games are head-and-shoulders above any others in the genre.  I know many people who buy these games specifically for the story, no consideration for the competitive and online communities.
And yet, with all the praise I have for NRS, I can never, ever recommend purchasing MKX on Steam.  The game is a mess of a port, updates for the PC version are weeks behind console versions, every patch is over 10 GB and tends to make things worse rather than better.  As someone with not great internet, having to download a 16 GB patch on a regular basis in order to play online is infuriatingly unrealistic.  I want to play the game I purchased, not be continuously downloading updates which only break the game further.
I love NRS games, but I will never purchase another one as long as the PC versions are passed off to the lowest bidder.

Updating my review completely- I've had this since it got released, been repeatedly coming back to it overtime, and it's just got better and better (still miss the old character shader though).
For anyone who still hasn't got this yet, RWBY:GE is a 1-4 player beat'm up based on RoosterTeeth's original animated series RWBY. You play as one of four young Huntresses (and main characters from the show)- Ruby, Weiss, Blake and Yang- as you are assigned to defeat armies of dark beasts known as Grimm. The game has 10 levels in its campaign, which can be played solo OR co-operatively with up to 3 other players, and a 'horde mode' has been announced for the immediate future.
Pros:
1- Simple Hack n' Slash mechanics, easy to pick up and not too hard to master. Controls are even simpler (so long as you use a controller/gamepad).
2- Beautiful art-style, even with the current [controversial] character shader (and I am not joking, majority of people were P****D when that was implimented).
3- The developers, RoosterTeeth Games, are very involved with the community behind this game- as most RT families are with their audiences. If there is a problem, you can guarantee they will fix it (eventually).
4- A lot of content is already announced to flesh out the game further- including the previously mentioned Horde Mode and new characters to play as (namely, the members of Team JNPR from the show).
5- Runs smooth as butter, most of the time- so long as your internet doesn't keep kicking you out of online games every 5 minutes while you're also in a Skype call (so not bitter). I'm running a basic rig with an i7-4790 CPU and a GTX960 GPU from Feburary last year [plus Win10], and it runs at 60fps with no issues. If you have anything newer, you should have no trouble at all.
Cons:
1- Keyboard controls are hard to get used to. This game was clearly designed with gamepads in mind, and that may turn away some people.
2- Content is admittedly lacking, especially for the asking price of nearly £19/$25. It's understandable, since it's the developers first game [of this scope], but some may want to wait for a sale or after more content becomes available.
3- Some people on older machines have reported some issues running the game, but most of these have been phased out during the E.A. period. If you've got a machine older than 2 years old, it'd be best to check your specifications before buying this game.
Verdict: 8-10. A must-have for any RWBY fan, and definitely something for most gamers to look into. Would slaughter Grimm as an almost-loli with a Sniper-Scythe again.

If gaming needed a game to showcase to the world that it's as good as any other story-telling medium, it's Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons.
This is a singleplayer co-op game. Yes. A singleplayer co-op game, where you control two characters, the brothers, at the same time on screen, preferably with two control sticks. This game, at least for me, needs you to play with a controller to take full advantage of it. The keyboard controls are not that good.
That being said, the game is always throwing you new mechanics at you and gets rid of them as soon as they fulfill their purpose, this makes for a compelling and never tedious gameplay experience. Each puzzle and platforming section is never the same.
This game may be short, but for good reason. It's a game that is better played in one sitting. It can be completed in 2 hours and a half or 3 hours, so it's not that much longer than your average movie. The game tells a story about two brothers on a journey to find the life water that'll cure they're widowed father from a fatal disease. Anything else would be spoiling the story so I highly suggest playing it on your own.
This game is a prime example of how to tell a story through gameplay mechanics and it does so, extremely effectively! Me, being a brother, really connected to the story and the story may be sad at times, but it's very well told and does what games should do in the first place: transmit emotion through gameplay, not just through story.
This game isn't quite a game... It's not that hard. But it's highly innovative both in terms of gameplay and storytelling. This game is an experience. Highly recommend it.

Bought this game as a long time fan of the genre. The RPG elements seemed cool to me and the Ikaruga-like color swapping held some appeal as well.
But the game is not good. Technically it runs alright but I encountered bugs with it not displaying an icon on my taskbar. The UI is lifeless, the music is horrible (really poor quality on the menus and ingame) and doesn't feel inspired or interesting in any way, the ship customization+player customization+drone customization is done very badly. You don't get any real description of what anything does, and the little bars that gauge offense and defense don't make sense. On the ship selection screen they work one way and on the drone upgrade screen they work in the opposite way.
The levels are typical for a SCHMUP but your ship+drones take up a ton of the screen. It is really hard to avoid getting hit (which makes the Ikaruga-like color swapping mechanic useful) and things just feel really... unpolished. I think it is safe to say that the whole product feels and plays like a mobile port.
Hopefully this sees some major patching but as-is it is not really worth a purchase at 9.99. if you get this 90% off you might feel like you got what you paid for but at full price it feels like a rip-off. Especially since some of the best games on Steam are cheaper (Binding of Isaac, for example).

If you have another friend with the game, or you can convince one to pick it up, 1v1 matches in this game are tense as ♥♥♥♥. There's nothing more unnerving than a sniper duel, and Sniper Elite is one of the best ways to experience that. If you're looking for a fun game to play with a friend where you can scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of each other from 300 feet away, this is it. The sniper duel experience alone is worth the price if you can get it on sale.
Pick up some weapon packs too, because finding rifle modifications in the field is a chore that weapon packs allow you to ignore entirely.

Second and more conerning is the DLC in this game. First off the pre order bonuses are one time use. Once you use them on one save they can not be used again. I'm talking about equipment like the special pistol and assult rifle. The cosmetic stuff can be used in as many saves as you want. This is just a cheap and sleezy move on the part of Square Equinx and it sets a bad example for other publishers. I really don't want to see that kind of crap in more games.
There is also basically a paid item shop where you can buy one time use equipment. I don't see any reason why you would HAVE to use it but it really should not be there in a $60 single player game.
I need to do some more research but I saw a post on reddit saying that there are two aguments that can only be obtained by purchasing them for real money. If that is truly the case then that REALLY bad. Shame on you Square.
All of these problems except the mouse issue are the fault of the publisher, the devs even made a post basically admiting that the DLC decisions above were forced on the by "first part limitations" aka Square making those decisions.
