It's been too long that we've run into a game that truely pulls on all our heart strings at the same time. Every now and then we're treated to a real gem in gaming history that leaves a little tender burn in our hearts that just.. feels so good. We can all be proud that sometimes games can tell a story better than movies or novels. I know I do. Get ready for something like nothing you've ever played, but even more so an experience you'll be glad you were a part of.
"Brothers: A tale of two brothers" hits home on more levels than you thought you even had. The ones underneath your FEELS sector that you almost forgot about. The story is amazingly well told without ever speaking a word. It's built so solidly, that even the deaf will shed a tear. I know I had a hard time holding back the tears at the trajedy and sufferings that these brothers had to endure in order to save their father, a man struck by a mysterious illness.
That being said, the game itself is not without flaws. You'll find it very difficult to manage controlling two characters at the same time, and often have one running into a wall because of a lose of coordination. Keeping one brother controlled from the left joystick and the other with the right takes a bit of practice, but not impossible and can feel a bit rewarding when you get the hang of it. You'll do well to take your time when navigating certain areas that require you to have really honed both sides of your brain, or you'll be falling to your death too often.
Battles are understandably missing. The focus was clearly on playing a game differently and like nothing you've ever done before. It's still a little disappointing that conflicts and enemies were too far inbetween. Fights aren't as much as a fight, as they are actually intense puzzles to solve. Fun puzzles to solve, but still just another puzzle.
Don't miss this game. Even though it has it's flaws, the story more than makes up everything else. It carries you throughout the game. It's only too bad it wasn't a little longer.

I'll preface this review with a quick warning: I would not necessarily recommend The Fractured But Whole to someone who is not a fan of South Park. I feel like a lot of my enjoyment of the games main story came from my familiarity with certain characters from the show, and I don't know if it would be nearly as funny or generally entertaining without that previous knowledge. Beyond that, this game is extremely South Park. So, if you generally don't like the show's humor or haven't liked recent seasons, you're probably not going to like the game.
I'm mostly writing a review because this game has been getting a lot of negative reviews since it came out. So much so that I almost didn't buy it myself. While some of the criticisms are justified, most of the negativity seems unwarranted. A lot of the non-recommendation reviews seem to be focused on the price, uplay, and the length of the game. Uplay is an annoyance but can always be uninstalled later. If paying $60 for 20+ hours of gameplay bothers you, then wait for a sale. Neither of these things affect the game itself.
The story was great. Personally, I found it to be hilarious with a couple surprisingly emotional moments which is all I can ever ask from South Park. A lot of reviews complain about the ending, but I thought that the third act was leagues above Stick of Truth. I don't remember the first game making me laugh nearly as much. It was probably the most South Park ending possible, which is perhaps part of the reason so many people seemed to dislike it. It ends like an episode of the show, not an epic video game.  I stand by my statement at the start of this review: if you don't like the show, you're not going to like the game.
One thing that I will say is a step down from Stick of Truth is the gameplay. It's nothing special. Playing a second play through on mastermind doesn't feel any harder than normal difficulty, and there was only really one fight that I found challenging. That being said, I love the battle banter that goes on in all the fights. The unique mechanics for bosses were a nice change of pace and kept them feeling tedious. Buddy abilities, however, do start to feel tedious. There are too many steps to summoning a buddy, and by the end of the game, when you have to use multiple different buddy abilities in a row to solve a single puzzle, it starts to get a little annoying. None of this ruined my overall game experience, though. Minor annoyances stayed minor annoyances.
Lastly, the game can be pretty buggy. I personally encountered two potentially game breaking bugs, one of which I was only able to fix by switching to another computer temporary which is not a viable option for most people. Other than that I had a few sound effect issues, a couple slightly broken cutscenes, and characters freezing up in combat once in a while. If you're concerned it might be better to wait and see if things get patched up.
TDLR; It's a good game. If you like South Park, you'll enjoy it. Gameplay wise, it's not quite as good as Stick of Truth, but I thought the story was a lot funnier and generally more entertaining. There are a still quite a few bugs, so watch out. Overall, would recommend to fans of the show.

Super Crate Box: Game of the Year, sorry, CENTURY
Super Crate Box a long awaited open world  third-person shooter/platformer, met not only what we were hoping for but gave us more than anyone could ever imagine. Super Crate Box sends us to another dimension in a world of only a few pixels (however the game still looks awesome) where you can fight aliens of all different kinds; big green, small green, angry little red ones etc. aliens kill you in one touch, so you the survivor has to gather guns with unlimited ammo that are supplied in crates to kill off these wretched creatures. You start off with a dead on ordinary pistol to then find loads of other random weapons in the crates, these include but are not limited to: the minigun, dual pistols, machine gun, laser gun, etc. At the bottom of the platforms there is a hole with some fire in it -for no apparent reason, if the monsters fall into the fire it turns them angry and they travel much faster making it a harder time for you.
Not only has the creator's given us so much already, but they provide us as well with not 1, not 2 but 3 maps to play in, each one getting harder as you unlock them.
Super Crate Box also gives us a range of characters to play as and to unlock as you get a higher score. For each map you get normal level or SFMT level, normal is obviously average and SFMT is… absolute carnage.
And last but not least the leveling up is spectacular, you would think that how many aliens you kill provide you points however it is actually how many crates you collect, you can tell the developers were really thinking out of the box this time. Players of SCB have reached miraculous scores, you can see their scores at
.
Despite the lack of textures in some places of the map Super Crate Box has well earned its place in in the hall of AWESOME games. I have 32 hours on the game now and I am looking forward to spending many more.

The best 3D fighting game on PC right now, and it will be for a long time.
The game runs fantastically and is very well optimized. You might want to deactivate the chromatic abberation and the film grain in the game's files.
Netcode works great and is more lenient concerning lag, the fastest moves in this game have a 10f startup so 1 or 2 more frame delay than usual isn't a big deal.
Offline content is okay, story mode lasts about 2hours + episodes which consist of one fight with a short cinematic for every character. You can earn gold in treasure battle which you can spend in the customisation shop.  However future characters won't be purchasable with in game money I think.
Of course you have the VS mode, and arcade mode.
Concerning the gameplay it can be a little overwhelming at first but once you understand the purpose of each type of attacks it all makes sense and it becomes very easy to remember the 100+ attacks per character.
But don't worry, Tekken 7 is more welcoming for new players with the new Rage system as a comeback mechanic; every character has a Rage Art, a kind of super attack that deals a devastating amount of damage but you need to have a low life. These moves are usually unsafe so use it with caution.
Rage Drive are somewhat similar and are strong attacks that deal more damage and increase juggle options.
Teching throw is also easier, in the previous installments you had to guess which button to use to tech but now you can do it with X or Y. Throws aren't the core of the gameplay so it doesn't really matter.
The only real complaint I have with the game is the lack of tutorial or trial/combo mode. In the story mode you have a few pop ups that explains briefly how to move and that A is left kick and B right kick etc but that's pretty much it.
Oh, and you can't move the camera in the customization menu if you play with an arcade stick.
Also, no rematch option in lobbies but we can expect it to be added soon, seeing how they reacted with the patch for the ps4.
It's my first TEKKEN, and I really appreciate it.

It's been 10 Years since Tekken 6 came out , Tekken Tag Tournament 2 has been released 6 Years ago.
And after waiting for that many years for a fighting game that stays true to it's Players we got Tekken 7 in 2017 on PC.
The Reason why this game for me personally is a pretty big deal is simple , i have been disappointed by many developers in the last few years that pushed out games that simply weren't worth playing or developed into a completely different direction over the course of developement.
The Tekken series has always been a rewarding experience once you took your time and learned the game , there are still the same mechanics from the Older Games of the series combined with new ones . There are New Characters that feel very Refreshing to play and just loads of fun to learn.
For me it has always been a fascinating experience to play Fighting games , where it doesn't really matter against what Character you're playing but with more depth in how your Opponent is playing. What kind of knowledge he has about the matchup , how good his execution is and how good his reactions are.
Tekken has always had what many games by now lost , Rewarding you for spending time in it. There is no easy way in this one , it's training mode , it's practicing the combos up and down and just getting stuck in Vortex of trying out new stuff for hours on hours with so many factors coming into play in an actual match where you can tell that a player knows what he's doing and can adapt and execute split second decisions perfectly through putting effort in the game.
I gotta be totally honest i was skeptic about this game , we've been here on PC and we got MK:X which was a flop.
We got Street Fighter V which just took all the veterans and slapped em in the face by catering to the Casuals.
But Tekken 7 has what i always loved about Tekken and has managed to improve all that without making the Veterans of the game unhappy.
We got a Game that runs perfectly on low-mid end hardware that's also The only Unreal Engine 4 game at this Point that is well polished (which is really hard to be honest . GJ NAMCO.)
The Old Characters that we loved , redefined by different Visuals and new moves in addition to the old ones.
The new Characters which just had me curious in trying them out since as Good of a game as TTT2 was it was just the Tekken 6 cast present.
Fantastic Visuals and Animations throughout the entire Game.
Great loading times and Superb Netcode in a fighting game!.
Pretty Good soundtrack , i only truly hate 1 song( you guys prolly know which one) and the fact that there's no Jukebox on PC is also pretty sad but not a dealbreaker.
Overall i gotta say that this is the best Fighting Game i've played in ages , it is a ton of fun to play , it has alot of depth to it and it doesn't cater to the Casuals.
What i mean by that is that there's nothing wrong with getting this game when you're new to Fighting Games or just Tekken and simply don't have that much time to Invest into a Video Game , you'll still have a blast playing it and there's nothing wrong with that aslong as you can get over the fact that you're going to get bodied at the start and that success in this Series requires commitment , motivation , proper inputs and reactions. (a Wired Connection with atleast 20mb/s Also helps)
The Game has a wide learningcurve and doesn't gimp the Experience of anyone who spent thousands of hours already in it's Predecessors , the Game has everything I loved it for and has managed to improve in all Aspects and with that many Fighting Games which just come with Rootkits or Absolute Garbage Netcode it is truly Amazing to see this Game perform that well on it's first time on PC.
Don't be biased by the PS4 version , the PC version is better in my eyes than the PS4 version in any regard.
Faster Loading Times.
Better Visuals.
Ability to customize settings as you please.
Exponentially less Wifi players.
Great Netcode (i do not know for sure if ps4's is actually worse i've just heard.)
You do not have to Pay for PS4 plus if you wanna play online by playing on PC.
This is also the only fighting game where i'm almost certain that the PC version will live for a long time simply due to it's almost Perfect execution.
To finish this . I Absolutely recommend this game to literally anyone that wants to get into a fighting game or even diehard players that want to have more.
This Game has it all and if i had more time i'd sink in as much as i did into T3/4/5/6 & TTT2.

I would love to rate this game higher, but I am affraid I can not. The question of course is why, because the game certainly does have several things that speak for it.
Brutal Legend is a game filled with humor that is akin to main man's introduction cult movie; The Pick of Destiny. Personally, I enjoy it for in the game it is not constantly bombarded at you if you are just cruising in the Druid Plow (that is your car), but fills the conversations with a light air that is certainly good for a laugh. If you are cruising Metal music (of different genres of metal) greets your ears. Something I enjoy and in fact made me appreciate some artists better, but certainly not for everyone. Okay so that gives it a rather niche public, but that doesn't make it bad does it? No, it doesn't.
However, the game also has real time combat and does so in a the old Warcraft/Starcraft format, but has the view not topdown but on you as well as you are a important player. With no pause function, bad overview, the fact that you need to fight as well as command constantly -  because the AI is just horrible - makes it stressful. A shrill constrast to the rest. Now a friend of mine has it and does well enough. The difference, a controller. I have mouse and keyboard and the controls are such .... finicky, that on a dial I can not even select the unit above or below it because it either won't move or will go down 2 in an instance. The solos you need to perform to boost you army also require key combinations which also go wrong at times due to this. No problem outside combat but in it... The problem is that this game is fun, looks nicely, has good humor, but was not properly developed for combat with mouse and keyboard.
Thus, the game has its niche in which it does well. However, if you do not like this niche or do not own a controller, I would say it is not worth the frustation of the combat and quirky controls (even with remapping!) - because that is the opposite of what the game is intended to be and would be a dissappointment over an otherwise well intended and decently executed (mainly music, humor and graphic wise) game.

Puzzle games vary in quality a lot, that's a given, but Alexia Crow is near the bottom of the heap.
is much better than this, and it's over twenty years old.
The number one reason why you shouldn't buy Alexia Crow, realistically, is that it has been released on several websites for free (legitimate sites, not pirate sites,) so there's no good reason to pay for it unless you really want to support the devs (or are desperate for Steam Achievements and Trading Cards.)
Beyond that, the game has several glaring flaws; the voice acting is poor and the writing (or translation, more likely) is terrible.  The story is incoherent.  The puzzles tend to the sort where figuring out
you're being asked to do is frequently harder than actually doing it.  The interface is annoying for many reasons, most notably because it uses tight target zones, but changes the mouse pointer to the object you're using, with no indication of the active point; if you use pointer icons without a clear active point, you need liberal target zones to make up for it.  A late-game puzzle involving a maze revealed only in fragments was particularly frustrating because confusion over the active point and general glitchiness caused my icon to get repeatedly stuck in walls.
Alexia Crow isn't all bad.  The art is very nice, and some of the puzzles were quite fun.  On the whole, though, this is a notably substandard puzzle game, and you can easily find much better ones.

I'll preface this review with a quick warning: I would not necessarily recommend The Fractured But Whole to someone who is not a fan of South Park. I feel like a lot of my enjoyment of the games main story came from my familiarity with certain characters from the show, and I don't know if it would be nearly as funny or generally entertaining without that previous knowledge. Beyond that, this game is extremely South Park. So, if you generally don't like the show's humor or haven't liked recent seasons, you're probably not going to like the game.
I'm mostly writing a review because this game has been getting a lot of negative reviews since it came out. So much so that I almost didn't buy it myself. While some of the criticisms are justified, most of the negativity seems unwarranted. A lot of the non-recommendation reviews seem to be focused on the price, uplay, and the length of the game. Uplay is an annoyance but can always be uninstalled later. If paying $60 for 20+ hours of gameplay bothers you, then wait for a sale. Neither of these things affect the game itself.
The story was great. Personally, I found it to be hilarious with a couple surprisingly emotional moments which is all I can ever ask from South Park. A lot of reviews complain about the ending, but I thought that the third act was leagues above Stick of Truth. I don't remember the first game making me laugh nearly as much. It was probably the most South Park ending possible, which is perhaps part of the reason so many people seemed to dislike it. It ends like an episode of the show, not an epic video game.  I stand by my statement at the start of this review: if you don't like the show, you're not going to like the game.
One thing that I will say is a step down from Stick of Truth is the gameplay. It's nothing special. Playing a second play through on mastermind doesn't feel any harder than normal difficulty, and there was only really one fight that I found challenging. That being said, I love the battle banter that goes on in all the fights. The unique mechanics for bosses were a nice change of pace and kept them feeling tedious. Buddy abilities, however, do start to feel tedious. There are too many steps to summoning a buddy, and by the end of the game, when you have to use multiple different buddy abilities in a row to solve a single puzzle, it starts to get a little annoying. None of this ruined my overall game experience, though. Minor annoyances stayed minor annoyances.
Lastly, the game can be pretty buggy. I personally encountered two potentially game breaking bugs, one of which I was only able to fix by switching to another computer temporary which is not a viable option for most people. Other than that I had a few sound effect issues, a couple slightly broken cutscenes, and characters freezing up in combat once in a while. If you're concerned it might be better to wait and see if things get patched up.
TDLR; It's a good game. If you like South Park, you'll enjoy it. Gameplay wise, it's not quite as good as Stick of Truth, but I thought the story was a lot funnier and generally more entertaining. There are a still quite a few bugs, so watch out. Overall, would recommend to fans of the show.

I've played a stupid amount of this game for an early access title.  This may not be a comprehensive guide, but it's long enough that I feel like it will give people a realistic glimpse into what to expect.
Things that rock about this game:
*  Large universe is LARGE.  The home island that I have customized the most seems small at first Glance.  I've been carving out huge swaths to make new buildings, dungeons, gardens, and landscaping projects as time goes on, yet an aeriel view on the smallest looking Island reveals I've still barely scratched the surface - and that's saying nothing about the vast caverns beneath.
*  Events.  There are some fun and interesting events.  The great part is resources.  Some of the rarest Items in the game come from these events, and certainly the most interesting monsters.
*  Soundtrack.  It's not my first choice in music style.  The compositions are solid throughout, and the clarity is top notch.  There is no 8-bit feel here - the instruments could (and might be, for all I know) real.
*  Pets.  The basic pets can be cool.  The rare pets are fantastic!  There is something satisfying about having a baby boss follow me around.  Cats, mice, owls, a panda, dragons (though I've only seen one), and a mini end boss adds a certain flair I find pleasing.
*  Blocks.  I've never played minecraft so perhaps I am not the best choice to comment on this, but there are some beautiful and interesting blocks in this game.  Carpets, intricate carved hard stones, shiny gem blocks, several shades of concrete, and various stone and wood blocks are sweet.  The _real_ cool ones are the neon and meteorite blocks.  Some are lit but cast no light, others are so bright a few too many in a room is blinding.
*  Co-op.  You can solo online or off, but the real fun when it comes to combat is with friends.  Multiplayer combat is fun to play around with, and effective.
*  Graphics. it's cartoonish, but it's all smooth and polished looking.  Curves aren't much of a reality in a box-block game, but none of the graphics are pixelated or jagged.  Edges are sharp.  Colors are vivid.
*  Lighting options.  Braziers, torches, chinese lanterns, candycane striped fixtures, colored lamps, Star lanterns, chandelier style fixtures, and some blocks make for some fun and interesting lighting patterns.
*  Statues.  Knights, gargoyles, lions, dragons, golden eggs, toads and giant alligator demigods give the option of some truly unique decoration styles.
*  Planting and gardening.  Putting aside the counterpoint to this I'm putting below, it's sweet to not have to judge lighting conditions, water, soil types, or much of anything - plant a seed and it grows!  Underwater gardens and floating forests are possible and beautiful once finished.
*  Character models.  So many options!  Better yet, they aren't restrictive in the least.  Just to test I put together a female character with a vibrant green pixie cut, bone ear necklace, monster eyes and a goatee.  It may not be a huge sell to many, but I ADORE the ability to customize any character as I like with all options in the game.  This is one of the few that truly does.
*  Vanity Items - Care for a monocle to go with your bumblebee wings and fluffy bunny pants?  Perhaps some jester/harlequin pants and shoes to Liven up your formal Mandarin robes?  Some Devil horns to make sure your enemies know you mean no good?  There are **way** more items than are displayed in the wiki page.  The best part is you don't have to give up armor bonuses!  Wear your armor and look like a million bucks at the same time!
Things that are not so awesome:
*  No access to water blocks.  You can craft water bombs to make pools, but the option for a player to use an item capable of creating such beauty is currently stripped from the game.  There is still fountains that generate with a world, but you can't collect them.  The water is **gorgeous**, and it's a shame that by and large we'll only ever see it during an event or in an underground cavern.
*  Enemies.  Each biome has it's own variants, but it feels like the same 10 monsters everywhere I go.  There are more than 10; but most of it is variations on slimes, skeletons, mummies, wraiths, turtles, and ogres.  There are a couple of really neat ones, like the merman and dogfish, that are truly rare.  For the most part once you've made it about 1/3 of the way through the game you've about seen them all outside of an event.
*  Event generation.  There are some creative and fun events that pop up, but whether by design or by accident it's been common for me to get the same event several days in a row.  There are some super cool trophies to get out of this but I'm about full on mummy and Bones trophies.
*  Combat mechanics.  I enjoy not having to read a tactics manual to do the combat.  The warrior is solid.  While the ranger and the mage are different, the execution of the attacks feels so similar t
*  Pet AI.  I know this is petty, but some of the coolest pets have a frustrating habit of blocking part of your view during combat in first person.  Doubly frustrating when it intereferes with building or causes you to walk off of an edge because it won't move away from a hole.
*  Difficulty scale.  It's a challenge at first.  To be fair, there is a balance through most of the game.  Once I got around level 27 that slipped, and once I hit 30 my choices were no challenge at all or a hard mode boss.  C'thiris kind of makes up for it, but one level isn't quite enough to recover from that.
*  biome restrictions on planting.  There are all sorts of cool flowers, trees, fruits and vegetables in this game.  A genuine plethora of colorst, shapes and textures.  I see all of these and imagine the gorgeous landscapes I could put together.  instead I plant a forest with perhaps three trees, two bushes, and and a couple veg.  I know it may not be the point of the game.  It is the part I most enjoy and a huge focus, however, so I don't feel like this is an unimportant complaint.
*  The lack of an ending.  This may end up being an obsolete complaint come release day.  At the moment you fight the end(?) boss, go to a portal at the end of the world, Aaaaaaand nothing.  No credits.  No congratulations.  Just a portal that doesn't activate or lead anywhere.  I suspect that part of the full release or an upcoming DLC will use this.  For the moment it is little more than a decoration and ambiguous sign of victory that isn't particularly satisfying.
*  Disappearing data.  I haven't had this happen in a few weeks, but I have lost three characters and two universes to...gremlins?  Elves?  I'll never know.  The error message that pops up and reads "data error" is accurate but uninformative.  It also was almost enough to ruin the game completely for me.  It did for a bit.  I now back up my files after every session, which is useful but leaves me with a kind of distrustful feeling.
The TL;DR

Pretty good, but needs improvement before I give it a wholehearted reccomendation.
Let's start with my biggest complaint: NO CHARACTER/CLASS SYNERGY! None whatsoever. CLass synergy is afantastic way to make multiplayer more fun for everyone, as it stands there is really no reason to play omline unmless it's with friends. Character/Class sybergy could go a long way towards making this game a bit less repetitive, which brings us nicely into my second complaint with the game: it gets repetitive quickly. You only have two regular attacks and three special attacks, and there are no combos in the game, turning what looks like a fun hack-and-slash into a repetitive button masher, where you spam regular attacks to recharge your special attack meter, rinse and repeat ad nauseum. ANd since all the characters start out with all of their special attacks unlocked, there is never any real sense of player progression, as all of the upgrades you get are either passive modifiers to the attack, or to the player character.
The game also lacks an offline mode for single player, so if you want to play solo, then you will need to create a private lobby and join the game with just you in in it. And finally, the RWBY stuff almost feels like window dressing. None of the characters handle all that differently, all of them feel the same, and the idea of each character in the show having a unique semblance isnt used AT ALL, which is a collosal missed opportunity to have the characters feel different from each other.
All that being said, there are a lot of good pinttts about this game as well. RT seems to undeerstand that "Early Access" doesn't mean &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥out an unfinished, buggy, broken game and charge twenty dollars US for it." The game is very well polished, and very stable, no crashes, no disconnects in the online, and aside from some issues with the character animations when moving over uneven terrain, no real technical issues to be found. And while I may have called the RWBY stuff "Window Dressing" a little bit ago, it is extremely beautiful window dressing. This game looks beautiful, and exactly the way a RWBY game shoulf look, the voice acting (recorded just fior this game) is top-notch, and the combat at least looks like something out of RWBY.
This game has so much potential, and I hope RT impliments some stuff to make it as good as we all know it can be. MAybe have us fight some neemies other than Grimm, maybe White Fang Members, or Roman Torchwick/Cinder's thugs. Maybe a stronger narrative in an offline campaign mode, and if RT is really feeling crazy, some kind of Loot System. That last one might be a bit too much to ask for, but there is an absoluitelty fantastic game here, trapped in a slightly-above-average game. We know that RT has immense talent, and that the original developer has nothing but love for RWBY, so I hopoe that this game gets more depth, because I would love to Power-Punch a Grimm as Yang so that Ruby can send it flying into the ari and sklice it in half. Or freeze and enemy as Weiss so another player can shatter it.

Something that I never thought I’d be bored of was watching German/Italian solders going all skeletal as a rifle round passed through some organ and broke various body parts.  Alas that’s really all this game gives you and after you see the same generic German and Italian WW2 solder do that for the 1,000th time I would say that it is an apt description of this title.
The game tries to portray realistic bullet behavior but some what fails because at the ranges that you are actually engaging people from there should be almost zero bullet drop.  Max range that I’ve seen across the entire campaign and 1 DLC mission was maybe 250 meters which for a WW2 era full power cartridge is nothing.  Accounting for windage and other conditions aside from basic gravity is ok but again because you’re actually shooting at targets much closer, the vast majority being within 100 meters you would not need that much compensation as this game tries to force you to take.  Even current small arms ballistics are not as bothered by environmental and range differences let alone some full power sniper load for a 30-06.  I’ve personally done some “long range”, out to 300 yards, shooting myself with a few firearms.  While I’m no expert at it I can honestly tell you that it was more me being unfamiliar with the weapon rather then the effects of the environment on the round at it went down range.  Again I have to reiterate that 300 yards is a range that you will not see for the vast majority of your play time within this title.
Gameplay wise it was surprisingly short, the base campaign was finished in about 10-14 hours and the DLC missions I estimate will not add more then maybe an hour or two total.  Keep in mind that I was pretty timid during my play time and did not rush a single mission so keep that in mind.  While I didn’t go back to every mission to get everything (simply because the missions are not worth revisiting and the game is repetitive) I did get a fair amount of all of the collectables on my first run.  That said a lot of the missions are pretty linier so there’s that aspect of them as well.
I wrote earlier that this game is very repetitive and after a while you quickly start to see the same thing pop up and quite frequently I might add.  The formula is as follows, scout, shoot a few solders, scout some more, possibly get caught and run away only to scout again.  Find some objectives then find some secondary objectives achieve those, mission over.  Oh did I mention in between all of those you need to relocate every 5 seconds?  That’s if there aren’t any conveniently placed sound sources for you to hide your shots behind… every minute or two that is.  The repetitive nature of this title extends into killing solders as well, when you get a killing shot your camera follows the round exiting your muzzle in the same exact way every single time, using the same slow motion sound effect for the shot and following it all the way down to the target and as it hits the camera goes into an x-ray vision so that you can see what vital organs that you hit.  Well that’s all great and all and it would be cool if the game didn’t give you this same x-ray kill shot almost very.single.sniper.kill that you make.  It ends up making killing multiple targets in rapid succession almost impossible because the time that you could be aiming at the guy right next to the one that you just shot that guy is already out of your line of fire or is alerted by his friend dropping next to him.
Mostly because the AI has beyond super human hearing, they will hear you through a mountain I kid you not.  There is a particular level or rather one or two where there is a system of tunnels in a hill or mountain and if you run around inside of them you will arouse suspicion.. somehow.  I’m sorry but when someone is standing above someone with about 15-30 foot of rock and or bunker material between them I think that the game’s aspect of stealth is a bit ruined don’t you think?
On the subject of enemy variation, this is none, you get the same 5 or 6 models throughout the entire game with almost no variation in types.  On that you also fight against armored vehicles, because that’s what sniper rifles were designed for right?  Taking out Panzer 4s, armored cars, half tracks and TIGER tanks!  Fighting armor in this game is beyond the pale in terms of how “fun” or “enjoyable” it is, you literally have to either sneak up on it, get lucky and place 2 mines in the right spot OR get into a shooting fight with the thing and watch in shock as the tank’s turret follows your every movement.  Somehow in WW2 they have turrets that can track a human running a full sprint without any problem what so ever.  They also have ESP abilities so if you’re looking at the tank from behind they will see you, even when there are no view ports available.  Have fun sneaking up on armor that is all seeing and all knowing, really it’s either luck of mine placement or restart that checkpoint and place explosives where the tanks end up going because otherwise there’s no real way to deal with them for the most part that will not involve you getting spotted instantly and shot with insane precision and speed.

Graphically this game isn't going to blow you away, but I do have to hand it to the developers for giving every single puzzle a different look and feel to it. You will be faced with a music challenge, a pipe-dream like challenge, a numbers puzzle, and much more.
The up and down side of the game is its length, yes there are seven rooms to enter, and each one has its own unique look and puzzles, but if you put your mind to it you can conquer Alexia Crow and the Cave of Heroes in about 45 minutes. Now some of you out there will think that this isn't worth it, but I have to say that even with the shortness of the game, it had me hooked from start to finish.
I will say this about the puzzles, though, there are no instructions, you are basically thrown into each puzzle, and you're going to have to figure out how the puzzle works, or what the end game is. I don't know if this was done intentionally or not, and maybe this tactic inflates the gameplay a little bit because of the fact that there is a trial and error element to it, but in the end the puzzles were fun.
The way the game ends you have to think that there's a sequel, there has to be, there's no way that the game could end like it does, and if you want to know how the game ends, you're just going to have to play it for yourself. This game gets a 7.2 out of 10.

I went into this game after being very frustrated by aspects of Divinity 2. Kingdoms of Amalur turned out to be a far more satisfying experience, albeit in unexpected ways.
A major selling point is that it was written by R.A. Salvatore, one of my favourite authors. However, the game's story is very forgettable. I mean that literally - I've played 60 hours, am nearly at the end, and can barely remember anything that's happened. There is a great set piece battle and a few clever side quests, but the rest just blurs together - something something "fate", something something "mortal". There's few choices and little reason to even read the dialogue most of the time - just follow the quest markers and do what the pop-up text tells you to do.
What it really gets right is the gameplay. Combat is varied enough to keep things interesting, despite making up the bulk of the gameplay. Enemies flail around when set on fire, dodge arrows, resist some forms of damage and have some neat skills and spells. The player character can be built in several different ways , and the paths are distinct enough to encourage re-specing (which is quite easy to do). Controls are straightforward, although the camera can be bothersome at times.
The inability to jump, with the resulting unpassable ankle-high obstacles, is irritating at first, but moving around the world is simple enough through a generous fast-travel system, and there's plenty to do as you walk around.
There's no shortage of loot, both from enemy drops and in numerous chests and hidden locations. The inventory fills up annoyingly quickly, with no option to screen items by quality, but there's no shortage of merchants around.
The crafting system is great, allowing all sorts of equipment, potions and gems to be made.
The game loads quickly, and looks lovely even on a mid-range system.
There's certainly plenty of gameplay - expect 60 or more hours to complete most of the sidequests.
It's a shame the game will never be followed up, because there is an excellent core game here.

Very solid early access game. This is the way early access should be: the gameplay is solid, its just bits and bobs that are missing. I haven't played many hack-and-slashers, but this one is the most satisfying one I've played. A fitting tribute to Mony Oum. He always talked about how good fight choreography has rhythm. After a little while playing this game, you begin to feel the rhythm of it. The enemie's attack patterns have rhythm, and your own attack sequences have a defenite rhythm to them. The characters feel nuanced, each with their own attack patterns and specials. I've played the most with Blake, but each has their weaknesses. There are some things that would be nice to have, such as a way to quickly switch characters without leaving a game, but as I said, the gameplay is solid. Pretty menus and more characters can come later. The voic acting is very well done. It's the real voice actors doing it (Lindsay, Barbra, Kara, Arryn, ect.). My recommendation? Buy it, play it, have fun, and watch it get better.

I haven't been this drawn into a fighting game since my childhood days of playing Soul Calibur 2 and 3 almost non stop when I had them. Every other recent fighting game has me feeling tired and bored of it after an hour or so, even with friends. This game, on the otherhand, is so satisfying to play that even spending a few hours of solo play on Treasure Battle feels amazing. And even after playing a few hours by myself, I could easily jump in with my friends and spend a few more hours just playing match after match, each being immensely fun.
The team at Bamco that worked on this game clearly put a lot of love, work, and polish into it. The game runs as good as it looks and just oozes quality. There are some minor issues (spectating sync comes into mind), but hopefully they will be ironed out in future patches.
The story is also a bit lackluster (get ready to hear a boring reporter drag on about "a war going on", stabbing Jin with a screwdriver, and focusing on people's eyes too much), but hey, at least it actually has one on release (looking at you SFV...).
Definitely get this game at some point. If you love fighting games, I don't see any way that you'd be disappointed by it.

Pros:
- Runs slick.  I mean, it *should* run fine on a i7-6800k, but I can get it to run on my work laptop (A8-6410 with 1gb vram for r5) at a solid 60fps on medium.  A 4 year old laptop should not be able to even touch a game this new and pretty, but it does.
-  pretty!  I'm still unlocking treasure mode items, and I spend about 80% time playing, and the rest making new outfits.  Some of these are amazing!  Yoshimitsu has a color changing head, some of the custom character-specific outfits are outstanding in design and effects.  The hit effect animations get insane, especially some of the unlockables.  Animated auras, particle effect animations, the metallics... rich, detailed animations from start to finsh.
-  Fun!  I haven't played since Tekken 3.  It's a new game, and it's different enough to be a learning experience, but I could step back in and feel at home.  The treasure mode is like survival with rewards, and at ~750 matches in I don't see this getting old anytime soon.  They also added a "close call" animation.  Totally adds tension when it's down to the last shot or two and the hits are so close that time slows down and I get to see just how close my win (or loss) was.  The story mode isn't what I was hoping for, but is a challenge and interesting anyway.  Story mode, chapters, and treasure hunt combined make for a good tutorial mode to boot!
- Netcode.  Stick with a connection 4 bars and above and you might as well be playing on the same machine.  Bonus points for not having to hear opponents screaming about how cheap the combos are or how their controller is broken.  Tournaments are slick as well.
Cons:
- Training mode.  It's not *bad*.  It could have been much, much more though.  I've been spoiled by games like DOA and Soul Caliber which had a robust training mode.  It still has some of the standard training structure, but it could use some situational conditions.
-  Online play.  While the netcode appears to be fine, the dropped connections are a thing.  It seems to go in streaks, and when it does there is no match possible for an undefined period of time.  Tournaments have a strange tendency to be ghost towns and populated by about ~30% hosts who will kick players who start winning.  it's not a jab against the game itself, but it is still a pain to deal with.
-  Character editor.  Don't get me wrong, it's freaking amazing.  It's a bit buggy and non-sensical.  The camera has a tendency to randomly raise itself to max height.  you can still edit, but good luck seeing what you are doing until the game is restarted.  some of the options don't mix together in ways that make little sense.  On Josie, for example, I can put shades, a monkey, and a hat on her - or I can change her hair color.  Cool hair, or any of three different customization options.  It's a minor complaint but it's one I don't feel is going away.
The TL;DR:
It's gorgeous, fun, and one of the few games I've pre-ordered and had it live up to the hype.  If you like tekken, Namco fighters, or pretty action games in general BUY IT.

I would love to rate this game higher, but I am affraid I can not. The question of course is why, because the game certainly does have several things that speak for it.
Brutal Legend is a game filled with humor that is akin to main man's introduction cult movie; The Pick of Destiny. Personally, I enjoy it for in the game it is not constantly bombarded at you if you are just cruising in the Druid Plow (that is your car), but fills the conversations with a light air that is certainly good for a laugh. If you are cruising Metal music (of different genres of metal) greets your ears. Something I enjoy and in fact made me appreciate some artists better, but certainly not for everyone. Okay so that gives it a rather niche public, but that doesn't make it bad does it? No, it doesn't.
However, the game also has real time combat and does so in a the old Warcraft/Starcraft format, but has the view not topdown but on you as well as you are a important player. With no pause function, bad overview, the fact that you need to fight as well as command constantly -  because the AI is just horrible - makes it stressful. A shrill constrast to the rest. Now a friend of mine has it and does well enough. The difference, a controller. I have mouse and keyboard and the controls are such .... finicky, that on a dial I can not even select the unit above or below it because it either won't move or will go down 2 in an instance. The solos you need to perform to boost you army also require key combinations which also go wrong at times due to this. No problem outside combat but in it... The problem is that this game is fun, looks nicely, has good humor, but was not properly developed for combat with mouse and keyboard.
Thus, the game has its niche in which it does well. However, if you do not like this niche or do not own a controller, I would say it is not worth the frustation of the combat and quirky controls (even with remapping!) - because that is the opposite of what the game is intended to be and would be a dissappointment over an otherwise well intended and decently executed (mainly music, humor and graphic wise) game.

I will start with the positives.  I really like the artwork, it has a nice painterly feel.  I also enjoyed the puzzles, though they perhaps could have been a little harder.  The voice acting, while short and a bit repeatative when clicking something incorrect, was decent.
And now for what I felt could have been improved.  The game is VERY short.  The story, while interesting, is not very interwoven into the game itself.  I felt like I was given a bit of the story then thrown into a series of rooms almost unrelated.  While trying not to include spoilers, which would completely ruin any gameplay this game has, some of the interactions could have been more intuitive.
For a game like this, I wish Steam had a neutral recommendation.  If you find it on sale, perhaps it is worth your while, but not for the full price.  If this had not been just Chapter 1, this review probably would have been a lot more positive.

I feel misled and cheated. This is *only* Chapter One - at no place in the description or title is that made clear. If I had known, I'd have waited for a full (or fuller, anyway) version. Perhaps I should have dug deeper, but it is the norm to post that info in the description.
As far as the game itself: the art is very good. That's about all I can say positive.
The puzzles are very simple; however, you are often left hanging with inadequate input. While I don't expect to be hand-held, basic info should be available (there is at least one puzzle where you can work it and work it - but nothing happens unless you "activate" the pieces - which is not indicated at all, not even a simple "Hmm, this fits but something's missing"). Frustrating. Nor is there any guide or indication that you can do things like combine pieces in your inventory; again, basic information.
The storyline is less than gripping, the scripting poor and the voice acting annoying. You cannot skip through it either, as far as I was able to tell.
I generally enjoy this type of game as a light, relaxing activity. Between the lack of information, simplicity of the puzzles and lack of fair description I have to downvote this, despite the very professional art. Simply not worth the price for one chapter.
If you like point and click adventures and puzzles, this one is for you.

Third installment of a pretty cool franchise. This time it is off to the Africa theatre in the hunt for the new nazi super weapon. Plot is simple and fairly straight forwarad with each new level letting you take another step towards finding out the big enemy plan and finally deal with it. Its enough to keep you entertained for a couple of hours, even though you will tire of shooting spooky skeletons about halfway through and just turn off the X-ray mech in order to keep the flow.
What I didnt like was the sneak mechanic. Despite this being the third game, the mechanic still sucks. At times you get discovered for no reason what so ever and all of a sudden you get shot at from 7 different angles at the same time. And everytime that happened, all you had to do was to slaugheter everything within that particular area and everything went back to normal. Polishing it up a bit and allowing you to actually being able to make a few stealth kills here and there would be nice.
A barely gave multiplayer a shot. The times I did, I spent 20 minutes crouched, camping in a house in the middle of the desert, successfully sniping another player after missing the first 20 rounds. The second time I was barely able to poke my head out before having it shot off... So yeah, not my kind of MP im afraid. Co-Op however was great fun! Being able to sneak in, wreak havoc, covering each other and to play the different challenges made the game worth to re-play a couple of more times before growing tired of it.
All in all: 6 mice out of 10. Enough to keep you occupied over the weekend.

Still, enough "once upon a time" remains here to make a lovely little experience.

Spelunky has so much depth. That is a puntendre and also a truthfact.
Not only do you go down a lot, vut very simple mechanics lead to insane, Rube Goldbergesque happenings. The snake triggers the arrow trap whose arrow stump then falls down and hits the caveman on the head and he gets stunned and falls down two levels into the mouth of the... okay, you get it.
This can lead to its only real problem: sometimes things happen offscreen that suddenly anger a shopkeeper and you're immediately shot to death, which is unfair. But if you're willing to accept that .5% of the time, the other 99.5% of runs are pretty much great.
Why I really love Spelunky is partly its hidden things (figuring out what the thing in the golden chest does is the start, but please don't deny yourself the satisfaction of working it out yourself) which take many many runs to figure out, and all the extra hidden depth that comes from that, and mostly, the sense of accomplishment you get as you feel yourself getting progressively better at it.

Kingdoms of Amalur manages to combine an interesting number of gameplay elements. To me at least, it seems to have a similar feel to an older, single-player computer RPG, like Gothic or Die by the Sword - yet at the same time, it contains many modern gameplay features and conventions. The combat is fairly button-combo heavy and is fairly similar to Fable - even the character progression paths (Warrior, Rogue, Wizard) follow the same lines. Each area is filled with NPCs who will offer various main or side quests, and tasks, all courtesy of the glowy exclamation points floating over their heads, as is the trend for seemingly every RPG nowadays (not just MMOs anymore, it seems!) The main quest is fairly good, but it is even easier to get lured off by the sheer amount of side quests and faction storylines to follow. The faction quest lines serve to drive you from one area to the next just as much as the main storyline does, so I suppose that in theory, you could ignore the main quest completely and just play the additional content - there is certainly enough of it to reach the level cap well before the game ends.
The game world itself is huge; it's easy to tell that this was designed as a prototype for an MMO, even though it still feels like a single-player map - the way much of it is designed, it's doubtful that it could've accomodated a large number of players. The areas are sprawling, however, though they can be traversed fairly easily on foot, in my opinion, without them feeling like a slog. Even the smallest area map has a number of small nooks and crannies off the beaten path that will yield treasure, lore, or crafting materials - although many of these cannot be acquired without the proper skills to unlock them. While in theory this provides an incentive to return to older areas later on when a character is more skilled, more often than not the treasure is not worth the effort. However, each area is dotted with a variety of runestones that provide you with lore and passive bonuses if you manage to find them all, which encourages full exploration.
The game has a robust crafting system that is based upon breaking down items into components that can then be used to forge new weapons and armor, depending on the type. Additional components can be added, if available, to make the final product better, and gems can be added to slotted gear to add extra magical effects (gems, too, can be combined to make more potent versions). While some fairly good gear can be purchased, the best items are rare, expensive, and hard to find - more often than not, by the mid-game, the best equipment you will end up with is stuff that you make yourself. A fairly good alchemy system also exists, with the standard gathering of plants and combining them to discover different effects, then using them to brew useful potions.
The game suffers from some bugs, namely in the inventory and quest system. Many quest or plot-related items remain in your inventory indefinitely, and whether or not they take up physical space in your collection seems to be an arbitrary distinction. While the ability to expand your inventory exists, these upgrades are fairly scarce, external storage is limited, and most quest items cannot even be stored - you're stuck carrying them forever. The lack of companions to carry excess items, combined with a limited inventory size, can make loot runs back into town frustratingly frequent. There is also no way to remove unwanted or incomplete quests from your journal, which can develop some annoying glitches once your total number of active quests tops a certain number. The simple gathering tasks you acquire in each town can be helpful to do once or twice, but having one from a place you visited four towns and twenty levels ago stuck in your quest list for the rest of the game can be irritating.
While the progression trees are fairly straightforwards and each contain some impressive abilities, the skill system is somewhat cumbersome. So many of the skills are so useful (arguably essential) that you really want, if not need, all of them - and yet skill progression, compared to level and ability gain, is painfully slow. You can pay certain NPCs to train you in a skill, giving you an extra point; however, the catch is that you can only receive this training if your skill is still below a certain rank. Early in the game, this is too expensive to pay for; by the time you can afford the training and return, chances are you will be too skilled to get the training, forcing you to repeatedly re-spec and travel backwards step by step, hunting for each trainer in the order that you found them in, if you want to acquire every skill point available (unless of course you choose to follow the Rogue's path).
Sadly, the collapse of the development studio and the lack of any further support for the game makes the chances of getting patches or other updates very remote. This is definitely a game that would benefit from some bug-fixes and mods. The fact that neither of the two DLC expansions bothered to increase the level cap means that even without using experience boosts, you will likely reach max level well before you finish the game (though I suppose it depends on how much of a completionist you are). The inclusion of ten to twenty more levels and some sort of alternate advancement/fourth ability tree would have made a nice addition to the extra content.
All in all, I think that KOA:R is an enjoyable game that is well worth picking up for the price. It has a fair amount of replay value and certainly has more than enough content to spare for anyone looking for a good fantasy adventure. The main story, while perhaps not quite original, is compelling enough, and the setting unique enough that it doesn't feel quite as cliched as some of the more standard fantasy RPG fare. While I do not think that it is for everyone, depending on your own personal taste, the gameplay is solid and the game itself quite enjoyable if you can get past the interface/game system bugs.

Long time fan of the action RPG genre.
I was wandering in a game store and picked this up for PS3 back in 2012, as I needed a break from Skyrim. One of the best decisions ever.
+ Good plot, not too complicated but still has its own complexity.
+ Very well written lore with lots of things left hidden for players to discover and theorize by ourselves.
+ At first I was a bit turned off by the cartoonish art style but it actually fits the game world really well.
+ Beautiful music
+ Huge map with lots of things to do
+ The combat system in this game is fantastic. Great variety of combat styles and they all fit with each other seamlessly. Until now the only other RPG that could come close to this is Dragon's Dogma.
+ The races and factions in the game are very nicely designed. The Kollossae are nice. I really feel sad doing the quests of the House of Sorrows. House of Ballads is really unique, I won't spoil it though.
+ The 2 DLCs are great, they add 2 very unique regions to the game.
- There are quite a few game breaking bugs, as well as many minor bugs. A few quests have bugs that will break your game. Beware of Her Righteous Fury!
- The player character doesn't talk, thus making us feel a bit colorless. This is a common problem among the genre. Conversations are long and boring at times, despite of the very decent voice acting.
- Monsters and loots are level locked the first time you enter a region. This discourages early exploring.
- Max level at 40 is too low. If you do most or all sidequests as you gain them, you will be 40 long before the game ends, especially now with 2 DLCs added.
I know my opinion might not be popular, but this right here is my most favourite RPG of all time.
Too bad we will never be able to see the sequel.

The fidelity to the animated series visuals and story line is something that I thoroughly appreciate and enjoy, so much so that it allowed me to easly overlook the rough edges of the current state of the game, and have a good few hours of fun. Not to say that the game doesn't have great potential, and a lot of value in its own right.
Even at the current state of development; with only a few more chapters to the story, a boss fight, and a decent lobby system, it could deliver enough of an experience to attract a lot of support from more than just fans of the series.
Some issues that I think it would need to be addressed before the game goes out of early access:
1.- The lobby system
There is nothing more frustrating in a game that losing your progress, players should be able to preserve their current game state after disconnecting (purposely or otherwise), and be able to look for other games at the same state to join.
2.- Difficulty level
After you have mastered the combat system, most fights become monotonous, which can easily be addressed by adding higher difficulty settings.
3.- Collisions
Collisions would have to be polished a fair bit, in order to deliver a more satisfying experience when hitting enemies and objects.
At its current state, I would recommend the game only for fans of the series that are willing to look past a few quirks, in exchange to be able to play your favorite RWBY character for a little while.

Here is my first review ever for a game. I've recently picked up gaming again and i've really indulged on the winter sale. This game popped up and after playing it, i felt inspired to give my opinion on the game. Brothers is probably one of the most unique games ive ever played. Playing co-op as 1 player is such an interesting concept and it turned out to be really fun. There is no dialogue, spoken or subtitles, within the game. The language is made up but you have no problem understanding everything you're supposed to do from the mood and gestures of the person telling you where to go. The game was not very difficult but i just got done playing portal 2 so i'm sure my puzzle solving skills are through the roof at the moment. The environment is absolutely beautiful and i loved utilizing the benches through out the game just to look at the time the devs must have put into making such a stunning visual experience. The thing i loved most about the game was the story. Simple, yes, but you feel so engaged and you feel every emotion, especially at the end. I will not drop any spoilers but the end was so perfectly done. The way you move and act in the end is exactly how i would respond in real life if i were put in such a situation. So much good to say about the game but as for complaints, the only thing i can think of was that i never fully got used to the controls but they weren't bad overall, just different. Loved the graphics, loved the story, loved the price at which i pretty much stole it from Steam.
Overall 10/10
